docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
Notable changes to ReactPy, newest first. Read the Unreleased section for what has landed since the last release, and the versioned sections for what shipped in each.

The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.

Note

Entries use the Keep a Changelog categories — Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security — and versions follow Semantic Versioning. Pre-release versions carry a bN suffix, and behaviour can shift between betas without a major-version bump, so pin an exact version if you depend on one.

The authoritative list of shipped artefacts, with downloads and commit ranges, is GitHub Releases; the published packages are on PyPI. This page is the curated narrative of what changed, not the release log.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Added support for Python 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14.
  • Added type hints to reactpy.html attributes.
  • Added support for nested components in web modules
  • Added support for inline JavaScript as event handlers or other attributes that expect a callable via reactpy.types.InlineJavaScript
  • Event functions can now call event.preventDefault() and event.stopPropagation() methods directly on the event data object, rather than using the @event decorator.
  • Event data now supports accessing properties via dot notation (ex. event.target.value).
  • Added support for partial functions in EventHandler
  • Added reactpy.types.Event to provide type hints for the standard data function argument (for example def on_click(event: Event): ...).
  • Added asgi and jinja installation extras (for example pip install reactpy[asgi, jinja]).
  • Added reactpy.executors.asgi.ReactPy that can be used to run ReactPy in standalone mode via ASGI.
  • Added reactpy.executors.asgi.ReactPyCsr that can be used to run ReactPy in standalone mode via ASGI, but rendered entirely client-sided.
  • Added reactpy.executors.asgi.ReactPyMiddleware that can be used to utilize ReactPy within any ASGI compatible framework.
  • Added reactpy.templatetags.ReactPyJinja that can be used alongside ReactPyMiddleware to embed several ReactPy components into your existing application. This includes the following template tags: {% component %}, {% pyscript_component %}, and {% pyscript_setup %}.
  • Added reactpy.pyscript_component that can be used to embed ReactPy components into your existing application.
  • Added reactpy.use_async_effect hook.
  • Added reactpy.Vdom primitive interface for creating VDOM dictionaries.
  • Added reactpy.reactjs.component_from_file to import ReactJS components from a file.
  • Added reactpy.reactjs.component_from_url to import ReactJS components from a URL.
  • Added reactpy.reactjs.component_from_string to import ReactJS components from a string.
  • Added reactpy.reactjs.component_from_npm to import ReactJS components from NPM.
  • Added reactpy.h as a shorthand alias for reactpy.html.
  • Added reactpy.config.REACTPY_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE to configure the maximum size of all ReactPy asyncio queues (e.g. receive buffer, send buffer, event buffer) before ReactPy begins waiting until a slot frees up. This can be used to constraint memory usage.
  • Events now support debounce and throttle, configurable per event via event.debounce = <milliseconds> and EventHandler(fn, throttle=<milliseconds>) respectively.
    • debounce waits until activity stops, then fires once. Default is 200 ms on input/select/textarea, 0 ms elsewhere.
    • throttle caps the rate how often an event is allowed to execute. No default; opt in per event.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The key attribute is now stored within attributes in the VDOM spec.
  • Substitute client-side usage of react with preact.
  • Script elements no longer support behaving like effects. They now strictly behave like plain HTML scripts.
  • The reactpy.html module has been modified to allow for auto-creation of any HTML nodes. For example, you can create a <data-table> element by calling html.data_table().
  • Change set_state comparison method to check equality with == more consistently.
  • Add support for rendering @component children within vdom_to_html.
  • Renamed the use_location hook's search attribute to query_string.
  • Renamed the use_location hook's pathname attribute to path.
  • Renamed reactpy.config.REACTPY_DEBUG_MODE to reactpy.config.REACTPY_DEBUG.
  • ReactPy no longer auto-converts snake_case props to camelCase. It is now the responsibility of the user to ensure that props are in the correct format.
  • Rewrite the event-to-object package to be more robust at handling properties on events.
  • Custom JS components will now automatically assume you are using ReactJS in the absence of a bind function.
  • Refactor layout rendering logic to improve readability and maintainability.
  • The JavaScript package @reactpy/client now exports React and ReactDOM, which allows third-party components to re-use the same React instance as ReactPy.
  • reactpy.html will now automatically flatten lists recursively (ex. reactpy.html(["child1", ["child2"]]))
  • reactpy.utils.reactpy_to_string will now retain the user's original casing for data-* and aria-* attributes.
  • reactpy.utils.string_to_reactpy has been upgraded to handle more complex scenarios without causing ReactJS rendering errors.
  • reactpy.core.vdom._CustomVdomDictConstructor has been moved to reactpy.types.CustomVdomConstructor.
  • reactpy.core.vdom._EllipsisRepr has been moved to reactpy.types.EllipsisRepr.
  • reactpy.types.VdomDictConstructor has been renamed to reactpy.types.VdomConstructor.
  • REACTPY_ASYNC_RENDERING can now de-duplicate renders where necessary.
  • REACTPY_ASYNC_RENDERING is now defaulted to True for up to 40x performance improvements in environments with high concurrency.

docs.title: Deprecated
docs.text:
• reactpy.web.module_from_file is deprecated. Use reactpy.reactjs.component_from_file instead.
  • reactpy.web.module_from_url is deprecated. Use reactpy.reactjs.component_from_url instead.
  • reactpy.web.module_from_string is deprecated. Use reactpy.reactjs.component_from_string instead.
  • reactpy.web.export is deprecated. Use reactpy.reactjs.component_from_* instead.
  • reactpy.web.* is deprecated. Use reactpy.reactjs.* instead.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• Removed support for Python 3.9 and 3.10.
  • Removed the ability to import reactpy.html.* elements directly. You must now call html.* to access the elements.
  • Removed backend specific installation extras (such as pip install reactpy[starlette]).
  • Removed support for async functions within reactpy.use_effect hook. Use reactpy.use_async_effect instead.
  • Removed deprecated function module_from_template.
  • Removed deprecated exception type reactpy.core.serve.Stop.
  • Removed deprecated component reactpy.widgets.hotswap.
  • Removed reactpy.sample module.
  • Removed reactpy.svg module. Contents previously within reactpy.svg.* can now be accessed via reactpy.html.svg.*.
  • Removed reactpy.html._ function. Use reactpy.html(...) or reactpy.html.fragment(...) instead.
  • Removed reactpy.run. See the documentation for the new method to run ReactPy applications.
  • Removed reactpy.backend.*. See the documentation for the new method to run ReactPy applications.
  • Removed reactpy.core.types module. Use reactpy.types instead.
  • Removed reactpy.utils.str_to_bool.
  • Removed reactpy.utils.html_to_vdom. Use reactpy.utils.string_to_reactpy instead.
  • Removed reactpy.utils.vdom_to_html. Use reactpy.utils.reactpy_to_string instead.
  • Removed reactpy.vdom. Use reactpy.Vdom instead.
  • Removed reactpy.core.make_vdom_constructor. Use reactpy.Vdom instead.
  • Removed reactpy.core.custom_vdom_constructor. Use reactpy.Vdom instead.
  • Removed reactpy.Layout top-level re-export. Use reactpy.core.layout.Layout instead.
  • Removed reactpy.types.LayoutType. Use reactpy.types.BaseLayout instead.
  • Removed reactpy.types.ContextProviderType. Use reactpy.types.ContextProvider instead.
  • Removed reactpy.core.hooks._ContextProvider. Use reactpy.types.ContextProvider instead.
  • Removed reactpy.web.utils. Use reactpy.reactjs.utils instead.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Fixed a bug where script elements would not render to the DOM as plain text.
  • Fixed a bug where the key property provided within server-side ReactPy code was failing to propagate to the front-end JavaScript components.
  • Fixed a bug where RuntimeError("Hook stack is in an invalid state") errors could be generated when using a webserver that reuses threads.
  • Fixed a bug where events on controlled inputs (e.g. html.input({"onChange": ...})) could be lost during rapid actions.
  • Allow for ReactPy and ReactJS components to be arbitrarily inserted onto the page with any possible hierarchy.

  • Fixed needless unmounting of JavaScript components during each ReactPy render.
  • Fixed missing event["target"]["checked"] on checkbox inputs.
  • Fixed missing static files on sdist Python distribution.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • Allow concurrently rendering discrete component trees - enable this experimental feature by setting REACTPY_ASYNC_RENDERING=true. This improves the overall responsiveness of your app in situations where larger renders would otherwise block smaller renders from executing.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ReactPy takes pull requests from anyone, and most of what gets rejected is not wrong — it is unreviewable. A short branch, a focused diff, and the checks run before you open the pull request is what makes a change easy to say yes to. This page covers the mechanics: where the code lives, how to branch, and what CI will run against you.

You will learn

  • Which branch a change belongs on, and why that matters here more than elsewhere
  • The commit and pull request conventions this repository enforces
  • What CI checks, before CI tells you

docs.title: Know which repository you are in
docs.text:
This documentation site and the library are separate bodies of work, and the commands that work in one do nothing in the other.

Change Repository / branch Library code, hooks, layout, backends reactive-python/reactpy → main JavaScript client (src/js/) Same, main These documentation pages (docs/src/, docs/examples/) reactive-python/reactpy → new-docs

The new-docs branch holds only docs/ — the package and tests/ were removed from it. A test command run there reports success without running anything.

Pitfall

Confirm the branch before you start typing, not after. A library fix committed onto the docs branch looks fine locally and becomes a rebase chore later. git branch --show-current costs nothing and settles it.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Look for an open discussion or issue that matches what you intend to do. If one exists, comment there before writing code — a maintainer who has already thought about the problem will usually redirect you in one sentence, and that sentence is cheaper than a rejected pull request. If none exists, open a discussion first.

For anything larger than a bug fix, expect the answer to be "show me the design first". A draft pull request is the right medium for that: it runs CI, it is reviewable, and it says plainly that it is not ready to merge.

docs.title: Branch, commit, push
docs.text:
Fork the repository if you do not have write access, then branch from an up-to-date main:

git checkout -b fix-my-change main

Name the branch for the change, not for you. fix-key-not-resetting-on-provider beats patch-1 and survives a month of review.

Match the convention of the branch you are landing on; they differ. Documentation commits on new-docs use Conventional Commits subjects — docs(learn): author X for ReactPy v2, docs(examples): fix include-marker cropping. Library history on main instead uses plain sentence subjects, because pull requests there are squash-merged and the summary is written at merge time — Fix PyScript root component not hiding after render error (#1347). In both cases the subject is the thing a reader scans to find the functional change in a long history, so write it for that reader.

One commit per logical change. If a commit only makes sense next to a later one, squash them before you push rather than asking the reviewer to mentally reassemble them.

docs.title: The checklist
docs.text:
The repository ships a pull request template; fill it in rather than deleting it.

  • [ ] Tests have been developed for bug fixes or new functionality.
  • [ ] The changelog has been updated, if necessary.
  • [ ] Documentation has been updated, if necessary.
  • [ ] GitHub Issues closed by this pull request have been linked.

By submitting, you agree that your contribution complies with the project's open source licenses.

Tests are not optional for a behaviour change. A bug fix should arrive with the test that reproduces the bug — write it first and watch it fail, then fix and watch it pass. A test that has never failed proves nothing about the thing it claims to protect.

The changelog rule is narrower than it looks: CHANGELOG.md gets an entry under Unreleased for user-facing changes only. Test-only, docs-only, and CI-only changes get none. Adding one for those is a small annoyance to the person doing the release, who then has to notice and delete it. See Changelog.

docs.title: What CI runs
docs.text:
Understanding the gate is cheaper than discovering it in a failed run.

hatch test --parallel --cover --retries 10          # coverage job
hatch test --parallel --retries 10                  # ubuntu, macos, windows × 3.11–3.14
hatch fmt src/reactpy --check                       # lint + format
hatch run python:type_check                         # pyright
hatch run javascript:test
hatch run javascript:check

Run the equivalents locally before you push — the same commands, not approximations of them:

hatch fmt --check
hatch run python:type_check
hatch test -k the_test_you_touched

CI retries flaky tests, which is a mercy and a trap: a genuinely racy test can go green on the third attempt and stay in the tree. If a test fails once and passes on retry, that is a bug in the test — usually a bare asyncio.sleep where poll(...) belongs.

A pull request into new-docs gets no CI at all, for two independent reasons. GitHub runs pull_request workflows from the base branch, and the only workflow that exists on new-docs is the docs deploy, which triggers on push — so nothing matches a PR. And the test-documentation job in check.yml on main is disabled outright with if: 0 (temporarily, while the Sphinx-to-MkDocs transition finishes), so even a PR targeting main runs lint and Python tests but never builds the docs. A docs change is verified by you or by nobody — run the mkdocs build --strict set from Running Tests and read its exit code. The one thing that does run: pushing to new-docs deploys with mkdocs gh-deploy --force, no --strict — expect a change to be live the moment it merges, whether or not it builds cleanly.

docs.title: Working with reviewers
docs.text:
Respond to every comment, including the ones you are not acting on. "Not taking this because X" is a complete reply and saves a round trip; silence invites a re-review of something you already considered.

Push fixes as new commits rather than force-pushing over the reviewed range. Reviewers read the delta between your last push and this one; a force-push that rewrites history they already read makes them re-read the whole diff, and they will notice when they skip it.

If a review asks for something you believe is wrong, say so once, with evidence, and then defer if the maintainer still wants it. Review is a conversation with an asymmetry: they own the file after you leave.

Note

When a review is posted by an automated tool, the maintainers still own the decision. Do not treat "the bot did not complain" as approval, and do not treat a bot comment as a demand — respond on the merits, the same as any other comment.

docs.title: After merge
docs.text:
Documentation changes on new-docs deploy to the live site on push, so a mistake there is visible immediately rather than at the next release. That is a reason to run the build check locally, not a reason to be nervous about contributing.

Library changes reach users only through a release, which the maintainers cut. Do not ask when your fix will ship, and do not close a closed-issue loop by demanding a release — the tag is a maintainer's call.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Library work on main; documentation work on new-docs. Check the branch first.
  • Start from a discussion; a one-sentence redirect beats a rejected pull request.
  • Conventional Commit subjects, one logical change per commit, branch named for the change.
  • Tests accompany behaviour changes, and they must have failed first.
  • Changelog entries for user-facing changes only.
  • Run CI's exact commands locally before pushing; treat a flaky test as a bug.

  • Community — where to raise the issue before you write the fix

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ReactPy is built in the open. Questions, bug reports, and ideas all have a home, and the same places are where you get help when an example on this site stops behaving. This page is a map of those places and what belongs in each.

You will learn

  • Where to ask a question, report a bug, and propose a feature
  • Which channels are official, and which are just links people repeat
  • What the code of conduct expects, and what to include in a report

docs.title: Where everything happens
docs.text:
The ReactPy repository on GitHub is the centre of gravity. Everything else points back to it.

You want to Go to Ask how to do something Discussions → Question Report something broken Discussions → Problem Propose a feature Discussions → Ideas Show off what you built Discussions → Share Publish a package you made Discussions → Downloadable Packages Track a confirmed defect Issues Chat in real time Discord

Discussions is the front door, not Issues. The repository's issue-template configuration disables blank issues and points new visitors at Discussions instead, so a question opened as an issue gets redirected rather than answered. Open an issue once a defect is confirmed and someone has reproduced it — the discussion that came first usually becomes the link inside it.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text:
There is a Discord server for ReactPy, announced in Discussion #997 and linked from the repository README. It is the fastest place to get an answer to a "why is this doing that" question, and quiet enough that nobody minds a beginner question.

Note

An invite URL is mutable third-party state. If discord.gg/uNb5P4hA9X ever stops resolving, read the current invite from the README badge or from Discussion #997 — those two are maintained together — rather than trusting a search result, which may point at a cloned server.

Discord is good for conversation and bad for searchability. A solution that exists only in chat is invisible to the next person with the same problem. If a chat thread solves something real, post it to Discussions afterwards; if it exposes an error on this site, that is a documentation contribution.

docs.title: Code of conduct
docs.text:
Participation is governed by the Contributor Covenant code of conduct, which lives at the repository root. It applies everywhere the project is discussed — Discussions, Issues, pull requests, Discord, and any other space where ReactPy maintainers show up.

The practical version: assume good faith, criticise code rather than people, and accept that "this is obvious" is rarely true of the person asking. The enforcement section of the document names the contact route for escalating a problem.

docs.title: Packages outside this repository
docs.text:
ReactPy's core deliberately stays small, so much of what you might expect to find here lives in sibling repositories. Each has its own issue tracker — do not file a Django problem against the core repo.

  • reactpy-router — URL routing
  • reactpy-django — Django integration
  • reactpy-jupyter — Jupyter integration
  • reactpy-js-component-template — starting point for a custom JavaScript component

Community-built packages are announced in Discussions → Downloadable Packages. Those are third-party: they are not reviewed before being posted, they are not pinned against a ReactPy release, and an unanswered thread there says nothing about the library. See Tools, Libraries, and Packages for how to evaluate one.

docs.title: Supporting the project
docs.text:
ReactPy is maintained by volunteers on their own time. GitHub Sponsors is the route the project uses, matching the maintainers listed in the repository's funding configuration.

Sponsoring buys maintenance, not priority. It does not queue your issue and does not entitle anyone to a feature. If you need a specific behaviour on a deadline, the reliable path is to write it — or fund someone to write it — and open a pull request.

docs.title: What to include when you ask
docs.text:
Most unanswered questions are unanswered because they cannot be reproduced. Four things turn a vague report into one someone can act on:

  • The exact ReactPy version. Run pip show reactpy and paste it. Behaviour shifts between pre-releases, so 2.0.0b13 and 2.0.0 are different answers.
  • The Python version and operating system.
  • The smallest snippet that still misbehaves. Cutting an app down to one component usually finds the bug before you post it.
  • Both sides of the comparison: what happened, and what you expected. For a rendering problem, include what the browser showed, not only what the code says.

Pitfall

"It doesn't work" with no traceback is not a question anyone can answer, and the error you think is irrelevant often is not the relevant one. Include the full traceback and the server-side console output. ReactPy logs failing event handlers and effects on the server while the browser stays silent, so a UI that merely stops responding usually has a server line that explains it — see Creating VDOM Event Handlers.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Ask in Discussions; open an issue only for a confirmed defect.
  • Real-time chat is on Discord; follow up anything durable in Discussions so it stays searchable.
  • The code of conduct governs every one of those spaces.
  • Integration packages live in sibling repos; file bugs against the repo that owns the behaviour.
  • Reproducible reports get answers: versions, smallest failing snippet, and the server log.

  • Contributing Documentation — fixing a page that misled you

  • Tools, Libraries, and Packages — choosing between built-in and third-party

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Most of these pages were ported from the ReactJS documentation, and the port is the whole job: a page is done when every claim in it is true of ReactPy and every snippet in it runs. That is a lower bound on effort and an upper bound on trustworthiness, which is the trade this project made deliberately. This page is how to do the work and how to know it is finished.

You will learn

  • What makes a ported page "done", and how the 🚧 marker works
  • The page structure, admonitions, and link conventions this site uses
  • Why snippets live in docs/examples/ instead of inside the markdown

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text:
docs/
├── mkdocs.yml          # nav: — every page must be listed here
├── src/                # the pages, in markdown
│   ├── learn/          #   tutorials and concepts
│   ├── reference/      #   API reference
│   └── about/          #   this section
├── examples/           # runnable Python, one directory per page slug
└── overrides/          # template overrides

Page files are kebab-case.md; example directories are the same name with underscores (learn/scaling-up-with-reducer-and-context.md → examples/scaling_up_with_reducer_and_context/). A new page must be added to nav: in mkdocs.yml, but the build will not tell you when you forget: a page missing from nav: is still built and served, and mkdocs build --strict exits 0. The only trace is an INFO line listing the unlisted pages. Read it: every page currently on that list carries a Planned / Undeveloped banner in its body and can be ignored, which is exactly how a page you did mean to publish would hide among them. Adding the entry is what puts the page in the site's navigation, which is the actual reason to do it.

docs.title: What "done" means
docs.text:
A page is authored, not migrated. Concretely:

  • Every code sample is ReactPy that runs. No JSX, no className= outside an attribute dict, no hook that does not exist.
  • Every behavioural claim has been checked against the package or its tests — by reading the source, and for anything about rendering or events, by running it.
  • React-only sections are removed or rewritten, not translated.
  • The 🚧 badge is gone from its nav: entry.

Note

🚧 in the navigation means "this is still a ReactJS page with the React names swapped". It is a promise to the reader that the content is unreliable, so removing it is the meaningful act — the badge should never come off before the checks above are true. 🚫 means the page is blocked on something outside this project and is parked; commented-out nav: entries work the same way.

docs.title: Port, do not rename
docs.text:
The pages derive from react.dev. Editing means deleting what is false as much as replacing what is named differently, and the failure mode is a page that reads fluently and is wrong.

Things that do not survive a rename:

  • Hooks that do not exist. ReactPy has twelve hooks. There is no use_id, use_transition, use_deferred_value, use_layout_effect, use_insertion_effect, use_imperative_handle, or use_sync_external_store. Some of the react.dev pages for them are parked as 🚫; use_id has no page at all, because the upstream issue was closed as not planned. Never port a page that depends on one as if it worked.
  • Naming rules. Components are snake_case and lowercase — my_button, not MyButton. React's capital-letter rule does not apply, because ReactPy distinguishes a component from a tag by the call, not the case. Attribute keys stay camelCase (className, onClick), because those pass through to the DOM untouched.
  • JSX mechanics. Children are positional arguments after an optional attribute dict. There is no JSX, and no PSX in this release.
  • StrictMode and memo. Neither exists. React's double-invoke warnings and its "skip re-rendering unchanged children" optimisation have no ReactPy equivalent, so port those sections as a warning that ReactPy will not catch the problem for you.
  • && rendering. {cond && <X/>} has no safe Python spelling — False and X leaks the word False into the page, since only None renders nothing. Rewrite such examples rather than transliterating them.
  • Dependency arrays. use_effect, use_memo, and use_callback infer dependencies from the closure when you omit the argument. React's "omit the array to run after every render" is simply wrong here.

Pitfall

A page can pass every automated check while teaching something false, because the checks are syntactic. The ReactJS FIXME that sat in thinking-in-react.md claiming event["target"]["checked"] does not work was wrong — a checkbox onChange receives checked=True. The only defence is running the example and reading what the client actually sent.

docs.title: Page structure
docs.text:
Every authored page opens the same way: an ## Overview heading, an intro paragraph in a <p class="intro"> block, then a You will learn summary.

## Overview

<p class="intro" markdown>

One or two paragraphs that say what the page solves and why it matters in ReactPy specifically.

</p>

!!! summary "You will learn"

    -   Bullet
    -   Bullet

Then the body as ## and ### sections, closing with ## Recap (bulleted, factual) and ## Related (links with a dash and a phrase explaining each).

Admonitions come from the Material theme plus assets/css/admonition.css. The set in use:

Admonition For !!! summary "You will learn" Objectives, once, after the intro !!! abstract "Note" Clarification that is not a warning !!! warning "Pitfall" A mistake the reader is likely to make !!! info "Deep Dive" Deeper mechanics a reader can skip !!! example "Terminal" A shell session

ReactJS's <Pitfall>, <DeepDive>, <Recap>, <Challenges>, <Solution>, and <Hint> JSX tags have no MkDocs equivalent. Convert them to admonitions or headings; never copy them through, since an unrecognised tag renders as literal text.

Links are relative .md paths from the current file — ../reference/use-state.md, ./extracting-state-logic-into-a-reducer.md#the-rule-reactpy-adds — not site-absolute paths like /learn/..., which break under versioned builds and make --strict unable to verify them.

Code fences: ```python linenums="0" for fragments, bare ```python for full-file tabs, and hl_lines="3-4 7" to mark the lines under discussion. Inline code that is Python gets the #!python prefix (\#!python use_state``) so it highlights.

docs.title: Examples are the source of truth
docs.text:
Snippets are not typed into the markdown. They are real files under docs/examples/<page_slug>/, pulled in by the include plugin:

=== "app.py"

    ```python

    @component
    def my_button():
        return html.button("I'm a button!")

    ```

=== ":material-play: Run"

    ```python
    # TODO
    ```

The rules that make this work:

  • The file is a complete, importable module — black-formatted at 88 columns, imports at the top.
  • A # start marker on its own line is what the include begins after; # end stops it. Crop at the marker so the marker itself never renders on the page.
  • A file with no marker is included whole.
  • Multiple variants of one idea go in sibling directories (task_state_props/, task_context/, task_wiring/), one tabbed group per example.
  • The :material-play: Run tab is a standing placeholder. Keep it.

Because the file is included, a snippet cannot drift from a runnable example — but nothing in the build proves the example behaves. Mount it and check the DOM before you write "this renders a list". When a page compares several versions, drive all of them through the same click sequence and assert the same observable output; "it looks the same" is how two versions of an example quietly disagree.

Also list children of a component with key= when they come from a list — html.ul([row(item, key=item["id"]) for item in items]). Omitting it renders fine and emits a debug-mode warning, which is exactly the lesson the page about keys is trying to teach.

docs.title: Verifying a page
docs.text:
From the repository root:

hatch fmt --check docs/
pyright --pythonpath <your-env>/bin/python docs/
cd docs && mkdocs build --strict; echo "exit=$?"

Then run the examples themselves and open the built page in a browser. mkdocs build --strict catches broken internal links and unresolvable includes — both abort the build with a nonzero exit. Two things it does not catch: a page missing from nav: (an INFO line, exit 0), and a link whose #anchor does not exist in an otherwise valid target file (also exit 0), so check both by eye. And it cannot catch a snippet that renders nothing.

You are the only gate. The single workflow on new-docs runs mkdocs gh-deploy --force on push, and gh-deploy does not pass --strict — a build with broken links exits 0 and publishes. A miss does not fail a pipeline; it goes live.

Pitfall

Do not trust a component that renders without error. Set REACTPY_DEBUG=1 when probing: with debug off, a component that raised produces {"tagName": "", "error": ""} — a blank region and a 200 response. See Running Tests for the harness traps that make a broken example look green.

docs.title: Process
docs.text:
Branch from new-docs, one page per branch, and use the same Conventional Commit subjects as the history there — docs(learn): author X for ReactPy v2. A commit that removes a 🚧 badge from nav: should be the same commit that authored the page, never a separate "mark done" commit that could be cherry-picked alone.

No CHANGELOG.md entry: documentation work is not user-facing in the sense the changelog means. See Changelog.

Note

docs/src/dictionary.txt exists for the spellcheck plugin, which is currently commented out in mkdocs.yml. New domain words belong there if the plugin is ever re-enabled; nothing fails while it stays off.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A page is done when it runs and every claim is verified — then remove its 🚧 badge.
  • Port, do not rename: delete JSX, non-existent hooks, StrictMode, memo, && rendering, and React's dependency-array semantics.
  • Fixed structure: Overview, intro paragraph, You will learn, sections, Recap, Related.
  • Relative .md links; admonitions instead of ReactJS's JSX tags.
  • Snippets are includes from docs/examples/, cropped at # start, formatted at 88 columns.
  • --strict checks links and nothing about behaviour. Run the example.

docs.text:
ReactPy's source is MIT-licensed. Much of the prose you are reading is derived from the ReactJS documentation, which carries a separate Creative Commons licence, and the two do not cover the same things. This page states which licence applies to what, and what you owe when you reuse either.

You will learn

  • Which licence covers the code, and which covers these pages
  • Why the distinction matters when you copy from one side
  • Where the third-party components in a ReactPy install come from

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
These pages are a different body of work from the code, and they are separately encumbered.

Much of this documentation — including its layout and much of its content — was created with heavy influence from react.dev, which is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence. ReactPy's behaviour often mirrors React's closely enough that the documents paraphrase, and in places copy, React's language and examples.

Note

CC BY 4.0 is also permissive, but its condition is attribution rather than keeping a licence block. If you copy substantial prose from these pages into your own documentation, credit ReactPy and, where the text is close to React's original, acknowledge the ReactJS documentation as the further source. Attributing to ReactPy alone is not sufficient for the passages that came from React.

The practical boundary: code you write against ReactPy is yours, unencumbered by either licence. These pages are text under a credit-bearing licence. A snippet in docs/examples/ is code that happens to be inside a document — treat it as MIT, since its purpose is to be pasted into a project.

docs.title: Third-party components
docs.text:
A working ReactPy install bundles more than this repository's source: the browser-side client, the vendored JavaScript dependencies, and, for client-side rendering, PyScript. Each keeps its own upstream licence, shipped with the distribution.

Check what a release actually contains rather than trusting a summary — the package metadata and the static/ directory of the release are authoritative, and the licence files travel inside the wheel.

docs.title: Licensing your own contribution
docs.text:
The pull request template ends with an agreement that contributions comply with the project's open source licences. It is a checkbox, but it is the whole of the provenance control this project has, so it is worth taking literally:

  • Do not paste code you do not have the right to redistribute. Code copied from a licence-incompatible project, or from an answer on a forum, is the common failure.
  • Do not copy substantial prose from react.dev into these pages without acknowledging the source on the page or in the commit.
  • If you adapted something, say what and from where in the pull request description. It costs you a sentence and saves the maintainer an investigation.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Source code: MIT, in LICENSE.md at the repository root.
  • These pages: derived from the ReactJS docs under CC BY 4.0 — attribution is the obligation.
  • Snippets in docs/examples/ exist to be pasted; treat them as MIT code.
  • Bundled JavaScript and PyScript keep their upstream licences, shipped with the release.
  • Contributions must be yours to license; say what you adapted and from where.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
There are two test suites in this project, and they live in different places. The Python and JavaScript suites exercise ReactPy itself and run through hatch; the documentation checks exercise the pages you are reading and run through mkdocs. Knowing which one a failing command belongs to is most of debugging it.

You will learn

  • How to run the Python test suite, and why it needs a browser installed
  • How to run the documentation build checks yourself, since no CI runs them for you
  • Which command failures are yours and which are environmental

Note

The ReactPy package and its tests/ directory live on the main branch. This documentation site is authored on the new-docs branch, which contains only docs/ — running a test command there collects zero tests rather than failing, which reads like a pass and is not one. If hatch test reports no tests ran, you are on the wrong branch, not on a clean tree.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The development environment is managed by Hatch, which creates and maintains its own virtual environments. Install Hatch, then clone:

git clone https://github.com/reactive-python/reactpy.git
cd reactpy

You also need Bun for the JavaScript packages. Python must be 3.11 or newer — requires-python in pyproject.toml is >=3.11, and the test matrix runs 3.11 through 3.14.

Pitfall

Do not install the project's dependencies with pip install -r into your own environment. Hatch owns those environments, and a hand-built one drifts from CI in ways that look like your fault. The one exception is the documentation requirements, which are installed separately below.

docs.title: Python tests
docs.text:
The suite is pytest-based and runs under Hatch:

hatch test                                    # current Python version
hatch test --all                              # every version in the matrix
hatch test -k test_use_connection             # a single test by name

CI runs hatch test --parallel --retries 10 across three operating systems and four Python versions, and a separate coverage job runs hatch test --parallel --cover --retries 10.

The suite needs a browser. Each test run installs Playwright's Chromium, builds the JavaScript client, and builds a wheel before it invokes pytest — that is what the hatch-test environment's run script does. A first run is therefore slow, and a failure inside Chromium installation looks identical to a failure in the test itself. Read the top of the output, not the bottom.

playwright install chromium
playwright install-deps chromium   # optional; fails harmlessly on some systems

Tests are session-scoped around one browser and one backend server, defined in tests/conftest.py, and that file also turns on REACTPY_DEBUG and REACTPY_ASYNC_RENDERING for the whole session. Two consequences:

  • A test that passes alone and fails in the suite may be reading state a previous test left behind. Reproduce with -k before you chase it.
  • Because debug mode is on in tests and off by default in production, some errors surface only in the suite. Debug-mode checks such as REACTPY_CHECK_VDOM_SPEC are exactly this.

Configuration lives under [tool.pytest.ini_options] in pyproject.toml: --strict-config, --strict-markers, xfail_strict, asyncio_mode = "auto", testpaths = "tests", and a 120-second per-test timeout. xfail_strict means an expected failure that unexpectedly passes is itself a failure, so an xfail you fixed must be deleted rather than left alone.

docs.title: What the helpers are for
docs.text:
reactpy.testing exists because a UI is only correct once it renders in a browser. The acceptance bar is that the real artefact behaves, not that a function returned the expected shape.

  • DisplayFixture — serves a component and gives you a Playwright page to drive it: await display.show(my_component), then display.page.
  • BackendFixture — the server side, usually paired with DisplayFixture as in conftest.py.
  • poll(...) — retries a condition until it holds or the timeout expires. Use it instead of asyncio.sleep, which passes vacuously on a slow machine and flakes on a fast one.
  • HookCatcher and StaticEventHandler — capture a component's life-cycle hook and an event handler's target, for delivering events without a click.
  • capture_reactpy_logs, assert_reactpy_did_log, assert_reactpy_did_not_log — assert on server-side log output, which is where ReactPy puts swallowed handler and effect errors.

conftest.py also installs an autouse fixture that fails a test if any ReactPy log record carries an exception. That is deliberate: an error logged server-side while the browser stays quiet is the most common way a ReactPy bug hides. If a new test trips it, the exception is real even when the assertion you wrote passes.

docs.title: JavaScript tests
docs.text:
The client packages are tested with Bun:

hatch run javascript:test     # run the JavaScript tests
hatch run javascript:check    # lint and format check
hatch run javascript:fix      # lint and write fixes to disk
hatch run javascript:build    # rebuild the client bundles

Changes under src/js/ need a rebuild before Python tests can see them. The test script does this itself, but a manual run against a stale bundle will not reflect your edit.

docs.title: Linting and type checking
docs.text:
hatch fmt                     # format and lint, writing fixes
hatch fmt --check             # the CI form: report, do not write
hatch run python:type_check   # pyright over src/reactpy

CI runs hatch fmt src/reactpy --check followed by hatch run python:type_check.

Pitfall

Run hatch fmt --check before you commit, not hatch fmt. Bare hatch fmt rewrites files, so a run that "passes" has already edited your working tree — including files you did not intend to touch. Scope it (hatch fmt docs/) if you only want part of the tree.

Formatting is Ruff at a line length of 88. The rules that bite most in this repository are set in pyproject.toml; docs/**/*.py already ignores E402, S102, T201, TID252, RUF059, and INP001, because example files are teaching snippets rather than importable modules.

docs.title: Documentation checks
docs.text:
Run these from the repository root before you commit.

Pitfall

Nothing checks the documentation for you. The only workflow on new-docs installs the requirements and runs mkdocs gh-deploy --force on push — which does not pass --strict, so a broken internal link exits 0 and deploys anyway. The commands below are the gate only because you run them; there is no CI to catch a miss, and the live site is where an uncaught one appears.

hatch fmt --check docs/             # formatting and lint
cd docs && mkdocs build --strict    # build, fail on warnings

Plus the type check over the example files, which are real Python:

pyright --pythonpath <your-env>/bin/python docs/

mkdocs build --strict is the important one: it turns broken internal links and unresolvable includes into build failures, both of which abort with a nonzero exit. It does not fail on two things you would expect it to: a page missing from nav: (only an INFO line, and the build still exits 0 while serving the orphaned page), and a link whose #anchor does not exist inside an otherwise valid target file (also exit 0). Read that nav: list yourself and check anchors by eye. Nor can it tell you whether a snippet works: the examples in docs/examples/ are the source of truth for every snippet on the site, and a snippet that does not run is a docs bug the build will not catch on its own. That part is on you.

Pitfall

Do not judge a build by its log output alone. A grep-style check on the output hides a nonzero exit:

cd docs && mkdocs build --strict; echo "exit=$?"

In a bash pipeline, use echo "${PIPESTATUS[0]}" instead — a trailing | grep that finds a match makes the pipeline's exit code meaningless.

docs.title: Running the site locally
docs.text:
pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
cd docs && mkdocs serve

Then follow the printed URL. Editing any file under docs/src/ or docs/examples/ reloads the page.

The requirements file pins mkdocs-material==9.7.7. Earlier revisions pinned 9.4.0, which pulled in regex~=2022.4 and resolved to a release shipping wheels only through CPython 3.11 — on newer Pythons that meant a source build and a hard failure without a C compiler. The current pin dropped the regex dependency altogether, so the install works on 3.12 and up. If you are on an older branch and the docs install dies inside regex, that is the reason: use Python 3.11 or raise the pin.

docs.title: Checking your work
docs.text:
Before calling anything done, run the gates in this order and read every failure:

  1. hatch fmt --check docs/ — formatting and lint
  2. pyright docs/ — types in the examples
  3. cd docs && mkdocs build --strict — links, includes, nav
  4. The relevant tests, for code changes
  5. The real user scenario, by hand — open the page, click the control

Steps 1–4 can all pass while the thing you built does not work. A status is not an acceptance test: run the artefact. For a docs example that means mounting it in a browser and confirming the DOM changed, because a ReactPy component can render, error server-side, and show a blank region while the HTTP response still reads 200.

Deep Dive

Two harness traps have made broken examples look green more than once. First, the decorated function is a constructor: counter itself has no .render() and Layout(counter) raises TypeError: Expected a ReactPy component, so you must pass an instance. The instance does have .render(), but calling it outside a Layout raises RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout? for any component that uses a hook — which silently skips the behaviour you meant to test. Render through async with Layout(counter()) as layout: await layout.render(). Second, ReactPy formats exception text into the model only when REACTPY_DEBUG is on; with it off, a component that raised renders as {"tagName": "", "error": ""} — an empty region and no message. Set the variable when you are probing failures, and unset it when you are checking what a user would actually see.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Two suites: hatch test for ReactPy (on main), mkdocs build --strict for the docs.
  • hatch test reporting no tests ran means the suite is not there, not that it passed.
  • Python tests need Playwright's Chromium and build a wheel before pytest starts.
  • conftest.py forces debug mode and fails any test that logs an exception.
  • Run hatch fmt --check, never bare hatch fmt, before committing.
  • Check exit codes, not log text; then verify the real behaviour by hand.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Contributing Code — branches, commits, and the pull request checklist
  • Contributing Documentation — page conventions and the example-file workflow
  • Changelog — when a change needs an entry

docs.title: Add React to an Existing Project
Overview
docs.text: If you want to add some interactivity to your existing project, you don't have to rewrite it in React. Add React to your existing stack, and render interactive React components anywhere.

docs.title: Using React for an entire subroute of your existing website
docs.text: Let's say you have an existing web app at example.com built with another server technology (like Rails), and you want to implement all routes starting with example.com/some-app/ fully with React.

docs.title: Using an ASGI subroute
docs.text:
Here's how we recommend to set it up:

  1. Build the React part of your app using one of the ReactPy executors.
  2. Specify /some-app/ as the base path in your executor's kwargs (path_prefix="/some-app/"). The trailing slash is load-bearing: executors/asgi/middleware.py validates the value and a missing slash raises ValueError from the constructor — Invalid path_prefix of "/some-app". URL path must end with a forward slash. — so the app never starts.
  3. Configure your server or a proxy so that all requests under /some-app/ are handled by your React app.

This ensures the React part of your app can benefit from the best practices baked into those frameworks.

docs.title: Using static site generation (SSG)
docs.text: Support for SSG is coming in a future version.

docs.title: Using React for a part of your existing page
docs.text:
Let's say you have an existing page built with another Python web technology (ASGI or WSGI), and you want to render interactive React components somewhere on that page.

The exact approach depends on your existing page setup, so let's walk through some details.

docs.title: Using ASGI Middleware
docs.text:
ReactPy supports running as middleware for any existing ASGI application. ReactPy components are embedded into your existing HTML templates using Jinja2. You can use any ASGI framework, however for demonstration purposes we have selected Starlette for the example below.

First, install ReactPy, Starlette, and your preferred ASGI webserver.

Terminal

pip install reactpy[asgi,jinja] starlette uvicorn[standard]

Next, configure your ASGI framework to use ReactPy's Jinja2 template tag. The method for doing this will vary depending on the ASGI framework you are using. Below is an example that follow's Starlette's documentation:

Note

The ReactPyJinja extension enables a handful of template tags that allow you to render ReactPy components in your templates. The component tag is used to render a ReactPy SSR component, while the pyscript_setup and pyscript_component tags can be used together to render CSR components.

from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.routing import Route
from starlette.templating import Jinja2Templates

from reactpy.templatetags import ReactPyJinja

jinja_templates = Jinja2Templates(
    env=Environment(
        loader=FileSystemLoader("path/to/my_templates"),
        extensions=[ReactPyJinja],
        autoescape=True,
    )
)


async def example_webpage(request):
    return jinja_templates.TemplateResponse(request, "my_template.html")


starlette_app = Starlette(routes=[Route("/", example_webpage)])

Now you will need to wrap your existing ASGI application with ReactPy's middleware, define the dotted path to your root components, and render your components in your existing HTML templates.

main.pymy_components.pymy_template.html 
from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.routing import Route
from starlette.templating import Jinja2Templates

from reactpy.executors.asgi import ReactPyMiddleware
from reactpy.templatetags import ReactPyJinja

jinja_templates = Jinja2Templates(
    env=Environment(
        loader=FileSystemLoader("path/to/my_templates"),
        extensions=[ReactPyJinja],
        autoescape=True,
    )
)


async def example_webpage(request):
    return jinja_templates.TemplateResponse(request, "my_template.html")


starlette_app = Starlette(routes=[Route("/", example_webpage)])
reactpy_app = ReactPyMiddleware(starlette_app, ["my_components.hello_world"])

from reactpy import component, html


@component
def hello_world():
    return html.div("Hello World")

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">

<head>
  <title>ReactPy in Django</title>
</head>

<body>
  {% component "my_components.hello_world" %}
</body>

</html>

Finally, use your webserver of choice to start ReactPy:

Terminal

uvicorn main:reactpy_app

docs.title: Using WSGI Middleware
docs.text: Support for WSGI executors is coming in a future version.

docs.title: External Executors
docs.text:
Note

External executors exist outside ReactPy's core library and have significantly different installation and configuration instructions.

Make sure to follow the documentation for setting up your chosen external executor.

docs.title: Django
docs.text:
Django is a full-featured web framework that provides a batteries-included approach to web development.

Due to it's batteries-included approach, ReactPy has unique features only available to this executor.

To learn how to configure Django for ReactPy, see the ReactPy-Django documentation.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Structuring state well is the difference between a component that is pleasant to modify and one that is a constant source of bugs. ReactPy makes these guidelines matter more than they do in React, because it detects state changes with == rather than by identity, and because it re-renders every child of a component that re-renders. Each principle below comes with the failure it prevents, measured.

You will learn

  • When to group state into one object, and what that trade actually costs
  • Why contradictions, redundancy, and duplication each buy you a bug
  • How ReactPy's == comparison changes the "never mutate state" rule
  • What a flat state shape does to the cost of an update

docs.title: Principles for structuring state
docs.text:
When you write a component that holds state, you choose how many state variables to use and what shape their data has. A poor shape still runs correctly; it just makes mistakes easier to make. Five principles point the other way:

  1. Group related state. If you always update two or more state variables together, merge them into one.
  2. Avoid contradictions in state. If two pieces of state can disagree, you have left room for a bug.
  3. Avoid redundant state. If you can calculate a value from props or existing state during render, do not put it in state.
  4. Avoid duplication in state. Data stored in two places must be kept in sync in two places.
  5. Avoid deeply nested state. To change one leaf you must rebuild every ancestor.

The goal is to make state easy to update without introducing mistakes — the same reason a database engineer normalizes a schema. To paraphrase Einstein: make your state as simple as it can be, but no simpler.

One fact about ReactPy changes how all five pay off, so it comes first.

docs.title: ReactPy compares state with ==
docs.text:
use_state compares the value you set against the current one with strictly_equal, which falls through to ==. If the two compare equal, nothing re-renders. Verified against a real Layout, one press each:

You set over Renders {"items": [1, 2]} — a brand-new dict {"items": [1, 2]} 0 [1, 2, 3] — a brand-new list [1, 2, 3] 0 [] [] 0 {"a": {"b": 2}} {"a": {"b": 1}} 1 [1, 2] (1, 2) 1

The first three rows are the ones to internalise. In React, setting a fresh object always re-renders, because React compares by identity. In ReactPy, a new object that reads the same as the old one is discarded.

That makes the "never mutate state" rule stricter, not looser:

rows["items"].append("x")
set_rows(rows)  # same object, and == equal -> no render at all

Verified: three presses of that handler leave the rendered count at n=0 with the component body having run once. The mutation did happen — the list really grew — but nothing re-rendered to show it, so the screen and the data now disagree. Build a new object instead ({**rows, "items": [*rows["items"], "x"]}) and the update becomes visible.

It also means a tuple and a list are different states: [1, 2] over (1, 2) renders, because strictly_equal checks type(x) is type(y) before anything else. Pick one container type per field. See Lifecycle of Reactive Effects for the full comparison rules.

docs.title: Group related state
docs.text:
Should you use several state variables or one object?

Technically either works. But if two state variables always change together, put them in one state variable, so there is no second setter call to forget. Here the two coordinates are separate, and one handler forgets the second call:

app.py Run 
@component
def marker():
    x, set_x = use_state(20)
    y, set_y = use_state(20)

    def move_diagonally(event):
        # The classic mistake: this handler remembers x and forgets y.
        set_x(x + STEP)

    def move_correctly(event):
        set_x(x + STEP)
        set_y(y + STEP)

    def reset(event):
        set_x(20)
        set_y(20)

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": move_diagonally}, "Move (forgot y)"),
        html.button({"onClick": move_correctly}, "Move (both)"),
        html.button({"onClick": reset}, "Reset"),
        html.div(
            STYLE,
            html.div(
                {
                    "style": {
                        "position": "absolute",
                        "left": f"{x}px",
                        "top": f"{y}px",
                        "width": "18px",
                        "height": "18px",
                        "borderRadius": "50%",
                        "background": "#d40000",
                    }
                }
            ),
        ),
        html.p({"id": "coords"}, f"x={x}  y={y}"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return html.div(html.h3("Two state variables"), marker())

# TODO

Press Move (forgot y): the dot travels horizontally and the readout confirms the split — x=44 y=20. Every later move compounds it, because each handler builds on the state it already has.

With one object, the mistake has nowhere to live:

app.py Run 
@component
def marker():
    position, set_position = use_state({"x": 20, "y": 20})

    def move_diagonally(event):
        # One setter, one object: there is no second call left to forget.
        set_position({"x": position["x"] + STEP, "y": position["y"] + STEP})

    def reset(event):
        set_position({"x": 20, "y": 20})

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": move_diagonally}, "Move diagonally"),
        html.button({"onClick": reset}, "Reset"),
        html.div(
            STYLE,
            html.div(
                {
                    "style": {
                        "position": "absolute",
                        "left": f"{position['x']}px",
                        "top": f"{position['y']}px",
                        "width": "18px",
                        "height": "18px",
                        "borderRadius": "50%",
                        "background": "#d40000",
                    }
                }
            ),
        ),
        html.p({"id": "coords"}, f"x={position['x']}  y={position['y']}"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return html.div(html.h3("One state variable"), marker())

# TODO

Two presses of Move diagonally give x=68 y=68. There is no second setter to omit: one set_position call carries both axes, and the dict you build has to say something about each one.

The trade is worth naming, because it is not free. A single object means every update rebuilds the whole object, and position["x"] is noisier than x. ReactPy does not sweeten it with fewer renders: verified, two presses of "move both" cost two renders in the separate version and two in the grouped version, and moving only x costs one render in both. Group related state to remove a class of bug, not to save work.

docs.title: Avoid contradictions in state
docs.text:
A feedback form tracks its send with two booleans:

app.py Run 
@component
def feedback():
    text, set_text = use_state("")
    is_sending, set_is_sending = use_state(False)
    is_sent, set_is_sent = use_state(False)

    async def submit(event):
        set_is_sending(True)
        await asyncio.sleep(DELAY)
        # Forget either line below and the two flags disagree forever.
        set_is_sending(False)
        set_is_sent(True)

    async def submit_with_bug(event):
        set_is_sending(True)
        await asyncio.sleep(DELAY)
        set_is_sent(True)  # set_is_sending(False) was never called

    if is_sent:
        return html.div(
            html.h3("Thanks for your feedback!"),
            html.p({"id": "flags"}, f"is_sending={is_sending}  is_sent={is_sent}"),
        )

    return html.div(
        html.p("How was your stay at The Prancing Pony?"),
        html.textarea(
            {
                "value": text,
                "onChange": lambda event: set_text(event["target"]["value"]),
                "disabled": is_sending,
            }
        ),
        html.br(),
        html.button({"onClick": submit, "disabled": is_sending}, "Send"),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": submit_with_bug, "disabled": is_sending}, "Send (buggy)"
        ),
        (html.p("Sending...") if is_sending else None),
        html.p({"id": "flags"}, f"is_sending={is_sending}  is_sent={is_sent}"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return html.div(html.h3("Two flags"), feedback())

# TODO

The code works — and it permits a state that should be impossible. Press Send (buggy), which sets is_sent without clearing is_sending, and the readout reports:

is_sending=True  is_sent=True

That is not hypothetical. Nothing in the data structure prevents those two flags being true together, so the only thing protecting you is remembering every setter in every handler. The readout exists so you can see the disagreement; in a real component you would instead see a spinner that never stops.

Since the flags can never both be true, replace them with one variable holding one of three values:

app.py Run 
@component
def feedback(speed="slow"):
    text, set_text = use_state("")
    status, set_status = use_state("typing")

    async def submit(event):
        set_status("sending")
        await asyncio.sleep(DELAYS[speed])
        set_status("sent")

    # Plain names, not state: they cannot drift apart because they are derived.
    is_sending = status == "sending"
    is_sent = status == "sent"

    if is_sent:
        return html.div(html.h3("Thanks for your feedback!"))

    return html.div(
        html.p("How was your stay at The Prancing Pony?"),
        html.textarea(
            {
                "value": text,
                "onChange": lambda event: set_text(event["target"]["value"]),
                "disabled": is_sending,
            }
        ),
        html.br(),
        html.button({"onClick": submit, "disabled": is_sending}, "Send"),
        (html.p("Sending...") if is_sending else None),
        html.p({"id": "flags"}, f"status={status}"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return html.div(html.h3("One status"), feedback())

# TODO

status passes through "sending" and ends at "sent", which swaps the form for a thank-you. There is no way to be in two states at once, because there is only one variable.

You can still write the readable names:

is_sending = status == "sending"
is_sent = status == "sent"

Those are plain local variables computed during render, not state. They cannot drift, which is exactly why they should not be state.

docs.title: Avoid redundant state
docs.text:
A check-in form shows a full name built from two fields:

app.py Run 
@component
def check_in():
    first_name, set_first_name = use_state("Ada")
    last_name, set_last_name = use_state("Lovelace")
    full_name, set_full_name = use_state("Ada Lovelace")

    def handle_first_name_change(event):
        set_first_name(event["target"]["value"])
        set_full_name(event["target"]["value"] + " " + last_name)

    def handle_last_name_change(event):
        set_last_name(event["target"]["value"])
        set_full_name(first_name + " " + event["target"]["value"])

    def rename_only_first(event):
        # The bug the extra state variable invites: one writer, one update.
        set_first_name("Grace")

    def rename_only_last(event):
        # This one does not touch full_name either.
        set_last_name("Hopper")

    return html.div(
        html.h2("Let's check you in"),
        html.label(
            {},
            "First name: ",
            html.input({"value": first_name, "onChange": handle_first_name_change}),
        ),
        html.br(),
        html.label(
            {},
            "Last name: ",
            html.input({"value": last_name, "onChange": handle_last_name_change}),
        ),
        html.br(),
        html.button({"onClick": rename_only_first}, "Rename first"),
        html.button({"onClick": rename_only_last}, "Rename last"),
        html.p({"id": "ticket"}, "Your ticket will be issued to: ", html.b(full_name)),
    )


@component
def app():
    return check_in()

# TODO

It has three state variables, and one is redundant — full_name is derivable from the other two at any moment. That is not merely wasteful; it is a second place every writer must remember. Press Rename first: first_name becomes "Grace", and the ticket still reads Ada Lovelace.

Remove the state variable and calculate it:

app.py Run 
@component
def check_in():
    first_name, set_first_name = use_state("Ada")
    last_name, set_last_name = use_state("Lovelace")

    # Not state. Every render recomputes it from whatever the two fields hold.
    full_name = f"{first_name} {last_name}"

    def rename_only_first(event):
        set_first_name("Grace")

    def rename_only_last(event):
        set_last_name("Hopper")

    return html.div(
        html.h2("Let's check you in"),
        html.label(
            "First name: ",
            html.input(
                {
                    "value": first_name,
                    "onChange": lambda event: set_first_name(event["target"]["value"]),
                }
            ),
        ),
        html.br(),
        html.label(
            "Last name: ",
            html.input(
                {
                    "value": last_name,
                    "onChange": lambda event: set_last_name(event["target"]["value"]),
                }
            ),
        ),
        html.br(),
        html.button({"onClick": rename_only_first}, "Rename first"),
        html.button({"onClick": rename_only_last}, "Rename last"),
        html.p({"id": "ticket"}, "Your ticket will be issued to: ", html.b(full_name)),
    )


@component
def app():
    return check_in()

# TODO

Now Rename first followed by Rename last gives Grace Hopper. The same two buttons cannot go wrong, because there is only one copy of the name.

The difference is not the render count — both versions render once per press, verified. It is that the derived version has no code path that produces a stale ticket.

Note

Deriving is the default, but not free when a calculation is genuinely expensive. The order is: derive first, then measure. If a render is too slow, cache the value with use_memo rather than promoting it to state — a cache adds no render, a state variable does. See You Might Not Need an Effect.

docs.title: Avoid duplication in state
docs.text:
A snack menu lets you choose one item and edit the titles. This version stores the selected item as an object:

app.py Run 
@component
def menu():
    items, set_items = use_state(INITIAL_ITEMS)
    selected_item, set_selected_item = use_state(INITIAL_ITEMS[0])

    def handle_item_change(item_id, event):
        new_title = event["target"]["value"]
        set_items(
            [
                {**item, "title": new_title} if item["id"] == item_id else item
                for item in items
            ]
        )

    return html.div(
        html.h2("What's your travel snack?"),
        html.ul(
            [
                html.li(
                    {"key": item["id"]},
                    html.input(
                        {
                            "value": item["title"],
                            "onChange": lambda event, i=item: handle_item_change(
                                i["id"], event
                            ),
                        }
                    ),
                    html.button(
                        {"onClick": lambda event, i=item: set_selected_item(i)},
                        "Choose",
                    ),
                )
                for item in items
            ]
        ),
        html.p({"id": "picked"}, f"You picked {selected_item['title']}."),
    )


@component
def app():
    return menu()

# TODO

Press Choose on pretzels, then edit that input to chips. The input updates; the line below it does not:

You picked pretzels.

selected_item is a second copy of data that also lives inside items. set_items updated one copy and nothing updated the other — the same bug as the stale full name, one level deeper.

Hold the id instead and look the item up during render:

app.py Run 
@component
def menu():
    items, set_items = use_state(INITIAL_ITEMS)
    selected_id, set_selected_id = use_state(0)

    # Derived: there is exactly one copy of the title, and it lives in items.
    selected_item = next(item for item in items if item["id"] == selected_id)

    def handle_item_change(item_id, event):
        new_title = event["target"]["value"]
        set_items(
            [
                {**item, "title": new_title} if item["id"] == item_id else item
                for item in items
            ]
        )

    return html.div(
        html.h2("What's your travel snack?"),
        html.ul(
            [
                html.li(
                    {"key": item["id"]},
                    html.input(
                        {
                            "value": item["title"],
                            "onChange": lambda event, i=item: handle_item_change(
                                i["id"], event
                            ),
                        }
                    ),
                    html.button(
                        {"onClick": lambda event, i=item: set_selected_id(i["id"])},
                        "Choose",
                    ),
                )
                for item in items
            ]
        ),
        html.p({"id": "picked"}, f"You picked {selected_item['title']}."),
    )


@component
def app():
    return menu()

# TODO

Editing the selected row now updates the line below it, because selected_item is a next(...) over items, re-evaluated on every render. The state went from:

  • items = [{"id": 0, "title": "pretzels"}, ...]
  • selected_item = {"id": 0, "title": "pretzels"}

to:

  • items = [{"id": 0, "title": "pretzels"}, ...]
  • selected_id = 0

Only the id is essential; the rest was a copy. The same reasoning turns a selected object into an id, a filter string into its own fields, and a sorted list into an unsorted list plus a sort.

Pitfall

"Store the id, derive the object" meets ReactPy's == comparison in one place worth knowing about. A derived object handed to use_effect as a dependency compares equal every render, so the dependency holds and the effect never restarts — usually what you want. But that also means a dependency cannot detect a change that == cannot see. Verified with a plain class instance held as a dependency and mutated in place: across three presses the component re-rendered each time and the screen showed n=3, while the effect ran once and kept reporting n=0. Use dict and list, or an immutable @dataclass(frozen=True), for anything that appears in a dependency array. See Removing Effect Dependencies.

docs.title: Avoid deeply nested state
docs.text:
A travel plan is planets, then continents, then countries. The tempting shape mirrors the picture. Two files make the example — app.py renders it, data.py holds the tree:

app.pydata.py Run 
def mark_visited(node, target_id):
    """Copy this node, and recurse — the whole tree is rebuilt top-down."""
    if node["id"] == target_id:
        return {**node, "visited": True}
    return {
        **node,
        "childPlaces": [
            mark_visited(child, target_id) for child in node["childPlaces"]
        ],
    }


@component
def place_tree(place, on_visit):
    children = place["childPlaces"]
    return html.li(
        {"key": place["id"]},
        place["title"],
        html.button(
            {"onClick": on_visit}, "Visited" if place.get("visited") else "Visit"
        ),
        html.ol([place_tree(child, on_visit) for child in children])
        if children
        else None,
    )


@component
def travel_plan():
    plan, set_plan = use_state(INITIAL_PLAN)

    return html.div(
        html.h2("Places to visit"),
        html.ol(
            [
                place_tree(
                    place,
                    lambda event, pid=place["id"]: set_plan(mark_visited(plan, pid)),
                )
                for place in plan["childPlaces"]
            ]
        ),
    )


@component
def app():
    return travel_plan()

"""The same tree as nested objects, the shape this section argues against."""

INITIAL_PLAN = {
    "id": 0,
    "title": "(Root)",
    "childPlaces": [
        {
            "id": 1,
            "title": "Earth",
            "childPlaces": [
                {
                    "id": 2,
                    "title": "Africa",
                    "childPlaces": [
                        {"id": 3, "title": "Botswana", "childPlaces": []},
                        {"id": 4, "title": "Egypt", "childPlaces": []},
                        {"id": 5, "title": "Kenya", "childPlaces": []},
                    ],
                },
                {
                    "id": 10,
                    "title": "Americas",
                    "childPlaces": [
                        {"id": 11, "title": "Argentina", "childPlaces": []},
                        {"id": 12, "title": "Brazil", "childPlaces": []},
                        {"id": 13, "title": "Barbados", "childPlaces": []},
                    ],
                },
                {
                    "id": 21,
                    "title": "Asia",
                    "childPlaces": [
                        {"id": 22, "title": "Japan", "childPlaces": []},
                        {"id": 23, "title": "Nepal", "childPlaces": []},
                    ],
                },
            ],
        }
    ],
}

# TODO

Marking one country visited calls mark_visited, which copies the root, copies Earth, copies the continent, and copies every sibling along the way — a new object for every node between the root and the leaf. Correct, and also easy to get wrong: miss one {**node, ...} and you have mutated shared state, which in ReactPy means the update may compare equal and never render.

Flatten the tree into one dict keyed by id, with child lists of ids:

app.pydata.py Run 
@component
def place_tree(place_id, on_visit, visited):
    place = PLACES[place_id]
    children = place["childIds"]
    return html.li(
        {"key": place_id},
        place["title"],
        html.button(
            {"onClick": on_visit}, "Visited" if place_id in visited else "Visit"
        ),
        (
            html.ol(
                [
                    place_tree(
                        child_id,
                        lambda event, cid=child_id: on_visit(event, cid),
                        visited,
                    )
                    for child_id in children
                ]
            )
            if children
            else None
        ),
    )


@component
def travel_plan():
    # One dict keyed by id, plus one set of visited ids. Marking a place visited
    # touches exactly one entry — there is no enclosing object to rebuild.
    visited, set_visited = use_state(set())

    def toggle(event, place_id=0):
        if place_id not in visited:
            set_visited({*visited, place_id})

    return html.div(
        html.h2("Places to visit"),
        html.ol(
            [
                place_tree(
                    place_id,
                    lambda event, pid=place_id: toggle(event, pid),
                    visited,
                )
                for place_id in PLACES[0]["childIds"]
            ]
        ),
    )


@component
def app():
    return travel_plan()

"""The same tree flattened into one dict keyed by id."""

PLACES = {
    0: {"id": 0, "title": "(Root)", "childIds": [1]},
    1: {"id": 1, "title": "Earth", "childIds": [2, 10, 21]},
    2: {"id": 2, "title": "Africa", "childIds": [3, 4, 5]},
    3: {"id": 3, "title": "Botswana", "childIds": []},
    4: {"id": 4, "title": "Egypt", "childIds": []},
    5: {"id": 5, "title": "Kenya", "childIds": []},
    10: {"id": 10, "title": "Americas", "childIds": [11, 12, 13]},
    11: {"id": 11, "title": "Argentina", "childIds": []},
    12: {"id": 12, "title": "Brazil", "childIds": []},
    13: {"id": 13, "title": "Barbados", "childIds": []},
    21: {"id": 21, "title": "Asia", "childIds": [22, 23]},
    22: {"id": 22, "title": "Japan", "childIds": []},
    23: {"id": 23, "title": "Nepal", "childIds": []},
}

# TODO

The same update now adds one entry to one set, and finding a place is a dict lookup rather than a recursion. The rendering component still walks the tree by id, so the display is unchanged — only the update path got shorter.

A useful test for whether nesting has gone too far: count the objects an update has to rebuild to change one field. If the answer is "everything above it", flatten. If the hierarchy is genuinely part of the data and updates are rare, nesting is fine — the cost is in writes, not reads.

Deep Dive

Flattening is what databases do, and ReactPy's == comparison gives you a concrete second reason — though it rewards less than you would expect. A state update is detected by handing the new value to == (core/hooks.py, strictly_equal, falls through to == for a dict). dict.__eq__ first compares lengths, which is free, then walks entries in insertion order and stops at the first difference. So the cost depends on where the changed entry sits, not on how big the object is.

Measured on dicts of 100,000 keys, comparing a copy against its original after changing one entry: about 0.00 ms when the changed key sorts first, about 1.3 ms when it sorts last, and about 3 ms when the two dicts hold identical content. Nested dicts recurse, so a rebuilt branch is compared down to its leaves while untouched sibling branches are still compared entry by entry too — sharing the sub-dict objects does not make the comparison skip them.

The honest conclusion: comparison cost is real but small and easy to over-engineer around, so flatten for the update-code reasons above rather than for this one. Where the shapes matter, measure instead of guessing — ReactPy ships no render profiler, so count renders with a use_ref counter in the component body, as the examples on this page do.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• ReactPy's use_state compares with ==: setting a new object that reads equal to the old one renders nothing. Copy objects rather than mutating them — verified, mutating leaves the screen and the data disagreeing.
  • type(x) is not type(y) makes (1, 2) and [1, 2] different states, so pick one container type per field.
  • Group state that always changes together. It removes the "forgot the second setter" bug; it does not reduce renders (verified: same count both ways).
  • Replace mutually exclusive booleans with one variable holding one of several values, so the impossible state is unrepresentable.
  • Derive anything you can calculate during render. Both versions of the name form render the same number of times; only one of them can show a stale ticket.
  • Store ids, not copies. Edit the selected row and the derived label follows while the stored one does not.
  • Count how many objects an update must rebuild. If nesting forces you to rebuild the path to every leaf, flatten and key by id.
