docs.title: Communicating Data Between Server and Client
Overview
docs.text:
ReactPy connects a Python process and a browser tab with one websocket and one message type in each direction. That single constraint decides how every kind of data moves between the two: values the server knows flow down as rendered models, values the user produces flow up as event payloads, and anything else needs a deliberate detour. This page is a map of those routes — what crosses, what cannot, and the honest workaround for each.

You will learn

  • Which channels actually exist, and the one direction that is not supported
  • How to push a server-side value into a view without the client asking
  • What an event payload really contains — including why file uploads do not work the way people expect
  • How to get real file bytes across, and how to keep blocking code off the loop

docs.title: The channels that exist
docs.text:
Direction Mechanism Your control server → client the rendered model, sent as layout-update patches total — return it from the component client → server an event handler, receiving layout-event total — read event server → client, arbitrary message none not supported shared mutable state none the two sides hold different objects

The server-to-client push row is the one people look for first, and its absence is a design choice, not an omission. A component's Connection has no send, no deliver, no close (User Connection), and the backend is the only code allowed to write to the socket. That keeps the model the single source of truth: if a component could scribble on the wire, the client's tree and the server's model would drift apart with nothing to reconcile them.

A hand-written message is dropped by the client, silently

A custom backend can write anything to the socket, so it is tempting to invent a message type. Verified against a real browser: a {"type": "my-custom", ...} frame arrives, and the client logs

[ReactPy] Received message without handler Object

and discards it. The client dispatches on message.type against a fixed registry — "layout-update" is the only one registered by the mount path — and an unregistered type warns and returns. Nothing throws, the socket stays up, and the UI never changes. The client bundle exports exactly one function and offers no onMessage hook to register against, so there is no supported way to add a handler. Do not build on this path; use one of the routes below.

docs.title: Down: push a value the client never asked for
docs.text:
Anything you can await on the server becomes a render, and a render reaches the client. An use_async_effect that loops is the whole pattern:

app.py Run 
async def fetch_price(symbol):
    """Stand-in for a request to an exchange, a sensor, a queue."""
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return f"{symbol}: 42.10"


@component
def ticker(symbol):
    price, set_price = use_state("loading...")

    async def poll():
        while True:
            try:
                set_price(await fetch_price(symbol))
            except Exception as error:
                set_price(f"error: {error}")
            try:
                await asyncio.sleep(1)
            except asyncio.CancelledError:
                break

    use_async_effect(poll)

    return html.div(html.h1(price))

# TODO

Verified end to end: the first patch carried ["loading..."], and about a second later a second patch arrived with ["BTC: 42.10"] — no client event in between. The client applied it like any other update.

Three things make or break this:

  • Use use_async_effect, not use_effect. An async def passed to use_effect raises TypeError: \use_effect` does not support async functions. Use `use_async_effect` instead.The effect takes **zero arguments** — the#!python async def effect(stop)shape from 1.x no longer works. Note where that error surfaces:#!python use_effectraises during the **render**, not inside the effect task, so you get a blank region — the model is#!python {"tagName": "", "error": ""}with debug off, and carries theTypeErrortext with#!python REACTPY_DEBUGon — and noError in effect` log line at all. That distinguishes it from a raising effect body, which is silent everywhere until unmount (Lifecycle of Reactive Effects).
  • Loop and honour cancellation. A long-lived effect is while True: with except asyncio.CancelledError: break. ReactPy cancels the task on unmount; shield=True opts out if the work must finish.
  • The dependency array is not React's. Omitted means inferred from the closure's free variables, dependencies=[] starts once, dependencies=None restarts every render. Never omit the array expecting "run after every render". See Use Async Effect.

Polling is fine for a demo and wrong at scale. For real work, prefer a server-sent queue that the effect awaits — the effect suspends on await queue.get() and the render happens the moment an item lands, with no timer at all.

docs.title: Up: read what the client sends
docs.text:
An event handler receives a dict, not a live event — the browser serialized it and your code is now on the other side of a network boundary. The client walks the target and copies enumerable properties, plus value, checked, files, type, name read off the element even though they are accessors, plus dataset, plus — on submit — the form's named controls. Functions, DOM nodes, and cycles are skipped rather than raising.

Two consequences to internalize:

An <input> arrives as the whole element. A measured onChange payload carried roughly ninety keys — accept, formAction, validity, validationMessage, and the rest of HTMLInputElement — of which you read value. Index what you need; do not count on a specific key surviving, and do not iterate the payload assuming it is small.

On submit, event["target"] is a list, not a dict. The named controls are serialized as list entries, so the read shape differs from every other event:

def handle_submit(event):
    event.preventDefault()
    controls = event["target"]  # list of control dicts
    payload = next((c["value"] for c in controls if c.get("name") == "payload"), "")

This is verified: submitting a form with a hidden name="payload" input produced [{"name": "", "type": "file", ...}, {"name": "payload", "type": "hidden", "value": "hello world\n"}, {"name": "", "type": "submit", ...}]. The full working example is in Files below. The protocol behind this is documented in Protocol Structure.

docs.title: Files: what actually crosses the wire
docs.text:
A file input does not send file contents. It sends file metadata. Verified with a real file chooser against a real browser — this is the entire files entry that arrived:

{
    "name": "upload.txt",
    "lastModified": 1791523914968,
    "lastModifiedDate": {},
    "webkitRelativePath": "",
    "type": "text/plain",
}

No bytes. File exposes its content through methods, which are functions, and functions are skipped by the walk. There is no FormData in the client and no chunked upload path. If you expected event["target"]["files"][0]["content"], it does not exist and never will from this mechanism.

docs.title: Reading real bytes
docs.text:
The route is: read the file in the browser with JavaScript, put the text into a normal form field, and let an ordinary submit carry it. This works — verified in Chrome, with a 12-character file arriving server-side as 'hello world\n':

app.py Run 
READ_FILE = (
    "const file = event.target.files[0];"
    "if (file) {"
    "    file.text().then((text) => {"
    "        document.getElementById('payload').value = text;"
    "    });"
    "}"
)


@component
def text_upload():
    received, set_received = use_state("Choose a file, then send.")

    def handle_submit(event):
        event.preventDefault()
        # On submit, target is the list of *named* controls in the form.
        controls = event["target"]
        payload = next(
            (c["value"] for c in controls if c.get("name") == "payload"),
            "",
        )
        set_received(f"{len(payload)} characters received")

    return html.form(
        {"onSubmit": handle_submit},
        html.input({"type": "file", "onChange": READ_FILE}),
        html.input({"type": "hidden", "id": "payload", "name": "payload", "value": ""}),
        html.button({"type": "submit"}, "Send"),
        html.pre(received),
    )

# TODO

The mechanics, each of which matters:

  • The onChange value is a string, which routes it to inlineJavaScript instead of eventHandlers — that is what makes it run in the page (Creating VDOM Event Handlers).
  • file.text() returns a promise, so the assignment happens in a callback — which is why a submit button is required. Sending immediately from the change handler races the promise and ships an empty string.
  • The hidden input needs both id (for the JavaScript to find it) and name (for the form walk to include it).
  • event.preventDefault() must appear literally in the handler's body. ReactPy detects it by bytecode inspection; calling a helper that calls it is not detected, and the page navigates away. See the bound-method caveat in Creating VDOM Event Handlers.

Untrusted content and eval

The inline-JavaScript string is eval'd. Build it from constants only — f"...{user_input}..." is an injection point. And anything you read off a user's file is untrusted data: cap the size before you buffer it, and never render it back without escaping.

Binary uploads work the same way via file.arrayBuffer() plus base64, but base64 costs a third of your bandwidth on top of a JSON string over a socket. For anything large, upload to a normal HTTP endpoint and pass the resulting id through state instead.

docs.title: Blocking code and other threads
docs.text:
Everything a component does runs on the connection's event loop. A synchronous, CPU-bound call inside a render or an effect freezes that connection — and the handlers on it. Move blocking work with asyncio.to_thread:

app.py Run 
def blocking_render(width):
    """A synchronous, CPU-bound library call. Never run this on the loop."""
    time.sleep(0.4)  # stands in for image encoding, model inference, ...
    return f"rendered {width}px"


@component
def preview(width):
    result, set_result = use_state("rendering...")

    async def render():
        # to_thread keeps the loop free; the setter runs back on the loop.
        set_result(await asyncio.to_thread(blocking_render, width))

    use_async_effect(render, dependencies=[width])

    return html.h1(result)

# TODO

Verified: the first patch says rendering..., the next says rendered 300px, and the loop stayed responsive across the 0.4 s call. Note that the setter is called from inside the effect, which is already on the loop.

Calling a state setter from another thread loses the update

Handing set_value to a raw threading.Thread is the natural mistake, and it fails with no user-visible symptom. Verified — the setter raises on the worker thread, and no render ever arrives:

Failed to schedule render via <function _make_life_cycle_state.<locals>.<lambda> ...>
RuntimeError: no running event loop
RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'Layout._create_layout_update' was never awaited

Nothing appears in the browser console; the component simply never updates. The fix is to capture the loop while you are on it and marshal back:

loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()  # inside the component, on the loop

def deliver_from_thread(value):
    loop.call_soon_threadsafe(set_value, value)

Verified working — the update arrived as a normal patch. Prefer asyncio.to_thread when you can, since it removes the bookkeeping entirely.

Do not hang state on the component function

my_component.started = True as a run-once guard looks harmless and is a cross-user leak: the function object is module-scope, so the first visitor flips it for everyone. Give the component a prop, key the child, or guard with use_ref. The general version of this is in VDOM Mutations.

docs.title: Client-only data
docs.text:
The mirror problem: something in the browser that Python cannot see. Computed style, scroll position, canvas pixels, localStorage, geolocation, the clipboard — none of it is in the payload, because the walk copies data properties and skips everything callable.

Your options, in order of preference:

  1. Move the computation server-side. If the value depends only on data you already have, compute it in Python. Server-side rendering is the default for a reason.
  2. Copy it into a form field and submit, exactly as the file example does. Clunky, and it works.
  3. Use the browser API in inline JavaScript and let it act locally — copy to clipboard, request fullscreen, scroll. Keep it to one call, and never interpolate user input into the string.
  4. Render the data yourself. A chart is usually better as a server-built <svg> or a generated image (reactpy.widgets.image) than as JavaScript in the page.

There is no use_ref-style handle to a DOM node, and {"ref": ...} either vanishes or throws in the browser — see Manipulating the DOM with Refs.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Only two channels exist: the model down, events up. An arbitrary server→client message is logged as Received message without handler and dropped.
  • Server push means use_async_effect plus a state setter — loop, handle CancelledError, and remember the dependency array infers by default.
  • Event payloads are serialized snapshots: an input arrives as the whole HTMLInputElement, and submit gives you a list of named controls.
  • File inputs send metadata only, never bytes. Read the file in the browser, put the text in a named hidden input, and submit.
  • Use asyncio.to_thread for blocking work. Calling a setter from a raw thread fails with no running event loop and no visible symptom — marshal with call_soon_threadsafe.
  • State never lives on the component function object; that is a leak across connections.

  • User Connection — the read-only connection view

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Your components will often need to display different things depending on different conditions. In ReactPy, you can conditionally render markup using Python syntax like if statements and conditional expressions.

You will learn

  • How to return different markup depending on a condition
  • How to conditionally include or exclude a piece of markup
  • Conditional syntax shortcuts you'll encounter in ReactPy codebases

docs.title: Conditionally returning markup
docs.text:
Let's say you have a packing_list() component rendering several item()s, which can be marked as packed or not. Notice that some of the item() calls have their is_packed prop set to True instead of False. You want to add a checkmark (✔) to packed items if is_packed is True.

You can write this as an if/else statement like so:

if is_packed:
    return html.li({"className": "item"}, f"{name} ✔")
return html.li({"className": "item"}, name)

If the is_packed prop is True, this code returns a different VDOM tree. With this change, some of the items get a checkmark at the end:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def item(name, is_packed):
    if is_packed:
        return html.li({"className": "item"}, f"{name} ✔")
    return html.li({"className": "item"}, name)


@component
def packing_list():
    return html.section(
        html.h1("Sally Ride's Packing List"),
        html.ul(
            item(is_packed=True, name="Space suit"),
            item(is_packed=True, name="Helmet with a golden leaf"),
            item(is_packed=False, name="Photo of Tam"),
        ),
    )

.item {
    list-style: none;
}

# TODO

Try editing what gets returned in either case, and see how the result changes!

Notice how you're creating branching logic with Python's if and return statements. In ReactPy, control flow (like conditions) is handled by Python.

docs.title: Conditionally returning nothing with None
docs.text:
In some situations, you won't want to render anything at all. For example, say you don't want to show packed items at all. A component must return something — in ReactPy, that something is None:

if is_packed:
    return None
return html.li({"className": "item"}, name)

If is_packed is true, the component will return nothing, None. Otherwise, it will return markup to render.

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def item(name, is_packed):
    if is_packed:
        return None
    return html.li({"className": "item"}, name)


@component
def packing_list():
    return html.section(
        html.h1("Sally Ride's Packing List"),
        html.ul(
            item(is_packed=False, name="Space suit"),
            item(is_packed=False, name="Helmet with a golden leaf"),
            item(is_packed=True, name="Photo of Tam"),
        ),
    )

.item {
    list-style: none;
}

# TODO

In practice, returning None from a component isn't common because it might surprise a developer trying to render it. More often, you would conditionally include or exclude the component in the parent component. Here's how to do that!

docs.title: Conditionally including markup
docs.text:
In the previous example, you controlled which (if any!) VDOM tree would be returned by the component. You may already have noticed some duplication in the render output:

html.li({"className": "item"}, f"{name} ✔")

is very similar to

html.li({"className": "item"}, name)

Both of the conditional branches return html.li({"className": "item"}, ...):

if is_packed:
    return html.li({"className": "item"}, f"{name} ✔")
return html.li({"className": "item"}, name)

While this duplication isn't harmful, it could make your code harder to maintain. What if you want to change the className? You'd have to do it in two places in your code! In such a situation, you could conditionally include a little markup to make your code more DRY.

docs.title: Conditional (ternary) expression
docs.text:
Python has a compact syntax for writing a conditional expression — the conditional expression or "ternary operator".

Instead of this:

if is_packed:
    return html.li({"className": "item"}, f"{name} ✔")
return html.li({"className": "item"}, name)

You can write this:

return html.li({"className": "item"}, f"{name} ✔" if is_packed else name)

You can read it as "if is_packed is true, then render f"{name} ✔", otherwise render name".

Now let's say you want to wrap the completed item's text into another HTML tag, like <del> to strike it out. You can add even more newlines and parentheses so that it's easier to nest more markup in each of the cases:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def item(name, is_packed):
    return html.li(
        {"className": "item"},
        html.del_(f"{name} ✔") if is_packed else name,
    )


@component
def packing_list():
    return html.section(
        html.h1("Sally Ride's Packing List"),
        html.ul(
            item(is_packed=True, name="Space suit"),
            item(is_packed=True, name="Helmet with a golden leaf"),
            item(is_packed=False, name="Photo of Tam"),
        ),
    )

.item {
    list-style: none;
}

# TODO

This style works well for simple conditions, but use it in moderation. If your components get messy with too much nested conditional markup, consider extracting child components to clean things up. In ReactPy, markup is a part of your code, so you can use tools like variables and functions to tidy up complex expressions.

Are these two examples fully equivalent?

If you're coming from an object-oriented programming background, you might assume that the two examples above are subtly different because one of them may create two different "instances" of html.li. But VDOM dictionaries aren't "instances" because they don't hold any internal state and aren't real DOM nodes. They're lightweight descriptions, like blueprints. So these two examples, in fact, are completely equivalent. Preserving and Resetting State goes into detail about how this works.

docs.title: Excluding a child with a conditional
docs.text:
In JavaScript React you'll often see the logical AND operator used to render a child only when a condition holds:

<li className="item">{name} {isPacked && "✔"}</li>

There is no equivalent of this idiom in ReactPy. Python's and returns one of its operands rather than a renderable-agnostic False, and ReactPy renders False as the literal text "False" instead of skipping it:

# WRONG: renders "Photo of Tam False" when is_packed is False
return html.li({"className": "item"}, name, is_packed and "✔")

Reach for a conditional expression that yields an empty list, and unpack it:

return html.li(
    {"className": "item"},
    name,
    *(["✔"] if is_packed else []),
)

Or build the children list up front, which reads better as the number of optional children grows:

@component
def item(name, is_packed):
    content = [name]
    if is_packed:
        content.append("✔")
    return html.li({"className": "item"}, *content)

Don't put a number on the left side of a conditional expression

The classic messageCount && <p>New messages</p> bug has an exact Python twin. and returns the left operand when it is falsy, and ReactPy renders numbers as text — so count and html.p("New messages") renders 0 rather than nothing when count is 0. Make the left side a genuine boolean test:

html.p("New messages") if count > 0 else None

docs.title: Conditionally assigning markup to a variable
docs.text:
When the shortcuts get in the way of writing plain code, try using an if statement and a variable. Start by providing the default content you want to display, the name:

item_content = name

Use an if statement to reassign a VDOM expression to item_content if is_packed is True:

if is_packed:
    item_content = html.del_(f"{name} ✔")

Embed the variable in the returned VDOM tree, nesting the previously calculated expression inside the parent element:

html.li({"className": "item"}, item_content)

This style is the most verbose, but it's also the most flexible:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def item(name, is_packed):
    item_content = name
    if is_packed:
        item_content = html.del_(f"{name} ✔")
    return html.li({"className": "item"}, item_content)


@component
def packing_list():
    return html.section(
        html.h1("Sally Ride's Packing List"),
        html.ul(
            item(is_packed=True, name="Space suit"),
            item(is_packed=True, name="Helmet with a golden leaf"),
            item(is_packed=False, name="Photo of Tam"),
        ),
    )

.item {
    list-style: none;
}

# TODO

Like before, this works not only for text, but for arbitrary markup too.

Tags that collide with Python keywords

del is a Python keyword, so the <del> tag is spelled with a trailing underscore: html.del_. The underscore is stripped before the tag name is emitted, so it still renders <del>. The same rule covers html.import_, html.object, and friends — and dashes become underscores, so <data-table> is html.data_table.

If you're not familiar with Python, this variety of styles might seem overwhelming at first. However, learning them will help you read and write any Python code — and not just ReactPy components! Pick the one you prefer for a start, and then consult this reference again if you forget how the other ones work.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• To conditionally return different markup from a component, use if statements and return.
  • To render nothing, return None from the component.
  • To tidy up duplicated markup, use a conditional expression: x if condition else y.
  • Don't use and to include a child — ReactPy renders False as the text "False". Unpack an empty list instead.
  • For anything more complex, assign children to variables with if statements.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ReactPy's UI is a plain dictionary. Two functions move it across the boundary to and from ordinary HTML text: reactpy_to_string() renders a VDOM dictionary or a component to an HTML string, and string_to_reactpy() parses an HTML string into a VDOM dictionary. Both live at the top of the package, and both are load-bearing inside ReactPy itself — the executors build the initial document and the PyScript head with them.

You will learn

  • How to turn VDOM into an HTML string, and what that conversion throws away
  • How to parse HTML text into a VDOM dictionary, and the renames it performs on the way in
  • Why className survives parsing but not serialization
  • When to reach for string_to_reactpy() instead of writing html.* calls

docs.title: The two functions
docs.text:
Function In Out Raises on bad input reactpy_to_string(root) VdomDict or a called Component str of HTML TypeError on a callable attribute string_to_reactpy(html, *transforms, strict=True, intercept_links=True) str of HTML VdomDict HTMLParseError, ValueError, TypeError

Both are exported from the package root:

from reactpy import reactpy_to_string, string_to_reactpy

Neither is a serializer for the wire. The socket protocol has its own shape, described in Protocol Structure; these two functions exist so you can hand ReactPy's output to something that speaks HTML, and hand HTML from somewhere else to ReactPy.

docs.title: VDOM to HTML: reactpy_to_string()
docs.text:
Give it an element, or a component that has already been called:

app.py Run 
todo_list = html.div(
    html.h1("My Todo List"),
    html.ul(
        html.li("Build a cool new app"),
        html.li("Share it with the world!"),
    ),
)

print(reactpy_to_string(todo_list))
# <div><h1>My Todo List</h1><ul><li>Build a cool new app</li><li>Share it with the world!</li></ul></div>

# TODO

There is no formatting option, no indent, no doctype. You get the tags and the attributes and nothing else.

docs.title: What it renders
docs.text:
reactpy_to_string() walks tagName, attributes, and children (utils.py, _add_vdom_to_etree). Everything else in the dictionary is ignored:

  • Event handlers disappear. A {"onClick": handler} produces no attribute at all. The value is a Python function; there is nothing sensible to write into HTML text.
  • Inline JavaScript disappears too. inlineJavaScript is not consulted, so reactpy_to_string(html.button({"onClick": "this.innerText = 1"}, "x")) returns <button>x</button> with the script gone.
  • An importSource disappears. A web-module component renders as its bare tag name, which no browser knows what to do with.
  • A component child is rendered. _add_vdom_to_etree calls component_to_vdom() on any child with a .render attribute, and component_to_vdom() recurses, so nested components come out as HTML — verified two levels down, html.section(mid()) becomes <section><div><p>deep</p></div></section>. The limit is hooks, not depth.

That list is why this function cannot render your average app. It has no Layout, so there is no hook stack: use_state, use_ref, use_effect, use_location all raise RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout? Only hook-free components and plain html.* elements convert. This is the same path ReactPy(prepend_body=...) uses, which is why that argument takes an element and not a stateful component.

Passing an uncalled component raises AttributeError

reactpy_to_string(my_component) fails with AttributeError: 'function' object has no attribute 'render' — the decorator has not run, so there is nothing to render. Call it: reactpy_to_string(my_component()).

docs.title: Attribute names are lowercased
docs.text:
This is the sharpest edge on the page, and it is silent. On the way out, every attribute name goes through .lower() (utils.py, _react_attribute_to_html), with the exception of data-* and aria-*, which are left exactly as you wrote them:

app.py Run 
# HTML in, ReactPy out: camelCase comes back.
print(string_to_reactpy('<label for="email">Email</label>'))
# {'attributes': {'htmlFor': 'email'}, 'children': ['Email'], 'tagName': 'label'}

# ReactPy out: every attribute name is lowercased on the way out.
print(reactpy_to_string(html.label({"htmlFor": "email"}, "Email")))
# <label htmlfor="email">Email</label>

print(reactpy_to_string(html.label({"for": "email"}, "Email")))
# <label for="email">Email</label>

print(reactpy_to_string(html.div({"className": "card"}, "x")))
# <div classname="card">x</div>

# TODO

htmlFor becomes htmlfor and className becomes classname — neither of which is a real HTML attribute, so the browser ignores both. The label stops labelling and the class stops styling, with no error anywhere.

Write the HTML name when the string is the destination. {"for": "email"} and {"class": "card"} produce correct markup; {"htmlFor": ...} and {"className": ...} do not. There is no single spelling that satisfies both this and live rendering — see Common Props for why className is what the browser-side path wants.

The one attribute ReactPy does translate is style, which it flattens from a dict into a key:value; string and kebab-cases on the way:

reactpy_to_string(html.div({"style": {"fontSize": "20px", "zIndex": 3}}, "s"))
# <div style="font-size:20px;z-index:3">s</div>

Note what did not happen to the 3: no unit is inferred. z-index:3 is fine because it takes no unit, but font-size:30 would be invalid CSS where the browser-side renderer would have applied it as 30px. Always put the unit in the string.

Some boolean attributes obey lxml, not HTML

ReactPy renders the string through lxml, which carries its own list of known boolean attributes. For a name on that list the value is discarded and only presence matters — so False still emits the attribute:

app.py Run 
# lxml knows a fixed list of boolean attributes. For those, the value is
# dropped and presence is all that survives -- False included.
print(reactpy_to_string(html.input({"type": "checkbox", "checked": False})))
# <input type="checkbox" checked>

# For everything else the value is str()-ed, so False leaks into the page.
print(reactpy_to_string(html.div({"hidden": False}, "still hidden")))
# <div hidden="False">still hidden</div>

# TODO

checked renders as <input type="checkbox" checked> even though you said False. Names outside that list get str(value) instead, which leaks the word False into your markup as in <div hidden="False">. Which names fall in which group depends on your lxml build, so test the attribute you care about. The safe form for a server-rendered string is to omit the key entirely rather than set it to False.

docs.title: HTML to VDOM: string_to_reactpy()
docs.text:
app.py Run 
model = string_to_reactpy('<div class="card"><h1>My Todo List</h1></div>')

print(model["tagName"])  # div
print(model["attributes"])  # {'className': 'card'}
print(model["children"])  # [{'tagName': 'h1', 'children': ['My Todo List']}]

# Nested children are full models too, which is easiest to see with pprint:
# pprint(model, sort_dicts=False)
# {'children': [{'children': ['My Todo List'], 'tagName': 'h1'}],
#  'attributes': {'className': 'card'},
#  'tagName': 'div'}

# TODO

Parsing is done by lxml.html, then each node is rebuilt through the normal html.* constructors (utils.py, _etree_to_vdom), which means what comes back is a genuine VdomDict you can render, patch, and send over the socket.

docs.title: What parsing renames and rewrites
docs.text:
The parser does not give you a mirror of the input. It runs a table of renames and a handful of node rewrites (transforms.py, attributes_to_reactjs and RequiredTransforms):

In the HTML In the VDOM Why class="card" {"className": "card"} React-style prop name for="email" {"htmlFor": "email"} React-style prop name checked {"defaultChecked": ...} Controlled-vs-uncontrolled accept-charset {"acceptCharset": ...} React-style prop name http-equiv {"httpEquiv": ...} React-style prop name style="font-size:20px" {"style": {"fontSize": "20px"}} Style strings become dicts <input value="ab"> {"defaultValue": "ab"} A value prop makes an input controlled <textarea>hi</textarea> {"defaultValue": "hi"}, no children Same reason <option selected> defaultValue on the parent <select> React puts the selection on the parent <a href="/x"> an onClick handler with prevent_default Keeps a client router in charge <div id="uniq"> {"id": "uniq", "key": "uniq"} A key is inferred from id, then name

The last two deserve a second look, because they change behaviour rather than spelling.

Every anchor gets a click handler. By default intercept_links=True installs a preventDefault-only onClick on every <a> (transforms.py, intercept_link_clicks). The link looks dead: clicking it does nothing, because ReactPy has no router to hand the navigation to. Pass intercept_links=False to keep real links.

An id becomes a key. infer_key_from_attributes copies id — or name on <input>, <select>, <textarea> — into attributes["key"]. That is usually what you want, since a stable id is a stable identity, but it also means two elements parsed with the same id collide: the layout rejects them with ValueError: Duplicate keys [...].

Whitespace you did not ask for

lxml is configured to drop comments, processing instructions, and blank text — but remove_blank_text only removes whitespace that is purely formatting. The newline and indentation between tags in a pretty-printed document survive as text children:

string_to_reactpy("<ul>
  <li>a</li>
  <li>b</li>
</ul>")["children"]
# [{'tagName': 'li', 'children': ['a']}, '
  ', {'tagName': 'li', 'children': ['b']}, '
']

Those strings render as visible whitespace. If you parse an indented template literal, expect stray spaces and newlines in the layout — write the markup flat, or strip the text children in a transform.

docs.title: Errors, and when to turn strictness off
docs.text:
string_to_reactpy() raises in four distinct ways:

string_to_reactpy(12)          # TypeError: Expected html to be a string, not int
string_to_reactpy("no tags here")  # ValueError: Expected html string to contain HTML tags, but no tags were found.
string_to_reactpy("<div <p>x</p>")  # HTMLParseError (a subclass of lxml.LxmlSyntaxError)
string_to_reactpy("<div <p>x</p>", strict=False)  # parses; '<p' becomes an attribute name

strict=True reaches lxml as recover=False, so a document lxml refuses to parse cleanly becomes an HTMLParseError whose message tells you to turn strictness off. Do that deliberately: recovery invents attribute names out of the malformed text rather than complaining, so you trade a loud failure for a quietly wrong model.

A few things you might expect strict to catch, and it does not:

  • Unclosed or mismatched tags — <div><span>x</div> parses fine and the span is closed for you.
  • Orphan fragments — <td>orphan</td> and <li>x</li> parse into bare td/li models, which then render somewhere HTML forbids them.
  • Unknown entities — ¬real; becomes the literal text ¬real;.

docs.title: Wrapping, empty input, and multiple roots
docs.text:
lxml wants a single well-formed root, so it adds one for you:

  • <p>a</p><p>b</p> comes back wrapped in a div.
  • <body>hi</body> comes back as a span, not a body — lxml.html's document scaffolding leaks through.
  • <meta http-equiv="refresh"> is likewise pulled into an html/head pair.
  • Empty or whitespace-only input returns {"tagName": ""} — a fragment, not an error.

Do not write code that indexes children by position on parsed input; the wrapper is lxml's decision, not yours.

docs.title: Transforming every node: the *transforms argument
docs.text:
string_to_reactpy() takes any number of one-argument callables and applies each to every node after parsing (utils.py, _etree_to_vdom). This is the supported way to post-process the model rather than editing it after the fact:

def add_card_class(vdom):
    if vdom["tagName"] == "div":
        vdom.setdefault("attributes", {})["className"] = "card"
    return vdom


string_to_reactpy("<div>x</div>", add_card_class)
# {'tagName': 'div', 'attributes': {'className': 'card'}, 'children': ['x']}

Mutate and return the same dictionary; the return value replaces the node, assigned unconditionally (utils.py, _etree_to_vdom). A transform that returns None deletes the node — for a child it leaves None in children, for the root it makes string_to_reactpy() itself return None. Always return the model.

Transforms run after the built-in ones, so a style value is already a dict by the time yours sees it, and an <a> already has its onClick. Use this hook to strip attributes you do not trust from third-party HTML — but note that removing an attribute is not the same as making untrusted HTML safe:

Never parse untrusted HTML without filtering

string_to_reactpy() does not sanitize. An <img src=x onerror="alert(1)"> comes back with the payload in inlineJavaScript, not in attributes — verified: {'attributes': {'src': 'x'}, 'inlineJavaScript': {'onError': 'alert(1)'}, 'tagName': 'img'} — and that is the more dangerous of the two outcomes: the client turns each inlineJavaScript entry into an event-handler prop whose body is eval(...) (static/index.js, the inline-JavaScript wrapper), so the code executes when the event fires. An <img src=x> fails to load, onError fires, and the payload runs. An <script> comes back as a script element with its content intact. ReactPy's own html.script refuses event handlers and injects an inferred key, but it does not inspect the JavaScript inside, and neither guard applies to what string_to_reactpy() produces. If the string came from a user, run it through a sanitizer first and pass intercept_links=False only once you have decided links are wanted.

docs.title: Using the result in a component
docs.text:
A parsed model is an ordinary element, so a component can return it directly:

app.py Run 
@component
def card():
    return string_to_reactpy('<div class="card"><b>rendered from a string</b></div>')


print(reactpy_to_string(card()))
# <div class="card"><b>rendered from a string</b></div>

# TODO

That is exactly how ReactPy builds its own document head: ReactPy(pyscript_setup=True) parses a block of PyScript markup with string_to_reactpy() and splices it into html_head (executors/asgi/standalone.py).

Do not parse inside the render body

The parse is a full lxml document build, and it runs on the server on every render. Parse once at module level and return the stored model, or memoize it with use_memo. Re-parsing per render is pure waste, and if you put the model in state you also hand yourself the mutation hazard covered in VDOM Mutations.

docs.title: Choosing a direction
docs.text:
Reach for these when the HTML exists somewhere other than in your Python code:

  • string_to_reactpy() when markup arrives from a CMS, a markdown renderer, an email body, or a template you do not control. It is also the shortest path to pasting a snippet of HTML from a design mock into a component.
  • reactpy_to_string() when you must hand ReactPy's output to something that is not the ReactPy client: server-rendered <head> content, an <noscript> fallback, an email or PDF generator, a test assertion.

If the markup is yours to write, write html.* calls. The constructors validate at the call site, keep their arguments JSON-serializable, and support handlers — none of which the string path gives you.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• reactpy_to_string() takes a VdomDict or a called component and returns HTML text; it drops event handlers, inline JavaScript, and import sources, and can only render components that use no hooks.
  • It lowercases every attribute name except data-* and aria-*, so write "class" and "for" when the string is the destination.
  • string_to_reactpy() parses HTML into a real VdomDict, renaming to React-style prop names, converting style strings to dicts, and moving value/<textarea> content to defaultValue.
  • It intercepts link clicks and infers a key from id unless you tell it not to.
  • strict=False turns a loud HTMLParseError into a guessed model; lxml never complained about unclosed tags anyway.
  • Neither function is the wire format — that is Protocol Structure.

docs.text:

  • Creating VDOM Event Handlers — the eventHandlers slot these functions ignore

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
If you want to build a new app or website with React, we recommend starting with a standalone executor.

If your app has constraints not well-served by existing web frameworks, you prefer to build your own framework, or you just want to learn the basics of a React app, you can use ReactPy in standalone mode.

docs.title: Using ReactPy for full-stack
docs.text:
ReactPy is a component library that helps you build a full-stack web application. For convenience, ReactPy is also bundled with several different standalone executors.

These standalone executors are the easiest way to get started with ReactPy, as they require no additional setup or configuration.

Note

Standalone ReactPy requires a server

In order to serve the initial HTML page, you will need to run a server. The ASGI examples below use Uvicorn, but you can use any ASGI server.

Executors on this page can either support client-side rendering (CSR) or server-side rendering (SSR).

docs.title: Running via ASGI SSR
docs.text:
ReactPy can run in server-side standalone mode, where both page loading and component rendering occurs on an ASGI server.

This executor is the most commonly used, as it provides maximum extensibility.

First, install ReactPy and your preferred ASGI webserver.

Terminal

pip install reactpy[asgi] uvicorn[standard]

Next, create a new file called main.py containing the ASGI application:

main.py 
from reactpy import component, html
from reactpy.executors.asgi import ReactPy


@component
def hello_world():
    return html.div("Hello World")


my_app = ReactPy(hello_world)

Finally, use your webserver of choice to start ReactPy:

Terminal

uvicorn main:my_app

docs.title: Running via ASGI CSR
docs.text:
ReactPy can run in client-side standalone mode, where the initial page is served using the ASGI protocol. This is configuration allows direct execution of Javascript, but requires special considerations since all ReactPy component code is run on the browser via WebAssembly.

First, install ReactPy and your preferred ASGI webserver.

Terminal

pip install reactpy[asgi] uvicorn[standard]

Next, create a new file called main.py containing the ASGI application, and a root.py file containing the root component:

main.pyroot.py 
from pathlib import Path

from reactpy.executors.asgi import ReactPyCsr

my_app = ReactPyCsr(Path(__file__).parent / "root.py", initial="Loading...")

from reactpy import component, html


@component
def root():
    return html.div("Hello World")

Finally, use your webserver of choice to start ReactPy:

Terminal

uvicorn main:my_app

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A ReactPy backend is the piece that owns the HTTP routes, serves the client bundle, accepts the websocket, and drives a Layout against it. ReactPy and ReactPyMiddleware are two backends. This page is about writing the third: what the framework actually does for you, which parts you have to reproduce, and where the quiet traps are. It is also the fastest way to understand the request lifecycle, even if you never ship a custom backend.

You will learn

  • The four jobs a backend performs, in the order a browser makes them necessary
  • The three ASGI routes ReactPy needs, and the exact shapes of the messages on each
  • How to run a Layout by hand with serve_layout()
  • Why Connection is yours to construct, and what carrier means

docs.title: What a backend owes you
docs.text:
Strip away the executors and there are exactly four responsibilities. Everything else — hot reloading, config validation, HTML assembly — is convenience on top.

  1. Serve the client bundle over HTTP, so the page can import it.
  2. Serve web modules over HTTP, so the client can import any importSource you emitted.
  3. Return a document containing a mount element and a mountReactPy(...) call.
  4. Accept a websocket and run one Layout against it, pumping messages in both directions.

The whole of the protocol is two message types. A rendered update goes down as {"type": "layout-update", "path": ..., "model": ...}; an event comes up as {"type": "layout-event", "target": ..., "data": [...]}. Protocol Structure documents them in full — this page is about plumbing, not the schema.

docs.title: The job, in one file
docs.text:
This is a complete, working backend: no framework, no executor. It was run, and the counter incremented in a real browser.

main.py Run 
"""A ReactPy backend with no framework: routing, static files, and Layout."""

import asyncio
from pathlib import Path

import orjson
from asgi_tools import ResponseHTML
from servestatic import ServeStaticASGI

import reactpy
from reactpy import component, html, use_state
from reactpy.config import REACTPY_WEB_MODULES_DIR
from reactpy.core.hooks import ConnectionContext
from reactpy.core.layout import Layout
from reactpy.core.serve import serve_layout
from reactpy.types import Connection, Location

PATH_PREFIX = "/reactpy/"
STATIC_PATH = f"{PATH_PREFIX}static/"
MODULES_PATH = f"{PATH_PREFIX}modules/"

STATIC_DIR = Path(reactpy.__file__).parent / "static"


@component
def counter():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)
    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"Count: {count}"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_count(count + 1)}, "Increment"),
    )


def index_html() -> str:
    mount = (
        "mountReactPy({mountElement: document.getElementById('app'),"
        "  pathPrefix:'" + PATH_PREFIX + "', componentPath:'counter/'});"
    )
    return (
        "<!doctype html><html><head><meta charset='utf-8'><title>Custom backend</title>"
        "<script type='module'>"
        f"import {{ mountReactPy }} from '{STATIC_PATH}index.js';"
        + mount
        + "</script></head><body><div id='app'>Loading...</div></body></html>"
    )


class Backend:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.components = {"counter": counter}
        self.static_app = ServeStaticASGI(
            self.not_found, root=STATIC_DIR, prefix=STATIC_PATH
        )
        self.modules_app = ServeStaticASGI(
            self.not_found, root=REACTPY_WEB_MODULES_DIR.current, prefix=MODULES_PATH
        )

    async def not_found(self, scope, receive, send) -> None:
        await ResponseHTML("Resource not found on this server.", status_code=404)(
            scope, receive, send
        )

    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send) -> None:
        path = scope["path"]
        if scope["type"] == "http" and path.startswith(STATIC_PATH):
            return await self.static_app(scope, receive, send)
        if scope["type"] == "http" and path.startswith(MODULES_PATH):
            return await self.modules_app(scope, receive, send)
        if scope["type"] == "http" and path == "/":
            return await ResponseHTML(index_html())(scope, receive, send)
        if scope["type"] == "websocket" and path.startswith(PATH_PREFIX):
            return await self.serve_component(scope, receive, send)
        return await self.not_found(scope, receive, send)

    async def serve_component(self, scope, receive, send) -> None:
        name = scope["path"][len(PATH_PREFIX) :].strip("/")
        if name not in self.components:
            raise RuntimeError(f"Attempting to use an unregistered root {name}.")

        await send({"type": "websocket.accept"})
        queue: asyncio.Queue = asyncio.Queue(1000)

        async def pump() -> None:
            while True:
                event = await receive()
                if event["type"] == "websocket.disconnect":
                    return
                if event["type"] == "websocket.connect":
                    continue
                await queue.put(orjson.loads(event["text"]))

        async def recv():
            return await queue.get()

        async def send_model(message):
            await send(
                {"type": "websocket.send", "text": orjson.dumps(message).decode()}
            )

        task = asyncio.create_task(pump())
        connection = Connection(
            scope=scope,
            location=Location(path="/", query_string=""),
            carrier=None,
        )
        try:
            await serve_layout(
                Layout(ConnectionContext(self.components[name](), value=connection)),
                send_model,
                recv,
            )
        finally:
            task.cancel()


app = Backend()

# TODO

Run it with anything that speaks ASGI:

uvicorn main:app --port 8000

Read it top to bottom and the four jobs map onto four spots: static_app and modules_app are jobs 1 and 2, index_html() is job 3, and serve_component() is job 4. The rest is __call__ dispatching on scope["type"].

docs.title: The routes
docs.text:
Route Serves Supplied by {path_prefix}static/ index.js and its chunks reactpy/static/ inside the wheel {path_prefix}modules/ authored JavaScript modules config.REACTPY_WEB_MODULES_DIR {path_prefix}<name>/ (websocket) the layout for <name> your components mapping

The trailing slash on the websocket path is not decoration. The stock executors match ^{path_prefix}(?P<dotted_path>[a-zA-Z0-9_.]+)/$, and the client builds that URL by concatenating pathPrefix and componentPath. A custom backend can match anything — but then componentPath has to agree with it, and pathPrefix must start and end with /. See The URL is built by concatenation for why a missing slash fails loudly in development and silently in production.

docs.title: Serving the bundle
docs.text:
Two directories, both plain static files:

import reactpy
from pathlib import Path

from servestatic import ServeStaticASGI

from reactpy.config import REACTPY_WEB_MODULES_DIR

static_app = ServeStaticASGI(
    not_found, root=Path(reactpy.__file__).parent / "static", prefix="/reactpy/static/"
)
modules_app = ServeStaticASGI(
    not_found, root=REACTPY_WEB_MODULES_DIR.current, prefix="/reactpy/modules/"
)

servestatic is what the executors use, and it is a normal ASGI app — swap in your own static handler if you have one. Two details matter more than the choice of library.

Resolve REACTPY_WEB_MODULES_DIR.current at request time or shortly after, never at import time. It is an Option, and the executors repoint it. Reading it too early hands you a directory that later ceases to be the live one.

The <script type="module"> must be a module. The bundle uses static import for its two sibling chunks, so an ordinary <script> fails before any of your code runs, usually with a bare SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module in the console.

Serve the bundle from your own path at your peril

The client imports its chunks by a path derived from where index.js was loaded. Serve it under a prefix that does not also serve static/, and the chunk requests 404 while index.js itself loaded fine — which reads as a partial success and is easy to misdiagnose. Keep static/ a child of your mount prefix, exactly as the executors do.

docs.title: Driving a layout
docs.text:
This is the part that is genuinely yours. Everything else is file serving.

The two primitives are Layout (core/layout.py) and serve_layout (core/serve.py). The latter is about twenty lines: it opens the layout, then runs one loop sending await layout.render() out and one loop calling await layout.deliver(event) on each received message — with the deliver not awaited to completion, so a slow handler never blocks the next event.

You supply send and recv coroutines:

async def send_model(message):
    await send({"type": "websocket.send", "text": orjson.dumps(message).decode()})


async def recv():
    return await queue.get()

Four things go wrong here, and all four are worth knowing before you hit them.

docs.title: 1. The first receive() is websocket.connect
docs.text:
await send({"type": "websocket.accept"}) completes the handshake, but the websocket.connect event is still sitting in the incoming stream. A pump loop that treats every event as a message will orjson.loads() a dict with no text key and die, typically with TypeError or KeyError: 'text', right at connection time. Skip it:

async def pump():
    while True:
        event = await receive()
        if event["type"] == "websocket.disconnect":
            return
        if event["type"] == "websocket.connect":
            continue
        await queue.put(orjson.loads(event["text"]))

This is the single most common way a hand-written backend fails, because everything looks right until the client connects: the page serves, the bundle loads, and the socket opens and closes immediately. The console shows [ReactPy] Disconnected! followed by an endless reconnect loop.

docs.title: 2. recv() must not return None
docs.text: If your recv returns None — which is what an unguarded await receive() does on disconnect — serve_layout calls layout.deliver(None) and raises inside a task group, surfacing as an ExceptionGroup that names neither your code nor the cause. Return a valid message or raise; never None.

docs.title: 3. ResponseWebSocket has no send_text, and receive() needs raw=True
docs.text:
asgi_tools.ResponseWebSocket is what the built-in executors use — ReactPyWebsocket subclasses it — and it works fine as a backend's socket. Two API details differ from raw ASGI, and getting either wrong fails inside an anyio task group with an ExceptionGroup that names neither your code nor the cause:

async with ResponseWebSocket(scope=scope, receive=receive, send=send) as ws:

    async def pump():
        while True:
            event = await ws.receive(raw=True)  # the ASGI dict, not the payload
            if event["type"] == "websocket.disconnect":
                return
            if event["type"] != "websocket.receive":
                continue
            await queue.put(orjson.loads(event["text"]))

    async def send_model(message):
        await ws.send(orjson.dumps(message).decode())  # not send_text(...)
  • There is no send_text. On asgi_tools.response.ResponseWebSocket the methods are send(msg) — which wraps a str as {"type": "websocket.send", "text": ...} and bytes as "bytes": ... — plus send_json(data). Send text frames. The stock send_json emits {"type": "websocket.send", "bytes": json_dumps(data)}, i.e. a binary frame, and that is precisely why the executors do not use it: executors/asgi/middleware.py, ReactPyWebsocket.send_json overrides it to self._send({"type": "websocket.send", "text": orjson.dumps(data).decode()}). The client never sets socket.binaryType (static/index.js), so a binary frame arrives as a Blob, and JSON.parse(blob) throws SyntaxError: ... "[object Blob]" is not valid JSON — verified in headless Chrome. Reusing a stock asgi_tools websocket object instead of overriding send_json therefore produces a socket that connects, accepts, and then parses nothing.
  • receive() returns the payload by default, not the ASGI event. Without raw=True you get a str, and event["type"] then raises TypeError: string indices must be integers. Pass raw=True.
  • Under async with, the handshake is already done — do not send websocket.accept yourself. That is why the websocket.connect skip above tests for != "websocket.receive" rather than naming connect.

Raw send/receive from the ASGI callable, as the main example does, is the interface guaranteed to be present on any host; that is the reason it is the default here.

docs.title: 4. One layout per connection, and never share one
docs.text:
A Layout owns the hook state for a single client. Creating it before the request, or caching it by component name, means every browser tab shares one set of use_state values — one user's click changes another's screen. Build the Layout inside the connection handler, as above, and let it be garbage-collected with the socket.

The mirror-image bug is at the component level: a module-level element rendered by every layout is shared too, and mutation by one client leaks to all of them. That is covered in VDOM Mutations.

docs.title: Connection and carrier
docs.text:
Wrap the component in ConnectionContext so the connection hooks work:

from reactpy.core.hooks import ConnectionContext
from reactpy.types import Connection, Location

connection = Connection(
    scope=scope,
    location=Location(path="/", query_string=""),
    carrier=None,
)
layout = Layout(ConnectionContext(my_component(), value=connection))

Without that wrapper, use_connection(), use_location(), and use_scope() all raise RuntimeError: No backend established a connection. — even inside a perfectly healthy socket.

Connection is a three-field dataclass, and as the backend author you decide what goes in it:

  • scope — pass the websocket scope through verbatim. use_scope() returns it, and users expect headers and query strings to be there.
  • location — the stock ASGI executors do not use scope["path"]. The browser reports where it is, and the executor parses it out of the websocket query string: ?path=%2Fdocs%2F&qs=a%3D1 becomes Location(path="/docs/", query_string="a=1"). If you hard-code path="/", every use_location() on your app reports the root regardless of the URL in the address bar. Parse it the same way if your app routes on it.
  • carrier — whatever mediates the connection. Nothing in ReactPy reads it; the executors put their websocket object there so your components can reach it. Put your own in, and document what it is, because User Connection tells people to check its type rather than assume. None is fine if nothing needs it.

Connection is a read-only view by design

There is no deliver, no send, no close on it. Components talk to the client through state, effects, and event handlers — not by pushing messages. Your backend is the only code allowed to touch the socket, precisely because letting a component write to the wire bypasses the protocol and desynchronizes the client. If you find yourself wanting a push channel, read Communicating Data Between Server and Client first.

docs.title: When to write one
docs.text:
Almost never, and it is worth naming the honest cases:

  • Embedding ReactPy in an ASGI app you cannot wrap. ReactPyMiddleware already covers this — it takes your existing app as its first argument. Reach for a custom backend only when the middleware's routing gets in your way, since it owns {path_prefix}* and nothing else.
  • A non-ASGI host. ReactPy's core is host-agnostic: Layout and serve_layout need only two coroutines, so a socket server on another loop is a routing problem, not a rewrite. This is the case the design genuinely supports.
  • Owning the document. If you generate HTML yourself and want ReactPy components inside it, you need the mount markup and the import map. You usually want server_side_component_html for that rather than a new backend — see Serving a component from your own route.
  • Understanding it. Writing the backend once is the clearest way to learn where the boundary between layout and transport is. It is a good exercise even when the result is deleted.

What it does not buy you: performance. serve_layout in your own code is the same loop. And you take on the pieces the executors handle quietly — config validation, the import-map injection, pyscript_setup, static caching, reconnect options, and the error paths in the four sections above.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• A backend serves the bundle, serves web modules, returns a mount document, and runs one Layout per websocket.
  • The message shapes are fixed: layout-update down, layout-event up.
  • Skip the websocket.connect event in your pump; it is the most common cause of an instantly-dying socket.
  • Speak raw ASGI on the socket; framework websocket wrappers do not have the methods serve_layout needs.
  • Build the Layout per connection, and wrap the component in ConnectionContext or the connection hooks raise.
  • You populate Connection; the stock executors parse location from the query string, not the scope path.
  • Components get a read-only view of the connection by design — that is the protocol's integrity, not an omission.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Every element you write in ReactPy is a function call that returns a dictionary. html.div(...) is not a keyword, a macro, or a parser — it is an attribute lookup that manufactures a constructor on first use, and a __call__ that assembles the model. Knowing how that works explains why there is no allow-list to fight, why html.del_ means <del>, and where the handful of hard errors come from.

You will learn

  • How html turns an attribute name into a tag name
  • The rule that decides whether your first argument is attributes or a child
  • Which elements reject children, and why html.script is stricter still
  • How to build fragments, SVG, and tag names that are not valid Python identifiers

docs.title: html manufactures tags on demand
docs.text:
html is an instance of HtmlConstructor with a single __getattr__ (_html.py). Ask it for anything and you get a Vdom constructor back, cached by name:

app.py Run 
# The tag name is whatever you ask for -- there is no allow-list to consult.
print(html.div({"id": "greeting"}, "Hello"))
# {'tagName': 'div', 'attributes': {'id': 'greeting'}, 'children': ['Hello']}

print(html.definitely_not_a_real_tag("still renders"))
# {'tagName': 'definitely-not-a-real-tag', 'children': ['still renders']}

# TODO

There is no allow-list. ReactPy does not know or care whether <definitely-not-a-real-tag> exists; the string travels to the browser and the browser decides. The names spelled out on HtmlConstructor exist only so your editor can autocomplete them — the comment in the source says as much. Two practical consequences:

  • A misspelled tag renders as an unknown element with your text inside it, silently. Nothing in ReactPy will tell you that html.hdeader is wrong.
  • Custom elements work with no ceremony: html.my_widget(...) produces {"tagName": "my-widget"} and the browser hands it to whatever registered that name.

docs.title: The underscore rules
docs.text:
__getattr__ applies exactly two transformations — value.rstrip("_").replace("_", "-") — which is how you write names Python will not let you spell:

app.py Run 
# Underscores become dashes, and a trailing underscore is stripped -- the name
# is translated, not looked up.
print(html.del_("removed")["tagName"])  # del
print(html.data_table()["tagName"])  # data-table
print(html.my_widget()["tagName"])  # my-widget

# The same constructor comes back every time, so identity checks are cheap.
print(html.my_widget is html.my_widget)  # True

# TODO

Read the rules literally, because they are applied blindly:

You write Tag name Rule html.del_ del trailing _ stripped (a keyword) html.data_table data-table every _ becomes - html.my_widget my-widget same html.h1 h1 no underscore, nothing changes html._private -private leading underscore is not special html.a__b a--b doubles are not collapsed

Casing is passed through untouched, so html.myWidget gives you myWidget. Because translation happens before the cache lookup, html.data_table is html.data_table holds — but two spellings that translate to the same tag are the same object, and two that do not are different elements.

If a name cannot be written as an attribute at all — a leading digit, or one you are building from a variable — construct it directly:

from reactpy import Vdom

tag = Vdom("2fa-code")
tag("123456")  # {'tagName': '2fa-code', 'children': ['123456']}

Vdom(tag_name, /, allow_children=True, custom_constructor=None, import_source=None) is the same class every html.* name is built from, so you get identical behaviour. It is exported from the package root. Reach for it only for generated or unspellable names; anything else should go through html so it reads consistently.

html is not a namespace of plain functions

html.div is a Vdom object, not a function — html.div("x") works because Vdom.__call__ is the constructor. So html.div.__name__ is the tag name rather than a qualified name, and any name you ask for is fair game: html.allow_children("x") returns a perfectly valid {"tagName": "allow-children"} element rather than tripping over the Vdom attribute of the same name.

docs.title: The two call shapes
docs.text:
Vdom.__call__ accepts either children only, or an attribute dictionary followed by children (core/vdom.py, Vdom.__call__):

app.py Run 
# Two call shapes: children only, or an attribute dict first.
print(html.button("Click Me"))
# {'tagName': 'button', 'children': ['Click Me']}

print(html.button({"id": "save", "disabled": True}, "Save"))
# {'tagName': 'button', 'attributes': {'id': 'save', 'disabled': True}, 'children': ['Save']}

# Only an *exact* dict counts as attributes -- a dict subclass is a child.
print(html.div(VdomDict(tagName="span")))
# {'tagName': 'div', 'children': [{'tagName': 'span'}]}

# TODO

The discriminator is exact-type, not isinstance: type(values[0]) is dict (core/vdom.py, separate_attributes_and_children). Two consequences that bite:

  • A VdomDict — which is a dict subclass — in first position is treated as a child, which is what you want when nesting models you built earlier.
  • Any other dict subclass in first position is also a child, so a custom mapping you meant as attributes becomes a rendered object instead. Pass a plain dict literal for attributes.

A dict in any later position is always a child. There is one slot for attributes and it is the first.

docs.title: Attribute values are forwarded verbatim
docs.text:
ReactPy renames nothing. className, class, htmlFor, and for all reach the DOM as whichever string you typed, and unknown names like data-* and aria-* pass straight through. Nothing validates names against a list, so a typo is a silent no-op — {"class_name": "card"} renders <div class_name="card">, an attribute nobody reads.

There are no exceptions to this rule on the live path. class_name is not a thing. See Common Props for the full picture, including the one case where numeric style values behave differently between executors.

Attributes must be JSON-serializable, but you may not be told

Everything in the attribute dict is JSON-encoded on its way to the browser. ReactPy checks that with json.dumps only when REACTPY_CHECK_JSON_ATTRS is on — and that option's parent is REACTPY_DEBUG, so turning debug on turns this on too:

from reactpy import config

config.REACTPY_DEBUG.current = True

With the check on, html.div({"data": object()}) raises TypeError: Object of type object is not JSON serializable at the tag call, pointing at your line. With it off, the model is accepted and the failure surfaces much later, inside the websocket send, as an orjson error in a server log. If a page renders nothing and the browser console is empty, this is why.

docs.title: Fragments
docs.text:
html.fragment(...) and the shorter html(...) build a child list with no element of its own — tagName is the empty string, and the client renders it as nothing:

app.py Run 
# Fragments carry no tag of their own: tagName is the empty string.
print(html.fragment(html.b("bold"), html.i("italic")))
# {'tagName': '', 'children': [{'tagName': 'b', ...}, {'tagName': 'i', ...}]}

# html(...) is html itself: HtmlConstructor.__call__ is the fragment call.
print(html(html.b("bold"))["tagName"])  # ''
print(html()["tagName"])  # '' -- an empty fragment

# A fragment may carry a key -- and nothing else.
print(html.fragment({"key": "row-1"}, html.b("x"))["attributes"])  # {'key': 'row-1'}

try:
    html.fragment({"className": "wrap"}, html.b("x"))
except TypeError as error:
    print(error)  # Fragments cannot have attributes besides 'key'

# TODO

A fragment accepts key and nothing else: a className, a style, or an event handler all raise TypeError: Fragments cannot have attributes besides 'key'. There is no node to put them on, so ReactPy refuses rather than dropping them quietly.

Use a fragment when a component must return siblings and a wrapper <div> would break the layout or the CSS. When the children are already in a list, pass the list — you do not need a fragment for that, though you do need keys, covered in Rendering Lists.

docs.title: Void elements
docs.text:
html.br("x") is a hard error, not a warning that scrolls past:

app.py Run 
# Void elements reject children -- loudly, at the call site.
try:
    html.br("oops")
except TypeError as error:
    print(error)  # 'br' nodes cannot have children.

print(html.br())  # {'tagName': 'br'}

# script is stricter still: one string child, no handlers, an inferred key.
print(html.script("var answered = 42;"))
# {'tagName': 'script', 'children': ['var answered = 42;'],
#  'attributes': {'key': 'var answered = 42;'}}

print(html.script({"src": "/chart.js"}))
# {'tagName': 'script', 'attributes': {'src': '/chart.js', 'key': '/chart.js'}}

try:
    html.script({"onLoad": lambda event: None}, "var x = 1;")
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)  # 'script' elements do not support event handlers

# TODO

The rejecting set is NO_CHILDREN_ALLOWED_HTML_BODY (_html.py): area, base, br, col, command, embed, hr, img, input, iframe, keygen, link, meta, param, portal, source, track, wbr. The check happens after the model is built, so the message names the tag rather than your mistake — read the name in the error.

iframe is on that list, which surprises people who put fallback content inside one. ReactPy will not let you, and the browser-side renderer would not have shown it anyway.

docs.title: html.script is its own thing
docs.text:
html.script uses a custom constructor (_html.py, _script) with three rules and a side effect:

  • At most one child, and it must be a str — ValueError: 'script' nodes may have, at most, one child. and The child of a 'script' must be a string.
  • No event handlers at all — ValueError: 'script' elements do not support event handlers. Attach behaviour to a sibling element instead, or use the inline-JavaScript handler form on a normal tag (Creating VDOM Event Handlers).
  • A key is injected from the script's content, or from its src if it has no content. Upstream documents the purpose as allowing the script "to be run multiple times if its key changes", browser permitting. Pass your own key to control re-execution yourself.

Scripts are an injection surface

The child string reaches the browser as JavaScript. Never interpolate untrusted text into it — ReactPy's own docstring on _script says so, and there is no escaping step to save you. Build the string from your own constants, or pass a src you control.

docs.title: SVG is a second constructor
docs.text:
html.svg is a separate SvgConstructor, so SVG element names live in their own namespace and cannot collide with HTML names. Children come off it:

app.py Run 
# SVG lives on a second constructor, so html.svg.circle() does not collide
# with a hypothetical html.circle().
print(
    html.svg(
        {"width": "100", "height": "100", "viewBox": "0 0 100 100"},
        html.svg.circle({"cx": "50", "cy": "50", "r": "40", "fill": "tomato"}),
    )
)
# {'tagName': 'svg', 'attributes': {...},
#  'children': [{'tagName': 'circle', 'attributes': {...}}]}

# TODO

It has its own void set (NO_CHILDREN_ALLOWED_SVG), and that set is broader and less intuitive than the HTML one — it includes text, tspan, title, desc, path, use, and foreignObject. So the element you most need children inside is exactly the one that rejects them:

html.svg.text("hello")  # TypeError: 'text' nodes cannot have children.

Build those nodes with Vdom, which shares all the behaviour minus the void check:

from reactpy import Vdom

Vdom("text")("hello")  # {'tagName': 'text', 'children': ['hello']}

The bundled client creates every element through document.createElementNS(namespace, ...), picking the namespace from the tag name: "svg" gets http://www.w3.org/2000/svg, "math" gets the MathML URI, everything else the XHTML one. That logic lives in the preact runtime ReactPy bundles into its client chunks, not in ReactPy's own @reactpy/client source — so grep there for createElementNS and you will find nothing. Inside the SVG namespace attribute names are forwarded verbatim rather than lower-cased, so viewBox keeps its capital B — write it that way, since viewbox is a different attribute to the DOM.

docs.title: Choosing children over attributes
docs.text:
html.div({"children": ["a", "b"]}) does not do what it looks like. The dict is attributes, so you get an attribute literally named children and no children at all. Children are always positional arguments after the attribute dict — that is the only way to supply them:

html.div({"id": "list"}, html.li("one"), html.li("two"))   # correct
html.ul({"children": [html.li("one")]})                     # an attribute named children

Children are flattened fully, not one level at a time, for any iterable that is not a string or a mapping — core/vdom.py, _flatten_children recurses, and verified html.div([[["a"], "b"]]) yields children: ['a', 'b']. A list or tuple comprehension therefore works at any nesting depth, and None is skipped by the layout. Two rules from there are worth internalizing now, because both failures are quiet:

  • Elements inside a list need keys, in debug mode, or you get Key not specified for child in list ....
  • A generator in place of a list skips that check entirely, with Did not verify key-path integrity of children in generator .... Pass a list. The deeper hazard — storing an iterator in state — is covered in Rendering Lists.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• html invents a tag for any attribute name; the two rules are trailing _ stripped and every _ turned into -. There is no allow-list and no warning for a typo.
  • The first argument is attributes only if it is exactly a dict; everything else, including VdomDict and dict subclasses, is a child.
  • Attribute names are forwarded verbatim — use the DOM's spelling. Turn on REACTPY_DEBUG to catch un-serializable attribute values at the call site.
  • html.fragment and html() take only a key.
  • The void elements in NO_CHILDREN_ALLOWED_HTML_BODY reject children with a TypeError; html.script additionally allows one string child, forbids handlers, and infers its own key.
  • html.svg.* uses a broader void set that includes text; build those with Vdom.
  • Vdom(tag_name) is the class behind every html.* name — use it for tag names you cannot spell as an attribute, and for the SVG nodes html.svg rejects.
