docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
An event handler in ReactPy is any callable you put in an element's attribute dict. ReactPy inspects the value, not the name, decides what it is, and files it under one of three keys in the model. Most of the surprises on this page come from that one decision point: what counts as a handler, what counts as JavaScript, and what happens to the options you thought you set.

You will learn

  • The three buckets an attribute value lands in, and the rule that sorts them
  • Why preventDefault() sometimes reaches the browser and sometimes does not
  • The difference in arguments between a plain callable and an EventHandler
  • How to set debounce and throttle, and what values are rejected

docs.title: The three buckets
docs.text:
When you call html.button({...}, ...), ReactPy walks the attribute dict once and routes every value by kind — callable first, then string-under-onXxx, then everything else (core/vdom.py, separate_attributes_handlers_and_inline_javascript):

app.py Run 
# ReactPy sorts each value in the attribute dict into one of three buckets
# by *kind*, not by name (core/vdom.py, separate_attributes_handlers_and_inline_javascript).
def save(event):
    print("saved", event["target"]["value"])


element = html.button(
    {
        "id": "save",  # str, not onXxx -> attribute
        "onClick": save,  # callable -> event handler
        "onHover": "console.log('hover')",  # str under onXxx -> inline JS
        "data-row": "3",  # str, not onXxx -> attribute
    },
    "Save",
)

print(sorted(element))
# ['attributes', 'children', 'eventHandlers', 'inlineJavaScript', 'tagName']
print(sorted(element["attributes"]))  # ['data-row', 'id']
print(sorted(element["eventHandlers"]))  # ['onClick']
print(sorted(element["inlineJavaScript"]))  # ['onHover']

# TODO

The rules, exactly:

Value Lands in Note Anything callable eventHandlers under any key name A BaseEventHandler eventHandlers stored as-is, untouched A str under a key matching ^on[A-Z]\w+ inlineJavaScript eval'd in the page A reactpy.types.InlineJavaScript string inlineJavaScript under any key Everything else attributes forwarded verbatim

Three of those rows have consequences worth spelling out.

callable wins over the key name. {"notAnHandler": my_function} registers a real listener whose target ends in :notAnHandler. It will never fire, because no DOM event is named that, but it is registered. Conversely {"onClick": True} is not a handler — a bool is not callable, so it becomes an attribute and no listener exists. Neither mistake produces an error.

None is not a handler. The classic {"onClick": handle_click()} — calling instead of passing — yields {"attributes": {"onClick": None}}. The button renders, looks dead, and logs nothing on either side. If a control "does nothing", check that you passed the function.

A dict is never a handler. The React-style {"function": fn, "preventDefault": True} becomes an ordinary attribute; no listener is attached. With REACTPY_DEBUG on it fails loudly instead — TypeError: Object of type function is not JSON serializable — which is the better outcome. Build handlers with @event or EventHandler, never with a dict.

docs.title: Plain callables, the shape you want most of the time
docs.text:
Pass a function and ReactPy wraps it. The browser sends a list of arguments; a plain callable receives it unpacked positionally (core/events.py, to_event_handler_function), which for a DOM event means one argument:

def handle_click(event):
    print(event["target"]["value"])


html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, "Click me")

Sync functions, coroutine functions, and lambdas all work. Name the parameter whatever you like — the value is positional, and its type is reactpy.types.Event, a dict subclass with attribute access into nested dicts, so event["target"]["value"] and event.target.value are the same read. See Responding to Events for the payload surface and Protocol Structure for what the client actually serializes.

Declare exactly one parameter

The list is unpacked onto your signature, so a handler declaring two required parameters fails at the moment of the click with TypeError: ... missing 1 required positional argument, logged server-side only — the browser stays silent and the button just stops working. Extra context has to be bound in Python, usually with a lambda:

html.button({"onClick": lambda event: delete(item.id)}, "Delete")

docs.title: EventHandler: the pre-built form, and its different argument
docs.text:
EventHandler is what the @event decorator returns, and you can construct it directly. Two things change when you do.

First, ReactPy stores an EventHandler as-is rather than wrapping it, so the same object can serve every element that uses it. It does not follow that they share a target. The target is derived per element: unless the handler carries an explicit target, core/layout.py builds target = f"{key_path}:{event}", and @event leaves target as None. Verified with one @event handler on two buttons: the targets came out /0/0:onClick and /0/1:onClick — one function object, two targets.

Do not try to force the sharing by setting target= yourself. Two elements registered under the same explicit target overwrite each other in the layout's handler table, and the unmount path then tries to del that one key twice — verified, the second deletion raises KeyError from Layout._unmount_model_states.

Second, and this is the trap: an EventHandler receives the list itself, not the unpacked arguments.

app.py Run 
# A plain callable gets the browser's argument list UNPACKED.
def plain_handler(event):
    print(event["target"]["value"])  # the event dict


# An EventHandler gets the LIST ITSELF.
async def list_handler(data):
    print(data[0]["target"]["value"])  # index first


html.button({"onClick": plain_handler}, "a")
html.button({"onClick": EventHandler(list_handler, prevent_default=True)}, "b")

# Converting one to the other without changing the body breaks it:
# TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str

# TODO

The failure when you get it backwards is TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str inside the handler — and the layout swallows it into a server-side Failed to execute event handler line. Nothing appears in the browser console, so the UI merely stops responding. Prefer the plain-callable form unless you specifically need to hand-build a handler; @event gives you the same options with the friendlier argument shape.

docs.title: Setting the four options
docs.text:
Four behaviours run in the browser before an event is sent. They are properties on the handler object, never attributes on the element:

Option Type Effect prevent_default bool calls preventDefault() in the page stop_propagation bool calls stopPropagation() in the page debounce int ms rate-limits server→client value updates on input elements throttle int ms rate-limits client→server outgoing events

There are two ways to set them, and the difference matters.

docs.title: Say it: @event
docs.text:
from reactpy import event


@event(prevent_default=True, stop_propagation=True, debounce=250, throttle=100)
async def handle_key_down(event_data): ...


html.input({"onKeyDown": handle_key_down})

This is explicit and it always works. Reach for it by default.

docs.title: Be discovered: bytecode inspection
docs.text:
ReactPy also reads your function's bytecode looking for three specific statements, so you can write them inline instead (core/_event_inspect.py, inspect_event_handler):

app.py Run 
# Same behaviour, discovered by reading your bytecode instead of a decorator.
def submit(event):
    event.preventDefault()
    event.stopPropagation()
    event.debounce = 250


handler = html.form({"onSubmit": submit}, "x")["eventHandlers"]["onSubmit"]
print(handler.prevent_default)  # True
print(handler.stop_propagation)  # True
print(handler.debounce)  # 250

# TODO

This is a source-parsing hack, not a runtime mechanism, and it has limits you should know before relying on it. Detection requires all of the following:

  • The call is written literally in the handler's own body. event.preventDefault() inside a helper the handler calls is invisible to the inspector — it does not follow calls.
  • The first parameter is the event. The inspector reads co_varnames[0] and matches against it.
  • For debounce, the assigned value must be resolvable at inspect time: an integer literal, a compile-time-folded expression like 100 * 5, a numeric default on a parameter (def h(event, ms=350)), or a numeric closure cell. It cannot resolve a parameter with no default, a module-level global, or an arbitrary expression — all three inspect to None. And it stops scanning at the first assignment it can settle — resolved or not — so with two assignments to event.debounce the result depends on which one the bytecode reaches first. Verified: if event: event.debounce = 200 / else: event.debounce = len(x) inspects to 200, while the same branches written in the other order inspect to None. Write one assignment and the question does not arise; with more than one, check the value you get.

The second rule produces the sharpest bug, so it deserves its own call-out:

Bound methods are not inspected correctly

For def on_submit(self, event), the first parameter is self, so the inspector never matches the event variable and reports prevent_default=False. The handler still fires — it is a perfectly good callable — but your event.preventDefault() call is silently discarded:

app.py Run 
# A bound method is a fine handler -- it fires. What is lost is detection of
# the event.preventDefault() inside it: the bytecode inspector reads the
# *first* parameter as the event, and for a method that is `self`.
class SearchForm:
    def on_submit(self, event):
        event.preventDefault()


plain = html.form({"onSubmit": SearchForm().on_submit})["eventHandlers"]["onSubmit"]
print(plain.prevent_default)  # False -- your call was never seen


# Say it explicitly with @event and it works.
@event(prevent_default=True)
async def submit(event_data):
    print("submitted")


explicit = html.form({"onSubmit": submit})["eventHandlers"]["onSubmit"]
print(explicit.prevent_default)  # True

# TODO

Attach a plain function defined inside the component instead, or pass @event(prevent_default=True) explicitly over the method. functools.partial is fine — the inspector unwraps .func — and so is a functools.wraps decorator, via __wrapped__.

An inline-JavaScript handler cannot be inspected at all

Detection runs on Python bytecode. {"onClick": "this.innerText = 'x'"} has none, so there is no preventDefault equivalent in the string form. Call it yourself in the JavaScript: "event.preventDefault(); doThing()".

docs.title: Inline JavaScript
docs.text:
A str under an onXxx key is stored under inlineJavaScript and eval'd in the page; if it evaluates to a function, that function is called with the event:

html.button({"onClick": '(event) => (event.target.innerText = "Thank you!")'}, "Click")
html.button({"onClick": "this.innerText = 'Thank you!'"}, "Click")

This is the way to touch the DOM from ReactPy, and the reason it exists is that the server has no node to hold (Manipulating the DOM with Refs). Keep each snippet to a single call, and never interpolate anything you did not write:

Trusted strings only

The string runs with your application's privileges, in the page. f"this.innerText = '{user_input}'" is an injection point. Build strings from constants, or use a Python handler and pass data through state.

Note also that the pattern is ^on[A-Z]\w+ — a lowercase {"onclick": "..."} matches nothing and becomes a plain attribute that never fires.

docs.title: Merging handlers
docs.text:
reactpy.core.events.merge_event_handlers combines several handlers into one that runs them concurrently in a task group. It is public API but nothing in the installed package calls it — verified by grepping the whole reactpy package, which finds only its own definition — so you will rarely have a reason to call it. Its failure mode is still worth knowing, because it is a ValueError at build time:

merge_event_handlers([a, b])
# ValueError: Cannot merge handlers - 'stop_propagation', 'prevent_default',
# 'debounce', 'throttle' or 'target' mismatch.

Handlers merge only if every option matches. An empty list raises ValueError: No event handlers to merge.

docs.title: What to check when a control does nothing
docs.text:
Every failure mode on this page is silent in the browser, so work through them in this order:

  1. Did you pass the function or call it? {"onClick": handler()} gives None, which becomes an inert attribute.
  2. Is the key a real DOM event name in camelCase? on_click and onclick never fire.
  3. Does the handler take exactly one parameter? Two required parameters means a server-side TypeError and a dead button.
  4. Is it a bound method? Then preventDefault/stopPropagation/debounce are not detected — use @event.
  5. Read the server log. Failed to execute event handler is where swallowed handler errors go; the browser console will show nothing.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Values are sorted by kind, not name: callable → eventHandlers, string under onXxx → inlineJavaScript, everything else → attributes.
  • None, True, and dict handlers all fail silently as attributes.
  • A plain callable receives the argument list unpacked (so, the event dict); an EventHandler receives the list.
  • Set options with @event(prevent_default=..., stop_propagation=..., debounce=..., throttle=...); the bytecode detector is a convenience with real limits, notably bound methods.
  • debounce limits server→client value updates; throttle limits client→server events. Invalid values are dropped with a console warning, not an error.
  • Handler errors surface in the server log only.

docs.text:

  • Common Props — the same surface from the reference side, including ReactPy's own options
  • Protocol Structure — the wire format, target, and how data is built
  • Creating HTML Tags — how the model these handlers live in is built
  • Manipulating the DOM with Refs — the inline-JavaScript escape hatch

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A properly configured editor can make code clearer to read and faster to write. It can even help you catch bugs as you write them! If this is your first time setting up an editor or you're looking to tune up your current editor, we have a few recommendations.

You will learn

  • What the most popular editors are
  • How to format your code automatically

docs.title: Your editor
docs.text:
VS Code is one of the most popular editors in use today. It has a large marketplace of extensions and integrates well with popular services like GitHub. Most of the features listed below can be added to VS Code as extensions as well, making it highly configurable!

Other popular text editors used in the React community include:

  • Sublime Text has support for syntax highlighting and autocomplete built in.
  • Vim is a highly configurable text editor built to make creating and changing any kind of text very efficient. It is included as "vi" with most UNIX systems and with Apple OS X.

docs.title: Recommended text editor features
docs.text: Some editors come with these features built in, but others might require adding an extension. Check to see what support your editor of choice provides to be sure!

docs.title: Linting
docs.text:
Linting is the process of running a program that will analyse code for potential errors. Ruff is Reactive Python's linter of choice due to its speed and configurability. Additionally, we recommend using Pyright as a performant type checker for Python.

Be sure you have Python installed before you proceed!

  • Install Ruff using the VSCode extension or the standalone package.
  • Install Pyright using the VSCode extension or the standalone package.

docs.title: Formatting
docs.text:
The last thing you want to do when sharing your code with another contributor is get into an discussion about tabs vs spaces! Fortunately, Ruff will clean up your code by reformatting it to conform to preset, configurable rules. Run Ruff, and all your tabs will be converted to spaces—and your indentation, quotes, etc will also all be changed to conform to the configuration. In the ideal setup, Ruff will run when you save your file, quickly making these edits for you.

You can install the Ruff extension in VSCode by following these steps:

  1. Launch VS Code
  2. Use Quick Open, press Ctrl+P
  3. Paste in ext install charliermarsh.ruff
  4. Press Enter

Formatting on save

Ideally, you should format your code on every save. VS Code has settings for this!

  1. In VS Code, press Ctrl+Shift+P
  2. Type "workspace settings"
  3. Hit Enter
  4. In the search bar, type "Format on save"
  5. Be sure the "Format on save" option is ticked!

docs.title: Extracting State Logic into a Reducer
Overview
docs.text:
A component whose state is updated by many handlers spread across its body gets hard to reason about. A reducer moves every update rule into one pure function, so the handlers say only what the user did. In ReactPy there is one rule to learn on top of React's: the reducer you pass on the first render is the one ReactPy keeps, so a reducer defined inside the component body closes over frozen values.

You will learn

  • What a reducer is, and how dispatching differs from setting
  • Why ReactPy keeps the first reducer, and what that forbids
  • Where a ReactPy reducer actually runs, and what that means for purity
  • When a reducer is worth the extra code

docs.title: Consolidate state logic with a reducer
docs.text:
This component holds a list of tasks and updates it from three handlers:

app.py Run 
INITIAL_TASKS = [
    {"id": 0, "text": "Packing", "done": False},
    {"id": 1, "text": "Passport", "done": True},
    {"id": 2, "text": "Camera", "done": False},
]


@component
def task_app():
    next_id, set_next_id = use_state(3)
    tasks, set_tasks = use_state(INITIAL_TASKS)

    def handle_add_task(event):
        set_tasks([*tasks, {"id": next_id, "text": "New task", "done": False}])
        set_next_id(next_id + 1)

    def handle_toggle(task_id):
        def handle_click(event):
            set_tasks(
                [
                    {**task, "done": not task["done"]}
                    if task["id"] == task_id
                    else task
                    for task in tasks
                ]
            )

        return handle_click

    def handle_delete(task_id):
        def handle_click(event):
            set_tasks([task for task in tasks if task["id"] != task_id])

        return handle_click

    return html.div(
        html.h3("Prague itinerary"),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_add_task}, "Add task"),
        html.ul(
            [
                html.li(
                    {"key": task["id"]},
                    html.span(
                        {
                            "style": {
                                "textDecoration": "line-through"
                                if task["done"]
                                else "none"
                            }
                        },
                        task["text"],
                    ),
                    html.button({"onClick": handle_toggle(task["id"])}, "Toggle"),
                    html.button({"onClick": handle_delete(task["id"])}, "Delete"),
                )
                for task in tasks
            ]
        ),
        html.p({"id": "summary"}, f"{len(tasks)} tasks, next id {next_id}"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return task_app()

# TODO

Each handler knows how to rebuild the list. That is fine at three handlers and one field. It stops being fine when a fourth handler appears, when a second field has to change alongside tasks, or when you are debugging which of the four produced a wrong list — and here handle_add_task already has to keep two state variables in step.

Managing state with a reducer inverts it. Instead of telling ReactPy what to do, each handler says what just happened, and one function decides what that means:

app.py Run 
INITIAL_TASKS = [
    {"id": 0, "text": "Packing", "done": False},
    {"id": 1, "text": "Passport", "done": True},
    {"id": 2, "text": "Camera", "done": False},
]


def tasks_reducer(state, action):
    """One place that knows how the task list may change."""
    kind = action["type"]
    if kind == "added":
        task = {"id": state["next_id"], "text": "New task", "done": False}
        return {
            **state,
            "tasks": [*state["tasks"], task],
            "next_id": state["next_id"] + 1,
        }
    if kind == "toggled":
        return {
            **state,
            "tasks": [
                {**task, "done": not task["done"]}
                if task["id"] == action["id"]
                else task
                for task in state["tasks"]
            ],
        }
    if kind == "deleted":
        return {
            **state,
            "tasks": [task for task in state["tasks"] if task["id"] != action["id"]],
        }
    raise ValueError(f"unknown action type {kind!r}")


@component
def task_app():
    state, dispatch = use_reducer(tasks_reducer, {"tasks": INITIAL_TASKS, "next_id": 3})

    def handle_add_task(event):
        dispatch({"type": "added"})

    def handle_toggle(task_id):
        def handle_click(event):
            dispatch({"type": "toggled", "id": task_id})

        return handle_click

    def handle_delete(task_id):
        def handle_click(event):
            dispatch({"type": "deleted", "id": task_id})

        return handle_click

    return html.div(
        html.h3("Prague itinerary"),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_add_task}, "Add task"),
        html.ul(
            [
                html.li(
                    {"key": task["id"]},
                    html.span(
                        {
                            "style": {
                                "textDecoration": "line-through"
                                if task["done"]
                                else "none"
                            }
                        },
                        task["text"],
                    ),
                    html.button({"onClick": handle_toggle(task["id"])}, "Toggle"),
                    html.button({"onClick": handle_delete(task["id"])}, "Delete"),
                )
                for task in state["tasks"]
            ]
        ),
        html.p(
            {"id": "summary"},
            f"{len(state['tasks'])} tasks, next id {state['next_id']}",
        ),
    )


@component
def app():
    return task_app()

# TODO

Both examples are verified to behave identically — add twice, toggle, delete produces the same readouts and the same single flipped row in each. The difference is where the knowledge lives. The handlers now read as a list of user intentions:

  • dispatch({"type": "added"})
  • dispatch({"type": "toggled", "id": task_id})
  • dispatch({"type": "deleted", "id": task_id})

next_id moved into the same state object as tasks, so added bumps both in one return value. That is the first concrete gain: there is no longer a pair of setters that can be called in the wrong combination.

The reducer ends with raise ValueError(f"unknown action type {kind!r}") rather than return state. A fallthrough that silently does nothing is the hardest bug in this pattern to find, because every other symptom looks correct.

Note

use_reducer(reducer, initial_value) takes exactly two arguments. There is no third "init function" parameter as in some React versions. If building the initial state is expensive, pass a zero-argument callable as initial_value — ReactPy calls it once and stores the result, the same way use_state does.

docs.title: The rule ReactPy adds: the first reducer wins
docs.text:
This is the part that differs from React, and it will bite you once. use_reducer builds its dispatcher once and reuses it, so the reducer function from the first render is the one that runs forever — core/hooks.py, use_reducer.

Swapping the reducer at runtime does nothing at all:

app.py Run 
def add_by_one(state, action):
    return {"n": state["n"] + 1, "by": "add_by_one"}


def add_by_hundred(state, action):
    return {"n": state["n"] + 100, "by": "add_by_hundred"}


@component
def counter():
    version, set_version = use_state(1)

    # The component body picks a different reducer each time version changes,
    # but use_reducer built its dispatcher on the first render and reuses it.
    reducer = add_by_one if version == 1 else add_by_hundred
    state, dispatch = use_reducer(reducer, {"n": 0, "by": "-"})

    def handle_add(event):
        dispatch({"type": "add"})

    def handle_switch(event):
        set_version(2)

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": handle_add}, "Add"),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_switch}, "Switch reducer"),
        html.p({"id": "readout"}, f"n={state['n']} by={state['by']} version={version}"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return counter()

# TODO

Press Switch reducer — the readout shows version=2, so the component body really did pick add_by_hundred — then press Add: by=add_by_one. Every later action still runs the original function.

The same mechanism is subtler, and much more common, when the reducer is defined inside the component:

app.py Run 
INITIAL = {"count": 0, "total": 0}


@component
def cart(item_price):
    # This reducer reads item_price from the enclosing scope. ReactPy keeps the
    # reducer from the first render, so it keeps the first price too.
    def reducer(state, action):
        if action["type"] == "add":
            return {
                "count": state["count"] + 1,
                "total": state["total"] + item_price,
            }
        return state

    state, dispatch = use_reducer(reducer, INITIAL)

    def handle_add(event):
        dispatch({"type": "add"})

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": handle_add}, "Add"),
        html.p(
            {"id": "cart"},
            f"count={state['count']} total={state['total']} price={item_price}",
        ),
    )


@component
def price_control():
    price, set_price = use_state(10)

    def raise_price(event):
        set_price(50)

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": raise_price}, "Raise price"),
        cart(price),
        html.p(f"parent price={price}"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return price_control()

# TODO

Press Add once: count=1 total=10. Then Raise price, which takes the displayed price to 50 — and press Add again. You get total=20, not 60. The line reads price=50 while the arithmetic used 10.

Nothing crashed and nothing was logged. The reducer still holds the closure from the first render, in which item_price was 10. This is the frozen-effect-body problem from Lifecycle of Reactive Effects wearing a different hat, and it is the single most likely way to be quietly wrong with a ReactPy reducer.

The fix is the same instinct as always: keep the reducer pure and self-contained. Define it at module level, and let the action carry every value it needs. Handlers are not frozen — they are rebuilt each render — so a handler can read the current prop and hand it over:

app.py Run 
INITIAL = {"count": 0, "total": 0}


def cart_reducer(state, action):
    """Pure and self-contained: every value it needs arrives in the action."""
    if action["type"] == "add":
        return {
            "count": state["count"] + 1,
            "total": state["total"] + action["price"],
        }
    return state


@component
def cart(item_price):
    # Defined at module level, so there is no enclosing scope to freeze.
    state, dispatch = use_reducer(cart_reducer, INITIAL)

    def handle_add(event):
        # The handler closes over the *current* price, and hands it over.
        dispatch({"type": "add", "price": item_price})

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": handle_add}, "Add"),
        html.p(
            {"id": "cart"},
            f"count={state['count']} total={state['total']} price={item_price}",
        ),
    )


@component
def price_control():
    price, set_price = use_state(10)

    def raise_price(event):
        set_price(50)

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": raise_price}, "Raise price"),
        cart(price),
        html.p(f"parent price={price}"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return price_control()

# TODO

Same buttons: Add, Raise price, Add now gives count=2 total=60 price=50. cart_reducer sits at module level with no enclosing scope to freeze, and dispatch({"type": "add", "price": item_price}) supplies the live value.

So the ReactPy rule is: a reducer must be a module-level function that reads nothing but its two arguments. That is stricter than React's "reducers must be pure", and it costs nothing — a reducer that closes over component scope is a reducer you cannot unit-test with two plain arguments anyway.

docs.title: Where a ReactPy reducer runs
docs.text:
React's docs say reducers run during rendering, because React queues actions and calls the reducer at the next render. ReactPy is more direct, and the difference is worth knowing when you reach for a print statement:

handler:enter
reducer(add)
handler:exit
render

Verified trace of one click. dispatch calls your reducer immediately, inside the handler, then compares the result against the current state with == and schedules a render only if it differs — core/hooks.py, _create_dispatcher.

Three consequences:

  • A reducer that raises surfaces as a failed event handler, not a reducer error. Verified: dispatching an action whose branch raises ValueError leaves the state untouched and produces zero renders. dispatch ran the reducer inside the handler, so the exception propagates to core/layout.py, Layout._process_event_queue, which catches it and calls logger.exception — one ERROR: Failed to execute event handler record on the reactpy.core.layout logger, with the reducer's traceback attached. ReactPy itself never reports "a reducer raised". The component stays mounted and keeps working for later actions.
  • Multiple dispatches in one handler batch into one render. Verified: three dispatch calls in a single handler produce three reducer calls, applied in order, and one render.
  • Purity is not optional, but for a different reason than in React. Since the result is compared with ==, mutating and returning the same object compares equal and schedules nothing.

That last one is the most common reducer bug in ReactPy, and it is silent:

app.py Run 
INITIAL_TASKS = [
    {"id": 0, "text": "Packing", "done": False},
    {"id": 1, "text": "Passport", "done": True},
]


def mutating_reducer(state, action):
    """Looks fine, edits the list in place, returns it. Nothing will re-render."""
    if action["type"] == "added":
        state["tasks"].append(
            {"id": state["next_id"], "text": "New task", "done": False}
        )
        return state
    return state


@component
def task_app():
    # A fresh list per component instance: this reducer mutates the list it is
    # given, so it must not be handed a module-level one.
    state, dispatch = use_reducer(
        mutating_reducer, {"tasks": [*INITIAL_TASKS], "next_id": 2}
    )

    def handle_add_task(event):
        dispatch({"type": "added"})

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": handle_add_task}, "Add task"),
        html.ul(
            [html.li({"key": task["id"]}, task["text"]) for task in state["tasks"]]
        ),
        html.p({"id": "summary"}, f"{len(state['tasks'])} tasks rendered"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return task_app()

# TODO

Press Add task three times. The rendered count stays at 2 tasks rendered and the component body never runs again — verified at zero renders. The list did grow; the returned state compared equal to the old one, so ReactPy decided nothing had changed. Return new objects ({**state, "tasks": [*state["tasks"], task]}), exactly as you would with use_state.

Pitfall

return state after modifying state is a no-op, and so is any branch that falls through to return state. If an action's "type" matches no branch — a typo, a renamed constant — the dispatch is silently ignored. End the reducer with raise ValueError(...) for unknown types instead of a bare return state, so the mistake surfaces where it is made.

docs.title: Comparing use_state and use_reducer
docs.text:
• Code size. use_state needs less code upfront: a reducer and actions is two artefacts, not one. A reducer pays off when many handlers mutate state in similar shapes, or when one transition touches several fields at once — moving next_id next to tasks above is that case.
  • Readability. With use_state the update logic lives in the handlers, which is where you want it while it is three lines. When handlers grow conditionals, the reducer lets you separate how state changes from what happened.
  • Debugging. With use_state you must find which setter was wrong. With a reducer you can log the two arguments of one function and reconstruct the session — in ReactPy the log also tells you the order, because dispatch is eager. If each action is right, the bug is in the reducer.
  • Testing. A module-level reducer — which ReactPy already requires — is a plain function. tasks_reducer(state, {"type": "deleted", "id": 1}) is an assertion, no rendering involved.
  • Render count. Neither is cheaper. Both compare with == and both skip a render when the value is unchanged; neither bails out of rendering the component, because ReactPy has no memo.

Use a reducer when a component has produced real bugs from the wrong update path, not as a default. Mixing is fine: use_state for a draft input, use_reducer for the form's submitted record, in the same component.

Deep Dive

ReactPy has no immer equivalent that earns its keep here, because {**state, ...} and [*items, item] are already the copy idioms a reducer needs. What is worth doing once a reducer grows past a couple of branches: make the state a frozen @dataclass. Then a mutation raises FrozenInstanceError at the line that did it instead of quietly comparing equal — verified, and with it the two halves that make this safe: strictly_equal compares dataclass instances field by field, so dispatching an action that changes nothing renders nothing, while one that changes a field renders once. Because the raise happens inside the event handler, though, it is caught like any other handler exception: it appears as a root-logger ERROR, not on screen. Use dataclasses.replace(state, ...), and read the server log. See Lifecycle of Reactive Effects for the full comparison table.

docs.title: Writing reducers well
docs.text:
• One action per user interaction, not per field. A "Reset" button on a five-field form should dispatch {"type": "reset_form"}, not five set_field actions. If you logged every action, the log should read like a transcript of the session.
  • Actions describe what happened, not what to change. {"type": "toggled", "id": 3} survives a change in how toggling is displayed. {"type": "set_done", "value": True} does not, and is usually shorter written as a setter.
  • Put the data in the action. {"type": "add_item", "item": item, "price": price} — this is also exactly what keeps a ReactPy reducer honest, since the reducer cannot read live values from a closure.
  • Keep transitions in the reducer, not in the handler. A handler that does dispatch(...) and set_something_else(...) has two sources of truth again.
  • Do not dispatch during render. Dispatch is eager, so it updates the pending state while the component body is still running; the render then reflects an update that has already happened. Put it in an effect or a handler.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A reducer collects every state transition in one pure function; handlers shrink to a description of what the user did.
  • ReactPy keeps the first reducer it is given. Verified: swapping the reducer argument changes the body, not the behaviour.
  • Therefore define reducers at module level, reading nothing but state and action. A reducer defined in the component body freezes its closure — verified charging total=20 at a displayed price=50.
  • dispatch runs the reducer immediately, inside the handler, not at the next render. Verified by trace.
  • Mutating the state and returning it compares equal, so nothing renders — verified: three presses, zero renders, no log line. Return new objects.
  • A raising reducer surfaces as ERROR: Failed to execute event handler from reactpy.core.layout, not as a reducer error; end the reducer with raise ValueError so unknown actions surface.
  • Several dispatches in one handler apply in order and cost one render (verified).
  • use_reducer takes two arguments; pass a callable as initial_value to build it lazily, once.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The magic of components lies in their reusability: you can create components that are composed of other components. But as you nest more and more components, it often makes sense to start splitting them into different files. This lets you keep your files easy to scan and reuse components in more places.

You will learn

  • What a root component module is
  • How to import a component from another file
  • How ReactPy expresses "private" and "public" components
  • How to import and export multiple components from one file
  • How to split components into multiple files

docs.title: The root component module
docs.text:
In Your First Component, you made a profile component and a gallery component that renders it:

app.pystyles.css 
from reactpy import component, html


@component
def profile():
    return html.img(
        {"src": "https://i.imgur.com/MK3eW3As.jpg", "alt": "Katherine Johnson"}
    )


@component
def gallery():
    return html.section(
        html.h1("Amazing scientists"),
        profile(),
        profile(),
        profile(),
    )

img {
    margin: 0 10px 10px 0;
    height: 90px;
}

These currently live in a single module. Whichever module holds the component you hand to an executor is your root component module — the ASGI executor in Creating a Standalone React App takes that component directly:

from reactpy.executors.asgi import ReactPy

from app import gallery

my_app = ReactPy(gallery)

Which module plays this role depends on your executor. The middleware executor takes dotted paths instead, e.g. ["my_components.hello_world"], and the CSR executor takes a path to a file whose root component it mounts.

docs.title: Exporting and importing a component
docs.text:
What if you want to change the landing screen in the future and put a list of science books there? Or place all the profiles somewhere else? It makes sense to move gallery and profile into their own module. This makes them more modular and reusable in other files. You can move a component in three steps:

  1. Make a new Python file to put the components in.
  2. Define your component functions in that file. Unlike JavaScript, Python has no export keyword — every name defined at module level is importable.
  3. Import it in the module where you'll use the component.

Here both profile and gallery have moved into a new file called gallery.py. Now app.py imports gallery from it:

app.pygallery.py 
from gallery import gallery

from reactpy import component


@component
def app():
    return gallery()

from reactpy import component, html

__all__ = ["gallery"]


@component
def _profile():
    """Used only inside this module, so it stays out of ``__all__``."""
    return html.img({"src": "https://i.imgur.com/QIrZWGIs.jpg", "alt": "Alan L. Hart"})


@component
def gallery():
    return html.section(
        html.h1("Amazing scientists"),
        _profile(),
        _profile(),
        _profile(),
    )

Notice how this example is broken down into two component files now:

  1. gallery.py:
    • Defines the _profile component, which is only used within the same file and is kept private.
    • Makes gallery the public component of the module.
  2. app.py:
    • Imports gallery from gallery.py.
    • Defines the root app component.

Note

ReactPy does not care which module a component is defined in, so unlike ReactJS there is no distinction between "default" and "named" exports. from gallery import gallery, profile and two separate import statements mean the same thing.

docs.title: Public and private components
docs.text:
ReactJS lets you keep a component unexported so that only its own file can use it. Python has no equivalent enforcement, but it has two widely respected conventions that express the same intent.

A leading underscore marks a name as private to its module:

@component
def _profile():
    ...

And __all__ lists the names a module publishes. It is what a star import exports, and what linters and type checkers read to decide what is public API:

__all__ = ["gallery"]

This is why _profile is both underscore-prefixed and absent from __all__ in the example above.

Pitfall

These conventions are advisory, not enforced. from gallery import _profile still works, because Python has no private keyword. Do not reach for underscore-prefixed names from another module, and do not rely on them being unavailable — treat a broken convention as a bug in the importing code, not as protection.

Deep Dive

docs.title: Naming modules and components
docs.text:
Because imports name modules rather than files, give both meaningful names. scientists.py defining gallery and _profile reads better than utils.py defining Gallery, and it also keeps you consistent with the rest of the docs, which write components in snake_case.

Components should still be called everywhere they are used, so a component used by two modules must be imported in both of them. There is no global component registry to fall back on.

docs.title: Exporting and importing multiple components from the same file
docs.text:
What if you want to show just one profile instead of a gallery? Then app.py needs profile too. Add it to the module's __all__ and import it by name:

app.pygallery.py 
from gallery import gallery, profile

from reactpy import component, html


@component
def app():
    return html.div(profile(), gallery())

from reactpy import component, html

__all__ = ["gallery", "profile"]


@component
def profile():
    return html.img({"src": "https://i.imgur.com/QIrZWGIs.jpg", "alt": "Alan L. Hart"})


@component
def gallery():
    return html.section(
        html.h1("Amazing scientists"),
        profile(),
        profile(),
        profile(),
    )

Now gallery.py publishes both components:

  • gallery.py:
    • Lists gallery and profile in __all__.
  • app.py:
    • Imports both gallery and profile from gallery.py.
    • Renders each of them.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
You've learned:

  • What a root component module is, and that it depends on your executor
  • How to import a component from another file
  • How ReactPy expresses public and private components with __all__ and a leading underscore
  • How to export multiple components from the same file

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Now that your components can live in separate files, continue to Passing Props to a Component to make them configurable.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
React has been designed from the start for gradual adoption. You can use as little or as much React as you need. Whether you want to get a taste of React, add some interactivity to an HTML page, or start a complex React-powered app, this section will help you get started.

You will learn

  • How to start a new React project
  • How to add React to an existing project
  • How to set up your editor
  • How to install React Developer Tools

docs.title: Start a new React project
docs.text: If you want to build an app or a website fully with React, start a new React project.

docs.title: Add React to an existing project
docs.text: If want to try using React in your existing app or a website, add React to an existing project.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: Head to the Quick Start guide for a tour of the most important React concepts you will encounter every day.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Some Python functions are pure. Pure functions only perform a calculation and nothing more. By strictly only writing your components as pure functions, you can avoid an entire class of baffling bugs and unpredictable behavior as your codebase grows. To get these benefits, though, there are a few rules you must follow.

You will learn

  • What purity is and how it helps you avoid bugs
  • How to keep components pure by keeping changes out of the render phase
  • Why ReactPy cannot check purity for you

docs.title: Purity: Components as formulas
docs.text:
In computer science (and especially the world of functional programming), a pure function is a function with the following characteristics:

  • It minds its own business. It does not change any objects or variables that existed before it was called.
  • Same inputs, same output. Given the same inputs, a pure function should always return the same result.

You might already be familiar with one example of pure functions: formulas in math.

Consider this math formula: y = 2 * x.

If x = 2 then y = 4. Always.

If x = 3 then y = 6. Always.

If x = 3, y won't sometimes be 9 or -1 or 2.5 depending on the time of day or the state of the stock market.

If y = 2 * x and x = 3, y will always be 6.

If we made this into a Python function, it would look like this:

def double(number):
    return 2 * number

In the above example, double is a pure function. If you pass it 3, it will return 6. Always.

ReactPy is designed around this concept. ReactPy assumes that every component you write is a pure function. This means that ReactPy components you write must always return the same VDOM given the same inputs:

app.py Run 
@component
def recipe(drinkers):
    return html.ol(
        html.li(f"Boil {drinkers} cups of water."),
        html.li(f"Add {drinkers} spoons of tea and {0.5 * drinkers} spoons of spice."),
        html.li(f"Add {0.5 * drinkers} cups of milk to boil and sugar to taste."),
    )


@component
def app():
    return html.section(
        html.h1("Spiced Chai Recipe"),
        html.h2("For two"),
        recipe(2),
        html.h2("For a gathering"),
        recipe(4),
    )

# TODO

When you pass drinkers=2 to recipe(), it will return VDOM containing 2 cups of water. Always.

If you pass drinkers=4, it will return VDOM containing 4 cups of water. Always.

Just like a math formula.

You could think of your components as recipes: if you follow them and don't introduce new ingredients during the cooking process, you will get the same dish every time. That "dish" is the VDOM that the component serves to ReactPy to render.

docs.title: Side Effects: (un)intended consequences
docs.text:
ReactPy's rendering process must always be pure. Components should only return their VDOM, and not change any objects or variables that existed before rendering—that would make them impure!

Here is a component that breaks this rule:

app.py Run 
guest = 0


@component
def cup():
    # Bad: changing a preexisting variable!
    global guest
    guest = guest + 1
    return html.h2(f"Tea cup for guest #{guest}")


@component
def tea_set():
    return html(cup(), cup(), cup())

# TODO

This component is reading and writing a guest variable declared outside of it. This means that calling this component multiple times will produce different VDOM! And what's more, if other components read guest, they will produce different VDOM, too, depending on when they were rendered! That's not predictable.

Render this once and you get the numbering you expect:

Tea cup for guest #1
Tea cup for guest #2
Tea cup for guest #3

Render it again — after a hot reload, a reconnect, or simply a second request in the same process — and the counters have silently moved on:

Tea cup for guest #4
Tea cup for guest #5
Tea cup for guest #6

Going back to our formula y = 2 * x, now even if x = 2, we cannot trust that y = 4. Our tests could fail, our users would be baffled, planes would fall out of the sky—you can see how this would lead to confusing bugs!

You can fix this component by passing guest as a prop instead:

app.py Run 
@component
def cup(guest):
    return html.h2(f"Tea cup for guest #{guest}")


@component
def tea_set():
    return html(cup(1), cup(2), cup(3))

# TODO

Now your component is pure, as the VDOM it returns only depends on the guest prop.

In general, you should not expect your components to be rendered in any particular order. It doesn't matter if you call y = 2 * x before or after y = 5 * x: both formulas will resolve independently of each other. In the same way, each component should only "think for itself", and not attempt to coordinate with or depend upon others during rendering. Rendering is like a school exam: each component should calculate VDOM on their own!

ReactPy has no Strict Mode to catch this for you

React ships a "Strict Mode" that calls every component function twice in development, which is how the example above gets caught: an impure counter jumps to #2, #4, #6. ReactPy has no equivalent — there is no StrictMode component and no double-invoke. A single render of an impure component looks completely correct, and the bug only appears later as drifting output or as a failure under a test that renders twice.

Two practical consequences:

  • Add a test that renders the component twice and asserts the two results are equal. That is the closest ReactPy gets to Strict Mode, and it is entirely in your hands.
  • Because there is no double-invoke to hide behind, impurity in ReactPy tends to surface as state that changes between reconnects rather than as an obvious warning. Treat any component that touches module-level state as suspect.

docs.title: Local mutation: Your component's little secret
docs.text:
In the above example, the problem was that the component changed a preexisting variable while rendering. This is often called a "mutation" to make it sound a bit scarier. Pure functions don't mutate variables outside of the function's scope or objects that were created before the call—that makes them impure!

However, it's completely fine to change variables and objects that you've just created while rendering. In this example, you create a [] list, assign it to a cups variable, and then append a dozen cups into it:

app.py Run 
@component
def cup(guest):
    return html.h2(f"Tea cup for guest #{guest}")


@component
def tea_gathering():
    cups = []
    for index in range(1, 13):
        cups.append(cup(index, key=index))
    return html.div(cups)

# TODO

If the cups variable or the [] list were created outside the tea_gathering() function, this would be a huge problem! You would be changing a preexisting object by appending items to that list.

However, it's fine because you've created them during the same render, inside tea_gathering(). No code outside of tea_gathering() will ever know that this happened. This is called "local mutation"—it's like your component's little secret.

docs.title: Where you can cause side effects
docs.text:
While functional programming relies heavily on purity, at some point, somewhere, something has to change. That's kind of the point of programming! These changes—updating the screen, starting an animation, changing the data—are called side effects. They're things that happen "on the side", not during rendering.

In ReactPy, side effects usually belong inside event handlers. Event handlers are functions that ReactPy runs when you perform some action—for example, when you click a button. Even though event handlers are defined inside your component, they don't run during rendering! So event handlers don't need to be pure.

app.py Run 
@component
def tea_counter():
    sips, set_sips = use_state(0)

    def take_a_sip(event):
        # Side effects belong here: this runs on click, not during rendering.
        set_sips(sips + 1)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"You have taken {sips} sips."),
        html.button({"onClick": take_a_sip}, "Take a sip"),
    )

# TODO

If you've exhausted all other options and can't find the right event handler for your side effect, you can still attach it to your returned VDOM with a use_effect or use_async_effect call in your component. This tells ReactPy to execute it later, after rendering, when side effects are allowed. However, this approach should be your last resort.

When possible, try to express your logic with rendering alone. You'll be surprised how far this can take you!

Why does ReactPy care about purity?

Writing pure functions takes some habit and discipline. But it also unlocks real opportunities:

  • Your components can run on the server, and be rendered to a string. Components already execute server-side in ReactPy; purity is what makes it safe for one component to serve many requests. The same property lets reactpy_to_string turn a component into HTML — with one limit worth knowing: it calls component.render() with no Layout behind it, so the component may use no hooks at all. Hand it html.* elements or a hook-free component; anything with use_state raises RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout?. It is a string helper for fragments and tests, not a way to server-render an app. A component that mutated module state would leak one request's output into another's.
  • Rendering can be restarted. ReactPy may need to discard an in-progress render, and purity makes it safe to stop calculating at any time.
  • Reasoning and testing become mechanical. A pure component is an ordinary Python function: call it inside a reactpy.core.layout.Layout, render it twice, and compare the results — no browser required.

Note that one React benefit is not available to you yet: React skips re-rendering components whose inputs have not changed, which is safe precisely because pure functions are safe to cache. ReactPy has use_memo for values, but no memo for components, so a child re-runs whenever its parent renders. Purity is still required; it simply isn't being used for caching today.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A component must be pure, meaning:

    • It minds its own business. It should not change any objects or variables that existed before rendering.
    • Same inputs, same output. Given the same inputs, a component should always return the same VDOM.

  • Rendering can happen at any time, so components should not depend on each others' rendering sequence.

  • You should not mutate any of the inputs that your components use for rendering. That includes props, state, and context. To update the screen, "set" state instead of mutating preexisting objects.
  • Strive to express your component's logic in the VDOM you return. When you need to "change things", you'll usually want to do it in an event handler. As a last resort, you can use_effect.
  • ReactPy will not double-render your components to find impurity for you; write the render-twice test yourself.
  • Writing pure functions takes a bit of practice, but it unlocks the power of the ReactPy paradigm.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
An Effect is a piece of synchronization code attached to a render. It runs, it may clean up after itself, and it runs again if its inputs change. Understanding that lifecycle — not a memorized list of rules — is what makes Effects predictable in ReactPy.

You will learn

  • How an Effect setup and clean-up pair forms one synchronization
  • Which values an Effect "reacts" to, and what happens to the ones it doesn't
  • Why a dependency list, not the Effect's own text, decides re-synchronization
  • How Effects are ordered, and what is not guaranteed
  • Why a broken Effect reports itself nowhere the user can see

docs.title: The lifecycle of an Effect
docs.text:
Think of an Effect as a synchronization process between a value your component holds and something outside ReactPy. Each Effect has a setup and, sometimes, a clean-up:

app.py Run 
@component
def room_view(room):
    def effect():
        # Setup: ReactPy runs this when the Effect is created.
        close = server.connect(room)

        # Clean-up: ReactPy runs this before the *next* run of this same
        # Effect, and again when the component unmounts. Together they make
        # one synchronization: connect this room, then leave it.
        def cleanup():
            close()

        return cleanup

    use_effect(effect, dependencies=[room])

    return html.p(f"{room} -- open connections: {server.open_count}")


@component
def app():
    room, set_room = use_state("lobby")

    return html.div(
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_room("dev" if room == "lobby" else "lobby")},
            f"Leave {room}",
        ),
        html.p("(server log is printed on the server console)"),
        room_view(room),
    )

# TODO

Verified against the server's own log: mount produces connect lobby; pressing Leave lobby produces close lobby then connect dev; and the last connection closes on unmount. The open-connection count never climbs above 1.

Read the pair as a single unit — "be connected to this room". Setup and clean-up are not two independent callbacks: ReactPy runs the clean-up of a run right before that run's successor sets up, using the same captured state. So switching rooms means leave the old room, join the new one, in that order, and the process is complete no matter how many times the inputs change.

docs.title: Why synchronization may need to happen more than once
docs.text:
The value being synchronized can change while the component is on screen: room above, a search query, an auth token. Every such change means the previous synchronization is describing the past, so ReactPy tears it down and starts a new one.

That is why the clean-up is not optional boilerplate. In a browser, forgetting it leaks one subscription until the tab closes. On a ReactPy server it leaks until the process exits — and the leaked callback still holds your component, still fires, and keeps a connection or file handle alive for a user who left hours ago.

docs.title: How ReactPy re-synchronizes an Effect
docs.text:
When a dependency changes, ReactPy runs this sequence:

  1. The component renders and registers the Effect again.
  2. A new Effect task starts, and its first act is to run the previous run's clean-up — core/hooks.py, use_effect calls run_effect_cleanup before invoking your function.
  3. Your setup runs and returns the next clean-up.

Two consequences worth internalizing:

  • The clean-up runs on the new task, not the old one. It sees the previous run's captured values, which is exactly what a teardown needs.
  • The old task is not cancelled. A sync Effect's task parks on stop.wait() and is only reaped when the component unmounts. Measured: three dependency changes leave 4 live Effect tasks where there was 1, and all 4 disappear at unmount. The clean-ups still ran in the right order; the parked tasks are simply waiting for a signal that will come at unmount. For a long-lived component re-synchronizing constantly, that is memory you are paying for.

docs.title: Thinking from the Effect's perspective
docs.text:
When you read an Effect, read it as the outside world would. The code above says: "while this component is on screen and room is X, stay connected to X." Everything in that sentence is checkable:

Sentence part Where it comes from "while this component is on screen" the component's mount/unmount "and room is X" the dependency list "stay connected to X" setup (leaving) the returned clean-up

If part of that sentence is a lie, the Effect is wrong — not the dependency list, not the linting setup. dependencies is how you spell "and room is X"; it is not a performance knob.

docs.title: Each Effect represents a separate synchronization process
docs.text:
Two Effects in one component are two processes, not one with two steps. Keep them apart when their synchronization targets differ, and let each own its own clean-up:

use_effect(connect_to_room, dependencies=[room])
use_effect(subscribe_to_feed, dependencies=[user_id])

Do not merge them because they live in the same component: merging means a room change tears down the feed subscription too. Two Effects in the same component run in declaration order, so ordering within a component is available to you when one genuinely depends on the other's setup having happened.

docs.title: Effects "react" to reactive values
docs.text:
Every value in the component body — props, state, anything computed from them — belongs to one render. An Effect created by that render reads that render's values and never sees a later one. The dependency list is how you say which values should trigger a new Effect.

Here an Effect reports an error flag but leaves it out of the dependency list:

app.py Run 
@component
def counter():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)
    show_error, set_show_error = use_state(True)
    reports, set_reports = use_state([])

    def effect():
        # Reads `show_error`, but dependencies=[count] never mentions it. So
        # flipping show_error does not re-synchronize, and this keeps
        # reporting whatever show_error was when the Effect was created.
        line = f"count={count} reported_error={show_error}"
        log.append(line)
        set_reports(lambda previous: [*previous, line])

    use_effect(effect, dependencies=[count])

    return html.div(
        html.h1(count),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_count(count + 1)}, "Add 1"),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_show_error(not show_error)},
            f"Toggle error (currently {show_error})",
        ),
        html.p("Effect reports:"),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": index}, line) for index, line in enumerate(reports)]),
    )

# TODO

Verified: pressing Toggle error re-renders the component and runs the Effect zero times — the list says dependencies=[count], so nothing happens. Press Add 1 and the Effect runs, and this time it reports the new value of the flag, because a brand-new Effect was created by that render.

That is the precise meaning of "stale": the Effect reports values from the render that created it. It does not freeze at mount, and it does not read the latest — it reads whichever render it was born in. Adding the missing value to the list is the fix.

A local function as a dependency never counts as changed

This one bites hard, and it contradicts the docstrings. ReactPy compares dependencies with core/hooks.py, strictly_equal — not by id. For two locally defined functions it compares their code: same co_* attributes means same dependency. So a def re-created on every render is never detected as changed:

app.py Run 
@component
def counter():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)
    label, set_label = use_state("count")
    runs, set_runs = use_state([])

    def describe():
        # A fresh function object on every render -- but ReactPy compares two
        # such local functions by their *code*, not by identity
        # (core/hooks.py, strictly_equal). So `describe` never counts as
        # changed, and the Effect below keeps the closure it captured first.
        return f"{label}={count}"

    def effect():
        line = f"effect ran, describe() -> {describe()}"
        log.append(line)
        set_runs(lambda previous: [*previous, line])

    use_effect(effect, dependencies=[describe])

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"{label}: {count}"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_count(count + 1)}, "Add 1"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_label(label + "!")}, "Rename"),
        html.p("Effect runs:"),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": index}, line) for index, line in enumerate(runs)]),
    )

# TODO

Verified: press Add 1 twice and Rename once — the heading shows count!!: 2, yet the Effect has run exactly once and describe() still returns 'count=0'. The Effect is permanently frozen on its first closure, and nothing warns you.

The same rule bites the other way: a fresh [1, 2] or {"a": 1} that compares equal is also "unchanged", so rebuilding an options dict on every render will not re-trigger an Effect that lists it. Depend on the scalar values you actually use, not on containers or local functions.

docs.title: What an Effect with empty dependencies means
docs.text:
dependencies=[] does not mean "run once, like a componentDidMount". It means create this Effect and never replace it — including its body:

def effect():
    print(f"body sees label={label}")

use_effect(effect, dependencies=[])

Verified: change label three times and the component re-renders three times; the Effect never runs again, and when something else finally forces it, it prints the first render's label. An [] Effect is sealed at mount. Reach for it only when the Effect genuinely reads nothing but stable values (module constants, a setter, a ref).

The four settings, restated with their lifecycle meaning:

Value Meaning dependencies=[a, b] Re-synchronize when a or b changes. dependencies=[] Synchronize once, at mount; the body is never replaced. dependencies=None Re-synchronize after every render. omitted Infer the list from the closure's free variables — then compare with ==, so a rebuilt-but-equal value will not re-trigger.

docs.title: All variables declared in the component body are reactive
docs.text:
Props, state, and anything derived from them are per-render values, so they belong in the dependency list whenever the Effect reads them. Module-level constants and imported singletons do not: they are the same object for every render and every connection.

Careful with the middle case. A dict built at module level looks like a constant and is not safe to mutate — every connection shares it (VDOM Mutations). And a mutable default argument is shared too. Neither is a dependency, because neither changes; both are bugs if you write to them.

Hooks are unusable inside an effect body

def effect():
    theme = use_context(theme_context)   # RuntimeError

Effects run in their own task, after rendering, with no life cycle hook on the stack. use_context, use_state, and every other hook raise RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout? — and that traceback reaches only the server log. Read what you need during render and let the closure carry it:

theme = use_context(theme_context)

def effect():
    apply(theme)

use_effect(effect, dependencies=[theme])

docs.title: What to do when you don't want to re-synchronize
docs.text:
Three legitimate reasons, three different answers.

The value is genuinely constant. Import it, define it at module level, or hoist it out of the component. Then it is not a dependency because it cannot change:

POLL_INTERVAL = 5


@component
def poller(topic):
    async def effect():
        ...

    use_async_effect(effect, dependencies=[topic])

You want the latest value without restarting the process. Keep it in a ref and read .current — the box persists across renders, so a long-lived Effect always reads the newest assignment (Synchronizing with Effects).

You want to switch the process off. Do not delete the hook call — that changes the hook order and corrupts every hook after it. Pass a flag and branch inside the Effect:

app.py Run 
@component
def feed(topic, enabled):
    def effect():
        if not enabled:
            # Nothing to set up, and nothing to clean up. The hook call below
            # still happens, so the hook order never changes.
            return None

        print(f"subscribe {topic}")

        def cleanup():
            print(f"unsubscribe {topic}")

        return cleanup

    use_effect(effect, dependencies=[topic, enabled])

    return html.p(f"{topic}")


@component
def app():
    topic, set_topic = use_state("news")
    enabled, set_enabled = use_state(True)

    return html.div(
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_enabled(not enabled)},
            "Stop" if enabled else "Start",
        ),
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": lambda event: set_topic(
                    "sports" if topic == "news" else "news"
                )
            },
            "Switch topic",
        ),
        feed(topic, enabled),
    )

# TODO

Verified: Stop runs unsubscribe news; while stopped, switching topics logs nothing (correct — there is nothing to synchronize); and Start then runs subscribe sports for the new topic. The hook call always happens; only the setup is conditional. Note the dependency list includes enabled — leaving it out would mean toggling did nothing at all.

Do not omit a dependency to dodge a loop

An Effect that re-triggers itself is telling you something. Measured: an Effect that sets a piece of state it also lists as a dependency rendered 86 times before the probe stopped. Deleting the dependency silences the symptom and leaves you with an Effect that reports the past. Fix the loop — usually by moving the value into the dependency list and making the setup idempotent, or by deriving the value during render instead (You Might Not Need an Effect).

docs.title: ReactPy will not verify your dependencies
docs.text:
React's side of this is eslint-plugin-react-hooks, which reads the Effect and its dependency list and warns when they disagree. ReactPy's equivalent is reactpy-flake8 — a real plugin, pinned in this repo's pyproject.toml — but it is far narrower than people expect. Every row below was produced by running the installed reactpy_flake8.run.run_checks over the snippet in question.

The rules-of-hooks half, always on:

What you wrote Reported? a hook called inside an if, for, while, try, match, or a conditional expression yes — REACTPY102 a hook used after an early return yes — REACTPY103 a hook used outside any component or hook yes — REACTPY101 a hook defined as a closure inside another function yes — REACTPY100

The dependency half, which needs exhaustive_hook_deps=True and is otherwise silent:

What you wrote Reported? an inline lambda Effect, use_memo, or use_callback missing a variable that is assigned at the top of the component body yes — REACTPY202 the same, but the missing variable is a component parameter no — parameters are not in the set of names it compares against a named def Effect missing a variable no a @use_effect-decorated function missing a variable no a dependency written as obj.attr rather than a bare name yes — REACTPY200 a dependency list that is a variable or call rather than a literal list, tuple, or None yes — REACTPY201

So the linter catches every call-site violation, and catches a missing dependency only for an inline lambda over a body-assigned variable — one shape among the several people actually write. The stale-value class of bug is largely on you.

Two habits replace the missing dependency check:

  1. Read the Effect and list the names. Every free variable in the body should appear in dependencies, or be provably module-level. This is mechanical — do it once per Effect at write time.

  2. Test the re-synchronization, not just the mount. Render, change the input, assert the outside world changed:

    async def test_switching_room_reconnects():
    async with Layout(app()) as layout:
        await layout.render()
        ...  # deliver the click that changes the room
        assert server.log == ["connect lobby", "close lobby", "connect dev"]

    A reactpy.core.layout.Layout in pytest is enough — no browser, and it catches exactly the bugs the linter cannot see.

docs.title: The order Effects run in
docs.text:
Verified output for a parent with two children, each declaring two Effects:

beta: first effect
beta: second effect
alpha: first effect
alpha: second effect
panel: my own effect
app.py Run 
@component
def leaf(name):
    @use_effect
    def first():
        print(f"{name}: first effect")

    @use_effect
    def second():
        print(f"{name}: second effect")

    return html.p(name)


@component
def panel():
    @use_effect
    def parent_effect():
        print("panel: my own effect")

    # Two children: the SECOND one's effects run first.
    return html.div(leaf("alpha"), leaf("beta"))


@component
def app():
    return html.div(
        html.h1("Watch the server console"),
        panel(),
    )

# TODO

Three rules, and nothing else:

  • Children before parent. A parent's own Effects run after everything below it has set up.
  • Siblings in reverse source order. beta before alpha. This surprises everyone and is worth knowing if two siblings write to the same external resource.
  • Within one component, declaration order. This one you can rely on.

Do not build anything on the first two. They are behaviour, not contract — the reverse-sibling rule in particular is an artifact of how effects are collected, and code that depends on a particular cross-component order is code that will break. Within a component, order Effects deliberately; across components, make each Effect self-contained.

docs.title: Async Effects: cancellation is not instant
docs.text:
use_async_effect wraps your coroutine in a task. On re-synchronization the old task is cancelled, which means it stops at its next await — not before, and not necessarily in time.

Two things follow, both measured.

Two runs can be alive at once. Switch topics three times quickly, before any 0.4 s poll resolves, and the log is:

start polling news
cancelled news
start polling sports
start polling news          # the older run is still awaiting
cancelled news
start polling sports
finished polling sports
finished polling sports

Verified, and identical across three repeats: two runs are simultaneously awaiting. Cancellation happens when the successor task starts, so a run that has already passed its awaits cannot be recalled — and notice the two finished lines belong to the same topic.

A superseded run can still write state. With a 0.4 s source and four rapid switches (a → b → c → d), the runs that actually applied their result were ['DATA FOR b', 'DATA FOR d'] — a and c were cancelled, b and d completed and called their setters. Reproducible across runs.

So cancellation is a bias toward the newest value, not a guarantee. If a stale write would be damaging, do not rely on being cancelled — tag the data with what produced it and check on write:

loaded, set_loaded = use_state({"name": None, "data": {}})

async def effect():
    data = await fetch(name)
    if name == expected_name.current:   # still the value we care about?
        set_loaded({"name": name, "data": data})

Put teardown that must run in the cancellation branch, and re-raise:

async def effect():
    handle = open_connection()
    try:
        while True:
            await handle.poll()
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        handle.close()
        raise

Swallowing CancelledError leaves the task in a state asyncio did not expect.

A sync Effect blocks the whole connection

use_effect runs on the connection's event loop. Measured: an Effect calling time.sleep(0.4) made the next click take 0.40 s to be served, and every other handler on that connection waited behind it. Only the browser's own local typing stays responsive. Long or blocking work belongs in use_async_effect, with blocking calls wrapped in asyncio.to_thread (Communicating Data Between Server and Client).

docs.title: When an Effect fails, nothing reports it
docs.text:
This is the section that saves the most hours. An Effect body that raises is invisible in three places at once:

  • the page looks completely fine,
  • the browser console is clean,
  • and — the part that misleads people — the server log stays silent too.
app.py Run 
@component
def dashboard():
    refreshes, set_refreshes = use_state(0)

    def effect():
        # Suppose this reads a metric from a database and the query fails.
        #
        # The page does not change, the browser console stays clean, and no
        # error reaches the model. The ONLY trace is a traceback on the
        # server -- and, as written here, it does not even appear until the
        # component unmounts. Test your Effects; the UI will not report them.
        msg = "metric query failed"
        raise RuntimeError(msg)

    use_effect(effect, dependencies=[refreshes])

    return html.div(
        html.h1("Dashboard looks fine"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_refreshes(refreshes + 1)}, "Refresh"),
    )

# TODO

Measured with a log handler attached to the reactpy logger: after mount, after three dependency changes, and after half a second idle, zero log records. The single ERROR Error in effect record appears only when the component unmounts — because core/_life_cycle_hook.py, affect_component_will_unmount is where the Effect tasks are finally awaited and their exceptions gathered (core/hooks.py parks each task on stop.wait(), so nobody looks at its result before then).

Consequences to design around:

  • Never diagnose an Effect from the page. Read the server log, and read it after navigating away — that is when failures surface.
  • Assert the external world in tests. A render assertion passes happily while your Effect is throwing; assert that the connection happened, the row was written, the file exists.

  • Catch inside the Effect and set state when a failure should be visible to the user. ReactPy will not do it for you:

    def effect():
    try:
        set_metrics(fetch_metrics())
    except Exception as error:
        set_error(str(error))   # now the user can see it

Contrast with the failure modes that are reported, so you can tell which one you have:

Symptom Cause Blank region, error in the model (debug on) or a server traceback the component body raised — e.g. an async def passed to use_effect ValueError: Cell is empty in the model an Effect registered above the state it reads Page looks fine, log silent until unmount the Effect body raised Page looks fine, log clean forever, Effect never runs wrong dependencies

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• An Effect is a synchronization process: setup, clean-up, and a dependency list that says when to redo it.
  • The clean-up of a run executes on its successor's task, before that successor's setup — so a re-synchronization is leave-then-join, in order.
  • An Effect reads the values of the render that created it. Not the latest, not necessarily the first.
  • The dependency list, not the Effect's own text, decides re-synchronization. dependencies=[] seals the body at mount.
  • Dependencies compare with == via strictly_equal, so local functions and rebuilt-but-equal containers never count as changed — and a frozen Effect is silent.
  • ReactPy will not check your dependency list: reactpy-flake8 reports hooks in branches, and missing dependencies only for inline lambdas. Write the list yourself and test the re-synchronization.
  • Children's Effects run before the parent's, siblings in reverse, and within a component in declaration order. Only the last is safe to depend on.
  • Async cancellation lands at the next await: runs can overlap and a superseded run can still write. Guard the write; don't trust the cancel.
  • A raising Effect shows nothing in the page, nothing in the browser, and nothing in the log until unmount. Verify Effects by asserting their effect on the world.
