docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Sometimes you need to do something a rendering model cannot express: focus an input, scroll an element into view, call a browser API ReactPy does not expose. In React you reach for a ref to hold the DOM node. ReactPy runs on the server and sends description-of-UI over a socket, so it has no DOM node to hand you — and the consequences shape everything on this page.

You will learn

  • Why there is no <div ref={myRef}> equivalent in ReactPy
  • What happens if you pass a "ref" attribute anyway
  • How to focus, scroll, and restyle declaratively, and when you can't
  • Why you must not mutate the DOM ReactPy renders

docs.title: There is no ref to the node
docs.text:
In React, you declare a ref, pass it to a tag, and React fills it in:

# This is React, not ReactPy. It does not work.
<div ref={myRef}>

myRef.current then holds a real DOM node you can call focus() or scrollIntoView() on. That works because React runs in the browser, next to the DOM.

ReactPy runs in your Python process. It builds a VDOM dictionary, serialises it to JSON, and sends it over a websocket; the browser-side client turns that JSON into DOM nodes. By the time a node exists, the code that described it has finished running, and there is no channel for the browser to send a node back. The "node" is on the other side of a network boundary.

docs.title: What "ref" actually does
docs.text:
It is tempting to copy the React shape and put "ref" in the attribute dict. Don't — both forms fail, and one of them fails quietly.

Passing a dict that looks like a ref is silently dropped:

html.div({"ref": {"current": None}}, "...")

The key travels to the browser as an ordinary attribute. Even if the client writes a node into that object, it writes into its own throwaway copy decoded from the JSON — nothing can travel back up the socket into your Python dict. Measured: the element renders normally, as_dict["current"] stays None forever, and there is no error and no warning. A "focus the input" button built this way simply never focuses anything.

Passing a string is worse, because it throws in the browser:

html.div({"ref": "my_ref"}, "...")

preact tries to assign to the string and the page dies with an uncaught:

TypeError: Cannot create property 'current' on string 'my_ref'

The server logs nothing. Check the browser console.

docs.title: Focusing an input
docs.text:
If the input should be focused when it first appears, that is declarative — use the browser's own attribute and let ReactPy render it:

app.py Run 
@component
def search_form():
    return html.form(
        html.label({"htmlFor": "search"}, "Search"),
        html.input({"id": "search", "type": "search", "autoFocus": True}),
    )

# TODO

No ref, no effect, no JavaScript. The attribute dict is the DOM.

To focus later, in response to a click, there is no server-side way to reach a node — but ReactPy has an escape hatch for exactly this. When the value of an on* key is a string, it runs as JavaScript in the browser (see Responding to Events). Give the element an "id" and reach it by id:

app.py Run 
@component
def search_form():
    return html.form(
        html.input({"id": "search", "type": "search"}),
        # A string in a handler slot runs in the browser (see Responding to
        # Events), which is the only way to reach an element by id.
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": "document.getElementById('search').focus()",
            },
            "Focus the input",
        ),
    )

# TODO

This is the honest equivalent of myRef.current.focus(). The trade-off is that the code doing the focusing now lives in a string, on the server, unchecked by your linter and invisible to your type checker. Keep it to one-line calls.

Re-rendering does not re-focus

A common wish is "re-fire autoFocus when the user clicks again". Changing the element's "key" really does remount it — ReactPy destroys and recreates the node, and a child's state resets — but autoFocus does not re-trigger on that remount, because the browser only applies autofocus on initial page load. Measured: after re-keying, focus stayed on the button that was clicked. Use the inline-JS form above instead.

docs.title: Scrolling to an element
docs.text:
The React version of this example keeps three refs, one per image, and calls scrollIntoView() on each. In ReactPy you give each item an id and let the browser find it:

app.pydata.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def cat_friends():
    return html(
        html.div(
            {"id": "carousel", "className": "carousel"},
            [
                html.li(
                    {"key": person["id"], "id": f"friend-{person['id']}"},
                    html.img({"src": get_image_url(person), "alt": person["name"]}),
                )
                for person in friends
            ],
        ),
        html.div(
            {"className": "buttons"},
            [
                html.button(
                    {
                        "key": person["id"],
                        "onClick": f"document.getElementById('friend-{person['id']}')"
                        ".scrollIntoView({behavior: 'smooth', inline: 'center'})",
                    },
                    person["name"].split()[0],
                )
                for person in friends
            ],
        ),
    )

friends = [
    {
        "id": 0,
        "name": "Creola Katherine Johnson",
        "image_id": "MK3eW3A",
    },
    {
        "id": 1,
        "name": "Mario José Molina-Pasquel Henríquez",
        "image_id": "mynHUSa",
    },
    {
        "id": 2,
        "name": "Mohammad Abdus Salam",
        "image_id": "bE7W1ji",
    },
]


def get_image_url(person):
    return f"https://i.imgur.com/{person['image_id']}.jpg"

.carousel {
    display: flex;
    gap: 10px;
    overflow-x: auto;
    scroll-snap-type: x mandatory;
    padding: 10px 0;
}

.carousel li {
    list-style: none;
    flex: 0 0 auto;
    scroll-snap-align: center;
}

.carousel img {
    width: 130px;
    height: 130px;
    border-radius: 100%;
    object-fit: cover;
    display: block;
}

.buttons {
    display: flex;
    gap: 10px;
    margin-top: 10px;
}

# TODO

Note the f-string building the JavaScript: the id is interpolated server-side, so each button gets its own literal scrollIntoView call. That is also the risk — the interpolation is not escaped. Interpolating anything a user controls into that string is an injection hole; interpolate your own integer keys, like person["id"] above, and nothing else.

docs.title: Showing and hiding
docs.text:
Toggling visibility is the case where React's ref example and ReactPy agree on the goal but differ completely in method. There is no element.style.display = 'none'; you render the difference:

app.py Run 
@component
def todo_list():
    shown, set_shown = use_state(True)

    return html(
        html.div(
            {"id": "todo", "hidden": not shown},
            html.p("Learn ReactPy"),
            html.p("Build something"),
        ),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_shown(not shown)},
            "Hide" if shown else "Show",
        ),
    )

# TODO

Pressing the button flips shown, the "hidden" attribute changes, and the client updates the element. Any style you would have set by hand goes in the attribute dict the same way — "style" accepts a dict of camelCased CSS properties:

html.div(
    {"style": {"color": "red", "fontSize": "20px", "fontWeight": "700"}},
    "styled text",
)

Changing a value in that dict from state re-renders the element with the new style, which is what you almost always want instead of touching element.style from the browser.

docs.title: Two component-only features you cannot port
docs.text:
Two sections of React's version of this page have no ReactPy equivalent at all, and it is worth knowing they are absent rather than hunting for them:

  • useImperativeHandle / forwardRef. React lets a component expose a hand-picked slice of its DOM to a parent. There is no forward_ref and no use_imperative_handle in ReactPy — a component cannot hand a parent a node it does not have. If a parent must drive a child, pass a prop and let the child render it.
  • flushSync. React lets you force a synchronous repaint so that a subsequent DOM read sees the new values. ReactPy renders by sending a message, so there is nothing to flush; the client applies updates as they arrive.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
Refs are an escape hatch, and here the hatch is even narrower: it is a string of JavaScript.

  • Prefer declarative. If the change can be expressed as an attribute, a class, a "style" dict, a "key", or a conditional render, write that. It survives re-renders, and it is visible to your tools.
  • Keep inline JavaScript to one call. "document.getElementById('x').focus()" is fine. A multi-statement script embedded in an attribute dict is unmaintainable and unlintable.
  • Never interpolate user input into an inline-JS string. Build the JS from your own constants and ids.
  • Do not mutate DOM that ReactPy renders. This is the same hazard as in React, and it is easier to hit because nothing warns you. If an inline-JS handler calls remove() on an element ReactPy believes it owns, the next render that tries to update that element is working against a node that is gone. Toggle a state value and let ReactPy remove it.
  • You may touch nodes ReactPy never manages. An element ReactPy renders empty and never writes children to is yours to fill from inline JavaScript. It has no reason to update that subtree, so nothing conflicts.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• ReactPy is server-side: there is no DOM node to store in a ref, and {"ref": ...} either vanishes (dict) or throws in the browser (string).
  • Express focus, visibility, and styling declaratively first: "autoFocus", "hidden", "style", conditional rendering.
  • For the imperative remainder — focus on click, scroll into view — give elements ids and use the inline-JavaScript handler form, keeping each snippet to a single call and interpolating only trusted values.
  • forwardRef, useImperativeHandle, and flushSync do not exist in ReactPy.
  • Never mutate nodes ReactPy owns; remove them by changing state instead.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
"Registering a client" in ReactPy means telling the browser three things: which component to mount, where the socket lives, and which JavaScript modules it may import. The executors do all three for you. This page is for the cases where they cannot — a page you render yourself, several components on one document, or a component written in JavaScript that the server has to describe but cannot run.

You will learn

  • What mountReactPy needs, and how to write the call by hand
  • How to mount several components in one document, and what breaks if you mount twice into the same node
  • How an author-supplied import map suppresses ReactPy's own
  • How to register a JavaScript component so ReactPy can render it

docs.title: The three registrations
docs.text:
What Where it lives Who normally writes it The root component to mount componentPath in mountReactPy, and the backend's component registry the executor's HTML template The socket address pathPrefix + componentPath, concatenated the executor's HTML template Bare-specifier resolution ("react", "react-dom") <script type="importmap"> injected only if no <script type="importmap" id="reactpy-importmap"> exists

The full reference for the JavaScript side, including every option and its quirks, is Client API. This page covers the parts the executors normally hide.

docs.title: Mounting by hand
docs.text:
The minimal call needs only an element and a path:

<div id="app"></div>
<script type="module">
    import { mountReactPy } from "/reactpy/static/index.js";

    mountReactPy({
        mountElement: document.getElementById("app"),
        pathPrefix: "/reactpy/",
        componentPath: "main.counter/",
    });
</script>

Three details are load-bearing, all verified in a real browser:

  • pathPrefix must start and end with /. The client builds the socket URL by string concatenation, so "reactpy/" on a host with a port throws TypeError: Failed to construct 'URL': Invalid URL — and on a host without a port silently connects to a hostname like example.comreactpy. The failure mode changes with deployment, which is what makes it nasty.
  • componentPath carries a trailing slash and must name a component the server knows. "main.counter/", not "main.counter".
  • The import must be <script type="module">. The bundle statically imports two sibling chunks; a classic script fails with SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module before anything ReactPy-related runs.

The component itself lives in a Python module the backend can import. Under ReactPyMiddleware, componentPath is the dotted path you listed in root_components plus a slash — the middleware matches ^{path_prefix}(?P<dotted_path>[a-zA-Z0-9_.]+)/$. Under ReactPy there is one root and componentPath must be omitted: the client builds the URL as pathPrefix + componentPath (static/index.js) and ReactPy.match_dispatch_path compares the result against dispatcher_path exactly, so a stray "/" produces /reactpy//, matches nothing, and the socket dies while the server logs a NotImplementedError — one whose %s placeholders were never filled in, so the line reads ("ReactPy app received unsupported request of type '%s' at path '%s'", 'websocket', '/reactpy//'). Grep for unsupported request of type, not for the literal you expect. See The executors route differently.

Nothing stops you from mounting twice into the same element

mountReactPy returns nothing and keeps no registry, so a second call into the same node is not rejected. Verified in Chrome with two mounts pointing at one <div>: the second component's markup wins the visible tree, and the first keeps a fully live websocket — its socket stays OPEN, its server-side layout stays alive, and events it registered can still reach the server. You get one visible component and one invisible one consuming a connection and a layout each.

The client does not unmount the first subtree; it renders over it. Nothing you can do from JavaScript will stop it — there is no unmountReactPy. The only clean teardown is navigation or reload. If you are building a client-side router that swaps components, mount into a fresh element each time and remove the old one, accepting that the orphaned layout lives until the page does.

docs.title: Several components in one document
docs.text:
Each mountReactPy call opens its own websocket and gets its own Layout, which means separate hook state and no shared memory between them. Verified with two counters on one page: incrementing one left the other at zero, and the console logged two independent [ReactPy] Connected! lines.

<div id="header"></div>
<div id="cart"></div>
<script type="module">
    import { mountReactPy } from "/reactpy/static/index.js";

    mountReactPy({
        mountElement: document.getElementById("header"),
        pathPrefix: "/reactpy/",
        componentPath: "shop.header/",
    });
    mountReactPy({
        mountElement: document.getElementById("cart"),
        pathPrefix: "/reactpy/",
        componentPath: "shop.cart/",
    });
</script>

Under ReactPyMiddleware, register both:

from reactpy.executors.asgi import ReactPyMiddleware

app = ReactPyMiddleware(
    starlette_app,
    root_components=["shop.header", "shop.cart"],
)

Separate roots do not share state

Two components on one page are two layouts. They cannot use_state their way to agreement, and there is no event bus between them. If they must agree, either make them one component tree, or pass the shared value in as props from a single root — see Sharing State Between Components and Passing Data Deeply with Context.

You can also mount later, from a click handler or after a fetch — the call is ordinary JavaScript and nothing about it is privileged.

docs.title: Import maps
docs.text:
An import map is only needed when your model contains an importSource, which is what JavaScript components produce. Bare specifiers like "react" and "react-dom" are resolved by the map; without one, the client falls back to its bundled preact and says so on console.debug, at a level most consoles filter out.

The executors inject a map only when one with a specific id is absent:

if (!document.querySelector("#reactpy-importmap")) { /* inject ReactPy's map */ }

The trigger is the id, not the content. Write your own map and give it that id, or ReactPy adds a second one alongside yours and the browser reports a conflict on the "react" rule. See The import map for the three-case table.

ReactPy ships a helper that produces exactly that element, so you can decide the framework per page:

from reactpy.executors.asgi import ReactPy
from reactpy.reactjs import import_reactjs

app = ReactPy(
    counter,
    html_head=html.head(import_reactjs("react", version="19")),
)

import_reactjs(framework=None, version=None, use_local=False) returns a html.script already carrying {"type": "importmap", "id": "reactpy-importmap"}, so putting it in html_head suppresses the automatic injection. "preact" (the default) maps the four react* specifiers onto esm.sh/v135/preact@10/compat; "react" uses real React at the version you pass ("19" if you omit it); use_local=True maps them to ReactPy's own bundled chunks, which is what the default injection does anyway.

use_local rejects companions

import_reactjs(use_local=True, framework="react") raises ValueError: use_local cannot be used with framework or version. Choose one source or the other.

docs.title: Registering a JavaScript component
docs.text:
Python describes; the browser runs. A JavaScript component is any ES module that exports the names you ask for. It can also export a bind function that tells the client how to create, render, and unmount nodes in a container the client owns — and that is what you want, because the alternative is silent:

// vdom.tsx, loadImportSource
let { bind } = module;
if (typeof bind !== "function") {
    bind = await infer_bind_from_environment();
}

bind is therefore optional. Leave it out and the client infers one — first trying real React through the import map, then falling back to its bundled preact — and logs ReactPy will render JavaScript components using internal bindings for 'react' at console.debug, with no [ReactPy] prefix. Your module still mounts and appears to work, so a missing or misnamed bind is easy to miss. Ship it explicitly:

badge.jsmain.py Run 
// The bind() export tells the client how to put nodes on screen. It receives
// the container element the client owns and a config object carrying
// sendMessage/onMessage, and must hand back create/render/unmount.
export function bind(node, config) {
  return {
    create: (component, props, children) => {
      const el = document.createElement("span");
      el.className = props.tone || "default";
      el.textContent = props.label + ": " + (children || []).join("");
      el.addEventListener("click", () => {
        if (props.onPick) {
          props.onPick({ label: props.label });
        }
      });
      node.appendChild(el);
      return el;
    },
    render: (el) => {
      node.innerHTML = "";
      node.appendChild(el);
    },
    unmount: () => {
      node.innerHTML = "";
    },
  };
}

// One export per component you intend to register by name.
export function Badge(props, children) {
  return { props, children };
}

HERE = Path(__file__).parent

Badge = component_from_file(
    HERE / "badge.js",
    "Badge",
    name="badge",
    fallback=html.p("loading badge..."),
)


@component
def product_card(title, tone):
    return html.div(
        html.h2(title),
        Badge({"label": "in stock", "tone": tone}, "ready to ship"),
    )

# TODO

The registration call gives you a normal constructor:

from pathlib import Path

from reactpy.reactjs import component_from_file

Badge = component_from_file(Path("badge.js"), "Badge", name="badge")

Badge({"label": "alpha", "tone": "warn"}, "hello")

which produces the element the client executes:

{
    "tagName": "Badge",
    "attributes": {"label": "alpha", "tone": "warn"},
    "children": ["hello"],
    "importSource": {
        "source": "badge.js",
        "sourceType": "NAME",
        "fallback": null,
        "unmountBeforeUpdate": false
    }
}

importSource is the whole mechanism: sourceType is "NAME" or "URL", and the client resolves them differently — "NAME" becomes await import("/<prefix>modules/" + source) and "URL" becomes await import(source) directly.

Verified in Chrome: the badge rendered as <span class="warn">alpha: hello</span>, with the <span> coming from JavaScript and the wrapper from Python.

docs.title: The four registration functions
docs.text:
All in reactpy.reactjs, all returning a VdomConstructor (or a list, if you pass a list of names):

Function Source Typical use component_from_url(url, import_names, ...) a URL the browser can reach a CDN build, a dev server component_from_npm(package, import_names, version="latest", cdn="https://esm.sh/v135", bundle=...) an NPM package, rewritten to a CDN URL third-party React components component_from_file(file, import_names, name="", symlink=False, ...) a file on disk, copied into the web-modules dir a component you ship in your package component_from_string(content, import_names, name="", ...) a string of JavaScript tiny inline modules, tests

reactpy.web.module_from_url / module_from_file / module_from_string / export do the same thing and are all deprecated — they warn(DeprecationWarning) telling you to use the component_from_* form.

docs.title: Serving the module
docs.text:
A "NAME" module is copied into config.REACTPY_WEB_MODULES_DIR and fetched from {path_prefix}modules/ — which is why a custom backend must serve that directory, and why the built-in ones do:

from reactpy.config import REACTPY_WEB_MODULES_DIR

modules_app = ServeStaticASGI(not_found, root=REACTPY_WEB_MODULES_DIR.current, prefix="/reactpy/modules/")

The default web-modules directory is a temporary directory

REACTPY_WEB_MODULES_DIR defaults to a fresh TemporaryDirectory created at import (config.py). It is per process: read it in one process and you get a path that does not exist in the next. Two consequences:

  • Under a multi-worker server, workers get different directories and a module registered by one is 404 for another. Pin it — pass web_modules_dir=Path(...) to the executor or set the REACTPY_WEB_MODULES_DIR environment variable to one shared path.
  • The upstream config docstring says the directory must be treated as a black box. Do not read from it yourself; register modules and let the client fetch them.

A "URL" module needs no serving at all — the browser goes to the URL. That makes CDN registration the simpler path when you have a network, and a self-hosted directory the right one for offline or air-gapped use.

docs.title: Options worth knowing
docs.text:
• fallback — what to show while the module loads. Pass an element (html.p("loading...")). Without it there is nothing, and a slow module reads as a broken page.
  • allow_children — set False for a component that takes props only. Passing a child then raises TypeError: 'Badge' nodes cannot have children. at the call site rather than silently dropping it.
  • unmount_before_update — unmount and rebuild on every update. Only for packages that fail to re-render on prop change; it costs a full DOM rebuild each time.
  • resolve_imports — parse the module to learn its export names, so a typo fails in Python at registration instead of in the browser at render. Off by default for component_from_file/component_from_string; it walks imports to resolve_imports_depth (default 5).

A wrong export name fails at different times depending on a flag

With resolve_imports=True, component_from_file("badge.js", "Nope") raises immediately:

ValueError: 'badge.js' does not contain 'Nope'

With it off — the default — you get no Python error, and instead the browser logs, verbatim including the typo:

Module from source {"source": "badge.js", "sourceType": "NAME"} does not export Nope

and nothing renders. Turn the flag on during development; it turns a console hunt into a stack trace.

A bad bind is a console error, not an exception

If your module's bind does not return an object with create, render, and unmount, the client logs <source> returned an impropper binding — misspelling in the upstream string — and renders nothing. Python stays happy. The message goes to console.error, so it is easy to miss when the component simply is not there.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Registering a client means the component path, the socket prefix, and an import map — the executors write all three for you.
  • pathPrefix needs both slashes, componentPath needs its trailing slash, and the import must be a module script.
  • Mount each component into its own element. Mounting twice into one node leaves a live, invisible websocket you cannot close.
  • Multiple mounts on a page are multiple layouts with no shared state; pass shared values as props instead.
  • ReactPy injects an import map only if no element with id="reactpy-importmap" exists — the id, not the content, is the trigger. import_reactjs() produces that element.
  • JavaScript components are ordinary ES modules with a bind export, registered with component_from_url/_npm/_file/_string, and served from {prefix}modules/ unless they are URL-sourced.
  • The default web-modules directory is a per-process temporary directory; pin it under any multi-worker deployment.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Passing data through components that only hand it on is tedious and easy to get wrong. Context lets a component read a value that an ancestor provides, skipping the middle of the tree. In ReactPy it is purely a plumbing tool — it carries values down and nothing else — and there are three behaviours worth knowing before you rely on it.

You will learn

  • How to recognise prop drilling worth replacing
  • The three steps: create, use, provide
  • Why a component cannot read the context it provides
  • Why removing a provider throws away the subtree's state

docs.title: The problem with passing props
docs.text:
Here is a list of places, and each row is coloured by the current theme. Only the deepest component cares about the theme, but the prop has to travel through everyone:

app.py Run 
PLACES = ["Almaty", "Astana", "Shymkent", "Karaganda", "Turkestan"]


@component
def place_label(place, theme):
    color = "coral" if theme == "dark" else "black"
    return html.li({"style": {"color": color}}, place)


@component
def place_list(places, theme):
    return html.ul([place_label(place, theme) for place in places])


@component
def list_of_places(places, theme):
    # Renders its children inside the list box.
    return html.div(
        {"style": {"border": "1px solid #ccc", "padding": "8px"}},
        place_list(places, theme),
    )


@component
def section(places, theme):
    return html.section(html.h3("Places"), list_of_places(places, theme))


@component
def app():
    theme, set_theme = use_state("dark")

    def toggle(event):
        set_theme("light" if theme == "dark" else "dark")

    return html.div(
        html.button(
            {"onClick": toggle}, f"Switch to {'light' if theme == 'dark' else 'dark'}"
        ),
        html.p({"id": "theme"}, f"theme={theme}"),
        html.div({"id": "places"}, section(PLACES, theme)),
    )

# TODO

app holds the theme. section receives it, list_of_places receives it, place_list receives it, and only place_label reads it. Three components mention a value they never use, and adding a row to list_of_places means threading theme through one more signature.

That is the shape worth replacing: a prop that a component only forwards. If a component would use a prop itself, pass it as a prop — that is easier to trace.

docs.title: Context: an alternative to passing props
docs.text: Three steps, and the order matters: create the context, read it where you need it, and provide it somewhere above.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the context
docs.text:
A context is an object you create once, usually at module level:

from reactpy import create_context

ThemeContext = create_context("light")

The argument is the default — what use_context returns when no provider sits above the reader. Pick something that renders sensibly on its own, because a component will occasionally render without a wrapper.

The object is matched by identity, so create it once and import it everywhere. Two create_context calls are two unrelated contexts even with identical defaults.

docs.title: Step 2: Use the context
docs.text:
In the component that needs the value:

from reactpy import use_context

theme = use_context(ThemeContext)

No parameter, no forwarding. The components in between never learn the value exists:

app.py Run 
ThemeContext = create_context("light")


@component
def place_label(place):
    # Reads the theme directly: no prop had to travel here.
    theme = use_context(ThemeContext)
    color = "coral" if theme == "dark" else "black"
    return html.li({"style": {"color": color}}, place)


@component
def place_list(places):
    # No theme parameter, and none to forward.
    return html.ul([place_label(place) for place in places])


@component
def list_of_places(places):
    return html.div(
        {"style": {"border": "1px solid #ccc", "padding": "8px"}},
        place_list(places),
    )


@component
def section(places):
    return html.section(html.h3("Places"), list_of_places(places))


@component
def app():
    theme, set_theme = use_state("dark")

    def toggle(event):
        set_theme("light" if theme == "dark" else "dark")

    return html.div(
        html.button(
            {"onClick": toggle}, f"Switch to {'light' if theme == 'dark' else 'dark'}"
        ),
        html.p({"id": "theme"}, f"theme={theme}"),
        # The provider is a component: it renders its children with no wrapper.
        ThemeContext(html.div({"id": "places"}, section(PLACES)), value=theme),
    )

# TODO

place_label calls use_context, and place_list, list_of_places, and section no longer mention theme at all. Verified: this version and the prop-drilling version above render the same five rows with the same colours, and both respond to the toggle identically.

Without any provider at all, every reader gets the default:

app.py Run 
ThemeContext = create_context("light")


@component
def label(text):
    theme = use_context(ThemeContext)
    return html.p({"id": f"label-{text}"}, f"{text}: theme={theme}")


@component
def app():
    # Nothing wraps these in ThemeContext, so use_context falls back to the
    # value passed to create_context.
    return html.div(html.h3("No provider"), label("a"), label("b"))

# TODO

Both labels read theme=light — the value from create_context, not None. This is what makes it safe to reuse a component in a page that never sets the theme up.

docs.title: Step 3: Provide the context
docs.text:
Wrap the subtree you want to see the value:

ThemeContext(children, value=theme)

The context object is a component. Calling it produces a provider element whose children render in place, adding no wrapper of its own — verified: the element with id="places" contains the whole tree with nothing extra between it and the list.

A provider only covers its own children. A sibling rendered after it sees the default, and a provider nested inside another one shadows it for its own subtree:

app.py Run 
@component
def deep_label(tag):
    # Three levels down, still no prop in sight.
    return html.p({"id": tag}, f"{tag} sees: {use_context(ThemeContext)}")


@component
def middle():
    return html.div(html.h4("middle"), deep_label("deep"))


@component
def wrapper():
    # An intermediate component that neither receives nor forwards a theme.
    return html.div(html.h4("wrapper"), middle())


@component
def inner_scope():
    return html.div(
        deep_label("inner"),
        # A provider nested inside another one shadows it for its subtree.
        ThemeContext(deep_label("deepest"), value="innermost"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return html.div(
        # Same context, several providers, several scopes.
        deep_label("outside"),
        ThemeContext(wrapper(), value="outer"),
        ThemeContext(inner_scope(), value="middle-provider"),
        deep_label("after"),
    )

# TODO

Verified readouts: outside and after see light (the default), deep — three levels below outer — sees outer, inner sees middle-provider, and deepest, inside the nested provider, sees innermost. The nearest provider wins; the search walks up and stops.

Pitfall

use_context belongs in the component that uses the value, not in the parent that places it. Write ThemeContext(deep_label(), value="x"), not ThemeContext(html.p(f"{use_context(ThemeContext)}"), value="x"). The second one calls the hook while the parent renders, so it reads the parent's context — the provider has not been entered yet. This is easy to hit by accident: a label formatted inline above a provider reported the default light while its own provider supplied middle-provider.

docs.title: Using and providing context from the same component
docs.text:
A component cannot read the context it provides. The provider applies to its children, and a component is not its own child:

app.py Run 
@component
def label(text):
    return html.p({"id": f"label-{text}"}, f"{text} sees: {use_context(ThemeContext)}")


@component
def section():
    theme, set_theme = use_state("dark")

    def toggle(event):
        set_theme("light" if theme == "dark" else "dark")

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": toggle}, "toggle"),
        # Reads the context the way any *consumer* does...
        html.p({"id": "self"}, f"section itself sees: {use_context(ThemeContext)}"),
        # ...and provides it for everything below, which is not itself.
        ThemeContext(label("child"), value=theme),
    )


@component
def app():
    return html.div(html.h3("Self-provider"), section(), label("outside"))

# TODO

The child reads child sees: dark while the component that rendered the provider reads section itself sees: light — the default, before and after the toggle. If the component needs the value too, read the state it comes from: theme is right there in section, so use it directly.

docs.title: Context passes through intermediate components
docs.text:
The value reaches any depth as long as the provider is a genuine ancestor. wrapper and middle in the nesting example above receive no props at all, and deep still resolves the theme.

This is also what makes context the right tool for a component you do not control — a third-party list renderer, a slot you pass children into. Anything rendered inside the provider's subtree can read it, however deep.

Note

A component's state, however, belongs to its position in the tree. Two sibling subtrees that both mount draft() get two independent pieces of state (verified: x#1 and x#2 under two providers of the same context). Context shares what flows down from the provider; it does not merge instances below it.

docs.title: Removing a provider resets the subtree below it
docs.text:
A provider is a component, so adding or removing one changes the shape of the tree — and ReactPy identifies a component by where it sits. The subtree below is unmounted and rebuilt, with its state. Press change value and the draft you typed survives; press toggle provider and it is gone:

app.py Run 
@component
def draft():
    # State owned by the leaf. It is lost if this component is remounted.
    text, set_text = use_state("")
    body = use_ref(0)
    body.current += 1
    return html.div(
        html.input(
            {
                "value": text,
                "onChange": lambda event: set_text(event["target"]["value"]),
                "placeholder": "type something",
            }
        ),
        html.p(
            {"id": "draft"},
            f"draft={text!r} renders={body.current} theme={use_context(ThemeContext)}",
        ),
    )


@component
def panel():
    wrap, set_wrap = use_state(True)
    theme, set_theme = use_state("dark")

    def toggle_wrap(event):
        # Adding or removing the provider changes the shape of the tree, so the
        # subtree below is unmounted and rebuilt: the draft text is lost.
        set_wrap(not wrap)

    def toggle_theme(event):
        # Changing only the value keeps the same tree: the draft survives.
        set_theme("light" if theme == "dark" else "dark")

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": toggle_wrap}, "toggle provider"),
        html.button({"onClick": toggle_theme}, "change value"),
        (ThemeContext(draft(), value=theme) if wrap else draft()),
    )


@component
def app():
    return html.div(html.h3("Provider identity"), panel())

# TODO

Verified sequence. Type hello: the readout shows draft='hello'. Press change value: draft='hello' ... theme=light, and the component's own render counter keeps counting, which is how you can tell it is the same instance — a changed value does not disturb the tree. Press toggle provider: the counter resets to renders=1 and draft=''. The leaf was unmounted and a fresh one mounted, so its state is not stale, it is new.

Flipping the conditional back does not restore it either — that is a third instance.

The rule: keep the provider in the tree and vary only its value. Toggling a theme off should be Theme(child, value="light"), not Theme(child, value=...) if dark else child.

Do not reach for key to fix this — it does not. Verified across four variants: a conditional provider loses the state, and adding a stable key to the child beneath it loses the state too. What keeps the state is having the provider element present in both branches, so the tree shape never changes.

The version that works moves the condition inside value, expressing "not provided" as the default rather than as an absent wrapper:

app.py Run 
@component
def draft():
    # State owned by the leaf. It survives as long as this component keeps the
    # same position in the tree.
    text, set_text = use_state("")
    body = use_ref(0)
    body.current += 1
    return html.div(
        html.input(
            {
                "value": text,
                "onChange": lambda event: set_text(event["target"]["value"]),
                "placeholder": "type something",
            }
        ),
        html.p(
            {"id": "draft"},
            f"draft={text!r} renders={body.current} theme={use_context(ThemeContext)}",
        ),
    )


@component
def panel():
    provide, set_provide = use_state(True)
    theme, set_theme = use_state("dark")

    def toggle_wrap(event):
        set_provide(not provide)

    def toggle_theme(event):
        set_theme("light" if theme == "dark" else "dark")

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": toggle_wrap}, "toggle provider"),
        html.button({"onClick": toggle_theme}, "change value"),
        # The provider is always in the tree, so nothing below it is unmounted.
        # "Not provided" is expressed as the default value, not as an absent
        # wrapper.
        ThemeContext(draft(), value=theme if provide else "light"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return html.div(html.h3("Provider always present"), panel())

# TODO

Type hello, press toggle provider: draft='hello' ... theme=light, and the render counter keeps counting. Same buttons, same user-visible behaviour as the broken version, state intact.

This is a special case of a rule that applies to all components, not just providers — see Preserving and Resetting State. Context makes it easier to hit by accident, because "wrap this in a provider" is a natural thing to put behind an if.

docs.title: Before you use context
docs.text:
• Does a component only forward the prop? If it uses the value, pass a prop. If it is one level deep, pass a prop. Context pays off when the value crosses several levels that do not care about it.
  • Is the value genuinely shared? A value used by one subtree is simpler as a prop, and easier to trace when it is wrong.
  • Are you hoping it saves renders? It does not. ReactPy has no render bailout, so when the provider re-renders, everything below it re-renders too, whether or not the value changed. Context is a plumbing feature, never a performance one — see What context does not do.
  • Do you want to change a value from below? Then context is the wrong shape. Put the state in a common ancestor and pass the setter (or a dispatch) down with it — see Scaling Up with Reducer and Context.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Context replaces props that components only forward. It does not replace props a component actually uses.
  • Three steps: create_context(default) once at module level, use_context(Context) in the component that needs it, Context(children, value=...) above that subtree.
  • The default from create_context is what an unprovided reader gets — not None. Verified.
  • The nearest provider wins; a nested provider shadows the outer one, and siblings outside a provider see the default. Verified across four readers.
  • Call use_context in the component that uses the value. Formatting it inside the parent's arguments reads the parent's context.
  • A component cannot read the context it provides — verified reading the default while its own child read the provided value. Read the underlying state instead.
  • Keep the provider element in the tree and vary only its value. Conditionally wrapping in a provider unmounts the subtree and discards its state; a key does not prevent it (verified).
  • Context is plumbing only: no render bailout, no reactivity, no shared state. See Use Context for the parameter-level detail and error messages.

docs.text:

  • Scaling Up with Reducer and Context — sharing a reducer and its dispatch, the usual next step
  • Choosing the State Structure — what belongs in state at all, and where
  • Queueing a Series of State Updates — the updater form, when two handlers race

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ReactPy components use props to communicate with each other. Every parent component can pass some information to its child components by giving them props. Props might remind you of HTML attributes, but you can pass any Python value through them, including dictionaries, lists, and functions.

You will learn

  • How to pass props to a component
  • How to read props from a component
  • How to specify default values for props
  • How to pass some markup to a component
  • How props change over time

docs.title: Familiar props
docs.text:
Props are the information that you pass to a tag. For example, className, src, alt, width, and height are some of the props you can pass to an <img>:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def avatar():
    return html.img(
        {
            "className": "avatar",
            "src": "https://i.imgur.com/1bX5QH6.jpg",
            "alt": "Lin Lanying",
            "width": 100,
            "height": 100,
        }
    )


@component
def profile():
    return avatar()


@component
def app():
    return profile()

body {
    min-height: 120px;
}

.avatar {
    margin: 20px;
    border-radius: 50%;
}

# TODO

The props you can pass to an html.img tag are predefined (the browser conforms to the HTML standard), and they keep their familiar camelCase spelling because they are handed straight to the DOM. But you can pass any props to your own components, such as avatar(), to customize them. Here's how!

docs.title: Passing props to a component
docs.text:
In this code, the profile() component isn't passing any props to its child component, avatar():

@component
def profile():
    return avatar()

You can give avatar() some props in two steps.

docs.title: Step 1: Pass props to the child component
docs.text:
First, pass some props to avatar(). For example, let's pass two props: person (a dictionary), and size (a number):

@component
def profile():
    return html.div(
        avatar(
            person={"name": "Lin Lanying", "image_id": "1bX5QH6"},
            size=100,
        ),
    )

Unlike an HTML tag, a component you write takes its props as ordinary Python arguments. There is no attributes dictionary here — the values land directly in the function's parameters.

docs.title: Step 2: Read props inside the child component
docs.text:
You read props by listing their names person, size directly after def avatar. This lets you use them inside the avatar() code, like you would with a variable.

@component
def avatar(person, size):
    # person and size are available here
    ...

Add some logic to avatar() that uses the person and size props for rendering, and you're done.

Now you can configure avatar() to render in many different ways with different props. Try tweaking the values!

app.pystyles.css Run 
def get_image_url(person, size="s"):
    return f"https://i.imgur.com/{person['image_id']}{size}.jpg"


@component
def avatar(person, size):
    return html.img(
        {
            "className": "avatar",
            "src": get_image_url(person),
            "alt": person["name"],
            "width": size,
            "height": size,
        }
    )


@component
def profile():
    return html.div(
        avatar(
            person={"name": "Lin Lanying", "image_id": "1bX5QH6"},
            size=100,
        ),
        avatar(
            person={"name": "Katsuko Saruhashi", "image_id": "YfeOqp2"},
            size=100,
        ),
    )

body {
    min-height: 120px;
}

.avatar {
    margin: 20px;
    border-radius: 50%;
}

# TODO

Props let you think about parent and child components independently. For example, you can change the person or the size props inside profile() without having to think about how avatar() uses them. Similarly, you can change how avatar() uses these props, without looking at profile().

You can think of props like "knobs" that you can adjust. They serve the same role as arguments serve for functions—in fact, props are the only argument to your component! A component is nothing but a Python function, and a function can only accept arguments.

Every argument is a prop

In JavaScript, a component receives a single props object which you then destructure into function Avatar({ person, size }). Python needs no such ceremony: the parameters are the props.

@component
def avatar(person, size): ...

is already the direct, Pythonic form of that idea. But it means every parameter you declare is a prop a caller can pass by name — so keep the signature of a component to the values it actually renders.

docs.title: Specifying a default value for a prop
docs.text:
If you want to give a prop a default value to fall back on when no value is specified, put = and the default value right after the parameter:

@component
def avatar(person, size=100):
    # ...

Now, if avatar(person=...) is rendered with no size prop, the size will be set to 100.

The default value is used only when the caller omits the argument entirely. If you pass size=None or size=0, the default value will not be used — Python applies defaults for missing arguments, not for "empty" ones.

app.pystyles.css Run 
def get_image_url(person, size="s"):
    return f"https://i.imgur.com/{person['image_id']}{size}.jpg"


@component
def avatar(person, size=100):
    return html.img(
        {
            "className": "avatar",
            "src": get_image_url(person),
            "alt": person["name"],
            "width": size,
            "height": size,
        }
    )


@component
def profile():
    return html.div(
        avatar(person={"name": "Lin Lanying", "image_id": "1bX5QH6"}),
        avatar(
            person={"name": "Katsuko Saruhashi", "image_id": "YfeOqp2"},
            size=200,
        ),
    )

body {
    min-height: 120px;
}

.avatar {
    margin: 20px;
    border-radius: 50%;
}

# TODO

docs.title: Forwarding props with keyword argument unpacking
docs.text:
Sometimes, passing props gets very repetitive:

@component
def profile(person, size, is_sepia, thick_border):
    return html.div(
        {"className": "card"},
        avatar(
            person=person,
            size=size,
            is_sepia=is_sepia,
            thick_border=thick_border,
        ),
    )

There's nothing wrong with repetitive code—it can be more legible. But at times you may value conciseness. Some components forward all of their props to their children, like this profile() does with avatar(). Because they don't use any of their props directly, it can make sense to use Python's keyword argument unpacking instead:

@component
def profile(**props):
    return html.div({"className": "card"}, avatar(**props))

This forwards all of profile()'s props to the avatar() without listing each of their names. Inside the function, props is a plain dictionary, so you can also merge or filter it before forwarding.

Use unpacking with restraint. If you're using it in every other component, something is wrong. It hides the component's real interface, so neither your editor nor a reader can tell which props it accepts. Often, it indicates that you should split your components and pass children as arguments. More on that next!

app.pystyles.css Run 
def get_image_url(person, size="s"):
    return f"https://i.imgur.com/{person['image_id']}{size}.jpg"


@component
def avatar(person, size=100):
    return html.img(
        {
            "className": "avatar",
            "src": get_image_url(person),
            "alt": person["name"],
            "width": size,
            "height": size,
        }
    )


@component
def profile(**props):
    return html.div({"className": "card"}, avatar(**props))


@component
def app():
    return profile(
        person={"name": "Lin Lanying", "image_id": "1bX5QH6"},
        size=100,
    )

body {
    min-height: 120px;
}

.avatar {
    margin: 20px;
    border-radius: 50%;
}

# TODO

docs.title: Passing children to a component
docs.text:
It is common to nest built-in browser tags:

html.div(html.img())

Sometimes you'll want to nest your own components the same way:

card(avatar())

Anything you pass positionally lands in a *args parameter of the parent component, which is the ReactPy equivalent of React's children prop. For example, the card() component below collects its children and renders them inside a wrapper <div>:

app.pystyles.css Run 
def get_image_url(person, size="s"):
    return f"https://i.imgur.com/{person['image_id']}{size}.jpg"


@component
def avatar(person, size=100):
    return html.img(
        {
            "className": "avatar",
            "src": get_image_url(person),
            "alt": person["name"],
            "width": size,
            "height": size,
        }
    )


@component
def card(*children):
    return html.div({"className": "card"}, *children)


@component
def profile():
    return card(
        avatar(person={"name": "Katsuko Saruhashi", "image_id": "YfeOqp2"}),
    )

body {
    min-height: 120px;
}

.avatar {
    margin: 20px;
    border-radius: 50%;
}

# TODO

Try replacing the avatar() inside card() with some text to see how the card() component can wrap any nested content. It doesn't need to "know" what's being rendered inside of it. You will see this flexible pattern in many places.

You can think of a component with a *children parameter as having a "hole" that can be "filled in" by its parent components with arbitrary markup. You will often use children for visual wrappers: panels, grids, etc.

Keyword-only children

Because positional arguments become children, a component that accepts both should make its props keyword-only to avoid an ambiguous signature:

@component
def card(*children, title=None):
    return html.div({"className": "card"}, title, *children)

Now title= can never be mistaken for a child.

docs.title: How props change over time
docs.text:
The clock() component below receives two props from its parent component: color and time.

Try changing the color in the select box below:

app.py Run 
@component
def clock(color, time):
    return html.h1({"style": {"color": color}}, time)


@component
def app():
    color, set_color = use_state("lightcoral")
    now, set_now = use_state(datetime.now(timezone.utc))

    async def tick():
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(1)
            set_now(datetime.now(timezone.utc))

    use_async_effect(tick, dependencies=[])

    def handle_change(event):
        set_color(event["target"]["value"])

    return html.div(
        html.p(
            "Pick a color: ",
            html.select(
                {"value": color, "onChange": handle_change},
                html.option({"value": "lightcoral"}, "lightcoral"),
                html.option({"value": "midnightblue"}, "midnightblue"),
                html.option({"value": "rebeccapurple"}, "rebeccapurple"),
            ),
        ),
        clock(color=color, time=now.strftime("%H:%M:%S")),
    )

# TODO

This example illustrates that a component may receive different props over time. Props are not always static! Here, the time prop changes every second, and the color prop changes when you select another color. Props reflect a component's data at any point in time, rather than only in the beginning.

However, props are immutable—a term from computer science meaning "unchangeable". When a component needs to change its props (for example, in response to a user interaction or new data), it will have to "ask" its parent component to pass it different props—a new set of arguments! ReactPy re-renders the child with those new values rather than editing the old ones in place.

Don't try to change props

When you need to respond to user input (like changing the selected color), you will need to "set state", which you can learn about in State: A Component's Memory. Assigning to a prop parameter inside a component only rebinds the local name; the parent's value is untouched, and the next render overwrites it anyway.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• To pass props, add them as arguments to the component call, just like you would with an HTML tag's attributes.
  • To read props, list them as parameters: def avatar(person, size).
  • You can specify a default value like size=100, which is used when the caller omits the argument.
  • You can forward all props with def profile(**props) and avatar(**props), but don't overuse it!
  • Nested children like card(avatar()) arrive as a *children parameter.
  • Props are read-only snapshots in time: every render receives a new version of props.
  • You can't change props. When you need interactivity, you'll need to set state.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
State is isolated between components. ReactPy keeps track of which state belongs to which component based on their place in the UI tree. You can control when to preserve state and when to reset it between re-renders.

You will learn

  • How state is tied to a position in the tree
  • When state is preserved, and when it resets
  • How to reset a component's state on purpose, with position or with key
  • Why defining a component inside another one loses state

docs.title: State is tied to a position in the tree
docs.text:
When you give a component state, you might think the state "lives" inside the component. It doesn't. ReactPy holds the state, and associates each piece of it with a component by where that component sits in the tree.

Here counter() is rendered at two different positions:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def counter():
    score, set_score = use_state(0)

    return html.div(
        {"className": "counter"},
        html.h1(score),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_score(score + 1)}, "Add one"),
    )


@component
def app():
    # The same component function, rendered at two different positions in the
    # tree. ReactPy tracks state by position, so these two counters each get
    # their own score.
    return html.div(counter(), counter())

.counter {
    width: 130px;
    text-align: center;
    border: 1px solid #aaa;
    border-radius: 4px;
    padding: 12px;
    margin: 0 12px 12px 0;
}

.counter h1 {
    font-size: 18px;
    margin: 0 0 6px;
}

.fancy {
    background: #ffffd8;
    border-color: #e0b400;
}

# TODO

Click both counters and notice they don't affect each other. Each position gets its own state, so counter() is really two separate components here.

It makes no difference whether you build the child once and reuse it, or call it twice:

one_counter = counter()
html.div(one_counter, one_counter)  # same as: html.div(counter(), counter())

Both render counter() at two positions, and both get independent state.

docs.title: Same component at the same position preserves state
docs.text:
In this example a checkbox flips a prop on the counter, but there is always exactly one counter() at that position:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def counter(is_fancy):
    score, set_score = use_state(0)

    return html.div(
        {"className": f"counter{' fancy' if is_fancy else ''}"},
        html.h1(score),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_score(score + 1)}, "Add one"),
    )


@component
def app():
    is_fancy, set_is_fancy = use_state(False)

    return html.div(
        # Only one counter() is ever rendered at this position, and it is the
        # same component function either way, so ReactPy keeps its state across
        # the toggle; only the is_fancy prop changes.
        counter(is_fancy),
        html.label(
            html.input(
                {
                    "type": "checkbox",
                    "checked": is_fancy,
                    "onChange": lambda event: set_is_fancy(event["target"]["checked"]),
                }
            ),
            "Use fancy styling",
        ),
    )

.counter {
    width: 130px;
    text-align: center;
    border: 1px solid #aaa;
    border-radius: 4px;
    padding: 12px;
    margin: 0 12px 12px 0;
}

.counter h1 {
    font-size: 18px;
    margin: 0 0 6px;
}

.fancy {
    background: #ffffd8;
    border-color: #e0b400;
}

# TODO

Raise the score, then toggle "Use fancy styling". The score survives, because the same component stayed at the same position — only its is_fancy prop changed.

This is the default, and usually what you want.

docs.title: Different components at the same position reset state
docs.text:
Now switch the child to something else entirely:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def counter():
    score, set_score = use_state(0)

    return html.div(
        {"className": "counter"},
        html.h1(score),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_score(score + 1)}, "Add one"),
    )


@component
def app():
    is_paused, set_is_paused = use_state(False)

    return html.div(
        # Switching between a counter() and an html.p() puts a *different* kind
        # of child at this position, so ReactPy discards the counter's state
        # and starts a brand new one when the break ends.
        html.p("See you later!") if is_paused else counter(),
        html.label(
            html.input(
                {
                    "type": "checkbox",
                    "checked": is_paused,
                    "onChange": lambda event: set_is_paused(event["target"]["checked"]),
                }
            ),
            "Take a break",
        ),
    )

.counter {
    width: 130px;
    text-align: center;
    border: 1px solid #aaa;
    border-radius: 4px;
    padding: 12px;
    margin: 0 12px 12px 0;
}

.counter h1 {
    font-size: 18px;
    margin: 0 0 6px;
}

.fancy {
    background: #ffffd8;
    border-color: #e0b400;
}

# TODO

Raise the score, tick "Take a break", then untick it. The counter comes back at zero. Replacing the child with an html.p() destroyed the old state, and the returning counter() is a brand new one.

The rule so far: same component at the same position keeps state; anything else at that position does not.

docs.title: Resetting state at the same position
docs.text:
Suppose a scoreboard shows one player's score at a time, and "Next player" swaps Taylor for Sarah:

counter("Taylor") if is_player_a else counter("Sarah")

Both branches call counter() at the same position, so ReactPy sees one component whose person prop changed — and the score follows the player over. That's wrong here: Taylor's score and Sarah's score are different things.

There are two ways to get them treated as separate components.

docs.title: Option 1: render them at different positions
docs.text:
Give each player a container that always exists:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def counter(person):
    score, set_score = use_state(0)

    return html.div(
        {"className": "counter"},
        html.h1(f"{person}'s score: {score}"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_score(score + 1)}, "Add one"),
    )


@component
def scoreboard():
    is_player_a, set_is_player_a = use_state(True)

    return html.div(
        # Two containers that always exist, so each player's counter has its
        # own position in the tree. Only one holds a counter at a time, and the
        # container that loses it destroys that state.
        #
        # Do not "simplify" this to *([] if cond else [counter(...)]): an empty
        # expansion contributes no children, so both counters end up at
        # position 0 and ReactPy treats them as one component -- no reset.
        html.div(counter("Taylor") if is_player_a else None),
        html.div(counter("Sarah") if not is_player_a else None),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_is_player_a(not is_player_a)},
            "Next player!",
        ),
    )

.counter {
    width: 130px;
    text-align: center;
    border: 1px solid #aaa;
    border-radius: 4px;
    padding: 12px;
    margin: 0 12px 12px 0;
}

.counter h1 {
    font-size: 18px;
    margin: 0 0 6px;
}

.fancy {
    background: #ffffd8;
    border-color: #e0b400;
}

# TODO
  • At first the first html.div() holds Taylor's counter and the second is empty.
  • After "Next player!" the first is empty and the second holds Sarah's.

Each counter is destroyed when its container empties, so every switch starts from zero. This works nicely when there are only a couple of alternatives to lay out side by side.

An empty list expansion is not a placeholder

The tempting Python spelling of "or nothing" collapses the whole mechanism:

*([] if not is_player_a else [counter("Taylor")]),  # wrong: no child at all

An empty expansion contributes no children, so the two counters land at position 0 and ReactPy treats them as one component — no reset, and Sarah inherits Taylor's score. It is the two html.div() containers above that create the positions. (React avoids this because false still occupies a JSX slot.)

docs.title: Option 2: reset state with a key
docs.text:
You have seen "key" when rendering lists. Keys are not only for lists. By default ReactPy identifies a child by its index within its parent — "the first counter", "the second counter" — and a key lets you say this is not the first counter, it is Taylor's counter.

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def counter(person):
    score, set_score = use_state(0)

    return html.div(
        {"className": "counter"},
        html.h1(f"{person}'s score: {score}"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_score(score + 1)}, "Add one"),
    )


@component
def scoreboard():
    is_player_a, set_is_player_a = use_state(True)

    return html.div(
        # Both branches render counter() at the same position, so without a key
        # ReactPy would treat them as the same component and carry the score
        # from one player to the next. The key gives each player their own
        # identity, so switching players resets the score.
        counter("Taylor", key="Taylor")
        if is_player_a
        else counter("Sarah", key="Sarah"),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_is_player_a(not is_player_a)},
            "Next player!",
        ),
    )

.counter {
    width: 130px;
    text-align: center;
    border: 1px solid #aaa;
    border-radius: 4px;
    padding: 12px;
    margin: 0 12px 12px 0;
}

.counter h1 {
    font-size: 18px;
    margin: 0 0 6px;
}

.fancy {
    background: #ffffd8;
    border-color: #e0b400;
}

# TODO

The two counters no longer share state, even though they appear in the same place. Give "key" a value that identifies what the component is — the contact id, the player name — not where it sits.

Keys are only unique within their parent

Two components with the same key under different parents are fine: keys are not globally unique, they only identify a position within one parent.

Note also that an unkeyed child is identified by its index, which shares a namespace with explicit keys. html.div(contact_list(...), chat(to, key=0)) raises ValueError: Duplicate keys [0], because the unkeyed contact_list() already occupies position 0. Prefix your keys (key=f"chat-{to['id']}") or key all the siblings.

docs.title: Resetting a form with a key
docs.text:
Keying is most useful for forms. In this chat app, chat() holds the half-written message:

app.pydata.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def chat(contact):
    draft, set_draft = use_state("")

    return html.section(
        {"className": "chat"},
        html.h3(f"To: {contact['name']} <{contact['email']}>"),
        html.textarea({"placeholder": "Write a message", "value": draft}),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_draft("")}, "Clear"),
    )


@component
def contact_list(selected_contact, on_select):
    return html.section(
        {"className": "contact-list"},
        html.ul(
            [
                html.li(
                    {"key": contact["id"]},
                    html.button(
                        {"onClick": lambda event, c=contact: on_select(c)},
                        contact["name"],
                    ),
                )
                for contact in contacts
            ]
        ),
    )


@component
def messenger():
    to, set_to = use_state(contacts[0])

    return html.div(
        contact_list(to, set_to),
        # Without the key, switching contacts keeps the half-written message,
        # because chat() stays at the same position. The key ties the draft to
        # the contact instead of the slot.
        chat(to, key=f"chat-{to['id']}"),
    )

contacts = [
    {"id": 0, "name": "Taylor", "email": "taylor@mail.com"},
    {"id": 1, "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@mail.com"},
    {"id": 2, "name": "Bob", "email": "bob@mail.com"},
]

.contact-list ul {
    list-style: none;
    padding: 0;
    display: flex;
    gap: 8px;
}

.chat {
    border: 1px solid #aaa;
    border-radius: 4px;
    padding: 10px;
    margin-top: 10px;
}

.chat textarea {
    display: block;
    width: 100%;
    min-height: 60px;
}

# TODO

Type a draft, then pick another contact. Without the key the draft would follow you over, because chat() never left its position. With key=f"chat-{to['id']}" the draft belongs to the conversation rather than the slot.

docs.title: Keeping state for a component that is no longer rendered
docs.text:
Resetting is often not what you want — a real chat app should restore the draft when you go back to Alice. Keying does not do that: an unmounted component loses its state, so returning to Taylor starts at zero. Options:

  • Render all the chats and hide the inactive ones with CSS. Nothing is unmounted, so state survives. Great for small UIs, wasteful when the hidden trees are large.
  • Lift the state up and keep each recipient's draft in the parent, in a dict keyed by recipient. Children coming and going stops mattering. This is the most common answer.
  • Keep it outside ReactPy entirely — a database, or localStorage in the browser — which you want anyway if a draft should survive a page reload.

Whichever you choose, a chat with Alice is conceptually different from a chat with Bob, so it still deserves a distinct key.

docs.title: Nested component definitions reset state accidentally
docs.text:
This one bites quietly:

@component
def outer():
    @component
    def nested():
        value, set_value = use_state(...)
        ...

    return html.div(nested())

Every render of outer() creates a new function object for nested(). A new function is a new component, so ReactPy discards the old state and mounts a fresh one on every render — your state resets itself, with no warning. Measured: a nested child's mount counter climbs by one on each parent render, while a module-level child mounted once.

Define components at module level, or pass data through props.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• ReactPy keeps state for as long as the same component is rendered at the same position.
  • State is not stored in the call that produced the VDOM; it belongs to the tree position you put it in.
  • Force a subtree to reset by rendering it at a different position, or by giving it a different "key".
  • Unkeyed siblings are identified by index, in the same key namespace as explicit keys — prefix your keys to avoid ValueError: Duplicate keys.
  • Don't define a component inside another component, or you'll reset state by accident.
