docs.title: Queueing a Series of State Updates
Overview
docs.text:
Setting a state variable will queue another render. But sometimes you might want to perform multiple operations on the value before queueing the next render. To do this, it helps to understand how ReactPy batches state updates.

You will learn

  • How ReactPy batches state updates
  • Updating the same state multiple times before the next render
  • What happens when you mix values and updater functions

docs.title: ReactPy batches state updates
docs.text:
You might expect that clicking the "+3" button will increment the counter three times, because it calls set_number(number + 1) three times:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def counter():
    number, set_number = use_state(0)

    def handle_click(event):
        set_number(number + 1)
        set_number(number + 1)
        set_number(number + 1)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(number),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, "+3"),
    )

button {
    display: inline-block;
    margin: 10px;
    font-size: 20px;
}

h1 {
    display: inline-block;
    margin: 10px;
    width: 30px;
    text-align: center;
}

# TODO

It lands on 1, not 3. Two things combine to produce that.

First, as you may recall from State as a Snapshot, each render's state values are fixed. Inside this render's event handler number is always 0, no matter how many times you call the setter, so all three lines evaluate to the same call:

set_number(0 + 1)
set_number(0 + 1)
set_number(0 + 1)

Second, a synchronous event handler never yields, so nothing can render until it returns. ReactPy's setter applies its value immediately and only flags the component for re-render (core/hooks.py, _CurrentState.dispatch), and the flag is deduplicated — a component already flagged is not scheduled twice (core/_life_cycle_hook.py, LifeCycleHook.schedule_render and its _scheduled_render guard). Three calls to the setter inside one def therefore leave one render queued, showing 1.

This lets you update several state variables — even across several components — without triggering a render for each. It also avoids "half-finished" renders in which only some variables have been updated.

Batching stops at an await

The batching above is a side effect of a synchronous handler, and it is narrower than React's. Because the values are already stored, an await hands the event loop to the queued render task — which clears the flag, so the next setter schedules a second render. Nothing about the handler is special; the only difference is who holds the loop.

Measured in a real browser, watching every value the counter takes after a single click:

Handler Observed sequence three set_number(lambda n: n + 1) in a def 0 → 3 (one render) the same, with await asyncio.sleep(0.3) between the calls 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 (three renders)

React 18+ would batch both into a single render. In ReactPy, an async def handler that awaits between updates renders — and repaints — in between. If that flicker matters, do the awaits first and set state once at the end, or collect the results and make a single setter call.

ReactPy does not batch across multiple intentional events like clicks — each click is handled separately. This ensures that, for example, if the first click disables a form, the second click cannot submit it again.

docs.title: Updating the same state multiple times before the next render
docs.text:
It is an uncommon use case, but if you would like to update the same state variable multiple times before the next render, pass a function that computes the next value from the previous one instead of the value itself: set_number(lambda n: n + 1). This is a way of saying "do something with the current state" rather than "replace the state".

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def counter():
    number, set_number = use_state(0)

    def handle_click(event):
        set_number(lambda n: n + 1)
        set_number(lambda n: n + 1)
        set_number(lambda n: n + 1)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(number),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, "+3"),
    )

button {
    display: inline-block;
    margin: 10px;
    font-size: 20px;
}

h1 {
    display: inline-block;
    margin: 10px;
    width: 30px;
    text-align: center;
}

# TODO

This time the counter reaches 3, because each updater receives whatever the previous one produced.

docs.title: What happens if you update state after replacing it
docs.text:
What does this handler produce?

app.py Run 
@component
def counter():
    number, set_number = use_state(0)

    def handle_click(event):
        # number is 0 for this render, so this reads as set_number(5).
        set_number(number + 5)
        set_number(lambda n: n + 1)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(number),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, "Increase the number"),
    )

# TODO

Step by step, starting from number == 0:

  1. set_number(number + 5) — number is 0, so this is set_number(5). The state becomes 5.
  2. set_number(lambda n: n + 1) — an updater, so it runs against the current value: 5 + 1.

The next render shows 6, confirmed by rendering the example.

set_number(5) behaves like set_number(lambda n: 5)

A plain value ignores the argument entirely — it just replaces. That equivalence is what makes the next case surprising.

docs.title: What happens if you replace state after updating it
docs.text:
One more:

app.py Run 
@component
def counter():
    number, set_number = use_state(0)

    def handle_click(event):
        set_number(number + 5)
        set_number(lambda n: n + 1)
        set_number(42)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(number),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, "Increase the number"),
    )

# TODO
  1. set_number(number + 5) — number is 0, so state becomes 5.
  2. set_number(lambda n: n + 1) — updater, so 5 + 1 = 6.
  3. set_number(42) — a plain value, so state becomes 42.

The result is 42. The two updaters still ran, and their work was then overwritten — which is the same answer React's queue produces, arrived at by a different route.

To summarize what you can pass to a state setter:

  • An updater function (e.g. lambda n: n + 1) is applied to the current value.
  • Any other value (e.g. 5) replaces the state outright, discarding whatever the updaters produced.

Updater functions run while your handler runs, inside the setter call itself, so — like components — they must be pure. Don't set state from inside one or perform side effects there. They are eager, not deferred, which means the one thing they can still get wrong is the closure: a name the updater reads from the enclosing render is the value that render saw, not the current one. The updater argument is the only value guaranteed fresh, so take everything you need from n.

An updater that raises fails silently

Updaters run eagerly, inside the setter call itself (core/hooks.py, _CurrentState.dispatch calls new(self.value) before scheduling anything) — not later during rendering. Verified: an updater's side effect lands before the line after its set_number(...).

That has a nasty consequence. If an updater raises, the state is never assigned and no render is scheduled; ReactPy logs Failed to execute event handler on the server and swallows the error. The browser shows nothing, the console stays quiet, and the component simply stops responding to that button. Reproduced: a lambda x: 1 / 0 updater produced a server-side traceback and then an indefinite absence of any render.

Two habits follow: keep updaters to one pure expression, and when a counter "stops working" with no error in the browser, check the server log for Failed to execute event handler.

docs.title: Naming conventions
docs.text:
Name the updater's argument after the state variable it updates. Python has no single-letter convention as strong as JavaScript's, but the intent is the same — the argument is the previous value:

set_enabled(lambda enabled: not enabled)
set_last_name(lambda last_name: last_name[::-1])
set_friend_count(lambda friend_count: friend_count * 2)

For clarity, prefer a descriptive name over n: lambda previous: previous + 1 reads better in a handler that also does other work.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Setting state does not change the variable in the existing render; it requests a new render.
  • ReactPy processes state updates after a synchronous event handler has finished. That is batching.
  • Batching does not survive an await inside an async def handler — each await can flush a render with partial updates.
  • To update the same state several times in one handler, use updater functions: set_number(lambda n: n + 1).
  • A plain value replaces the state and discards earlier updater results; an updater is applied to the current value.
  • Updater functions must be pure, and ReactPy will not check them for you.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Welcome to the ReactPy documentation! This page will give you an introduction to the 80% of React concepts that you will use on a daily basis.

You will learn

  • How to create and nest components
  • How to add markup and styles
  • How to display data
  • How to render conditions and lists
  • How to respond to events and update the screen
  • How to share data between components

docs.title: Creating and nesting components
docs.text:
React apps are made out of components. A component is a piece of the UI (user interface) that has its own logic and appearance. A component can be as small as a button, or as large as an entire page.

React components are Python functions that return markup:

@component
def my_button():
    return html.button("I'm a button!")

Now that you've declared my_button, you can nest it into another component:

@component
def my_app():
    return html.div(
        html.h1("Welcome to my app"),
        my_button(),
    )

Have a look at the result:

app.py Run 
from reactpy import component, html


@component
def my_button():
    return html.button("I'm a button!")


@component
def my_app():
    return html.div(
        html.h1("Welcome to my app"),
        my_button(),
    )

# TODO

docs.title: Adding styles
docs.text:
In React, you specify a CSS class with className. It works the same way as the HTML class attribute:

html.img({"className": "avatar"})

Then you write the CSS rules for it in a separate CSS file:

/* In your CSS */
.avatar {
    border-radius: 50%;
}

React does not prescribe how you add CSS files. In the simplest case, you'll add a <link> tag to your HTML. If you use a build tool or web framework, consult its documentation to learn how to add a CSS file to your project.

docs.title: Displaying data
docs.text:
You can fetch data from a variety of sources and directly embed it into your components. You can also use the style attribute when your styles depend on JavaScript variables.

app.pystyles.css Run 
from reactpy import component, html

user = {
    "name": "Hedy Lamarr",
    "image_url": "https://i.imgur.com/yXOvdOSs.jpg",
    "image_size": 90,
}


@component
def profile():
    return html.div(
        html.h3(user["name"]),
        html.img(
            {
                "className": "avatar",
                "src": user["image_url"],
                "alt": f"Photo of {user['name']}",
                "style": {
                    "width": user["image_size"],
                    "height": user["image_size"],
                },
            }
        ),
    )

.avatar {
    border-radius: 50%;
}

.large {
    border: 4px solid gold;
}

# TODO

docs.title: Conditional rendering
docs.text:
In React, there is no special syntax for writing conditions. Instead, you'll use the same techniques as you use when writing regular Python code. For example, you can use an if statement to conditionally include components:

@component
def my_component():
    if is_logged_in:
        content = admin_panel()
    else:
        content = login_form()
    return html.div(content)

If you prefer more compact code, you can use the ternary operator.:

@component
def my_component():
    return html.div(admin_panel() if is_logged_in else login_form())

When you don't need the else branch, unpack a list that is either one item or empty — and not Python's logical and, which React's cond && <X/> habit tempts people into writing:

@component
def my_component():
    # No `else` branch needed: unpack a one-item list, or an empty one.
    # Unpack the *component*, never the dict it returns -- `*admin_panel()`
    # would iterate the dict and emit its keys as text.
    # `is_logged_in and admin_panel()` would render the word "False".
    return html.div(*([admin_panel()] if is_logged_in else []))

is_logged_in and admin_panel() returns False when the test fails, and ReactPy renders that as the literal word False on the page — only None and an absent child disappear. See Conditional Rendering for the same trap with numbers.

All of these approaches also work for conditionally specifying attributes. If you're unfamiliar with some of this Python syntax, you can start by always using if...else.

docs.title: Rendering lists
docs.text:
You will rely on Python features like for loop and list comprehension to render lists of components.

For example, let's say you have an array of products:

products = [
    {"title": "Cabbage", "id": 1},
    {"title": "Garlic", "id": 2},
    {"title": "Apple", "id": 3},
]

Inside your component, use list comprehension to transform an array of products into an array of <li> items:

list_items = [html.li({"key": product["id"]}, product["title"]) for product in products]

Notice how <li> has a key attribute. For each item in a list, you should pass a string or a number that uniquely identifies that item among its siblings. Usually, a key should be coming from your data, such as a database ID. React uses your keys to know what happened if you later insert, delete, or reorder the items.

app.py Run 
from reactpy import component, html

products = [
    {"title": "Cabbage", "is_fruit": False, "id": 1},
    {"title": "Garlic", "is_fruit": False, "id": 2},
    {"title": "Apple", "is_fruit": True, "id": 3},
]


@component
def shopping_list():
    list_items = [
        html.li(
            {
                "key": product["id"],
                "style": {"color": "magenta" if product["is_fruit"] else "darkgreen"},
            },
            product["title"],
        )
        for product in products
    ]

    return html.ul(list_items)

docs.title: Responding to events
docs.text:
You can respond to events by declaring event handler functions inside your components:

@component
def my_button():
    def handle_click(event):
        print("You clicked me!")

    return html.button(
        {"onClick": handle_click},
        "Click me",
    )

Notice how "onClick": handle_click has no parentheses at the end! Do not call the event handler function: you only need to pass it down. React will call your event handler when the user clicks the button.

docs.title: Updating the screen
docs.text:
Often, you'll want your component to "remember" some information and display it. For example, maybe you want to count the number of times a button is clicked. To do this, add state to your component.

First, import use_state from reactpy:

from reactpy import use_state

Now you can declare a state variable inside your component:

@component
def my_button():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)
    # ...

You’ll get two things from use_state: the current state (count), and the function that lets you update it (set_count). You can give them any names, but the convention is to write something, set_something = ....

The first time the button is displayed, count will be 0 because you passed 0 to use_state(). When you want to change state, call set_count() and pass the new value to it. Clicking this button will increment the counter:

@component
def my_button():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    def handle_click(event):
        set_count(count + 1)

    return html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, f"Clicked {count} times")

React will call your component function again. This time, count will be 1. Then it will be 2. And so on.

If you render the same component multiple times, each will get its own state. Click each button separately:

app.pystyles.css Run 
from reactpy import component, html, use_state


@component
def my_app():
    return html.div(
        html.h1("Counters that update separately"),
        my_button(),
        my_button(),
    )


@component
def my_button():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    def handle_click(event):
        set_count(count + 1)

    return html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, f"Clicked {count} times")

button {
    display: block;
    margin-bottom: 5px;
}

# TODO

Notice how each button "remembers" its own count state and doesn't affect other buttons.

docs.title: Using Hooks
docs.text:
Functions starting with use are called Hooks. use_state is a built-in Hook provided by ReactPy. You can find other built-in Hooks in the API reference. You can also write your own Hooks by combining the existing ones.

Hooks are more restrictive than other functions. You can only call Hooks at the top of your components (or other Hooks). If you want to use use_state in a condition or a loop, extract a new component and put it there.

docs.title: Sharing data between components
docs.text:
In the previous example, each my_button had its own independent count, and when each button was clicked, only the count for the button clicked changed:

However, often you'll need components to share data and always update together.

To make both my_button components display the same count and update together, you need to move the state from the individual buttons "upwards" to the closest component containing all of them.

In this example, it is my_app.

Now when you click either button, the count in my_app will change, which will change both of the counts in my_button. Here's how you can express this in code.

First, move the state up from my_button into my_app:

@component
def my_app():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    def handle_click(event):
        set_count(count + 1)

    return html.div(
        html.h1("Counters that update separately"),
        my_button(),
        my_button(),
    )


@component
def my_button(): ...  # this code is being moved up into `my_app`

Then, pass the state down from my_app to each my_button, together with the shared click handler. You can pass information to my_button using props:

@component
def my_app():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    def handle_click(event):
        set_count(count + 1)

    return html.div(
        html.h1("Counters that update together"),
        my_button(count, handle_click),
        my_button(count, handle_click),
    )

The information you pass down like this is called props. Now the my_app component contains the count state and the handle_click event handler, and passes both of them down as props to each of the buttons.

Finally, change my_button to read the props you have passed from its parent component:

@component
def my_button(count, on_click):
    return html.button({"onClick": on_click}, f"Clicked {count} times")

When you click the button, the on_click handler fires. Each button's on_click prop was set to the handle_click function inside my_app, so the code inside of it runs. That code calls set_count(count + 1), incrementing the count state variable. The new count value is passed as a prop to each button, so they all show the new value. This is called "lifting state up". By moving state up, you've shared it between components.

app.pystyles.css Run 
from reactpy import component, html, use_state


@component
def my_app():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    def handle_click(event):
        set_count(count + 1)

    return html.div(
        html.h1("Counters that update together"),
        my_button(count, handle_click),
        my_button(count, handle_click),
    )


@component
def my_button(count, on_click):
    return html.button({"onClick": on_click}, f"Clicked {count} times")

button {
    display: block;
    margin-bottom: 5px;
}

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ReactPy provides a declarative way to manipulate the UI. Instead of manipulating individual pieces of the UI directly, you describe the different states your component can be in, and switch between them in response to the user input. This is similar to how designers think about the UI.

You will learn

  • How declarative UI programming differs from imperative UI programming
  • How to enumerate the different visual states your component can be in
  • How to trigger the changes between the different visual states from code

docs.title: How declarative UI compares to imperative
docs.text:
When you design UI interactions, you probably think about how the UI changes in response to user actions. Consider a form that lets the user submit an answer:

  • When you type something into the form, the "Submit" button becomes enabled.
  • When you press "Submit", both the form and the button become disabled, and a spinner appears.
  • If the request succeeds, the form gets hidden, and a "Thank you" message appears.
  • If the request fails, an error message appears, and the form becomes enabled again.

In imperative programming, the above corresponds directly to how you implement interaction. You have to write the exact instructions to manipulate the UI depending on what just happened. Here's another way to think about this: imagine riding next to someone in a car and telling them turn by turn where to go. They don't know where you want to go, they just follow your commands. (And if you get the directions wrong, you end up in the wrong place!) It's called imperative because you have to "command" each element, from the spinner to the button, telling the computer how to update the UI:

async function handleFormSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    disable(textarea);
    disable(button);
    show(loadingMessage);
    hide(errorMessage);
    try {
        await submitForm(textarea.value);
        show(successMessage);
        hide(form);
    } catch (err) {
        show(errorMessage);
        errorMessage.textContent = err.message;
    } finally {
        hide(loadingMessage);
        enable(textarea);
        enable(button);
    }
}

function handleTextareaChange() {
    if (textarea.value.length === 0) {
        disable(button);
    } else {
        enable(button);
    }
}

function hide(el) {
    el.style.display = "none";
}

function show(el) {
    el.style.display = "";
}

function enable(el) {
    el.disabled = false;
}

function disable(el) {
    el.disabled = true;
}

Manipulating the UI imperatively works well enough for isolated examples, but it gets exponentially more difficult to manage in more complex systems. Adding a new UI element or a new interaction would require carefully checking all existing code to make sure you haven't introduced a bug (for example, forgetting to show or hide something).

ReactPy was built to solve this problem.

In ReactPy, you don't directly manipulate the UI — meaning you don't enable, disable, show, or hide components directly. Instead, you declare what you want to show, and ReactPy figures out how to update the UI.

This is less a stylistic preference than a physical constraint: a ReactPy server component has no DOM to manipulate. Your code runs on the server and returns a description of the UI; there is no element object to set .style.display on. See Manipulating the DOM with Refs for the one narrow escape hatch and why it rarely helps.

docs.title: Thinking about UI declaratively
docs.text:
You've learned that CSS enables declarative string-based styling so you can describe what to show, not how to show it. You can also learn to think about your ReactPy components declaratively.

ReactPy stands at the intersection of design and computer science, so both of these ideas are sources of inspiration. To think declaratively, take each possible state of a component's UI, break it down into a list, and then write code to describe each state at once.

docs.title: Step 1: Identify your component's different visual states
docs.text:
First, enumerate the visual states of the UI the user could see:

  1. Empty — the form has no answer yet.
  2. Typing — the form has a non-empty answer.
  3. Submitting — the answer has just been submitted and nothing else can be clicked.
  4. Success — the user wants to see a "Correct!" message instead of the form.
  5. Error — like Typing, but with an error message.

Replace the form() component with a mock that returns the right UI based on a status prop:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def form(status="empty"):
    """A mock: the visual states are driven by a prop, not by real logic.

    Rendering this with each status is the fastest way to enumerate the states
    before writing any interaction code.
    """
    if status == "success":
        return html.h1("That's right!")

    return html.div(
        html.h2("City quiz"),
        html.p(
            "In which city is there a billboard that turns air into drinkable water?"
        ),
        html.form(
            html.textarea({"disabled": status == "submitting"}),
            html.br(),
            html.button(
                {"disabled": status in {"empty", "submitting"}},
                "Submit",
            ),
            html.p({"className": "Error"}, "Good guess but a wrong answer. Try again!")
            if status == "error"
            else None,
        ),
    )

.Error {
    color: red;
}

textarea {
    width: 260px;
    height: 60px;
}

section {
    border-bottom: 1px solid #ddd;
    padding-bottom: 10px;
    margin-bottom: 10px;
}

h4 {
    margin: 4px 0;
    color: #888;
}

# TODO

The status prop is a "mock" of the state inside the component, and controls which visual states the user will see. This mock is controlled by a prop called status with a default value of "empty".

You could call that prop anything you like, the naming is not important. Try changing the default to status="success" to see the success message appear. Mocking lets you quickly iterate on the UI before you wire up any logic.

Two details in that mock are worth pointing out. "Typing" and "Submitting" render the same layout, differing only in whether the controls are disabled — so the difference is expressed as data, not as a different branch of markup:

html.button({"disabled": status in {"empty", "submitting"}}, "Submit")

And the error state deliberately keeps the form enabled. A state that showed an error while also disabling the input would leave the user unable to correct their answer — imperative code has to enforce that by hand, and it is exactly the kind of thing that gets forgotten.

Displaying many visual states at once

You could try each state by editing the source, but then you'd navigate back and forth many times. It's often easier to show many visual states at once, like a "living styleguide" or "storybook":

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def form(status="empty"):
    if status == "success":
        return html.h1("That's right!")

    return html.div(
        html.h2("City quiz"),
        html.p(
            "In which city is there a billboard that turns air into drinkable water?"
        ),
        html.form(
            html.textarea({"disabled": status == "submitting"}),
            html.br(),
            html.button(
                {"disabled": status in {"empty", "submitting"}},
                "Submit",
            ),
            html.p({"className": "Error"}, "Good guess but a wrong answer. Try again!")
            if status == "error"
            else None,
        ),
    )


@component
def app():
    """Render every visual state at once -- a "living styleguide".

    Because the mock is driven by a prop, all five states can sit side by side
    in one page and be compared without clicking anything.
    """
    statuses = ["empty", "typing", "submitting", "success", "error"]
    return html.div(
        [
            html.section(
                {"key": status},
                html.h4(status),
                form(status=status),
            )
            for status in statuses
        ]
    )

.Error {
    color: red;
}

textarea {
    width: 260px;
    height: 60px;
}

section {
    border-bottom: 1px solid #ddd;
    padding-bottom: 10px;
    margin-bottom: 10px;
}

h4 {
    margin: 4px 0;
    color: #888;
}

# TODO

Because the mock is driven by a prop, all five states mount side by side and can be compared without a single click. Each html.section() carries a "key" because they are children of a list.

docs.title: Step 2: Determine what triggers those state changes
docs.text:
There are two categories of "cause" that can change state in a component:

  • Input (the user typing, clicking, changing a field, and so on)
  • Output (one of the component's effects completing — a timer firing, a request finishing, and so on)

In both cases, you must set state variables to update the UI.

  • Changing the text input (human) should switch it from the Empty state to the Typing state or back, depending on whether the text box is empty or not.
  • Clicking the Submit button (human) should switch it to the Submitting state.
  • A successful response (computer) should switch it to the Success state.
  • A failed response (computer) should switch it to the Error state with the matching error message.

Notice that human inputs often require event handlers!

docs.title: Step 3: Represent the state in memory with use_state
docs.text:
Next you'll need to represent the visual states of your component in memory with use_state.

Simplicity is key: each piece of state is a "moving piece", and you want as few "moving pieces" as possible. More complexity leads to more bugs!

Start with the state that everyone agrees on:

answer, set_answer = use_state("")
error, set_error = use_state("")

Then you'll need a state variable representing which of the visual states to display. There's usually more than a single way to represent that in memory, so you'll need to experiment with it. Here's one attempt — a boolean per state:

is_empty, set_is_empty = use_state(True)
is_typing, set_is_typing = use_state(False)
is_submitting, set_is_submitting = use_state(False)
is_success, set_is_success = use_state(False)
is_error, set_is_error = use_state(False)

docs.title: Step 4: Remove any non-essential state variables
docs.text:
You want to avoid duplication in the state content so you're only tracking what is essential. Spending a little time refactoring your state structure will make your components easier to understand, reduce duplication, and avoid unintended meanings. Your goal is to prevent the cases where the state in memory doesn't represent any valid UI that you'd want a user to see.

Take those five booleans:

  • is_typing and is_submitting can't both be True. A paradox usually means the state is not constrained enough. There are four possible combinations of two booleans, but only three correspond to valid states. To remove the "impossible" state, combine them into a status that must be one of three values: "typing", "submitting", or "success".
  • Another paradox: is_empty and is_typing can't both be True. Keeping them as separate state variables risks them going out of sync and causing bugs. Fortunately you can drop is_empty and check len(answer) == 0 instead.
  • is_error is not needed, because you can check if error instead.

After this clean-up you're left with 3 (down from 7!) essential state variables:

answer, set_answer = use_state("")
error, set_error = use_state("")
status, set_status = use_state("typing")  # 'typing', 'submitting', or 'success'

You know they are essential, because you can't remove any of them without breaking the functionality.

Eliminating 'impossible' states with a reducer

These three variables are a good enough representation of this form's state. However, some intermediate states still don't fully make sense. A non-empty error doesn't make sense when status is "success". Reducers let you unify multiple state variables into a single object and consolidate all the related logic!

docs.title: Step 5: Connect the event handlers to set state
docs.text:
Finally, connect the event handlers to the set functions from Step 4:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def form():
    answer, set_answer = use_state("")
    error, set_error = use_state("")
    status, set_status = use_state("typing")  # 'typing', 'submitting', or 'success'

    if status == "success":
        return html.h1("That's right!")

    async def handle_submit(event):
        # Awaiting inside the handler is fine: ReactPy still suppresses the
        # form's default navigation, because it detects the preventDefault()
        # call by reading this function's bytecode -- whether or not the handler
        # ever finishes does not matter. The call must appear in this function
        # itself, though: hiding it in a helper defeats the inspection.
        event.preventDefault()
        set_status("submitting")
        try:
            await submit_form(answer)
        except ValueError as exc:
            set_status("typing")
            set_error(str(exc))
        else:
            set_status("success")

    def handle_textarea_change(event):
        set_answer(event["target"]["value"])

    return html.div(
        html.h2("City quiz"),
        html.p(
            "In which city is there a billboard that turns air into drinkable water?"
        ),
        html.form(
            {"onSubmit": handle_submit},
            html.textarea(
                {
                    "value": answer,
                    "onChange": handle_textarea_change,
                    "disabled": status == "submitting",
                }
            ),
            html.br(),
            html.button(
                {
                    "disabled": len(answer) == 0 or status == "submitting",
                    "type": "submit",
                },
                "Submit",
            ),
            html.p({"className": "Error"}, error) if error else None,
        ),
    )

.Error {
    color: red;
}

textarea {
    width: 260px;
    height: 60px;
}

section {
    border-bottom: 1px solid #ddd;
    padding-bottom: 10px;
    margin-bottom: 10px;
}

h4 {
    margin: 4px 0;
    color: #888;
}

# TODO

Three things are worth noticing.

The handlers only set state. You never say "hide the textarea" or "enable the button". The disabled attributes and the error paragraph are computed from status and error on every render, so it's impossible to end up in a state where one was updated and the other wasn't. Submitting a wrong answer really does lock the form, then bring back the form with the error message and the input usable again.

The error is stored as a string, not an exception. React's version keeps an Error object and reads .message off it. In Python, store the message — str(exc) — and render it directly.

event.preventDefault() matters here, and ReactPy reads your code to find it. Without it the browser navigates away and your app is gone. Detection happens by inspecting the handler's code rather than at call time, so an async def handler that calls event.preventDefault() before its await is still detected. What defeats it is indirection: rebinding the argument (e = event) or delegating to a helper hides the call from the handler's own code, and the default is not prevented. If you can't put the call in the handler itself, declare it with @event(prevent_default=True).

An await in the handler means an extra paint

Calling set_status("submitting") before await submit_form(answer) is what makes the locked-form state visible at all: ReactPy renders what has been set so far when the handler suspends, so you see the form lock, then the result arrive. That is the behaviour you want here.

It is narrower than React's batching, and will surprise you when you don't want the intermediate paint. See Queueing a Series of State Updates for the measured difference.

Although this code is longer than the original imperative example, it is much less fragile. Expressing all interactions as state changes lets you introduce new visual states later without breaking existing ones. It also lets you change what should be displayed in each state without changing the logic of the interaction itself.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Declarative programming means describing the UI for each visual state rather than micromanaging the UI (imperative).
  • Identify the visual states, and mock them with a prop so all of them can be seen at once.
  • Then:
    • Determine the possible causes — user inputs and computer outputs.
    • Represent those states with as few state variables as possible, and remove any that can be derived.
    • Connect the event handlers to set state.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
When you want a component to "remember" some information, but you don't want that information to trigger new renders, you can use a ref.

You will learn

  • How to add a ref to your component
  • How to update a ref's value
  • How refs are different from state
  • How to use refs safely

docs.title: Adding a ref to your component
docs.text:
You can add a ref to your component by importing the use_ref hook from ReactPy:

from reactpy import use_ref

Inside your component, call the use_ref hook and pass the initial value that you want to reference as the only argument. For example, here is a ref to the value 0:

clicks = use_ref(0)

use_ref returns a Ref object holding that value:

Ref(0)  # holds the value you passed to use_ref

You can access the current value of that ref through the clicks.current attribute. This value is intentionally mutable, meaning you can both read and write to it. It's like a secret pocket of your component that ReactPy doesn't track. (This is what makes it an "escape hatch" from ReactPy's one-way data flow — more on that below!)

Here, a button will increment clicks.current on every click:

app.py Run 
@component
def counter():
    clicks = use_ref(0)

    def handle_click(event):
        clicks.current += 1
        # Nothing on screen changes, but the server console proves the ref is
        # really incrementing between clicks.
        print(f"You clicked {clicks.current} times!")

    return html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, "Click me!")

# TODO

The ref points to a number, but, like state, you could point to anything: a string, an object, or even a function. Unlike state, a ref is a plain Python object with a current attribute that you can read and modify.

Note that the component doesn't re-render with every increment. Like state, refs are retained by ReactPy between re-renders. However, setting state re-renders a component. Changing a ref does not! Watch the server console: each click prints a new count, yet the page never redraws.

Pass the initial value

Unlike useRef() in React, use_ref() has no no-argument form — initial_value is required, so use_ref() fails outright with TypeError: use_ref() missing 1 required positional argument: 'initial_value'. Pass None explicitly when you have no better starting value: tick_task = use_ref(None).

The lower-level reactpy.utils.Ref() is the one that accepts no arguments, and there current starts unset rather than at None, so the first read raises AttributeError: 'Ref' object has no attribute 'current'. Components should call use_ref rather than construct a Ref directly.

docs.title: Example: building a stopwatch
docs.text:
You can combine refs and state in a single component. For example, let's make a stopwatch that the user can start or stop by pressing a button. In order to display how much time has passed since the user pressed "Start", you will need to keep track of when the Start button was pressed and what the current time is. This information is used for rendering, so you'll keep it in state:

elapsed, set_elapsed = use_state(0.0)
running, set_running = use_state(False)

When the user presses "Start", you'll update the elapsed time about ten times a second. ReactPy has no setInterval, but it runs on asyncio, so the equivalent is a coroutine that sleeps and sets state, started with use_async_effect.

Now the awkward part. That coroutine runs for a long time, and it needs to know when the user pressed Start in order to compute time.monotonic() - <start>. It cannot read it from a local variable, because the render that created the coroutine is long gone by the time the coroutine wakes up. Since the start time is not used for rendering directly, you can keep it in a ref:

app.py Run 
@component
def stopwatch():
    # What the UI renders lives in state. What only the handlers and the
    # ticking effect read -- and which must never trigger a render of its own
    # -- lives in a ref.
    elapsed, set_elapsed = use_state(0.0)
    running, set_running = use_state(False)
    started_at: Ref[float | None] = use_ref(None)

    async def tick():
        # The ref is the same object on every render, so this long-lived loop
        # always sees whatever the button handlers wrote into it.
        while started_at.current is not None:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
            set_elapsed(time.monotonic() - started_at.current)

    use_async_effect(tick, dependencies=[running])

    def start(event=None):
        started_at.current = time.monotonic()
        set_running(True)

    def stop(event=None):
        if started_at.current is not None:
            # Write the exact final value; the ticking effect only samples
            # every 0.1s, so relying on it alone would leave the display
            # slightly behind.
            set_elapsed(time.monotonic() - started_at.current)
            started_at.current = None
        set_running(False)

    def reset(event=None):
        started_at.current = None
        set_running(False)
        set_elapsed(0.0)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"{elapsed:.1f}s"),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": stop if running else start},
            "Stop" if running else "Start",
        ),
        html.button({"onClick": reset}, "Reset"),
    )

# TODO

Press Start and the counter climbs; press Stop and it freezes at the exact final value. The started_at ref is the same object on every render, so the button handlers and the long-lived ticking coroutine all see whatever the others wrote into it.

Note what the ref is not doing here: it is not holding the asyncio.Task. The ticking coroutine is owned by use_async_effect, which cancels it when running flips to False and when the component unmounts. Storing a manually created task in a ref is tempting — tick_task.current = asyncio.create_task(keep_ticking()) — but nothing ever cancels it. Measure it by unmounting the component while it runs and the loop keeps rendering forever. Reach for an effect to own background work, and use the ref for the plain values the handlers need to share.

When a piece of information is used for rendering, keep it in state. When a piece of information is only needed by event handlers and changing it doesn't require a re-render, using a ref may be more efficient.

docs.title: Differences between refs and state
docs.text:
Perhaps you're thinking refs seem less "strict" than state — you can mutate them instead of always having to use a state setting function, for instance. But in most cases, you'll want to use state. Refs are an "escape hatch" you won't need often. Here's how state and refs compare:

refs state use_ref(initial_value) returns Ref(current=initial_value) use_state(initial_value) returns the current value of a state variable and a state setter function Doesn't trigger re-render when you change it. Triggers re-render when you change it. Mutable — you can modify and update current outside of the rendering process. "Immutable" — you must use the state setting function to modify state variables to queue a re-render. You shouldn't read (or write) current during rendering. You can read state at any time. However, each render has its own snapshot of state which does not change.

Here is a counter button that's implemented with state:

app.py Run 
@component
def counter():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    def handle_click(event):
        set_count(count + 1)

    return html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, f"You clicked {count} times")

# TODO

Because the count value is displayed, it makes sense to use a state value for it. When the counter's value is set with set_count(), ReactPy re-renders the component and the screen updates to reflect the new count.

If you tried to implement this with a ref, ReactPy would never re-render the component, so you'd never see the count change! See how clicking this button does not update its text:

app.py Run 
@component
def counter():
    count = use_ref(0)

    def handle_click(event):
        # This doesn't re-render the component!
        count.current += 1

    return html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, f"You clicked {count.current} times")

# TODO

This is why reading ref.current during render leads to unreliable code. If you need that, use state instead.

docs.title: How does use_ref work inside?
docs.text:
Although both use_state and use_ref are provided by ReactPy, use_ref really is implemented on top of use_state. In reactpy/core/hooks.py:

def use_ref(initial_value):
    return _use_const(lambda: Ref(initial_value))


def _use_const(function):
    return HOOK_STACK.current_hook().use_state(function)

During the first render, use_ref stores a Ref object as if it were state. That object is retained by ReactPy, so every later render gets the very same object back. There is no setter in the picture because use_ref always needs to return the same object — which is exactly why it can reuse state machinery without re-rendering.

If you're familiar with object-oriented programming, refs might remind you of instance fields — but instead of self.something you write something.current.

docs.title: When to use refs
docs.text:
Typically, you will use a ref when your component needs to "step outside" ReactPy and communicate with external APIs — often an API that won't impact the appearance of the component. Here are a few of these rare situations:

  • Storing asyncio tasks or timer handles, as in the stopwatch above
  • Storing other objects that aren't needed to calculate the VDOM — a client, a cache, a handle from an external library

If your component needs to store some value, but it doesn't impact the rendering logic, choose refs.

A ref cannot hold a DOM node

React's docs list "accessing a DOM element" among the top reasons to reach for a ref. That one does not carry over: reactpy.utils.Ref is a plain Python box that lives on the server, and there is no attribute that hands a browser node to Python. What you do instead — give the element an "id" and reach it from inline JavaScript — uses no ref at all. See Manipulating the DOM with Refs for why the name is a misnomer and what replaces each React example.

docs.title: Best practices for refs
docs.text:
Following these principles will make your components more predictable:

  • Treat refs as an escape hatch. Refs are useful when you work with external systems. If much of your application logic and data flow relies on refs, you might want to rethink your approach.
  • Don't read or write ref.current during rendering. If some information is needed during rendering, use state instead. Since ReactPy doesn't know when ref.current changes, even reading it while rendering makes your component's behavior difficult to predict. (The only exception to this is code like if not ref.current: ref.current = Thing(), which only sets the ref once during the first render.)

Limitations of ReactPy state don't apply to refs. For example, state acts like a snapshot for every render and doesn't update synchronously. But when you mutate the current value of a ref, it changes immediately:

clicks.current = 5
print(clicks.current)  # 5

This is because the ref itself is a regular Python object, and so it behaves like one.

You also don't need to worry about avoiding mutation when you work with a ref. As long as the object you're mutating isn't used for rendering, ReactPy doesn't care what you do with the ref or its contents.

docs.title: Refs and the DOM
docs.text: You can point a ref to any value — but not to a DOM element. ReactPy has no ref attribute to pass to a tag, and no server-side handle on a browser node: use_ref lives in the Python process, the node lives in the page. The React idiom input_ref.current.focus() therefore has no Python spelling at all. What replaces it is to give the element an "id" and reach it from inline JavaScript, which runs in the page — and which uses no ref. The trap to avoid is reaching for it from an effect: effects run on the server too, where document does not exist. Manipulating the DOM with Refs walks through focus, scrolling, and play/pause.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• A ref is a value that lets a component "remember" something without triggering a re-render.
  • Call use_ref(initial_value) and read or write ref.current.
  • Setting state re-renders; changing a ref does not, which makes refs suitable for values only event handlers need.
  • Don't read or write ref.current during rendering — use state for anything that affects what's on screen.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Every dependency you list is a promise: "when this changes, redo the work." Removing one you don't need is fine — and proving it is not needed is the whole job. This page covers what counts as a change in ReactPy, and the six legitimate reasons a value can leave the list.

You will learn

  • How to prove a value is not a dependency, rather than guess
  • How ReactPy actually compares dependencies — not what the docstring says
  • The six safe ways to remove a dependency
  • Why a rebuilt object is not "new" here, and when that saves you
  • What to do when a value must stay out of the list for real

docs.title: Dependencies should match the code
docs.text:
The list describes the code, not your intent. Look at the Effect body, list every name it reads that came from the component body, and that is the list. Nothing more, nothing less.

A missing dependency is a correctness bug: the Effect reports values from an older render. An extra dependency is a behaviour bug: the work runs when it shouldn't, tearing down something that should have stayed up. Both are worth fixing, and they are fixed differently.

To remove a dependency, prove one of these about it:

  • it cannot change between renders (module constant, imported helper)
  • it is read only to compute a new value, not to decide what to do
  • it is read for a "latest value" snapshot, and reacting to it is unwanted
  • the code that reads it should be in an event handler, not an Effect
  • the Effect is doing two jobs and only one of them needs it
  • it changes unintentionally, and the real fix is to stop it changing

If none of those is true, the value stays. Deleting it from the list to quiet a symptom produces an Effect that looks fine and reports the past.

docs.title: A missing dependency is visible if you look
docs.text:
This Effect writes a summary into state but lists only topic:

app.py Run 
@component
def reporter(topic):
    count, set_count = use_state(0)
    theme, set_theme = use_state("light")
    summary, set_summary = use_state("no report yet")

    def report():
        # reads `count` and `theme`, but neither is in the dependency list
        set_summary(f"topic={topic} count={count} theme={theme}")
        print(f"report topic={topic} count={count} theme={theme}")

    use_effect(report, dependencies=[topic])

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_count(count + 1)}, f"Count {count}"),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda e: set_theme("dark" if theme == "light" else "light")},
            f"Theme {theme}",
        ),
        html.p(f"live: count={count} theme={theme}"),
        html.p(f"summary: {summary}"),
    )


@component
def app():
    topic, set_topic = use_state("news")
    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_topic(topic + "x")}, f"Topic {topic}"),
        reporter(topic),
    )

# TODO

Verified: press Count twice and Theme once, and the page reads

live:    count=2 theme=dark
summary: topic=news count=0 theme=light

The summary describes the render that created the Effect. Press Topic and both lines agree again — because a new Effect was built from the current render. That pair of lines is the whole missing-dependency bug made visible: it is not frozen at mount, and it is not current. It is from some render.

docs.title: How ReactPy compares dependencies
docs.text:
This is where React's advice and ReactPy's behaviour part ways, and it decides which removals are safe.

Dependencies go through core/hooks.py, strictly_equal:

  1. Type gate first. If type(x) is not type(y), it is a change — 1 and 1.0 never compare equal here.
  2. Local functions compare code. If both values have a __qualname__ containing <locals> or <lambda> and both expose __code__, their co_* bytecode attributes are compared — same code, and the same __qualname__, means unchanged. One side qualifying is not enough: a locally-defined function compared against an import is not code-compared.
  3. Otherwise ==, but only if the value has an __eq__ at all (hasattr(x, "__eq__")), and falling back to is if == raises.

Note step 3. The strictly_equal docstring claims only int, float, str, bytes and friends are compared by equality, but the implementation reaches x == y for anything with an __eq__ — which is everything. Measured over 5 renders each (mount plus four unrelated state changes), counting how many times the Effect ran:

Dependency, rebuilt on every render Runs {"sort": "date", "limit": 10} — never changes 1 [1, 2, 3] — never changes 1 DataFilter("a") (@dataclass) — content changed twice 3 TupleFilter("a") (NamedTuple) — content changed twice 3 {"sort": "date", "limit": count} — content tracks state 3 plain class instance, no __eq__ 5 (every render) (1, 2, 3) alternating with [1, 2, 3] 3 (type gate)

Consequences:

  • React's "a rebuilt object is a new dependency" warning does not apply here. A dict or list you rebuild on every render is not a dependency change, so it will not loop. That is why the classic infinite-loop example needs no fix in ReactPy — and why you must not rely on it either, since it depends on values comparing equal, not on identity.
  • A plain class instance always counts as changed, because it inherits object.__eq__ and identity never holds across renders. That is the shape that genuinely spins.
  • The type gate catches things == would not: strictly_equal(1, True) is False even though 1 == True, and a tuple swapped for a list is a change.

Because ReactPy cannot check your list for you — reactpy-flake8 reports a missing dependency only for an inline lambda, never for a named def or a decorated Effect — proving the list is yours to do. See Separating Events from Effects and Lifecycle of Reactive Effects for the linter's exact coverage and for the Layout-based test that catches what it cannot.

docs.title: Should this code move to an event handler?
docs.text: If the work should happen because the user did something, it belongs in the handler, and the dependency disappears along with the Effect. This is the most common removal and the one that deletes the most code — see Separating Events from Effects.

docs.title: Is your Effect doing several unrelated things?
docs.text:
One Effect connecting a socket and loading rows means each job inherits the other's dependencies:

app.py Run 
@component
def feed(topic):
    page, set_page = use_state(1)
    rows, set_rows = use_state([])
    online, set_online = use_state(True)

    def subscribe():
        # one Effect doing two unrelated jobs: connect AND load rows
        if not online:
            print("offline — nothing to do")
            return
        print(f"connect {topic} page={page}")
        set_rows([f"{topic} row {i} (page {page})" for i in range(3)])

        def close():
            print(f"disconnect {topic} page={page}")

        return close

    use_effect(subscribe, dependencies=[topic, page, online])

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_page(page + 1)}, f"Page {page}"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_online(not online)}, "Toggle online"),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": row}, row) for row in rows]),
    )


@component
def app():
    topic, set_topic = use_state("news")
    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_topic(topic + "x")}, f"Topic {topic}"),
        feed(topic),
    )

# TODO

Verified: press Toggle online and the log shows disconnect news page=2 before offline — nothing to do. Going offline tears down a connection by way of a page number. Split the Effect in two and each list shrinks to what its own job reads.

docs.title: Are you reading some state to calculate the next state?
docs.text:
Then that state is not a dependency — it is an input to the next value. Take an updater and it leaves the list:

app.py Run 
@component
def log_viewer(topic):
    lines, set_lines = use_state([])
    visible, set_visible = use_state(3)

    def record():
        # `lines` is only used to build the next value, so it is not a
        # dependency — and listing it would make this Effect re-trigger itself
        def append(current):
            return [*current, f"opened {topic}"]

        set_lines(append)

    use_effect(record, dependencies=[topic])

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_visible(visible + 1)}, f"Show {visible}"),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": i}, line) for i, line in enumerate(lines[-visible:])]),
    )


@component
def app():
    topic, set_topic = use_state("news")
    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_topic(topic + "x")}, f"Topic {topic}"),
        log_viewer(topic),
    )

# TODO

Verified: each topic change appends exactly one entry; changing Show does not append anything.

Now the reason this rule matters. Listing lines as well — "just to be safe", exactly the mistake the ReactJS page warns about in the other direction — gives:

def record():
    def append(current):
        return [*current, f"opened {topic}"]

    set_lines(append)

use_effect(record, dependencies=[topic, lines])   # never settles

Measured: the connection rendered 400 times without settling and the component body ran 800 times. The Effect appends, lines changes, the Effect runs again. A functional updater is not a micro-optimisation here; it is what breaks the cycle.

docs.title: Do you want to read a value without reacting to its changes?
docs.text:
Keep it in a ref that you update during render, and leave it out of the list. The difference is easy to see on a poll loop with a user-adjustable delay.

The version that lists the delay:

app.py Run 
@component
def poller(topic):
    delay, set_delay = use_state(0.2)
    polls, set_polls = use_state(0)

    async def loop():
        print(f"start polling {topic} delay={delay:.1f}s")
        try:
            while True:
                await asyncio.sleep(delay)
                print(f"tick {topic} delay={delay:.1f}s")
                # the loop is created once per run, so read state via an updater
                set_polls(lambda current: current + 1)
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            print(f"stop polling {topic} delay={delay:.1f}s")
            raise

    # `delay` here means adjusting it cancels and recreates the whole loop
    use_async_effect(loop, dependencies=[topic, delay])

    return html.div(
        html.p(f"{topic}: {polls} polls"),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda e: set_delay(delay + 0.2)}, f"Delay {delay:.1f}s"
        ),
    )


@component
def app():
    topic, set_topic = use_state("news")
    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_topic(topic + "x")}, f"Topic {topic}"),
        poller(topic),
    )

# TODO

The version that keeps it in a ref:

app.py Run 
@component
def poller(topic):
    delay, set_delay = use_state(0.2)
    polls, set_polls = use_state(0)
    # updated during render, so the loop always sleeps with the newest value
    delay_ref = use_ref(delay)
    delay_ref.current = delay

    async def loop():
        print(f"start polling {topic}")
        try:
            while True:
                await asyncio.sleep(delay_ref.current)
                print(f"tick {topic} delay={delay_ref.current:.1f}s")
                # the loop is created once, so read state through an updater
                set_polls(lambda current: current + 1)
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            print(f"stop polling {topic}")
            raise

    # `delay` is deliberately absent: adjusting it must not reconnect
    use_async_effect(loop, dependencies=[topic])

    return html.div(
        html.p(f"{topic}: {polls} polls"),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda e: set_delay(delay + 0.2)}, f"Delay {delay:.1f}s"
        ),
    )


@component
def app():
    topic, set_topic = use_state("news")
    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_topic(topic + "x")}, f"Topic {topic}"),
        poller(topic),
    )

# TODO

Verified with the same script on both — two delay adjustments, half a second of ticking, then a topic change:

Loop starts Loop stops delay in the list 4 2 delay in a ref 2 1

Two of those restarts are pure waste: adjusting a setting nobody asked to reconnect for. And because the ref is assigned during render, the loop still sleeps with the newest delay — tick news delay=0.6s appears in the log of the ref version even though the Effect never re-ran.

The ref assignment during render looks like a write in a render, and it is the one case that is safe: the box is created once, the write is idempotent, and nothing derived from it feeds the render output.

docs.title: Does some reactive value change unintentionally?
docs.text:
Sometimes the dependency is correct and the value is the problem.

Move static values out of the component. A module-level constant, an imported helper, or a frozen config is the same object on every render and every connection, so it is not a dependency at all:

app.py Run 
PAGE_SIZE = 20
HEADERS = {"Accept": "application/json"}


def format_rows(topic, raw):
    """Module-level helper: same object on every render and every connection."""
    return [f"{topic}: {name}" for name in raw]


@component
def directory(topic):
    query, set_query = use_state("")
    rows, set_rows = use_state([])

    def load():
        raw = [f"user-{i}" for i in range(PAGE_SIZE // 4)]
        print(f"load topic={topic} page_size={PAGE_SIZE} headers={HEADERS}")
        set_rows(format_rows(topic, raw))

    # neither PAGE_SIZE, HEADERS, nor format_rows belongs in this list
    use_effect(load, dependencies=[topic])

    return html.div(
        html.input(
            {
                "value": query,
                "onChange": lambda e: set_query(e["target"]["value"]),
            }
        ),
        html.p(f"query={query!r} rows={len(rows)}"),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": row}, row) for row in rows]),
    )


@component
def app():
    topic, set_topic = use_state("news")
    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_topic(topic + "x")}, f"Topic {topic}"),
        directory(topic),
    )

# TODO

Verified: typing in the box re-renders the component and the Effect does not run; only the topic change logs load topic=newsx page_size=20 headers={'Accept': 'application/json'}.

Read primitive values out of objects. user.id is a dependency; user is a wider promise than you need, and any unrelated field change re-runs the Effect. Depend on the scalars you actually use.

Calculate primitives from functions, not objects. This is also the fix for the trap that silently freezes an Effect: a locally defined function passed as a dependency compares code-wise and therefore never changes. Depend on the string or number the function would have produced.

docs.title: Rebuilding an object is not a dependency change — but don't rely on it
When a dependency must come out
docs.text:
There are cases where the honest answer is "I read this value, I do not want to react to it, and a ref is the wrong shape for it." Then be explicit about the exception rather than quietly deleting the name:

def effect():
    notify(user_id, channel_id)   # reads channel_id

use_effect(effect, dependencies=[user_id])
# channel_id is read but not reacted to: it changes only when the user
# switches channel, which unmounts this component anyway.

The comment is the review surface. An unexplained missing name is indistinguishable from the bug in the first example on this page — and, as measured, nothing in ReactPy will tell you which one you wrote.

What dependencies=None does not mean

None is not "no dependencies"; it means re-run after every render. To create the Effect once and never replace it, use dependencies=[] — which also seals the body against future renders. See the four-way table in Lifecycle of Reactive Effects.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• The list describes the code. Prove a value is not a dependency; don't vote it off.
  • ReactPy compares dependencies with strictly_equal: type gate, then code comparison for local functions, then ==. Rebuilt dicts and lists are not changes; plain class instances always are.
  • A missing dependency is silent — no warning, no log. Make the staleness visible in the page, as the first example does, or assert it in a test.
  • The six removals: hoist what cannot change, take an updater for next-state reads, keep latest-value reads in a ref, move interaction logic to handlers, split Effects that do two jobs, and stop values changing unintentionally.
  • Listing state you only append to is the classic self-triggering loop: measured, 400 renders and no settle.
  • reactpy-flake8 will not check the list for you, so an explanatory comment is the only reviewer you have.
