docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Before your components are displayed on screen, they must be rendered by ReactPy. Understanding the steps in this process will help you think about how your code executes and explain its behavior.

You will learn

  • What rendering means in ReactPy
  • When and why ReactPy renders a component
  • The steps involved in displaying a component on screen
  • Why rendering does not always produce a DOM update

A ReactPy component is a Python function that returns a description of the UI. That description has to travel from your server to someone else's browser before it becomes pixels. The journey has four steps:

  1. Triggering a render — mounting the app, or updating state.
  2. Rendering the component — Python calls your functions and builds a VDOM tree.
  3. Committing to the DOM — the diff is sent over the websocket and patched into the page.
  4. Painting — the browser redraws.

The first two happen in Python, on your server. The last two happen in the browser. Keeping that boundary in mind explains a lot of ReactPy's behavior that differs from a browser-only React app — most obviously the round-trip latency on every interaction.

docs.title: Step 1: Trigger a render
docs.text:
There are two reasons for a component to render:

  1. It's the component's initial render, caused by mounting it.
  2. The component's (or one of its ancestors') state has been updated.

docs.title: Initial render
docs.text:
When your app starts, you need to mount a root component. Unlike React, where you call createRoot yourself, in ReactPy the executor does the mounting, and which executor you pick determines what the mounting line looks like:

app.py Run 
@component
def image():
    return html.img(
        {
            "src": "https://i.imgur.com/ZF6s192.jpg",
            "alt": "'Floralis Genérica' by Eduardo Catalano: a gigantic "
            "metallic flower sculpture with reflective petals",
        }
    )


# Mounting is what triggers the initial render. Which line you use depends on
# how the app is served; see the executors reference.
my_app = ReactPy(image)

# TODO

ReactPy(image) is the line that matters. It registers image as the root component and, when a browser connects, calls it and sends the result down. There is no DOM node to hand in — the executor owns the mount point (<div id="app"> in the page it generates).

The other executors mount differently: ReactPyMiddleware takes dotted paths to components so a URL can select one, and ReactPyCsr mounts a component from a Python file that the browser runs itself. See Creating a Standalone React App for those.

docs.title: Re-renders when state updates
docs.text:
Once the component has been initially rendered, you can trigger further renders by updating its state with the set function from use_state. Updating your component's state automatically queues a render.

app.py Run 
@component
def clock():
    now, set_now = use_state(datetime.now(timezone.utc))

    async def tick():
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(1)
            set_now(datetime.now(timezone.utc))

    use_async_effect(tick, dependencies=[])

    return html.h1(now.strftime("%H:%M:%S"))

# TODO

Note the difference from a browser-only React app: the state lives on the server. Calling set_now(...) schedules a render on the server, and the new VDOM reaches the browser a websocket message later. That is why an interaction in ReactPy feels slightly laggy compared to the same UI written in JavaScript, and why holding a lock or sleeping inside an event handler stalls the whole connection.

Setting the same value does not re-render

Calling a setter with a value equal to the current one renders nothing — verified: set_n(0) when n is already 0 produces no further render at all, while set_n(n + 1) does. The comparison is not an identity check: it accepts anything that compares equal, so even a freshly built list or dict schedules nothing when its contents match. Note this is a state-update bailout only; it is not component memoization — see step 2.

docs.title: Step 2: ReactPy renders your components
docs.text:
After you trigger a render, ReactPy calls your components to figure out what to display. "Rendering" is ReactPy calling your functions.

  • On initial render, ReactPy calls the root component.
  • For subsequent renders, ReactPy calls the function component whose state update triggered the render.

This process is recursive: if the updated component returns some other component, ReactPy renders that component next, and if that component returns yet another, ReactPy renders that one too. In this way, a state update inside a component can trigger renders all the way down its children.

Under the hood, Layout._render_component compares the new component against the previous one at the same position. Two things matter here, and both are worth internalizing:

  • A component is matched by its function object identity. If you define a @component inside another component, it is a brand-new function object on every render, so ReactPy unmounts the old one and loses all its state. Always define components at module level.
  • Children are matched by key, falling back to position. See Keeping list items in order with key.

Every child re-renders; there is no memo

ReactPy has no component-level memo. A child function runs again whenever its parent renders, even when its props are identical — verified by instrumenting a sibling: it re-ran on the parent's state update. use_memo caches values inside a component, not whole component subtrees.

This makes the "don't nest component definitions" rule above more than a style preference, and it means expensive children stay expensive. If a subtree is genuinely costly, the tools are use_memo for the computation and moving state down so fewer components re-render — not wrapping the child.

ReactPy will not render twice to catch you

React's Strict Mode double-invokes components in development to expose impure rendering. ReactPy has no Strict Mode and never double-invokes. A component that mutates module state or reads the clock will render perfectly once and misbehave later. If you want that safety net, write the test: render the component twice inside a reactpy.core.layout.Layout and assert the two results are equal.

docs.title: Step 3: Commit to the DOM
docs.text:
After a component renders, ReactPy has a Python description of the UI. This is not yet on the screen — ReactPy must deliver it to the browser, which must then update the DOM:

  1. Update the DOM. ReactPy's client applies the changes to existing DOM nodes, patching rather than replacing wherever it can.
  2. Display the DOM. The browser updates the screen to reflect the changes.

The first half happens on the server: ReactPy walks the new tree, computes a diff, and sends it over the websocket as a path plus a partial model. The second half happens in the browser, where the bundled client patches that subtree in place.

This is where ReactPy is most different from React, and it's the most useful thing to understand. React re-renders from the root and diffs the whole tree; ReactPy sends a patch addressed to one path in the tree. Observed directly: after clicking a button inside the first of two children, the update carried the path "/children/0/children/0" and a model describing only that button's subtree. Nothing about the untouched sibling went over the wire.

Because the patch is applied to existing nodes rather than rebuilt, DOM state that ReactPy doesn't know about survives. Verified in a browser: an <input> with no value attribute kept both its typed text and its focus across a parent re-render, and was the same node object before and after.

That is the practical payoff of the "controlled vs uncontrolled" distinction:

app.py Run 
@component
def app():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_count(count + 1)}, "Re-render"),
        html.p(f"Rendered {count} times"),
        # No `value`: the browser owns this field, so ReactPy never rewrites it.
        html.input({"placeholder": "Type here and then click the button"}),
    )

# TODO

Type into the field, then click Re-render. The text stays. ReactPy re-runs app(), produces a new tree, and the diff for the untouched input is empty — so the browser never touches it, and neither the user's text nor their cursor position is disturbed.

Had that input carried "value": something, ReactPy would own it and rewrite it on every render, which is what you want when the value is genuinely derived from state — and what makes typing feel broken when you forget the matching onChange.

You can skip the browser entirely

Because rendering is pure Python, the same components can be rendered to an HTML string with reactpy_to_string from reactpy.utils — no browser, no websocket. That is useful for email bodies, static fragments, and tests. It is not server-side rendering of an app: it calls component.render() directly, with no Layout behind it, so a component that uses any hook raises RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout? — including the use_state example further up this page. Plain html.* elements and hook-free components are all it can render. And it is only safe because rendering is pure: a component that reads the clock or mutates a global will leak one request's output into another's.

docs.title: Epilogue: Browser paint
docs.text:
After ReactPy has patched the DOM, the browser repaints the screen. Although this process is known as "browser rendering", we'll refer to it as "painting" to avoid confusion throughout the docs.

Because a round trip sits between the click and the paint, ReactPy apps feel more like a networked app than a local one. Two habits follow from that: keep event handlers short (they run on the server, blocking that connection), and prefer optimistic UI where a wrong guess is cheap.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Any screen update in a ReactPy app happens in four steps:
    1. Trigger
    2. Render (Python, on the server)
    3. Commit (a path-addressed patch over the websocket)
    4. Paint (the browser)
  • Mounting a root component triggers the initial render; the executor decides how.
  • Setting state queues a render; setting it to an equal value queues nothing.
  • Children always re-run — there is no memo, so keep definitions at module level and expensive work in use_memo.
  • ReactPy has no Strict Mode, so nothing will double-render your components to expose impurity for you.
  • Untouched parts of the tree are neither recomputed for the wire nor rewritten in the DOM, which is why an uncontrolled input keeps what the user typed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You will often want to display multiple similar components from a collection of data. You can use Python's list comprehensions to manipulate a list of data. On this page, you'll use comprehensions with ReactPy to filter and transform your data into lists of components.

You will learn

  • How to render components from a list using a comprehension
  • How to render only specific components using a filtering condition
  • When and why to use ReactPy keys

docs.title: Rendering data from lists
docs.text:
Say that you have a list of content.

html.ul(
    html.li("Creola Katherine Johnson: mathematician"),
    html.li("Mario José Molina-Pasquel Henríquez: chemist"),
    html.li("Mohammad Abdus Salam: physicist"),
    html.li("Percy Lavon Julian: chemist"),
    html.li("Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar: astrophysicist"),
)

The only difference among those list items is their contents, their data. You will often need to show several instances of the same component using different data when building interfaces: from lists of comments to galleries of profile images. In these situations, you can store that data in Python dictionaries and lists and use comprehensions to render lists of components from them.

Here's a short example of how to generate a list of items from a list:

  1. Move the data into a list:
people = [
    "Creola Katherine Johnson: mathematician",
    "Mario José Molina-Pasquel Henríquez: chemist",
    "Mohammad Abdus Salam: physicist",
    "Percy Lavon Julian: chemist",
    "Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar: astrophysicist",
]
  1. Build a new list of VDOM nodes from people:
list_items = [html.li(person) for person in people]
  1. Return list_items from your component wrapped in a <ul>:
return html.ul(list_items)

Here is the result:

app.pystyles.css Run 
people = [
    "Creola Katherine Johnson: mathematician",
    "Mario José Molina-Pasquel Henríquez: chemist",
    "Mohammad Abdus Salam: physicist",
    "Percy Lavon Julian: chemist",
    "Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar: astrophysicist",
]


@component
def people_list():
    list_items = [html.li(person) for person in people]
    return html.ul(list_items)

li {
    margin-bottom: 10px;
}

# TODO

If you run this with REACTPY_DEBUG=1, ReactPy prints a warning for each child:

Key not specified for child in list row(7f2c11ac75e0, person={...})

You'll learn how to fix this warning later on this page. Before we get to that, let's add some structure to your data.

docs.title: Filtering lists of items
docs.text:
This data can be structured even more. Rather than strings, each person becomes a dictionary:

people = [
    {
        "id": 0,
        "name": "Creola Katherine Johnson",
        "profession": "mathematician",
        "accomplishment": "spaceflight calculations",
        "image_id": "MK3eW3A",
    },
    # ...
]

Say you want to display only the chemists. In JavaScript React you would chain filter() and map(); in Python a single comprehension with an if clause does both:

chemists = [person for person in people if person["profession"] == "chemist"]
list_items = [html.li(person["name"]) for person in chemists]
app.pydata.pystyles.css Run

            html.p(
                html.b(person["name"]),
                f" {person['profession']} known for {person['accomplishment']}",
            ),
        )
        for person in chemists
    ]
    return html.ul(list_items)

A helper that forgets return renders nothing

The JavaScript "=> with a block body needs a return" trap has a direct Python twin that is worse, because Python fails silently. If a helper used inside a comprehension forgets its return, it evaluates to None — and ReactPy skips None children instead of raising:

def render_person(person):  # WRONG: no return
    html.li(person["name"])


list_items = [render_person(person) for person in people]

list_items becomes a list of None values and the <ul> renders empty, with no error. Use a comprehension directly when the expression is simple, and add a -> VdomDict return annotation to helpers so type checkers catch the omission.

docs.title: Keeping list items in order with key
docs.text:
When you render children from a list, ReactPy needs a way to tell which child is which. Give each item a key — a string or a number that uniquely identifies it among the other items in that list. Unlike React, where key is a special JSX attribute, in ReactPy it lives in the attributes dictionary like any other attribute:

html.li({"key": person["id"]}, ...)

Children built from a list always need keys

Any child that comes out of a comprehension — or any other list — should carry a key. ReactPy does not warn about this by default; the check is part of its debug mode, so run your app with REACTPY_DEBUG=1 (or set reactpy.config.REACTPY_DEBUG.current = True) while developing to surface them.

Keys tell ReactPy which list item each component corresponds to, so that it can match them up later. This becomes important if your list items can move (e.g. due to sorting), get inserted, or get deleted. A well-chosen key helps ReactPy infer what exactly has happened, and make the correct updates to the DOM tree.

Rather than generating keys on the fly, you should include them in your data:

app.pydata.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def people_list():
    list_items = [
        html.li(
            {"key": person["id"]},
            html.img({"src": get_image_url(person), "alt": person["name"]}),
            html.p(
                html.b(person["name"]),
                f" {person['profession']} known for {person['accomplishment']}",
            ),
        )
        for person in people
    ]
    return html.ul(list_items)

docs.title: Displaying several DOM nodes for each list item
docs.text:
What do you do when each item needs to render not one, but several DOM nodes?

A plain html(...) fragment takes no positional attributes, but it does accept an attributes dictionary — so pass the key there:

[
    html(
        {"key": person["id"]},
        html.h1(person["name"]),
        html.p(person["profession"]),
    )
    for person in people
]
app.pydata.py Run 
@component
def people_list():
    list_items = [
        html(
            {"key": person["id"]},
            html.h1(person["name"]),
            html.p(person["profession"]),
        )
        for person in people
    ]
    return html.div(list_items)

people = [
    {
        "id": 0,  # used as the key
        "name": "Creola Katherine Johnson",
        "profession": "mathematician",
        "accomplishment": "spaceflight calculations",
        "image_id": "MK3eW3A",
    },
    {
        "id": 1,  # used as the key

Fragments disappear from the DOM, so this produces a flat list of <h1>, <p>, <h1>, <p>, and so on.

docs.title: Where to get your key
docs.text:
Different sources of data provide different sources of keys:

  • Data from a database: If your data is coming from a database, you can use the database keys/IDs, which are unique by nature.
  • Locally generated data: If your data is generated and persisted locally (e.g. notes in a note-taking app), use an incrementing counter from itertools.count or a UUID from uuid.uuid4 when creating the item — never while rendering.

docs.title: Rules of keys
docs.text:
• Keys must be unique among siblings. However, it's okay to use the same keys for nodes in different lists.
  • Keys must not change or that defeats their purpose! Don't generate them while rendering.

Duplicate keys are a hard error in ReactPy

React logs a warning for duplicate keys and carries on. ReactPy raises instead:

ValueError: Duplicate keys [1] at '/children/0'

The whole component fails to render, so a data set with repeated IDs takes down the section rather than degrading it. If your data can legitimately repeat — for example, two rows that render the same underlying record — make the key unique among siblings by combining the fields that distinguish them.

docs.title: Why does ReactPy need keys?
docs.text:
Imagine that files on your desktop didn't have names. Instead, you'd refer to them by their order — the first file, the second file, and so on. You could get used to it, but once you delete a file, it would get confusing. The second file would become the first file, the third file would be the second file, and so on.

File names in a folder and keys in a list serve a similar purpose. They let us uniquely identify an item between its siblings. A well-chosen key provides more information than the position within the list. Even if the position changes due to reordering, the key lets ReactPy identify the item throughout its lifetime.

This is observable. Give each row its own use_state seeded from the person it renders, then reverse the list. With keys, every row's state travels with its person. Without keys, the state stays behind in the old slot:

keyed=True
   before: shown=ada   state=ada#0
   after : shown=alan  state=alan#2

keyed=False
   before: shown=ada   state=ada#0
   after : shown=alan  state=ada#0    # the row for "alan" inherited ada's state

Index-based keys are a trap

You might be tempted to use an item's index in the list as its key. In fact, that's effectively what ReactPy uses if you don't specify a key at all. But the order in which you render items will change over time if an item is inserted, deleted, or if the list gets reordered, and — as the output above shows — state then attaches to the wrong item.

Similarly, do not generate keys on the fly, e.g. with key=uuid.uuid4() or key=id(person) inside the render. Keys that differ on every render never match up, so every component and DOM node is recreated each time. Not only is this slow, it will also lose any user input inside the list items. Instead, use a stable ID that comes from the data.

Note that your component never receives key as a prop — ReactPy reserves it. Declaring a key parameter raises immediately:

TypeError: Component render function <function row ...> uses reserved parameter 'key'

If your component needs an ID, pass it as a separate prop: profile(id=id, key=id).

Pass a list, not a generator

html.ul(html.li(person) for person in people) renders, but a generator has no length, so ReactPy cannot verify key integrity and warns about it in debug mode. Bracket the comprehension so the children are a real list: html.ul([html.li(person) for person in people]).

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
On this page you learned:

  • How to move data out of components and into data structures like lists and dictionaries.
  • How to generate sets of similar components with a list comprehension.
  • How to create filtered lists with an if clause in a comprehension.
  • Why and how to set key on each component in a collection so ReactPy can keep track of each of them even if their position or data changes.
  • That ReactPy checks keys only in debug mode, treats duplicate keys as an error, and reserves key so components can never receive it as a prop.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ReactPy lets you add event handlers to your VDOM. Event handlers are your own functions that will be triggered in response to interactions like clicking, hovering, focusing form inputs, and so on.

You will learn

  • Different ways to write an event handler
  • How to pass event handling logic from a parent component
  • How events propagate and how to stop them
  • What the event object actually contains

docs.title: Adding event handlers
docs.text:
To add an event handler, you first define a function and then pass it as a prop to the appropriate tag. For example, here is a button that doesn't do anything yet:

app.py Run 
@component
def button():
    return html.button("I don't do anything")

# TODO

You can make it show a message when a user clicks by following these three steps:

  1. Declare a function called handle_click inside your def button() component.
  2. Implement the logic inside that function (use print to show the message).
  3. Add "onClick": handle_click to the html.button attributes dictionary.
app.pystyles.css Run 
from reactpy import component, html


@component
def button():
    def handle_click(event):
        print("You clicked me!")

    return html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, "Click me")

button {
    margin-right: 10px;
}

# TODO

You defined the handle_click function and then passed it as a prop to html.button. handle_click is an event handler. Event handler functions:

  • Are usually defined inside your components.
  • Have names that start with handle, followed by the name of the event.

By convention, it is common to name event handlers as handle followed by the event name. You'll often see "onKeyDown": handle_key_down, "onMouseEnter": handle_mouse_enter, and so on.

The handler key is camelCase, and it lives in the attributes dict

This is the single most common mistake when moving from ReactJS examples. The key is the DOM event name in camelCase — "onClick", "onChange", "onSubmit" — and it goes inside the attributes dictionary, not as a keyword argument:

html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, "Click me")   # correct

Writing html.button({"on_click": handle_click}, ...) does not raise. ReactPy ships it to the browser verbatim as a handler for an event called _click — the client registers a listener for the key with the leading on stripped — and no browser ever fires one. The button looks fine and simply never responds. Only the names you define (variables, components, component props) are snake_case.

Note what does and does not decide "this is a handler". In core/vdom.py, separate_attributes_handlers_and_inline_javascript the test is callable(v) on the value, checked before the key is ever looked at: a callable under "on_click", or even under "foo", lands in eventHandlers. The key pattern ^on[A-Z]\w+ (core/vdom.py, EVENT_ATTRIBUTE_PATTERN) is used only for the string case below — it decides whether a string becomes inlineJavaScript or a plain attribute. So {"onClick": "alert(1)"} runs as JavaScript, while {"onclick": "alert(1)"} and {"on_click": "alert(1)"} become inert attributes.

Alternatively, you can define an event handler inline with a lambda:

html.button(
    {"onClick": lambda event: print("You clicked me!")},
    "Click me",
)

Inline event handlers are convenient for short functions.

A string is not a handler — it is JavaScript

ReactPy has a second, easy-to-miss form. If the value of an on* key is a string, ReactPy treats it as JavaScript to run in the browser instead of calling your Python code:

html.button({"onClick": "alert('You clicked me!')"}, "Click me")

That renders into an inlineJavaScript field on the VDOM node rather than an eventHandlers field, and nothing on the server ever runs. It is a real escape hatch for things only the browser can do, but it is never what you want when you meant to write a Python function. If your handler silently does nothing, check whether you passed a string.

Pass the function, don't call it

Functions passed to event handlers must be passed, not called:

html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, "...")    # correct: fires on click
html.button({"onClick": handle_click()}, "...")  # wrong: fires during render

In the second case the () calls handle_click immediately during rendering, without any clicks — because the Python inside the call is evaluated right away, exactly like an expression inside JSX braces. Whatever it returns is what gets stored, and a function that ends without a return gives None. ReactPy does not reject that: handlers are picked out by callable(v), and None is not callable, so it falls through to the plain attributes and ships as {"onClick": None} — a DOM attribute named onClick holding null. Nothing registers, nothing fires, and the button renders and does nothing, forever.

The same trap appears with inline code:

# This prints when the component renders, not when clicked!
html.button({"onClick": print("You clicked me!")}, "Click me")

# Wrap it in a lambda so it becomes a function to call later.
html.button({"onClick": lambda event: print("You clicked me!")}, "Click me")

In both working cases, what you pass is a function.

docs.title: Reading props in event handlers
docs.text:
Because event handlers are declared inside a component, they have access to the component's props. Here is a button that, when clicked, displays its message prop:

app.py Run 
@component
def alert_button(message, *children):
    shown, set_shown = use_state("")

    def handle_click(event):
        set_shown(message)

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, *children),
        html.p(shown),
    )


@component
def toolbar():
    return html.div(
        alert_button("Playing!", "Play Movie"),
        alert_button("Uploading!", "Upload Image"),
    )

# TODO

This lets the two buttons show different messages. Try changing the messages passed to them.

Note the set_shown(message) line: the handler closes over the message prop, which is a plain function parameter, so this behaves like any other Python closure.

docs.title: Passing event handlers as props
docs.text:
Often you'll want the parent component to specify a child's event handler. Consider buttons: depending on where you're using a button() component, you might want to execute a different function—perhaps one plays a movie and another uploads an image.

To do this, pass a prop the component receives from its parent as the event handler:

app.py Run 
@component
def button(on_click, *children):
    return html.button({"onClick": on_click}, *children)


@component
def play_button(movie_name):
    shown, set_shown = use_state("")

    def handle_play_click(event):
        set_shown(f"Playing {movie_name}!")

    return html.div(
        button(handle_play_click, f'Play "{movie_name}"'),
        html.p(shown),
    )


@component
def upload_button():
    shown, set_shown = use_state("")

    def handle_upload_click(event):
        set_shown("Uploading!")

    return html.div(
        button(handle_upload_click, "Upload Image"),
        html.p(shown),
    )


@component
def toolbar():
    return html.div(play_button("Kiki's Delivery Service"), upload_button())

# TODO

Here, toolbar() renders a play_button() and an upload_button():

  • play_button() passes handle_play_click as the on_click prop to the button() inside.
  • upload_button() passes handle_upload_click as the on_click prop.

Finally, the button() component accepts a prop called on_click and passes it straight to the built-in browser button with {"onClick": on_click}. This tells ReactPy to call the passed function on click.

Notice the two levels of naming: the prop your own component accepts is an ordinary Python parameter (on_click, snake_case), while the key handed to the browser tag is "onClick". A design system commonly puts styling in components like buttons but leaves the behavior to callers, so play_button() and upload_button() pass handlers down.

docs.title: Naming event handler props
docs.text:
Built-in tags like html.button and html.div only support DOM event names as handler keys — "onClick", "onChange", and so on. When you build your own components, however, you can name their handler props anything you like, because they are just Python parameters.

By convention, name them on_ followed by the interaction:

app.py Run 
@component
def button(on_smash, *children):
    return html.button({"onClick": on_smash}, *children)


@component
def app():
    status, set_status = use_state("Nothing selected")

    return html.div(
        html.p(status),
        button(lambda event: set_status("Playing!"), "Play Movie"),
        button(lambda event: set_status("Uploading!"), "Upload Image"),
    )

# TODO

In this example {"onClick": on_smash} shows that the browser button still needs the key "onClick", but the prop name received by your own button() component is up to you.

When a component supports multiple interactions, name handler props after app-specific concepts. A toolbar() could receive on_play_movie and on_upload_image. The calling app() does not need to know what toolbar() will do with them — that's an implementation detail. It could wire them to a click today and a keyboard shortcut tomorrow. Naming props after app-specific interactions gives you that flexibility.

Use the right tag

Use the semantically correct HTML tag for the interaction. To handle clicks, use html.button({"onClick": handle_click}) rather than html.div({"onClick": handle_click}). A real browser <button> gives you built-in behavior such as keyboard navigation and focus handling. If you dislike the default styling, restyle it with CSS rather than downgrading it to a <div>. Learn more about writing accessible markup.

docs.title: The event object
docs.text:
Handlers receive the event data as their single positional argument. By convention it's called event.

It is not React's SyntheticEvent. There is no nativeEvent, no persist(), no event pooling. It is JSON that the browser sent over the websocket, wrapped in reactpy.types.Event — a dict subclass that adds attribute access into nested dictionaries:

def handle_change(event):
    event["target"]["value"]   # dictionary style
    event.target.value         # identical, attribute style

Both forms are equivalent, and each step down re-wraps the nested dictionary so chaining works. But a missing key reads as None instead of raising, so a typo such as event.target.vallue fails silently. Reach for event.get("target", {}) when a missing value should be a real error.

The properties that reliably arrive are those the client deliberately keeps:

Read Meaning event["target"]["value"] Text of an <input>, <textarea>, or selected <option> event["target"]["checked"] Whether a checkbox or radio is on (use "onChange", which the client maps to input for checkboxes) event["target"]["files"] Files from an <input type="file"> event["key"] Which key, on onKeyDown / onKeyUp event["type"] The event name, e.g. "click" event["target"]["dataset"] The element's data-* attributes event["target"][name] On onSubmit, each named control of the form

ReactPy's client serializes the DOM event's own enumerable properties, plus the five highlighted ones (value, checked, files, type, name) which it re-reads directly from the element so they survive even when the element hides them, and the current text selection.

It drops methods, anything __-prefixed or all-caps, and — to avoid enormous payloads and layout thrash — a long denylist of element properties including innerHTML, outerHTML, childNodes, parentNode, offsetWidth, and scrollTop. So event.target.parentNode is simply not there, and neither is anything that would need the real DOM node.

Form submits hand you the named fields

For onSubmit the target is the <form> itself, and each control that has a name is flattened onto it. That makes it easy to read a whole form without a use_state per field.

docs.title: Event propagation
docs.text:
Event handlers also catch events from any children a component has. We say that an event "bubbles" or "propagates" up the tree: it starts where the event happened, and then goes up.

ReactPy attaches an ordinary DOM listener to each element, so bubbling is the browser's native behavior rather than something ReactPy implements. That has one consequence worth knowing: unlike React, which delegates every event to the document root and then replays it down your component tree, ReactPy's handlers follow the real DOM tree. A parent handler fires for events from anything nested inside it, including elements you did not render yourself.

This <div> contains a button. Both the <div> and the button have their own "onClick" handlers. Which do you think fire when you click the button?

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def toolbar():
    messages, set_messages = use_state([])

    def handle_toolbar_click(event):
        set_messages([*messages, "You clicked on the toolbar!"])

    def handle_play_click(event):
        set_messages([*messages, "Playing!"])

    return html.div(
        {"className": "Toolbar", "onClick": handle_toolbar_click},
        html.button({"onClick": handle_play_click}, "Play Movie"),
    )

.toolbar {
    background: #aaa;
    padding: 5px;
}

button {
    margin: 5px;
}

# TODO

If you click the button, its "onClick" runs first, followed by the parent <div>'s. Two messages appear. If you click the toolbar itself, only the parent's handler runs.

Scroll does not bubble

Because propagation is the browser's own, the browser's exceptions apply. "onScroll" does not bubble: attaching it to an ancestor will not catch scrolls from descendants. Attach it to the element that actually scrolls.

docs.title: Stopping propagation
docs.text:
To prevent an event from reaching parent components, call event.stopPropagation():

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def button(on_click, *children):
    def handle_click(event):
        # Detected from this line, so the client stops the event before
        # it reaches the parent's handler.
        event.stopPropagation()
        on_click()

    return html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, *children)


@component
def toolbar():
    messages, set_messages = use_state([])

    def handle_toolbar_click(event):
        set_messages([*messages, "You clicked on the toolbar!"])

    def handle_play_click():
        set_messages([*messages, "Playing!"])

    return html.div(
        {"className": "Toolbar", "onClick": handle_toolbar_click},
        button(handle_play_click, "Play Movie"),
    )

.toolbar {
    background: #aaa;
    padding: 5px;
}

button {
    margin: 5px;
}

# TODO

Now clicking the button produces only "Playing!".

ReactPy detects this call by reading your bytecode

event.stopPropagation() is a no-op on the server — by the time your handler runs, the browser event is long gone. What actually stops propagation is a flag sent to the browser in advance, and ReactPy derives it by inspecting the bytecode of your handler (core/_event_inspect.py, inspect_event_handler).

It looks for .stopPropagation (and .preventDefault) accessed directly on the first parameter. That produces some sharp edges, all of them observable:

  • The handler must take a parameter at all. def handler(): can never be detected.
  • It must be the first positional parameter. Renaming it is fine; the position is what matters.
  • Rebinding defeats it. e = event followed by e.stopPropagation() is not detected, and propagation silently continues.
  • Passing the event into a helper that calls it is likewise not detected.

When in doubt, skip detection and declare the intent explicitly:

from reactpy import event

@event(stop_propagation=True, prevent_default=True)
async def handle_click(event): ...

docs.title: Preventing default behavior
docs.text:
Call event.preventDefault() the same way to stop the browser's built-in action. The classic case is a form submit, which would otherwise navigate away from the page:

app.py Run 
@component
def signup():
    signed_up, set_signed_up = use_state(0)
    name, set_name = use_state("")

    def handle_name_change(event):
        set_name(event["target"]["value"])

    def handle_submit(event):
        # Without this line the browser would navigate away from the page.
        event.preventDefault()
        set_signed_up(signed_up + 1)
        set_name("")

    return html.form(
        {"onSubmit": handle_submit},
        html.input({"value": name, "onChange": handle_name_change}),
        html.button({"type": "submit"}, "Sign up"),
        html.p(f"{signed_up} signed up"),
    )

# TODO

The same detection rules — and the same @event(prevent_default=True) escape hatch — apply.

Capture-phase handlers

To see an event on the way down, before your children handle it, append Capture to the event name:

html.div(
    {"onClickCapture": handle_toolbar_click},
    html.button({"onClick": handle_play_click}, "Play Movie"),
)

ReactPy forwards the key untouched, and the client registers it with addEventListener("click", handler, True), so "onClickCapture" fires before the button's own "onClick". This works because it maps onto a real DOM capability rather than a React invention — which also means the ordering is the browser's, not ReactPy's.

docs.title: Can event handlers have side effects?
docs.text: Yes. Unlike component bodies, which must stay pure, event handlers run in response to an action rather than during rendering, so they are the correct place to change things. See Where you can cause side effects for where side effects belong and why.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Add a handler by putting the DOM event name in camelCase into the attributes dictionary: {"onClick": handle_click}.
  • Only names you define are snake_case; "on_click" renders but never fires.
  • Pass a function, never the result of calling one; a string value means client-side JavaScript, not Python.
  • Handlers may read props, call setters, and have side effects.
  • The event object is a dict-subclass snapshot of browser data, not a SyntheticEvent; read event["target"]["value"], event["key"], and friends, and don't expect DOM-node properties.
  • Events bubble natively, with the browser's own exceptions such as "onScroll". Stop them with event.stopPropagation(), which is detected from your bytecode — or declare it with @event(stop_propagation=True).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A custom Hook is a plain Python function whose name starts with use_ and which calls other Hooks. It lets you reuse stateful logic between components — each caller still gets its own state, and nothing about it is special to ReactPy beyond the naming rule that makes the linter work.

You will learn

  • How to extract a custom Hook, and what it does and does not share
  • Why each call site gets independent state
  • Why passing a callback into a Hook silently freezes it
  • What actually happens when a Hook is called conditionally
  • What reactpy-flake8 can and cannot see inside a custom Hook

docs.title: Custom Hooks: sharing logic between components
docs.text:
Consider a shopping list where each row can be selected. The selection logic is stateful, and a second screen will need it too. Pulling it out gives you a function that reads like a Hook and behaves like one:

app.py Run 
def use_cart(items):
    """Selection logic for a list of items — the state lives in the caller."""
    selected, set_selected = use_state([])

    def handler_for(item):
        def toggle(event):
            if item in selected:
                set_selected([name for name in selected if name != item])
            else:
                set_selected([*selected, item])

        return toggle

    return selected, handler_for


@component
def checkout(items):
    selected, handler_for = use_cart(items)
    total = 10 * len(selected)
    return html.div(
        html.ul(
            [
                html.li(
                    {"key": item},
                    html.button(
                        {"onClick": handler_for(item)},
                        f"{item} {'[x]' if item in selected else '[ ]'}",
                    ),
                )
                for item in items
            ]
        ),
        html.p(f"{len(selected)} selected, total ${total}"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return checkout(["apple", "bread", "cheese"])

# TODO

Verified: pressing apple, cheese, bread, then apple again walks the counter 1 → 2 → 3 → 2 and the total follows it. Nothing about use_cart is registered, exported, or declared — it is an ordinary function that happens to call use_state.

Two rules make it a Hook rather than a helper:

  • Its name starts with use_. This is not cosmetic; see below.
  • It is called during rendering, at the top level of a component or another Hook — never in an if, a loop, a callback, or after an early return.

docs.title: Hook names must match ^_*use_\w+$
docs.text:
reactpy_flake8 decides what counts as a Hook with a regex, DEFAULT_HOOK_FUNCTION_PATTERN = r"^_*use_\w+$" (reactpy_flake8/run.py). Measured against the same file with only the function name changed, calling it conditionally from a component:

Function name Reported use_form REACTPY102 — hook used inside if _use_form REACTPY102 useForm REACTPY101 — hook used outside component or hook get_form REACTPY101

So the naming rule is what buys you the good diagnostic. A camelCase useForm still gets flagged — but as REACTPY101 at every use_state line inside it, which points at the wrong thing and reads like you called a Hook from the wrong place. Name them use_snake_case, and the linter can tell control-flow violations apart from misplaced calls.

Not every render-time function needs the prefix

Add use_ when the function calls Hooks. Leave it off when it does not — a format_rows() or total_price() is an ordinary function, and prefixing it would make the linter police it as a Hook.

docs.title: Custom Hooks share logic, not state
docs.text:
A common fear is that a Hook is a singleton. It is not: state is stored per call site, in order. Call the same Hook twice in one component and you get two independent boxes.

app.py Run 
def use_toggle(initial=False):
    on, set_on = use_state(initial)
    return on, (lambda event: set_on(not on))


@component
def panel():
    left, flip_left = use_toggle()
    right, flip_right = use_toggle()
    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": flip_left}, f"left {'ON' if left else 'off'}"),
        html.button({"onClick": flip_right}, f"right {'ON' if right else 'off'}"),
        html.p(f"both on: {left and right}"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return panel()

# TODO

Verified: pressing left gives left ON right off; pressing right gives left ON right ON; pressing left again gives left off right ON. Same function, same arguments, two unrelated pieces of state — and both on only when both are flipped.

The same Hook called from two different components is equally independent, since each component instance has its own Hook slots. There is no shared registry, no module-level store, and no Context involved.

This is also why a custom Hook is not a place to put values you want everyone to see. For that, pass props or use create_context (Passing Data Deeply with Context).

docs.title: Passing reactive values between Hooks
docs.text:
A Hook receives plain values during render and returns plain values. It re-runs whenever its caller re-renders, so it sees the same props and state the caller does.

def use_selection(items, limit):
    selected, set_selected = use_state([])
    too_many = len(selected) > limit          # re-evaluated every render
    return selected, set_selected, too_many

What you cannot do is pass a callback in and list it as a dependency.

docs.title: The callback you pass in will go stale
docs.text:
use_polling below takes a result handler and lists it as the Effect's dependency — which looks exactly right, and never works:

app.py Run 
def use_polling(on_result):
    async def loop():
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
            on_result("poll finished")

    # `on_result` looks like a sensible dependency; it never counts as changed
    use_async_effect(loop, dependencies=[on_result])


@component
def dashboard():
    topic, set_topic = use_state("news")
    last, set_last = use_state("nothing yet")
    tick = use_ref(0)

    def on_result(value):
        tick.current += 1
        # reads `topic` from whichever render created this callback
        set_last(f"{value} #{tick.current} (handler saw topic={topic})")

    use_polling(on_result)

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_topic(topic + "x")}, f"Topic {topic}"),
        html.p(last),
    )


@component
def app():
    return dashboard()

# TODO

Verified: press Topic once so the page reads Topic newsx, and the line still says handler saw topic=news. The poll counter keeps climbing, so it looks alive — but it is calling the handler from the first render, forever.

The reason is in core/hooks.py, strictly_equal: a def nested in a component is compared by its co_* bytecode attributes, not by identity. on_result re-created on the next render compares code-equal, so the dependency never changes and the Effect is never replaced.

The fix is to keep the callback in a ref that is refreshed during render, and leave it out of the list:

app.py Run 
def use_polling(topic, on_result):
    latest = use_ref(on_result)
    # always the newest callback, without making it a dependency
    latest.current = on_result

    async def loop():
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
            latest.current(f"result for {topic}")

    # deliberately excludes on_result: listing it would never help anyway
    use_async_effect(loop, dependencies=[topic])


@component
def dashboard():
    topic, set_topic = use_state("news")
    last, set_last = use_state("nothing yet")

    def on_result(value):
        # reads `topic` from the render that created it
        set_last(f"{value} (topic was {topic})")

    use_polling(topic, on_result)

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_topic(topic + "x")}, f"Topic {topic}"),
        html.p(last),
    )


@component
def app():
    return dashboard()

# TODO

Verified: after changing the topic, the same line reads (topic was newsx). The Effect still has exactly one dependency; only the ref's contents changed.

This is the same trap as a locally defined function used as an Effect dependency (Lifecycle of Reactive Effects), and it is nastier inside a Hook because the code that lists the dependency and the code that created the callback live in different files.

docs.title: When a Hook is called conditionally, nothing fails
docs.text:
This is the section React's version of the page does not need, because React's compiler and dev-mode warnings are not present here.

ReactPy matches Hooks to their state slots by call order. Nothing names them, and nothing checks them. When the number of Hooks called changes between renders, the slots shift and values land in the wrong variables:

app.py Run 
def use_profile(show_nickname):
    name, set_name = use_state("name")
    if show_nickname:
        nickname, set_nickname = use_state("nickname")
    else:
        nickname = "-"
    # `bio` is the third hook when the branch is taken and the second when it
    # is not, so it inherits the slot that `nickname` used to own
    bio, set_bio = use_state("bio")
    return name, nickname, bio, set_bio


@component
def profile(show_nickname):
    name, nickname, bio, set_bio = use_profile(show_nickname)

    def extend_bio(event):
        set_bio(bio + "!")

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": extend_bio}, f"bio={bio}"),
        html.p(f"name={name} nickname={nickname}"),
    )


@component
def app():
    show, set_show = use_state(True)
    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_show(not show)}, "toggle nickname"),
        profile(show),
    )

# TODO

Verified: press bio= twice, then toggle nickname. The page prints

bio=bio!!          # before the branch changes
bio=nickname       # after — bio is now nickname's state

No exception. No warning. No log record — the probe captured a completely silent reactpy logger across the whole transition. bio is the third Hook when the branch is taken and the second when it is not, so after the flip it reads the box that nickname used to own.

The corrected version calls every Hook unconditionally and makes only the return value conditional:

app.py Run 
def use_profile(show_nickname):
    name, set_name = use_state("name")
    # the hook is called unconditionally; only the returned value is conditional
    nickname, set_nickname = use_state("nickname")
    bio, set_bio = use_state("bio")
    return name, (nickname if show_nickname else "-"), bio, set_bio


@component
def profile(show_nickname):
    name, nickname, bio, set_bio = use_profile(show_nickname)

    def extend_bio(event):
        set_bio(bio + "!")

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": extend_bio}, f"bio={bio}"),
        html.p(f"name={name} nickname={nickname}"),
    )


@component
def app():
    show, set_show = use_state(True)
    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_show(not show)}, "toggle nickname"),
        profile(show),
    )

# TODO

Verified with the same script: bio=bio!! before and after the toggle. The toggle now changes only what is displayed.

docs.title: What the linter can see
docs.text:
REACTPY102 does fire on the broken file above — hook 'use_state' used inside if statement — provided the function is named as a Hook. That coverage is real and worth wiring into CI. So does REACTPY103, which catches the early-return case: a hook after a return reports hook 'use_state' used after an early return on line N. REACTPY101 catches hooks used outside any component or hook, and REACTPY100 hooks defined as closures. All four are in reactpy-flake8's RulesOfHooksVisitor. What it does not extend to:

  • calling a Hook-conditionally through a wrapper that the linter does not recognise (see the name table above),
  • a Hook list in one branch matching the caller's expectation in another,
  • the order the hooks actually run in — that is a runtime property, and nothing checks it.

And it checks dependency lists only under exhaustive_hook_deps=True, and even then only for a narrow set of shapes. See Lifecycle of Reactive Effects for exactly which. Treat the linter as a partial net and the fix — Hooks at the top level, always — as the actual rule.

Do not branch to disable a Hook

# wrong: the second Hook disappears when polling is off
if polling:
    use_async_effect(loop, dependencies=[topic])
Keep the call and branch inside the Hook body instead, returning None when there is nothing to do. See Lifecycle of Reactive Effects.

docs.title: Passing event handlers into custom Hooks
docs.text:
A handler is an ordinary value: pass it in, call it, done — it does not need to be a dependency, and listing it does not make it fresher (measured above). The two shapes that work:

# the Hook calls it; the ref keeps it current
def use_polling(on_result):
    latest = use_ref(on_result)
    latest.current = on_result
    ...

# or the caller owns the callback entirely and the Hook just hands back a value
selected, toggle = use_cart(items)

If you find yourself wanting to store a callback so it stays fresh, that is the same problem useEffectEvent solves in React — and ReactPy has no such Hook. The ref-updated-during-render idiom above is the equivalent, with the caveat that reading .current during render makes the render depend on an external value (Manipulating the DOM with Refs).

docs.title: When to use custom Hooks
docs.text:
Write one when you have logic — not markup — that two components genuinely need in the same shape. Good candidates in ReactPy:

  • selection, pagination, and form-draft logic
  • a subscription or polling loop with its clean-up wired correctly
  • reading a value from a use_connection-scoped resource
  • a compound updater that several components apply to the same kind of state

Keep them focused on a concrete use case. A use_async(fetcher, deps) that wraps use_async_effect in generic terms tends to encode one person's cancellation assumptions for everyone; the specific use_polling(topic, on_result) is easier to reason about and easier to change.

Two things a custom Hook is not:

  • A render bailout. ReactPy has no memo, so extracting a Hook does not reduce how often a component's body runs (Separating Events from Effects).
  • A state container. It cannot share state between components; only props and Context can.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A custom Hook is a function named use_* that calls Hooks; extract one to reuse stateful logic.
  • State is per call site, in call order: the same Hook called twice is two independent boxes (verified).
  • Name them use_snake_case — the linter's regex is ^_*use_\w+$, and camelCase versions get flagged as REACTPY101 instead of the accurate REACTPY102.
  • Never list a callback you were handed as a dependency: it compares code-equal and freezes the Effect on the first render. Read it through a ref updated during render.
  • Conditional Hook calls do not raise; state slots shift and values silently migrate between variables (verified: bio became nickname). Call every Hook unconditionally and branch on the return value.
  • reactpy-flake8 sees control-flow violations inside recognised Hooks, and nothing else — no dependency checks, no wrapper coverage.

docs.title: Scaling Up with Reducer and Context
Overview
docs.text:
A reducer keeps a component's update logic in one pure function; context carries values past components that only forward them. Together they let a deep tree read and change shared state without any wiring through props. In ReactPy there is one extra fact that makes this work cleanly: dispatch has a stable identity across renders, so it is safe to put in a context value.

You will learn

  • How to combine a reducer with context, in three steps
  • Why dispatch is safe to share through context in ReactPy
  • How to move all the wiring into a single module the UI never imports from directly

docs.title: Combining a reducer with context
docs.text:
Start with the version where state and dispatch travel as props. Only task_form and task want dispatch, but it has to be handed to everyone in between:

app.py Run 
@component
def task_form(state, dispatch, task):
    # The only component that actually wants dispatch...
    def handle_toggle(event):
        dispatch({"type": "toggled", "id": task["id"]})

    return html.div(
        {"style": {"textDecoration": "line-through" if task["done"] else "none"}},
        task["text"],
        html.button({"onClick": handle_toggle}, "Toggle"),
    )


@component
def task(state, dispatch, task):
    # ...but must receive it and hand it on, unchanged.
    def handle_delete(event):
        dispatch({"type": "deleted", "id": task["id"]})

    return html.li(
        {"key": task["id"]},
        task_form(state, dispatch, task),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_delete}, "Delete"),
    )


@component
def task_list(state, dispatch):
    # ...and this one forwards both, without reading either.
    return html.ul(
        [task(state, dispatch, item, key=item["id"]) for item in state["tasks"]]
    )


@component
def task_app():
    state, dispatch = use_reducer(tasks_reducer, {"tasks": INITIAL_TASKS, "next_id": 2})

    def handle_add(event):
        dispatch({"type": "added"})

    return html.div(
        html.h3("Prague itinerary"),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_add}, "Add task"),
        task_list(state, dispatch),
        html.p({"id": "summary"}, f"{len(state['tasks'])} tasks"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return task_app()

# TODO

Read the signatures: task_list(state, dispatch) receives both and reads neither — it only builds children and passes both along. task forwards state untouched to task_form, which uses only dispatch. Every new layer in the middle copies the same two parameters.

The reducer is already correct for ReactPy: module-level, reading nothing but its two arguments, returning new objects, and raising on an unknown action type. See Extracting State Logic into a Reducer for why each of those matters here.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the context
docs.text:
One context carries both halves — the state to read and the dispatch to change it with. Keep it beside the reducer, in a module that does not import the UI:

app.pytasks.py Run 
@component
def task_form(task):
    # Reads dispatch from context; no prop arrived.
    _, dispatch = use_context(TaskContext)

    def handle_toggle(event):
        dispatch({"type": "toggled", "id": task["id"]})

    return html.div(
        {"style": {"textDecoration": "line-through" if task["done"] else "none"}},
        task["text"],
        html.button({"onClick": handle_toggle}, "Toggle"),
    )


@component
def task(task):
    _, dispatch = use_context(TaskContext)

    def handle_delete(event):
        dispatch({"type": "deleted", "id": task["id"]})

    return html.li(
        {"key": task["id"]},
        task_form(task),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_delete}, "Delete"),
    )


@component
def task_list():
    # Reads only the state; dispatch never has to come through here.
    state, _ = use_context(TaskContext)
    return html.ul([task(item, key=item["id"]) for item in state["tasks"]])


@component
def task_app():
    state, dispatch = use_reducer(tasks_reducer, INITIAL_STATE)

    def handle_add(event):
        dispatch({"type": "added"})

    return html.div(
        html.h3("Prague itinerary"),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_add}, "Add task"),
        # One provider for the whole subtree.
        TaskContext(task_list(), value=(state, dispatch)),
        html.p({"id": "summary"}, f"{len(state['tasks'])} tasks"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return task_app()

"""The reducer, the context, and the initial state — all outside the UI."""

from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Any

from reactpy import create_context
from reactpy.types import Context

TaskState = dict[str, Any]
TaskValue = tuple[TaskState, Callable[[dict[str, Any]], None]]

# The reducer never mutates what it is given, so one shared constant is
# safe as the initial state for every instance.
INITIAL_TASKS = [
    {"id": 0, "text": "Packing", "done": False},
    {"id": 1, "text": "Passport", "done": True},
]

INITIAL_STATE: TaskState = {"tasks": INITIAL_TASKS, "next_id": 2}

# One context carries both halves: the state to read and the dispatch to change
# it with. Annotate the name, or the default narrows the value type.
TaskContext: Context[TaskValue] = create_context((INITIAL_STATE, lambda action: None))


def tasks_reducer(state: TaskState, action: dict[str, Any]) -> TaskState:
    kind = action["type"]
    if kind == "added":
        task = {"id": state["next_id"], "text": "New task", "done": False}
        return {
            **state,
            "tasks": [*state["tasks"], task],
            "next_id": state["next_id"] + 1,
        }
    if kind == "toggled":
        return {
            **state,
            "tasks": [
                {**task, "done": not task["done"]}
                if task["id"] == action["id"]
                else task
                for task in state["tasks"]
            ],
        }
    if kind == "deleted":
        return {
            **state,
            "tasks": [task for task in state["tasks"] if task["id"] != action["id"]],
        }
    raise ValueError(f"unknown action type {kind!r}")

# TODO

Two things to notice in tasks.py.

The context object is matched by identity, so create it once and import it from here everywhere. The annotation is load-bearing: create_context infers the value type from its default, so without Context[TaskValue] a type checker fixes the value to the default's shape and rejects a real one. Write the default first, then annotate. See Use Context.

The default value is a usable value, not None: an empty state and a dispatch that does nothing. A component rendered without a provider then renders an empty list instead of crashing when a handler fires.

docs.title: Step 2: Put state and dispatch into context
docs.text:
Call use_reducer once, in the component that owns the state, and provide both halves:

state, dispatch = use_reducer(tasks_reducer, INITIAL_STATE)
...
TaskContext(task_list(), value=(state, dispatch))

A tuple is the simplest value that carries both. If you prefer a dict or a dataclass, the same rules apply — but do not expect the value to control how often consumers render. ReactPy compares nothing here: use_context hands back whatever the provider is currently holding, and a provider that re-renders re-renders its children whether the value is new, equal, or literally the same object. Re-render cost is governed by where you place the provider, not by how you build the value.

docs.title: Step 3: Use context anywhere in the tree
docs.text:
Now the middle of the tree forgets both parameters:

@component
def task_list():
    state, _ = use_context(TaskContext)
    return html.ul([task(item, key=item["id"]) for item in state["tasks"]])

task_list no longer mentions dispatch at all, and task and task_form each call use_context themselves. Verified: this version and the prop version above are behaviourally identical — the same initial two tasks, the same row struck through by Toggle, the same count after Add task, the same rows after Delete. All three versions in this page pass the same user-journey comparison.

Note

use_context reserves no state slot, so unlike use_state it is safe to call conditionally. That is not an invitation to hide it: read it at the top of the component, the way you would a prop, so it is obvious where the value comes from.

docs.title: Why dispatch is safe to share in ReactPy
docs.text:
In React, sharing dispatch through context is safe because React guarantees its identity. In ReactPy it is safe for a more concrete reason you can check in the source: use_reducer builds the dispatcher once with _use_const — a use_state holding the function — and returns that same object on every render. Verified: across five renders and four dispatches, id(dispatch) took exactly one value.

That matters because the dispatcher closes over the reducer, which ReactPy also freezes at the first render. A stale dispatcher is not a hazard here as long as the reducer is module-level — which is exactly the rule the reducer page already imposes. Share dispatch freely; do not share a value you expect to be re-read from a closure.

What context does not do: it is not a render optimisation. ReactPy has no memo, so when the provider re-renders with a new value, the whole subtree re-renders, including every component whose read value did not change. Context removes parameters, not work. See What context does not do.

docs.title: Moving all wiring into a single file
docs.text:
Once the UI reads everything from context, the reducer, the context object, and even use_reducer can disappear from it. Move the whole mechanism into tasks.py, and expose exactly two names — a provider component and an accessor hook:

app.pytasks.py Run 
@component
def task_form(task):
    # No props. The dispatch comes from the wiring file.
    _, dispatch = use_tasks()

    def handle_toggle(event):
        dispatch({"type": "toggled", "id": task["id"]})

    return html.div(
        {"style": {"textDecoration": "line-through" if task["done"] else "none"}},
        task["text"],
        html.button({"onClick": handle_toggle}, "Toggle"),
    )


@component
def task(task):
    _, dispatch = use_tasks()

    def handle_delete(event):
        dispatch({"type": "deleted", "id": task["id"]})

    return html.li(
        {"key": task["id"]},
        task_form(task),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_delete}, "Delete"),
    )


@component
def task_list():
    state, _ = use_tasks()
    return html.ul([task(item, key=item["id"]) for item in state["tasks"]])


@component
def task_app():
    state, dispatch = use_tasks()

    def handle_add(event):
        dispatch({"type": "added"})

    return html.div(
        html.h3("Prague itinerary"),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_add}, "Add task"),
        task_list(),
        html.p({"id": "summary"}, f"{len(state['tasks'])} tasks"),
    )


@component
def app():
    # One name from the wiring file: the provider component.
    return task_store(task_app())

"""All the reducer, context, and wiring lives here; the UI imports two names."""

from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import Any

from reactpy import component, create_context, use_context, use_reducer
from reactpy.types import Context

TaskState = dict[str, Any]
TaskValue = tuple[TaskState, Callable[[dict[str, Any]], None]]

# The reducer never mutates what it is given, so one shared constant is
# safe as the initial state for every instance.
INITIAL_TASKS = [
    {"id": 0, "text": "Packing", "done": False},
    {"id": 1, "text": "Passport", "done": True},
]

INITIAL_STATE: TaskState = {"tasks": INITIAL_TASKS, "next_id": 2}

TaskContext: Context[TaskValue] = create_context((INITIAL_STATE, lambda action: None))


def tasks_reducer(state: TaskState, action: dict[str, Any]) -> TaskState:
    kind = action["type"]
    if kind == "added":
        task = {"id": state["next_id"], "text": "New task", "done": False}
        return {
            **state,
            "tasks": [*state["tasks"], task],
            "next_id": state["next_id"] + 1,
        }
    if kind == "toggled":
        return {
            **state,
            "tasks": [
                {**task, "done": not task["done"]}
                if task["id"] == action["id"]
                else task
                for task in state["tasks"]
            ],
        }
    if kind == "deleted":
        return {
            **state,
            "tasks": [task for task in state["tasks"] if task["id"] != action["id"]],
        }
    raise ValueError(f"unknown action type {kind!r}")


@component
def task_store(*children: Any):
    """Owns the reducer and provides it. The UI never sees the reducer."""
    state, dispatch = use_reducer(tasks_reducer, INITIAL_STATE)
    return TaskContext(*children, value=(state, dispatch))


def use_tasks() -> TaskValue:
    """The only accessor the UI needs: current state plus dispatch."""
    return use_context(TaskContext)

# TODO

The UI file now imports only task_store and use_tasks. It never mentions use_reducer, create_context, tasks_reducer, or TaskContext. Two consequences worth having:

  • The UI cannot reach the reducer except through an action, so there is no way to bypass it.
  • Changing how the state is stored — a different reducer, a different initial shape, even dropping context entirely — touches one file and no component.

task_store is a component that calls use_reducer and returns the provider. A component's render may return another component, so this composes without ceremony. Note that use_tasks is a plain function that calls use_context: it is a custom Hook, so name it use_* — the linter's regex is ^_*use_\w+$, and camelCase variants get a less accurate diagnostic. See Reusing Logic with Custom Hooks.

Pitfall

Because the provider is now a component, removing it from the tree unmounts everything below it and throws their state away. Do not write task_store(page()) if logged_in else page(). Keep the provider in the tree and vary only its value — verified: a conditional provider resets a leaf's state (its render counter returns to 1 and its draft text clears), while a stable key on the child does not prevent it. See Removing a provider resets the subtree below it.

Two task_store instances are two independent stores, not one shared store: verified, three presses on one side moved one=5 while the other stayed at its initial two=2. Context propagates down from the provider that happens to be above you. To genuinely share state, there must be one provider above both consumers — usually near the root.

Deep Dive

Should you also provide a derived value, such as a filtered list or a total? Compute it in the component that needs it. ReactPy re-renders the subtree whenever the provided state changes anyway, so a cached derivation saves nothing, and use_memo around it adds a dependency list to keep correct. Reserve the context value for what is genuinely shared: the state object and dispatch. For the caching rules, see You Might Not Need an Effect.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• A reducer owns the transitions; context carries (state, dispatch) past components that would only forward them. Both are needed together — context without a reducer leaves the update logic scattered, a reducer without context leaves the props.
  • Create the context beside the reducer, at module level, with a usable default and a Context[...] annotation so the value type is not narrowed by the default.
  • Provide (state, dispatch) from one component that owns use_reducer; read it in each component that needs it.
  • dispatch is identity-stable across renders in ReactPy (verified: one id over five renders), which is what makes sharing it through context sound.
  • A module that exports a provider component and a use_* accessor lets the UI import two names and never touch the reducer.
  • Keep the provider in the tree. Removing it remounts the subtree and discards state; a key does not save it (verified).
  • One provider per shared store. Two providers are two stores (verified).
  • Context removes parameters, not renders — ReactPy has no render bailout.
