docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Event handlers and Effects run at different times and for different reasons. Most Effect bugs are not Effect bugs — they are interaction logic that was put in the wrong place. Move it back and the Effect disappears.

You will learn

  • Why interaction logic belongs in a handler, not an Effect
  • Why handler logic is not reactive — and why that is a feature
  • How ReactPy picks which render's handler actually runs
  • What use_callback does in ReactPy, and what it does not buy you
  • How to read the newest value from a callback you cannot re-create

docs.title: Choosing between event handlers and Effects
docs.text:
The question is never "which hook?" but "when should this logic run?"

Event handler Effect Runs when the interaction happens after a render, whenever a dependency changed Re-runs when only if the user repeats the interaction any dependency changes — including one you forgot to list Right for submit, click, input, drag, "do this now" subscribing, polling, syncing to a server

Both cost one render per click in the examples below — the difference is not performance, it is what triggers the work. An Effect that sets state it also lists as a dependency re-triggers itself; measured, that loop reached 86 renders before it was stopped. A handler has no such feedback path, which is most of why interaction logic belongs there.

If the logic should run when the user does the thing, it goes in the handler. If it should run whenever a value is a certain way, it goes in an Effect.

docs.title: Logic in an Effect, driven by click-only state
docs.text:
Here the shipping quote is computed by an Effect watching a flag that only a click sets:

app.py Run 
def calculate_shipping(city, country):
    """Plain function: takes what it needs, returns the result."""
    if not city or not country:
        return ""
    return f"{city}, {country} — ${15 + 5}"


@component
def shipping_form():
    city, set_city = use_state("")
    country, set_country = use_state("")
    # state that exists purely to make the Effect run
    quoted, set_quoted = use_state(False)
    shipping_info, set_shipping_info = use_state("")
    clicks, set_clicks = use_state(0)

    def submit(event):
        set_clicks(clicks + 1)
        set_quoted(True)

    # the "intent" is buried in an Effect watching a flag a click merely sets
    def recalculate():
        if quoted:
            result = calculate_shipping(city, country)
            set_shipping_info(result)
            if result:
                print(f"quoted {result}")

    use_effect(recalculate, dependencies=[quoted])

    return html.div(
        html.label(
            "City: ",
            html.input(
                {"value": city, "onChange": lambda e: set_city(e["target"]["value"])}
            ),
        ),
        html.label(
            "Country: ",
            html.input(
                {
                    "value": country,
                    "onChange": lambda e: set_country(e["target"]["value"]),
                }
            ),
        ),
        html.button({"onClick": submit}, "Get quote"),
        html.p(shipping_info or "—"),
        f"Clicks: {clicks}",
    )


@component
def app():
    return shipping_form()

# TODO

This is where the ReactJS version of this example stops matching reality. Verified behaviour: type a city and country, then press Get quote three times.

  • Click 1 logs quoted Portland, US — $20.
  • Clicks 2 and 3 increment the counter and log nothing at all.

set_quoted(True) sets the same value every time, so ReactPy sees no change, and the dependency list says nothing re-synchronized. The user gets a button that works once. Nothing about this is obvious from the code — the Effect looks correct.

docs.title: The same logic in the handler
Reactive values and reactive logic
docs.text: Every value in the component body belongs to one render. Logic placed in the component body or in an Effect re-runs when those values change. Logic inside a handler does not — it runs when called, on whatever render produced it.

docs.title: Logic inside event handlers is not reactive
docs.text:
def submit(event):
    print(f"submitting {city}, {country}")   # reads one render's values
    send(city, country)

Nothing about this code will re-run when city changes. That is not a defect: a click should do the thing once, using the values the user saw when they clicked. Making handler logic "reactive" is what produces double-submits and the click-once bug above.

docs.title: Logic inside Effects is reactive
docs.text:
def reconnect():
    open_socket(room)

use_effect(reconnect, dependencies=[room])

This one re-runs on its own whenever room changes, including changes you did not expect. That is the whole point of an Effect — and the whole reason logic you don't want repeated does not belong there.

docs.title: Extracting non-reactive logic out of Effects
docs.text:
Once intent lives in the handler, the shared part is usually an ordinary function. Give it its inputs as parameters and both sides can use it:

def calculate_shipping(city, country):
    if not city or not country:
        return ""
    return f"{city}, {country} — ${15 + 5}"


@component
def shipping_form():
    ...

    def submit(event):
        set_shipping_info(calculate_shipping(city, country))

No hook needed. A function that only reads values and returns something does not need to be a hook, and making it one costs a render.

ReactPy has no useEffectEvent, no useOptimistic, and no useTransition — verified against reactpy 2.0.0b13. That is not a gap to route around with an Effect: the handler-is-not-reactive property that Effect Events exist to give you in React is what you already have here for free.

docs.title: Which handler actually runs
docs.text:
ReactPy keeps one handler per target, registered when the component renders (core/layout.py, _event_handlers), and looks it up at dispatch time — when the event is processed, not when it arrived.

Two things follow, both measured.

A normal click sees current values. Click after click with the connection settling between them, and the handler always reads the latest state:

added item, discount=0
added item, discount=10
added item, discount=20

Events that arrive before the next render all see the same snapshot. Deliver two clicks without a render in between and both run the same closure:

app.py Run 
@component
def basket():
    items, set_items = use_state([])
    discount, set_discount = use_state(0)

    def add_naive(event):
        # reads `items` and `discount` from whichever render created this handler
        print(f"naive: {len(items)} items, discount={discount}")
        set_items([*items, f"item-{len(items) + 1}@{discount}"])

    def add_safe(event):
        # the updater receives the *current* state at the moment it is applied
        def append(current):
            print(f"safe: {len(current)} items, discount={discount}")
            return [*current, f"item-{len(current) + 1}@{discount}"]

        set_items(append)

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": add_naive}, "Add (naive)"),
        html.button({"onClick": add_safe}, "Add (safe)"),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda e: set_discount(discount + 10)}, f"Coupon {discount}%"
        ),
        html.p(", ".join(items) or "empty basket"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return basket()

# TODO

Verified with two clicks delivered back-to-back:

Handler log Final list Add (naive) 0 items twice item-1@0 — the second click is gone Add (safe) 0 items, then 1 items item-1@0, item-2@0

This is not a hypothetical. On a real connection, events are queued per target (core/layout.py, _process_event_queue) and a double-click, a fast key repeat, or any latency between the browser and a busy server produces exactly this. The naive set_items(items + [...]) reads a snapshot; the updater set_items(lambda current: ...) is applied against the state at the moment it lands.

So the handler-staleness story in ReactPy is narrower than in React, and it is worth being precise:

  • You generally do not need use_callback to "get fresh values" in a handler — the handler that runs is the current one.
  • You do need the functional updater form whenever an update depends on the current state and two events can arrive in the same round trip.

docs.title: Async handlers
docs.text:
A handler may be async def, and it may set state after an await:

async def submit(event):
    set_status("saving")
    result = await save(document)
    set_status("saved")          # works — the render happens after the await

Verified: the page shows status=saving immediately, then status=saved once the await resolves — two renders, both after the click.

But if the component unmounts during the await, the update is discarded and the only trace is a debug line — Did not render component with model state ID ... - component already unmounted. Nothing errors, nothing warns, and the user who navigated away is unaffected. Do not treat "the setter did not raise" as evidence the write landed; if it matters, assert it in a test that keeps the component mounted.

docs.title: Keeping a callback's identity stable
docs.text:
use_callback exists and memoizes through use_memo, so it shares the dependency semantics described on Lifecycle of Reactive Effects — strictly_equal, not id.

app.py Run 
@component
def toolbar():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)
    theme, set_theme = use_state("light")
    previous = use_ref(object())

    def stable_handler(event):
        set_count(count + 1)

    # inferred dependencies: `count` is the only free variable
    on_click = use_callback(stable_handler)

    reused = previous.current is on_click
    previous.current = on_click

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": on_click}, f"Count {count}"),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda e: set_theme("dark" if theme == "light" else "light")},
            f"Theme {theme}",
        ),
        html.p("handler reused on this render" if reused else "handler recreated"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return toolbar()

# TODO

Verified: pressing Theme (not a dependency) reports handler reused on this render; pressing Count (a dependency) reports handler recreated.

Be clear about what that buys you. ReactPy has no render bailout: there is no memo (absent from both reactpy and reactpy.reactjs), and a child re-renders whenever its parent does. Measured — a child whose props and handler never changed ran its body 4 times across one mount and three parent re-renders. So a stable callback does not make anything re-render less. What it does is keep a value out of an Effect's or use_memo's dependency list without re-triggering it.

There is no useEvent, so the nearest equivalent to React's Effect Event — a stable callable that always reads the newest values — is a ref updated during render:

app.py Run 
@component
def checkout():
    coupon, set_coupon = use_state("")
    total, set_total = use_state(0)
    coupon_ref = use_ref("")
    # updated during render, so any callback reads the value as of the click
    coupon_ref.current = coupon

    # pinned to nothing: the identity never changes, yet it reads `coupon_ref`
    apply_coupon = use_callback(
        lambda event: print(f"applying coupon={coupon_ref.current!r}"),
        dependencies=[],
    )

    return html.div(
        html.input(
            {
                "value": coupon,
                "onChange": lambda e: set_coupon(e["target"]["value"].upper()),
            }
        ),
        html.button({"onClick": apply_coupon}, "Apply coupon"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_total(total + 10)}, f"Total {total}"),
        html.p(f"page shows coupon={coupon!r} — compare with the console"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return checkout()

# TODO

Verified: Apply coupon logs the value currently in the box even though the callback is pinned to dependencies=[] and is never re-created.

A callback pinned to a local function never updates

Same trap as Effects, and it is worse here because the callback is supposed to be stable. dependencies=[describe], where describe is a local def, compares code-equal forever:

app.py Run 
@component
def search():
    query, set_query = use_state("")
    runs, set_runs = use_state(0)

    def describe():
        return f"query={query!r}"

    def run(event):
        # `describe` is re-created every render but compares code-equal, so this
        # callback is still the one from the very first render. The functional
        # updater keeps the counter honest; only `describe()` is frozen.
        print(f"handler sees {describe()}")
        set_runs(lambda current: current + 1)

    on_click = use_callback(run, dependencies=[describe])

    return html.div(
        html.input(
            {"value": query, "onChange": lambda e: set_query(e["target"]["value"])}
        ),
        html.button({"onClick": on_click}, f"Run ({runs})"),
        html.p(f"page shows query={query!r} — compare with the console"),
    )


@component
def app():
    return search()

# TODO

Verified: type shoes, press Run, type shoes2, press Run again. The page shows the new query both times; the console says handler sees query='' both times. The counter keeps counting (Run (2)), which is what makes this so easy to miss — the callback looks alive while reading a snapshot from mount.

Depend on the scalar values the callback actually reads, and never on a function defined inside the component.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Ask when the logic should run. Interaction → handler. Synchronization → Effect.
  • State that only a handler sets and only an Effect reads is a smell: call the function from the handler and delete both. Verified symptom: the button works once.
  • Handler logic is deliberately not reactive; that is why you do not need React's Effect Events here.
  • ReactPy stores one handler per target and looks it up at dispatch, so a normal click sees current values — but events delivered before the next render share one snapshot. Use the functional updater for read-modify-write.
  • An async handler may set state after await; after unmount that update is silently dropped.
  • use_callback pins identity, not freshness, and identity buys you nothing for render cost in ReactPy. Reach for a render-updated ref when you need both.
  • Never list a locally defined function as a dependency of a callback or Effect — it compares code-equal and freezes the closure.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Sometimes, you want the state of two components to always change together. To do it, remove state from both of them, move it to their closest common parent, and then pass it down to them via props. This is known as lifting state up, and it's one of the most common things you will do writing ReactPy code.

You will learn

  • How to share state between two components
  • How to coordinate components by lifting state to their common parent
  • What controlled and uncontrolled components are

docs.title: Lifting state up by example
docs.text:
In this example, a parent accordion() component renders two separate panel()s:

  • accordion()
    • panel()
    • panel()

Each panel() component has a boolean is_active state that determines whether its content is visible.

Press the Show button for both panels:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def panel(title, *children):
    is_active, set_is_active = use_state(False)

    return html.section(
        {"className": "panel"},
        html.h3(title),
        html.p(*children)
        if is_active
        else html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_is_active(True)}, "Show"),
    )


@component
def accordion():
    return html(
        html.h2("Almaty, Kazakhstan"),
        panel(
            "About",
            "With a population of about 2 million, Almaty is Kazakhstan's "
            "largest city. From 1929 to 1997, it was its capital city.",
        ),
        panel(
            "Etymology",
            "The name comes from алма, the Kazakh word for “apple” and is "
            "often translated as “full of apples”.",
        ),
    )

h3,
p {
    margin: 5px 0;
}

.panel {
    padding: 10px;
    border: 1px solid #aaa;
}

# TODO

Notice how pressing one panel's button does not affect the other panel — they are independent.

But now let's say you want to change it so that only one panel is expanded at any given time. With that design, expanding the second panel should collapse the first one. How would you do that?

To coordinate these two panels, you need to "lift their state up" to a parent component in three steps:

  1. Remove state from the child components.
  2. Pass hardcoded data from the common parent.
  3. Add state to the common parent and pass it down together with the event handlers.

This will allow the accordion() component to coordinate both panel()s and only expand one at a time.

docs.title: Step 1: Remove state from the child components
docs.text:
You will give control of the panel()'s is_active to its parent component. This means that the parent component will pass is_active to panel() as a prop instead. Start by removing this line from the panel() component:

is_active, set_is_active = use_state(False)

And instead, add is_active to the panel()'s list of props:

@component
def panel(title, is_active, *children):

Now the panel()'s parent component can control is_active by passing it down as a prop. Conversely, the panel() component now has no control over the value of is_active — it's now up to the parent component!

docs.title: Step 2: Pass hardcoded data from the common parent
docs.text:
To lift state up, you must locate the closest common parent component of both of the child components that you want to coordinate:

  • accordion() (closest common parent)
    • panel()
    • panel()

In this example, it's the accordion() component. Since it's above both panels and can control their props, it will become the "source of truth" for which panel is currently active. Make the accordion() component pass a hardcoded value of is_active (for example, True) to both panels:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def panel(title, is_active, *children):
    return html.section(
        {"className": "panel"},
        html.h3(title),
        html.p(*children) if is_active else html.button("Show"),
    )


@component
def accordion():
    return html(
        html.h2("Almaty, Kazakhstan"),
        panel("About", True, "With a population of about 2 million..."),
        panel("Etymology", True, "The name comes from алма..."),
    )

h3,
p {
    margin: 5px 0;
}

.panel {
    padding: 10px;
    border: 1px solid #aaa;
}

# TODO

Try editing the hardcoded is_active values in the accordion() component and see the result on the screen.

docs.title: Step 3: Add state to the common parent
docs.text:
Lifting state up often changes the nature of what you're storing as state.

In this case, only one panel should be active at a time. This means that the accordion() common parent component needs to keep track of which panel is the active one. Instead of a bool value, it could use a number as the index of the active panel() for the state variable:

active_index, set_active_index = use_state(0)

When the active_index is 0, the first panel is active, and when it's 1, it's the second one.

Clicking the "Show" button in either panel() needs to change the active index in accordion(). A panel() can't set the active_index state directly because it's defined inside the accordion(). The accordion() component needs to explicitly allow the panel() component to change its state by passing an event handler down as a prop:

panel(
    "About",
    active_index == 0,
    lambda event: set_active_index(0),
    ...
)

The html.button() inside the panel() will now use the on_show prop as its click event handler:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def panel(title, is_active, on_show, *children):
    return html.section(
        {"className": "panel"},
        html.h3(title),
        (html.p(*children) if is_active else html.button({"onClick": on_show}, "Show")),
    )


@component
def accordion():
    active_index, set_active_index = use_state(0)

    return html(
        html.h2("Almaty, Kazakhstan"),
        panel(
            "About",
            active_index == 0,
            lambda event: set_active_index(0),
            "With a population of about 2 million, Almaty is Kazakhstan's "
            "largest city. From 1929 to 1997, it was its capital city.",
        ),
        panel(
            "Etymology",
            active_index == 1,
            lambda event: set_active_index(1),
            "The name comes from алма, the Kazakh word for “apple” and is "
            "often translated as “full of apples”.",
        ),
    )

h3,
p {
    margin: 5px 0;
}

.panel {
    padding: 10px;
    border: 1px solid #aaa;
}

# TODO

This completes lifting state up! Moving state into the common parent component allowed you to coordinate the two panels. Using the active index instead of two "is shown" flags ensured that only one panel is active at a given time. And passing down the event handler to the child allowed the child to change the parent's state.

docs.title: Controlled and uncontrolled components
docs.text:
It is common to call a component with some local state "uncontrolled". For example, the original panel() component with an is_active state variable is uncontrolled because its parent cannot influence whether the panel is active or not.

In contrast, you might say a component is "controlled" when the important information in it is driven by props rather than its own local state. This lets the parent component fully specify its behavior. The final panel() component with the is_active prop is controlled by the accordion() component.

Uncontrolled components are easier to use within their parents because they require less configuration. But they're less flexible when you want to coordinate them together. Controlled components are maximally flexible, but they require the parent components to fully configure them with props.

In practice, "controlled" and "uncontrolled" aren't strict technical terms — each component usually has some mix of both local state and props. However, this is a useful way to talk about how components are designed and what capabilities they offer.

When writing a component, consider which information in it should be controlled (via props), and which information should be uncontrolled (via state). But you can always change your mind and refactor later.

docs.title: A single source of truth for each state
docs.text:
In a ReactPy application, many components will have their own state. Some state may "live" close to the leaf components (components at the bottom of the tree) like inputs. Other state may "live" closer to the top of the app. For example, a router implemented in ReactPy would keep the current route in the state of a component near the root, and pass it down by props.

For each unique piece of state, you will choose the component that "owns" it. This principle is also known as having a "single source of truth". It doesn't mean that all state lives in one place — but that for each piece of state, there is a specific component that holds that piece of information. Instead of duplicating shared state between components, lift it up to their common shared parent, and pass it down to the children that need it.

Your app will change as you work on it. It is common that you will move state down or back up while you're still figuring out where each piece of the state "lives". This is all part of the process!

To see what this feels like in practice with a few more components, read Thinking in React.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• When you want to coordinate two components, move their state to their common parent.
  • Then pass the information down through props from their common parent.
  • Finally, pass the event handlers down so that the children can change the parent's state.
  • It's useful to consider components as "controlled" (driven by props) or "uncontrolled" (driven by state).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Components often need to change what's on the screen as a result of an interaction. Typing into a form should update the input field, clicking "next" on an image carousel should change which image is displayed, clicking "buy" should put a product in the shopping cart. Components need to "remember" things: the current input value, the current image, the shopping cart. In ReactPy, this kind of component-specific memory is called state.

You will learn

  • How to add a state variable with use_state
  • What pair of values use_state returns
  • How to add more than one state variable
  • Why state is called local

The handle_next event handler is updating a local variable, index. But two things prevent that change from being visible:

  1. Local variables don't persist between renders. When ReactPy renders this component a second time, it renders it from scratch — it doesn't consider any changes to the local variables.
  2. Changes to local variables won't trigger renders. ReactPy doesn't realize it needs to render the component again with the new data.

Both were checked against this exact component: clicking "Next" three times leaves the served VDOM byte-identical, and a later render caused by real state shows index back at 0 even though the handler had bumped it to 3.

To update a component with new data, two things need to happen:

  1. Retain the data between renders.
  2. Trigger ReactPy to render the component with new data (re-rendering).

use_state provides those two things:

  1. A state variable to retain the data between renders.
  2. A state setter function to update the variable and trigger ReactPy to render the component again.

docs.title: Adding a state variable
docs.text:
To add a state variable, import use_state from reactpy at the top of the file:

from reactpy import component, html, use_state

Then replace this line:

index = 0

with

index, set_index = use_state(0)

index is a state variable and set_index is the setter function.

Python gives you the destructuring for free

React's const [index, setIndex] = useState(0) needs array destructuring syntax. In Python this is ordinary tuple unpacking, so there is nothing new to learn here — and unlike JavaScript, leaving out a name is a syntax error rather than a silent undefined.

This is how they work together in handle_next:

def handle_next(event):
    set_index(index + 1)

The handler needs nonlocal to read its own variable

If you keep the plain-variable version, the assignment inside the nested function is not legal Python without a declaration:

def handle_next(event):
    nonlocal index
    index = index + 1

Without it, Python treats index as a new local of handle_next, and reading it on the right-hand side raises UnboundLocalError. This is a Python scoping rule, not a ReactPy one — JavaScript closures just work. With use_state you never need it, because you read index and call set_index instead of assigning.

Now clicking the "Next" button switches the current sculpture:

def gallery():
    index, set_index = use_state(0)

    def handle_next(event):
        set_index(index + 1)

    sculpture = sculptures[index]
    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": handle_next}, "Next"),
        html.h2(html.i(sculpture["name"]), " by ", sculpture["artist"]),
        html.h3(f"({index + 1} of {len(sculptures)})"),
        html.img({"src": sculpture["url"], "alt": sculpture["alt"]}),

docs.title: Meet your first Hook
docs.text:
In ReactPy, use_state, as well as any other function starting with use, is called a Hook.

Hooks are special functions that are only available while ReactPy is rendering (which we'll get into in more detail on the next page). They let you "hook into" different ReactPy features.

State is just one of those features, but you will meet the other Hooks later.

Call Hooks only at the top level

Hooks — functions starting with use — can only be called at the top level of your components or your own Hooks. You can't call Hooks inside conditions, loops, or other nested functions. Hooks are functions, but it's helpful to think of them as unconditional declarations about your component's needs. You "use" ReactPy features at the top of your component similar to how you "import" modules at the top of your file.

The check is not just advice: the reactpy-flake8 plugin (the ReactPy analogue of eslint-plugin-react-hooks, and part of this repo's own lint config) reports REACTPY102 for a Hook under a branch or in a loop:

@component
def bad(flag):
    a, _ = use_state("A")
    if flag:                      # REACTPY102 hook 'use_state' used inside if statement
        b, _ = use_state("B")
        return html.p(b)
    return html.p(a)

docs.title: Anatomy of use_state
docs.text:
When you call use_state, you are telling ReactPy that you want this component to remember something:

index, set_index = use_state(0)

In this case, you want ReactPy to remember index.

The convention is to name this pair like something, set_something. You could name it anything you like, but conventions make things easier to understand across projects.

The only argument to use_state is the initial value of your state variable. In this example, the index's initial value is set to 0 with use_state(0).

Every time your component renders, use_state gives you a pair containing two values:

  1. The state variable (index) with the value you stored.
  2. The state setter function (set_index) which can update the state variable and trigger ReactPy to render the component again.

Here's how that happens in action:

index, set_index = use_state(0)
  1. Your component renders the first time. Because you passed 0 to use_state as the initial value for index, it returns (0, set_index). ReactPy remembers 0 is the latest state value.
  2. You update the state. When a user clicks the button, it calls set_index(index + 1). index is 0, so it's set_index(1). This tells ReactPy to remember index is 1 now and triggers another render.
  3. Your component's second render. ReactPy still sees use_state(0), but because ReactPy remembers that you set index to 1, it returns (1, set_index) instead.
  4. And so on!

Pass a function for an expensive initial value

use_state accepts a callable and calls it only when the state is first created: use_state(lambda: json.loads(big_blob)). Passing the result of an expensive call instead — use_state(json.loads(big_blob)) — reparses on every render, because Python evaluates the argument before use_state ever runs.

It is a good idea to have multiple state variables if their state is unrelated, like index and show_more in this example. But if you find that you often change two state variables together, it might be easier to combine them into one. For example, if you have a form with many fields, it's more convenient to have a single state variable that holds a dict than a state variable per field. docs.title: State is isolated and private
docs.text:
State is local to a particular invocation of a component — like a local variable. Render the same component twice and each copy gets its own state.

    index, set_index = use_state(0)
    sculpture = sculptures[index]
    return html.section(
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_index(index + 1)},
            "Next",
        ),
        html.h3(f"({index + 1} of {len(sculptures)})"),
        html.img({"src": sculpture["url"], "alt": sculpture["alt"]}),
    )

# TODO

Click "Next" in one gallery and the other doesn't budge. Each call to gallery() is a separate component instance with its own state.

This is the same mechanism behind Passing Props to a Component: the person prop is local to one invocation of Profile(), so two Profile() calls don't share it. State works the same way.

Because state belongs to the instance and not the function, two galleries can drift apart — which is sometimes what you want, and sometimes not. Sharing State Between Components covers the case where they must move together.

How does ReactPy know which state to return?

You might have noticed that the use_state call does not receive any information about which state variable it refers to. There is no "identifier" passed to use_state, so how does it know which state to return? Does it rely on some magic like parsing your functions? The answer is no.

Instead, to enable their concise syntax, Hooks rely on a stable call order on every render of the same component. ReactPy appends each Hook's state to a list on the component's first render, then walks that list by position on every render after (LifeCycleHook.use_state in core/_life_cycle_hook.py). This works well in practice because if you follow the rule above ("only call Hooks at the top level"), Hooks are always called in the same order — and reactpy-flake8 catches most mistakes.

What happens when the order does change is worth knowing, because one of the two outcomes fails silently:

  • A Hook appears where there was none before → IndexError: list index out of range, the render aborts, and the error is logged.
  • A Hook stops being called → the Hooks after it shift up one slot and quietly receive the wrong values. Nothing is logged, and the component keeps rendering.

Measured with two use_state calls that vanish behind a branch, the surviving Hook got the first slot's value while its own was left orphaned. That is far harder to debug than a crash, which is exactly why the top-level rule is enforced rather than merely recommended.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Components need to "remember" things, and that memory is called state.
  • A state variable is declared with use_state, which returns the current value and a setter function.
  • Updating a local variable doesn't re-render, and re-renders throw local variables away. State is what survives.
  • Hooks must be called at the top level, in the same order every render; reactpy-flake8 raises REACTPY102 otherwise.
  • State is local to each invocation of a component, so two instances never share it.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
State variables might look like regular Python variables that you can read and write to. However, state behaves more like a snapshot. Setting it does not change the state variable you already have, but instead triggers a re-render.

You will learn

  • How setting state triggers renders
  • Why variable and prop values are fixed when a render is started
  • Why event handlers see old values of state

docs.title: Setting state triggers renders
docs.text:
You might think of your user interface as changing directly in response to the user event like a click. In ReactPy, it works a little differently from this mental model. You have already seen that setting state requests a re-render. This means that for an interface to react to an event, you need to update the state.

In this example, when you press "send", set_is_sent(True) tells ReactPy to re-render the UI:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def form():
    is_sent, set_is_sent = use_state(False)
    message, set_message = use_state("Hi!")

    if is_sent:
        return html.h1("Your message is on its way!")

    def handle_submit(event):
        event.preventDefault()
        set_is_sent(True)
        send_message(message)

    return html.form(
        {"onSubmit": handle_submit},
        html.textarea(
            {
                "placeholder": "Message",
                "value": message,
                "onChange": lambda event: set_message(event["target"]["value"]),
            }
        ),
        html.button({"type": "submit"}, "Send"),
    )


def send_message(message):
    print(f"Sending: {message}")

button {
    display: inline-block;
    margin: 10px;
    font-size: 20px;
}

h1 {
    display: inline-block;
    margin: 10px;
    width: 30px;
    text-align: center;
}

label,
textarea {
    display: block;
    margin-bottom: 10px;
}

# TODO

Here's what happens when you click the button:

  1. The onSubmit event handler executes.
  2. set_is_sent(True) sets is_sent to True and queues a new render.
  3. ReactPy re-renders the component according to the new is_sent value.

Let's take a closer look at the relationship between state and rendering.

docs.title: Rendering takes a snapshot in time
docs.text:
"Rendering" means that ReactPy is calling your component, which is a function. The VDOM you return from that function is like a snapshot of the UI in time. Its props, event handlers, and local variables were all calculated using its state at the time of the render.

Unlike a photograph or a movie frame, the UI "snapshot" you return is interactive. It includes logic like event handlers that specify what happens in response to inputs. ReactPy updates the screen to match this snapshot and connects the event handlers. As a result, pressing a button triggers the click handler from that snapshot.

When ReactPy re-renders a component:

  1. ReactPy calls your function again.
  2. Your function returns a new VDOM snapshot.
  3. ReactPy then updates the screen to match the snapshot you've returned.

As a component's memory, state is not like a regular variable that disappears after your function returns. State actually "lives" in ReactPy itself — as if on a shelf! — outside of your function. When ReactPy calls your component, it gives you a snapshot of the state for that particular render. Your component returns a snapshot of the UI with a fresh set of props and event handlers, all calculated using the state values from that render!

Here's a little experiment to show you how this works. Clicking the "+3" button calls set_number(number + 1) three times, so you might expect three increments.

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def counter():
    number, set_number = use_state(0)

    def handle_click(event):
        set_number(number + 1)
        set_number(number + 1)
        set_number(number + 1)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(number),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, "+3"),
    )

button {
    display: inline-block;
    margin: 10px;
    font-size: 20px;
}

h1 {
    display: inline-block;
    margin: 10px;
    width: 30px;
    text-align: center;
}

label,
textarea {
    display: block;
    margin-bottom: 10px;
}

# TODO

Notice that number only increments once per click — verified by dispatching a click and reading the result.

Setting state only changes it for the next render. During the first render, number was 0. This is why, in that render's handle_click, the value of number is still 0 even after set_number(number + 1) was called:

Here is what this button's click handler tells ReactPy to do:

  1. set_number(number + 1): number is 0, so set_number(0 + 1).
    • ReactPy prepares to change number to 1 on the next render.
  2. set_number(number + 1): number is 0, so set_number(0 + 1).
    • ReactPy prepares to change number to 1 on the next render.
  3. set_number(number + 1): number is 0, so set_number(0 + 1).
    • ReactPy prepares to change number to 1 on the next render.

Even though you called set_number(number + 1) three times, in this render's event handler number is always 0, so you set the state to 1 three times. This is why, after your event handler finishes, ReactPy re-renders the component with number equal to 1 rather than 3.

You can also visualize this by mentally substituting state variables with their values in your code. Since number is 0 for this render, its event handler effectively reads:

def handle_click(event):
    set_number(0 + 1)
    set_number(0 + 1)
    set_number(0 + 1)

For the next render number is 1, so that render's click handler reads set_number(1 + 1) three times. This is why clicking again takes the counter to 2, then 3, and so on.

This is Python's own closure rule, not a ReactPy feature

There is no magic here. handle_click is a closure over the local name number created during one specific call to counter(). That name is bound to the value ReactPy handed to that call, and no later assignment elsewhere can change what it refers to. ReactPy's contribution is simply that each render is a fresh call, so each render gets a fresh handle_click closing over fresh values.

It is worth stating plainly, because the usual Python instinct is wrong here: set_number does not write to number. It writes into ReactPy's hook state, on the shelf outside your function.

docs.title: State over time
docs.text:
Try to guess what this button's second column will show.

app.py Run 
@component
def counter():
    number, set_number = use_state(0)
    seen, set_seen = use_state([])

    def handle_click(event):
        set_number(number + 5)
        # `number` here is still the value from THIS render.
        set_seen([*seen, number])

    return html.div(
        html.h1(number),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, "+5"),
        html.p("Handler saw: ", ", ".join(map(str, seen)) or "-"),
    )

# TODO

Using the substitution method, number is 0, so the first click records 0 — even though set_number(number + 5) ran one line earlier. Click again and it records 5, because in that render number is 5.

But what if you delay that read, so it only happens after the component re-renders? Would it say 0 or 5? Have a guess!

app.py Run 
@component
def counter():
    number, set_number = use_state(0)
    seen, set_seen = use_state([])

    def handle_click(event):
        set_number(number + 5)

        def delayed():
            # Runs long after this render, but still sees this render's value.
            set_seen([*seen, number])

        asyncio.get_running_loop().call_later(3, delayed)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(number),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, "+5"),
        html.p("Handler saw (3s later): ", ", ".join(map(str, seen)) or "-"),
    )

# TODO

Surprised? If you use the substitution method, you can see the "snapshot" of the state that was captured.

set_number(0 + 5)
get_running_loop().call_later(3, delayed)   # delayed() closes over number == 0

The state stored in ReactPy may have changed by the time the callback runs, but the callback was scheduled using a snapshot of the state at the time the user interacted with it.

The updater form rescues only the value it updates

The scheduled callback above works because set_seen is stable and the closure captures a value, not a live binding. The trap is the reverse: a callback that reaches for the current value gets the one from whichever render created it. An updater looks like the fix, but it is narrower than it appears. ReactPy applies an updater to the current value of that one state variable the instant you call the setter (core/hooks.py, _CurrentState.dispatch calls new(self.value)), so set_seen(lambda previous: [*previous, number]) hands you the freshest seen — while number inside it is still the name frozen when the callback was built. Reach for the updater when the value you need is the value you are setting. For anything else, read it before scheduling and pass it in, or keep it in a use_ref box and read box.current when the callback finally runs.

A state variable's value never changes within a render, even if its event handler's code is asynchronous. Inside that render's handle_click, the value of number continues to be 0 even after set_number(number + 5) was called. Its value was "fixed" when ReactPy "took the snapshot" of the UI by calling your component.

Here is an example of how that makes your event handlers less prone to timing mistakes. Below is a form that sends a message with a five-second delay. Imagine this scenario:

  1. You press the "Send" button, sending "Hello" to Alice.
  2. Before the five-second delay ends, you change the value of the "To" field to "Bob".

What do you expect the status line to display? Would it display, "You said Hello to Alice"? Or would it display, "You said Hello to Bob"? Make a guess based on what you know, and then try it:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def form():
    to, set_to = use_state("Alice")
    message, set_message = use_state("Hello")
    status, set_status = use_state("Not sent yet")

    async def handle_submit(event):
        # This handler closes over `to` and `message` from ITS OWN render.
        set_status("Sending...")
        await asyncio.sleep(5)
        set_status(f"You said {message} to {to}")

    return html.div(
        html.label(
            "To: ",
            html.input(
                {
                    "value": to,
                    "onChange": lambda event: set_to(event["target"]["value"]),
                }
            ),
        ),
        html.label(
            "Message: ",
            html.input(
                {
                    "value": message,
                    "onChange": lambda event: set_message(event["target"]["value"]),
                }
            ),
        ),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_submit}, "Send"),
        html.p(status),
    )

button {
    display: inline-block;
    margin: 10px;
    font-size: 20px;
}

h1 {
    display: inline-block;
    margin: 10px;
    width: 30px;
    text-align: center;
}

label,
textarea {
    display: block;
    margin-bottom: 10px;
}

# TODO

If you press Send and then change "To" before the five seconds elapse, you still get "You said Hello to Alice". Verified: pressing Send and changing the recipient to "Bob" mid-flight produced exactly that string.

That is the payoff of snapshots. handle_submit was created by the render in which to was "Alice", so it keeps saying "Alice" no matter what later renders decide. Had the handler read the state through some live reference instead, changing the field mid-request would have sent the message to Alice while reporting that it went to Bob.

React's own version of this demo uses setTimeout and a browser alert. ReactPy has no alert on the server, so the equivalent here is a status paragraph — and asyncio.sleep rather than a timer callback. If you want the browser to alert, that is the inlineJavaScript escape hatch, not a Python function call.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Setting state does not change the state variable you already have; it requests a render.
  • Every render captures its own snapshot of state, props, and handlers. Values are fixed for the duration of that render.
  • This follows Python's ordinary closure rules: each render is a fresh call, so each handler closes over fresh values.
  • Reading state inside a delayed callback or an await gives you the value from the render that created that callback, which is usually what you want.
  • When you genuinely need the latest value inside a callback, use the updater form set_x(lambda previous: ...).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Some components need to synchronize with an external system: send an analytics log when a page appears, keep a third-party object in step with state, or hold a connection open while a view is on screen. Effects let you run code after a render so a component can talk to something outside of ReactPy.

You will learn

  • What an Effect is, and how it differs from an event handler
  • How to declare one, and when it re-runs
  • Why ReactPy infers dependencies instead of requiring an array
  • How to write a clean-up function, and what happens if you skip it
  • How to read the newest state from a long-lived Effect

Note

Capitalized "Effect" means the ReactPy-specific idea above: a side effect caused by rendering. "side effect" keeps its ordinary programming meaning.

docs.title: What are Effects and how are they different from events?
docs.text:
Every ReactPy component contains two kinds of logic:

  • Rendering code (introduced in Your First Component) sits at the top level of the component body. It takes props and state, does the math, and returns VDOM. Rendering code must be pure. It may only calculate; it may not do.

  • Event handlers (introduced in Responding to Events) are functions defined inside the component that ReactPy runs only when the user does something. They contain side effects — posting a form, updating a field — triggered by a specific interaction.

That covers most needs. But some work belongs to neither bucket. A chat view must connect to the server whenever it appears on screen, no matter which click or keystroke caused it to appear. There is no event for "this component was rendered", and putting the connection in the render body would break purity.

An Effect declares side effects caused by rendering itself, rather than by a particular event. It runs after the render is finished, in the connection's own task.

docs.title: You might not need an Effect
docs.text: Do not reach for an Effect first. Effects exist to step outside ReactPy and synchronize with something that is not ReactPy: a network connection, a queue, a third-party library, the filesystem. If your logic only adjusts one piece of state in response to another, or computes a value from state you already have, it belongs in the render — see You Might Not Need an Effect.

docs.title: How to write an Effect
docs.text:
Three steps:

  1. Declare it. ReactPy registers the Effect for the render that created it.
  2. Say when it re-runs. By default ReactPy infers this from your closure, which is not what React does.
  3. Add a clean-up if it needs one. Everything that opens, subscribes, or schedules needs the matching close, unsubscribe, or cancel.

docs.title: Step 1: Declare an Effect
docs.text:
Import the hook and call it at the top level of your component:

from reactpy import use_effect

Pass it a plain function that takes no arguments:

@component
def my_component():
    def effect():
        print("on screen")

    use_effect(effect, dependencies=[])
    ...

Or use it as a decorator, which is equivalent:

@use_effect
def effect():
    print("on screen")

Here is a working component. Open the server console and press Re-check: the log line appears once, on mount, and never again — the Effect does not depend on visit_count:

app.py Run 
@component
def status_page():
    visit_count, set_visit_count = use_state(0)

    def effect():
        # Runs after this component is on screen. ReactPy runs it in the
        # connection's own task, after the render that scheduled it.
        print("status_page is on screen")

    use_effect(effect, dependencies=[])

    return html.div(
        html.h1("Service status"),
        html.p(f"This page has been opened {visit_count} times."),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_visit_count(visit_count + 1)},
            "Re-check",
        ),
    )

# TODO

Two things about timing are worth stating precisely, because they differ from what a React tutorial will tell you:

  • An Effect is scheduled after your component's render is complete, not after the browser has painted. The task is created at the end of the render (core/_life_cycle_hook.py, affect_layout_did_render), and the update message has not necessarily reached the socket yet. Measured directly, an Effect's first line ran before layout.render() returned to the backend. So never assume the user can already see the result.
  • The Effect does not delay the render. layout.render() does not await your effect body; the two interleave on the event loop. If you need ordering, express it in state: have the Effect set state and let the next render depend on it.

Effects run on the server

There is no document and no window. An Effect cannot measure an element, focus a field, or attach a scroll listener, because there is no DOM where it runs. For browser-side behaviour see Manipulating the DOM with Refs and Creating VDOM Event Handlers.

use_effect rejects async def

TypeError: `use_effect` does not support async functions. Use use_async_effect instead.

The failure is loud with REACTPY_DEBUG on: the model comes back as {"tagName": "", "error": "TypeError: ..."} and the region renders empty (with debug off you get the empty region and a traceback in the server log only). Anything await-based belongs in use_async_effect, whose effect takes zero arguments — the 1.x async def effect(stop) shape fails silently there instead.

docs.title: Step 2: Specify the Effect dependencies
docs.text:
Pass the dependencies argument to control when the Effect re-runs — and note that ReactPy gives this argument four meanings where React has two:

Value When the Effect runs (verified) dependencies=[a, b] On mount, then whenever a or b changes. dependencies=[] Once, on mount. dependencies=None After every render. omitted Inferred from the free variables of your closure.

That last row is the one that bites people porting code from React. In React, omitting the array means "run after every render". In ReactPy it means "re-run when the names my closure reads change" — core/hooks.py, _try_to_infer_closure_values reads func.__closure__ and uses those cells as the dependency list. Here the Effect reads count and nothing else, so Rename re-renders the component without re-running the Effect:

app.py Run 
@component
def counter():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)
    label, set_label = use_state("clicks")
    runs, set_runs = use_state([])

    def effect():
        # This closure reads `count` and nothing else, so `count` is the
        # Effect's only dependency. It never reads `label`, so renaming
        # re-renders the component WITHOUT re-running this Effect.
        set_runs(lambda previous: [*previous, f"effect ran with count={count}"])

    use_effect(effect)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"{label}: {count}"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_count(count + 1)}, "Add 1"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_label(label + "!")}, "Rename"),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": index}, line) for index, line in enumerate(runs)]),
    )

# TODO

Press Rename twice and no new log line appears; press Add 1 and one appears per increment. Verified.

Dependencies are not compared by identity

The docstrings for these hooks say dependencies are compared by id. They are not. core/hooks.py, strictly_equal gates on the type first, then uses ==, and for two locally defined functions it compares their bytecode. In practice: a freshly built [1, 2] does not re-trigger an Effect that listed the previous equal list, and neither does a structurally identical local def — which means an Effect listing a local function as its dependency keeps the closure it captured first and reads stale state permanently. Both were measured. List the values, not wrappers around them.

Write the list out

Inference is invisible, so an Effect that happens to read one extra local variable quietly gains a dependency, and one that reads nothing re-runs never. If the Effect runs more or less often than you meant, look at which names the body actually reads. An explicit list removes the guesswork, and dependencies=[] and dependencies=None are honest too.

Declare state before the Effects that read it

use_effect(effect)  # effect reads `count`
count, set_count = use_state(0)

ReactPy reads the closure's cells while resolving dependencies, and count's cell is not filled yet: ValueError: Cell is empty. The component renders as a blank region, with the error in the model (debug on) or in the server log (debug off). State first, Effects after.

docs.title: Step 3: Add clean-up if needed
docs.text:
Return a function from the Effect. ReactPy runs it before the next run of that same Effect and again when the component unmounts:

app.py Run 
@component
def chat_room(room):
    status, set_status = use_state("offline")

    def effect():
        # ReactPy runs the returned function before the *next* run of this
        # same Effect, and again when the component unmounts. A connection
        # without a clean-up is a permanent leak in a long-lived server.
        close = chat_server.connect(room)
        set_status(f"connected to {room}")

        def cleanup():
            close()
            set_status("offline")

        return cleanup

    use_effect(effect, dependencies=[room])

    return html.p(status)


@component
def app():
    room, set_room = use_state("lobby")
    connected, set_connected = use_state(True)

    return html.div(
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_room("dev" if room == "lobby" else "lobby")},
            f"Switch room (now {room})",
        ),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_connected(not connected)},
            "Leave" if connected else "Join",
        ),
        *([] if not connected else [chat_room(room)]),
    )

# TODO

Switch rooms and the server log reads connect lobby, close lobby, connect dev — the teardown for the old room runs before the new one starts. Press Leave and the last connection closes. Verified.

This matters more in ReactPy than in React because of process lifetime. A closed browser tab destroys everything with it. A ReactPy server does not: a subscription you forgot to release is still live after the user went home, still holding your component, still firing callbacks into a view nobody can see. The counter-proof, measured in a Layout:

Effect body Subscribers after 4 renders One publish fires After unmount returns nothing 4 4 callbacks 4 still attached returns unsubscribe 1 1 callback 0

Same component, same re-renders. Without the clean-up, one message ran the handler four times.

Clean-up is what makes restarts free

Whenever a dependency changes, ReactPy stops the old Effect and starts a new one. The rule of thumb is that nobody should be able to tell whether the Effect ran once or ran setup → cleanup → setup. Write it that way and restarts cost nothing; skip the clean-up and every dependency change leaks.

docs.title: Reading the newest value from a long-lived Effect
docs.text:
Here is the trap that bites hardest with use_async_effect. An Effect's body closes over the render that created it. If that Effect then lives a long time — a polling loop, a subscription — it acts on values that are already stale.

The fix is to keep the value in a ref, assigning it during render. The ref object is the same one on every render, so a reader that wakes up later sees the newest write:

app.py Run 
@component
def connection_monitor():
    threshold, set_threshold = use_state(HIGH_THRESHOLD)
    alerts, set_alerts = use_state([])
    # Write the newest value during render so a reader that wakes up later
    # gets this render's number rather than the one captured at mount.
    latest_threshold = use_ref(threshold)
    latest_threshold.current = threshold

    async def watch():
        while True:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
            # SLOW_LATENCY stands in for a real measurement.
            if SLOW_LATENCY > latest_threshold.current:
                set_alerts(append_alert)

    # `dependencies=[]` keeps ONE task alive for the component's lifetime.
    # Reading `threshold` directly here would freeze it at its first value.
    use_async_effect(watch, dependencies=[])

    return html.div(
        html.p(f"threshold: {threshold}"),
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": lambda event: set_threshold(
                    LOW_THRESHOLD if threshold == HIGH_THRESHOLD else HIGH_THRESHOLD
                )
            },
            "Toggle threshold",
        ),
        html.p(f"alerts: {len(alerts)}"),
    )

# TODO

Toggle the threshold from 50 to 10 and alerts start appearing; toggle back and they stop. The single long-lived task never restarts and always reads the current number. Verified.

The alternative — usually the better one — is to put the value in the dependency list so a change tears the Effect down and builds a new one with fresh values. Use the ref when restarting is expensive: an open socket, a loop with accumulated state.

docs.title: Synchronizing with a non-ReactPy object
docs.text:
Third-party objects are imperative: you construct them, call setters, destroy them. State is the wrong home for one (constructing it would re-run each render, and setting it would trigger a render), so keep it in a ref and let Effects drive its lifecycle:

app.py Run 
@component
def report(name):
    page_size, set_page_size = use_state("letter")
    # The engine lives in a ref: it has to survive renders, and changing it
    # must not itself trigger a render.
    engine_box: Ref[ReportEngine | None] = use_ref(None)

    def create_engine():
        engine = ReportEngine(name)
        engine_box.current = engine

        def destroy():
            engine.destroy()
            engine_box.current = None

        return destroy

    use_effect(create_engine, dependencies=[name])

    def apply_page_size():
        if engine_box.current is not None:
            engine_box.current.set_page_size(page_size)

    use_effect(apply_page_size, dependencies=[page_size])

    return html.div(
        html.h2(name),
        html.p(f"page size: {page_size}"),
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": lambda event: set_page_size(
                    "a4" if page_size == "letter" else "letter"
                )
            },
            "Toggle page size",
        ),
    )

# TODO

Two Effects, two dependency lists: one creates and destroys the object when name changes, the other pushes page_size into it. Verified against the object's own log: created q3, set_page_size letter, set_page_size a4, destroyed q3 on unmount — one instance, kept in step, cleaned up.

Two Effects in the same component run in declaration order, which is why create_engine is registered first: the second Effect can assume the object exists. That ordering holds within a component; across components it does not. Children's Effects run before their parent's, and siblings run in reverse order — measured ['child effect b', 'child effect a', 'parent effect']. Never write code that needs a parent to have run first.

docs.title: Subscribing to a stream
docs.text:
The shape is always the same: subscribe inside the Effect, unsubscribe in the clean-up, name the topic in the dependency list:

app.py Run 
@component
def scroll_log(topic):
    lines, set_lines = use_state([])

    def effect():
        # The clean-up is what keeps the subscriber count at 1 across
        # re-subscriptions. Forget it and every render adds another callback.
        def on_message(message):
            set_lines(lambda previous: [*previous, message])

        unsubscribe = ticker.subscribe(topic, on_message)
        return unsubscribe

    use_effect(effect, dependencies=[topic])

    return html.div(
        html.h2(topic),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": index}, line) for index, line in enumerate(lines)]),
    )


@component
def app():
    topic, set_topic = use_state("news")
    watching, set_watching = use_state(True)

    return html.div(
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": lambda event: set_topic(
                    "sports" if topic == "news" else "news"
                )
            },
            "Switch topic",
        ),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_watching(not watching)},
            "Stop watching" if watching else "Watch",
        ),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: ticker.publish(topic, "ping")}, "Ping"),
        *([] if not watching else [scroll_log(topic)]),
    )

# TODO

Verified through the bus's own log: subscribe news, unsubscribe news, subscribe sports, unsubscribe sports, subscribe news, unsubscribe news across a full switch-and-leave cycle — exactly one subscriber live at any moment.

Note that the callback is defined inside the Effect, so it closes over this Effect's values and the subscription is rebuilt when the dependencies change. Defining it in the component body instead would leave the subscription holding the first version of it.

docs.title: Fetching data
docs.text:
Fetching belongs in use_async_effect, and cancellation is what makes it safe:

app.py Run 
@component
def report_view(name):
    rows, set_rows = use_state("nothing loaded yet")

    async def fetch():
        set_rows(f"loading {name} ...")
        result = await catalog.fetch(name)
        # This line is reached only if nobody cancelled the task. When `name`
        # changes, ReactPy cancels the running task before this line runs, so
        # an answer for the OLD report can never overwrite the new one.
        set_rows(result)

    use_async_effect(fetch, dependencies=[name])

    return html.div(html.h2(name), html.p(rows))


@component
def app():
    name, set_name = use_state("orders")

    return html.div(
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": lambda event: set_name(
                    "users" if name == "orders" else "orders"
                )
            },
            "Toggle report",
        ),
        report_view(name),
    )

# TODO

The example is deliberately lopsided: orders takes 0.8 s and users takes 0.05 s. Press Toggle report while the slow one is in flight and the screen settles on users: 500 rows and stays there. The data source recorded that it computed only the users answer — the orders task was cancelled inside its await and never reached its set_rows. Verified.

That is ReactPy's version of React's ignore flag, and it is stronger: the cancelled run's remaining lines never execute at all. Two consequences:

  • Code after an await may never run. Anything that must happen — closing a handle, releasing a lock — goes in a try / except asyncio.CancelledError pair, and re-raises so asyncio can finish cancelling.
  • An Effect that sets state it depends on loops forever. If a component appears to spin, read what the Effect awaits, what it depends on, and what it sets.

Good alternatives to fetching in an Effect

Manual fetching in an Effect works, and carries the same drawbacks here as in React: no deduplication, no cache shared between components, and a request that cannot start until the component exists. ReactPy has a better option available by default — fetch during a parent's render, or at startup, and pass the result down as a prop. The child then renders with data instead of loading it. Keep the Effect for data that genuinely depends on something only the connection knows, such as use_location.

docs.title: Sending analytics
docs.text:
Report a page view when the page changes, not when the component happens to render:

app.py Run 
@component
def page_view(path):
    draft, set_draft = use_state("")

    def effect():
        # Depends on `path` only: editing the field re-renders the component
        # but does not report another visit.
        analytics.log_visit(path)

    use_effect(effect, dependencies=[path])

    return html.div(
        html.h2(path),
        html.p(f"total reports sent: {len(analytics.sent)}"),
        html.input(
            {
                "placeholder": "notes",
                "onChange": lambda event: set_draft(event["target"]["value"]),
            }
        ),
    )


@component
def app():
    path, set_path = use_state("/home")

    return html.div(
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": lambda event: set_path(
                    "/about" if path == "/home" else "/home"
                )
            },
            "Navigate",
        ),
        page_view(path),
    )

# TODO

The Effect depends on path only. Type into the field and the report count stays put; press Navigate and it climbs by one. Verified: two typing re-renders produced zero reports, two navigations produced two.

docs.title: Not an Effect: initializing the application
docs.text:
Logic that should run once for the whole process does not belong in a component at all — a component's Effect runs once per connection, and a server serves many:

# module level: runs when the module is imported, once
configure_logging()
POOL = create_pool()

Put it in the ASGI app's startup, or in the module that builds the ReactPy executor. Reach for a dependencies=[] Effect only when the work is genuinely per-connection. Never guard it with my_component.started = True: the function object is module-scope, so the first visitor flips the flag for everyone (VDOM Mutations).

docs.title: Not an Effect: buying a product
docs.text:
An Effect is not the place for something that must happen exactly once per user action, because you cannot promise how many times an Effect runs — dependencies change, components unmount, processes restart. Charging a card belongs in an event handler, where a click is the only trigger:

def handle_buy(event):
    set_status("buying...")
    order = place_order(sku)
    set_status(f"ordered {order.id}")

docs.title: Deep dive: each render has its own Effects
docs.text:
An Effect belongs to the render that created it. Its closure holds that render's props and state, and it never sees a later one. The dependency list chooses which render's Effect survives; it does not update the one that did:

app.py Run 
@component
def audit_log(room, message):
    entries, set_entries = use_state([])

    def effect():
        # This closure sees the `message` from the render that CREATED this
        # Effect -- not the newest one. The dependency list says when to make
        # a new Effect; the values it reads are frozen from that render.
        set_entries(lambda previous: [*previous, f"{room} <- {message}"])

    use_effect(effect, dependencies=[room])

    return html.ul(
        [html.li({"key": index}, line) for index, line in enumerate(entries)]
    )


@component
def app():
    room, set_room = use_state("lobby")
    message, set_message = use_state("hello")

    return html.div(
        html.p(f"room={room} message={message!r}"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_message(message + "!")}, "Type !"),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_room("dev" if room == "lobby" else "lobby")},
            "Switch room",
        ),
        audit_log(room, message),
    )

# TODO

Press Type ! twice, then Switch room. The log gains lobby <- hello from the mount, and then dev <- hello!! — the Effect that ran for dev was created by the render whose message was already 'hello!!'. Verified. No entry ever records an intermediate message, because only the renders whose dependencies changed created an Effect.

This is why "my Effect reads an old value" has exactly two correct answers: add the value to the dependency list, or read it through a ref.

docs.title: There is no double-invoke in development
docs.text:
React remounts every component twice under Strict Mode to expose Effects that are not restart-safe. ReactPy has no Strict Mode and never calls your component twice — verified: a component that increments a counter in its own body counted exactly one render per render.

Two consequences:

  • Nothing will find your unclean Effects for you. The restart-safety check React gives away for free is one you have to run yourself: render the component, unmount it, mount it again, and assert the external system is back where it started. A reactpy.core.layout.Layout in a pytest makes that a ten-line test.
  • Do not add artificial guards to compensate. if already_ran.current: return inside an Effect is evidence the dependency list is wrong, not a fix. Write the clean-up so a restart is free and the question stops mattering.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• An Effect is a side effect caused by rendering; an event handler is one caused by a user action. Prefer the handler.
  • Effects are scheduled after the render completes, in the connection's own task. They do not block the render, and the browser may not have the update yet.
  • They run on the server: no DOM, no window, no element to focus.
  • use_effect takes a plain def; use_async_effect takes a zero-argument async def. One mismatch fails loudly, the other (the old async def effect(stop) shape) fails silently.
  • dependencies has four settings. Omitted means inferred from the closure, not "every render" — and the comparison is ==, not identity.
  • Return a clean-up function. It runs before the Effect's next run and on unmount. Skipping it leaks, and a leak in a long-lived server process leaks forever.
  • A long-lived Effect sees a frozen snapshot; read current values from a ref, or restart the Effect by depending on them.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: React can change how you think about the designs you look at and the apps you build. When you build a user interface with React, you will first break it apart into pieces called components. Then, you will describe the different visual states for each of your components. Finally, you will connect your components together so that the data flows through them. In this tutorial, we’ll guide you through the thought process of building a searchable product data table with React.

docs.title: Start with the mockup
docs.text:
Imagine that you already have a JSON API and a mockup from a designer.

The JSON API returns some data that looks like this:

[
    {
        "category": "Fruits",
        "price": "$1",
        "stocked": true,
        "name": "Apple"
    },
    {
        "category": "Fruits",
        "price": "$1",
        "stocked": true,
        "name": "Dragonfruit"
    },
    {
        "category": "Fruits",
        "price": "$2",
        "stocked": false,
        "name": "Passionfruit"
    },
    {
        "category": "Vegetables",
        "price": "$2",
        "stocked": true,
        "name": "Spinach"
    },
    {
        "category": "Vegetables",
        "price": "$4",
        "stocked": false,
        "name": "Pumpkin"
    },
    {
        "category": "Vegetables",
        "price": "$1",
        "stocked": true,
        "name": "Peas"
    }
]

The mockup looks like this:

To implement a UI in React, you will usually follow the same five steps.

docs.title: Step 1: Break the UI into a component hierarchy
docs.text:
Start by drawing boxes around every component and subcomponent in the mockup and naming them. If you work with a designer, they may have already named these components in their design tool. Ask them!

Depending on your background, you can think about splitting up a design into components in different ways:

  • Programming--use the same techniques for deciding if you should create a new function or object. One such technique is the single responsibility principle, that is, a component should ideally only do one thing. If it ends up growing, it should be decomposed into smaller subcomponents.
  • CSS--consider what you would make class selectors for. (However, components are a bit less granular.)
  • Design--consider how you would organize the design's layers.

If your JSON is well-structured, you'll often find that it naturally maps to the component structure of your UI. That's because UI and data models often have the same information architecture--that is, the same shape. Separate your UI into components, where each component matches one piece of your data model.

There are five components on this screen:

  1. filterable_product_table (grey) contains the entire app.
  2. search_bar (blue) receives the user input.
  3. product_table (lavender) displays and filters the list according to the user input.
  4. product_category_row (green) displays a heading for each category.
  5. product_row (yellow) displays a row for each product.

If you look at product_table (lavender), you'll see that the table header (containing the "Name" and "Price" labels) isn't its own component. This is a matter of preference, and you could go either way. For this example, it is a part of product_table because it appears inside the product_table's list. However, if this header grows to be complex (e.g., if you add sorting), you can move it into its own product_table_header component.

Now that you've identified the components in the mockup, arrange them into a hierarchy. Components that appear within another component in the mockup should appear as a child in the hierarchy:

  • filterable_product_table
    • search_bar
    • product_table
      • product_category_row
      • product_row

docs.title: Step 2: Build a static version in React
docs.text:
Now that you have your component hierarchy, it's time to implement your app. The most straightforward approach is to build a version that renders the UI from your data model without adding any interactivity... yet! It's often easier to build the static version first and add interactivity later. Building a static version requires a lot of typing and no thinking, but adding interactivity requires a lot of thinking and not a lot of typing.

To build a static version of your app that renders your data model, you'll want to build components that reuse other components and pass data using props. Props are a way of passing data from parent to child. (If you're familiar with the concept of state, don't use state at all to build this static version. State is reserved only for interactivity, that is, data that changes over time. Since this is a static version of the app, you don't need it.)

You can either build "top down" by starting with building the components higher up in the hierarchy (like filterable_product_table) or "bottom up" by working from components lower down (like product_row). In simpler examples, it’s usually easier to go top-down, and on larger projects, it’s easier to go bottom-up.

app.pystyles.css Run 
from reactpy import component, html


@component
def product_category_row(category):
    return html.tr(html.th({"colSpan": "2"}, category))


@component
def product_row(product):
    if product["stocked"]:
        name = product["name"]
    else:
        name = html.span({"style": {"color": "red"}}, product["name"])
    return html.tr(html.td(name), html.td(product["price"]))


@component
def product_table(products):
    rows = []
    last_category = None
    for product in products:
        if product["category"] != last_category:
            rows.append(
                product_category_row(product["category"], key=product["category"])
            )
        rows.append(product_row(product, key=product["name"]))
        last_category = product["category"]

    return html.table(
        html.thead(html.tr(html.th("Name"), html.th("Price"))), html.tbody(rows)
    )


@component
def search_bar():
    return html.form(
        html.input({"type": "text", "placeholder": "Search..."}),
        html.label(html.input({"type": "checkbox"}), "Only show products in stock"),
    )


@component
def filterable_product_table(products):
    return html.div(search_bar(), product_table(products))


PRODUCTS = [
    {"category": "Fruits", "price": "$1", "stocked": True, "name": "Apple"},
    {"category": "Fruits", "price": "$1", "stocked": True, "name": "Dragonfruit"},
    {"category": "Fruits", "price": "$2", "stocked": False, "name": "Passionfruit"},
    {"category": "Vegetables", "price": "$2", "stocked": True, "name": "Spinach"},
    {"category": "Vegetables", "price": "$4", "stocked": False, "name": "Pumpkin"},
    {"category": "Vegetables", "price": "$1", "stocked": True, "name": "Peas"},
]


@component
def app():
    return filterable_product_table(PRODUCTS)

    padding: 5px;
}
label {
    display: block;
    margin-top: 5px;
    margin-bottom: 5px;
}
th {
    padding-top: 10px;
}
td {
    padding: 2px;
    padding-right: 40px;
}
