(If this code looks intimidating, go through the Quick Start first!)

After building your components, you'll have a library of reusable components that render your data model. Because this is a static app, the components will only return non-interactive HTML. The component at the top of the hierarchy (filterable_product_table) will take your data model as a prop. This is called one-way data flow because the data flows down from the top-level component to the ones at the bottom of the tree.

Pitfall

At this point, you should not be using any state values. That’s for the next step!

docs.title: Step 3: Find the minimal but complete representation of UI state
docs.text:
To make the UI interactive, you need to let users change your underlying data model. You will use state for this.

Think of state as the minimal set of changing data that your app needs to remember. The most important principle for structuring state is to keep it DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself). Figure out the absolute minimal representation of the state your application needs and compute everything else on-demand. For example, if you're building a shopping list, you can store the items as an array in state. If you want to also display the number of items in the list, don't store the number of items as another state value--instead, read the length of your array.

Now think of all of the pieces of data in this example application:

  1. The original list of products
  2. The search text the user has entered
  3. The value of the checkbox
  4. The filtered list of products

Which of these are state? Identify the ones that are not:

  • Does it remain unchanged over time? If so, it isn't state.
  • Is it passed in from a parent via props? If so, it isn't state.
  • Can you compute it based on existing state or props in your component? If so, it definitely isn't state!

What's left is probably state.

Let's go through them one by one again:

  1. The original list of products is passed in as props, so it's not state.
  2. The search text seems to be state since it changes over time and can't be computed from anything.
  3. The value of the checkbox seems to be state since it changes over time and can't be computed from anything.
  4. The filtered list of products isn't state because it can be computed by taking the original list of products and filtering it according to the search text and value of the checkbox.

This means only the search text and the value of the checkbox are state! Nicely done!

Deep Dive

Props vs State

There are two types of "model" data in ReactPy: props and state. The two are very different:

  • Props are like arguments you pass to a function. They let a parent component pass data to a child component and customize its appearance. For example, a search_bar() component can pass a color prop to a badge() component you wrote. This is about your components: html.form and html.button are tag constructors, and what you hand them is an attribute dictionary, not props a component reads.
  • State is like a component’s memory. It lets a component keep track of some information and change it in response to interactions. For example, a badge() component you wrote might keep track of is_hovered state. Tags cannot hold state — html.button is a function that returns a dictionary, and a dictionary has no memory between renders.

Props and state are different, but they work together. A parent component will often keep some information in state (so that it can change it), and pass it down to child components as their props. It's okay if the difference still feels fuzzy on the first read. It takes a bit of practice for it to really stick!

docs.title: Step 4: Identify where your state should live
docs.text:
After identifying your app’s minimal state data, you need to identify which component is responsible for changing this state, or owns the state. Remember: React uses one-way data flow, passing data down the component hierarchy from parent to child component. It may not be immediately clear which component should own what state. This can be challenging if you’re new to this concept, but you can figure it out by following these steps!

For each piece of state in your application:

  1. Identify every component that renders something based on that state.
  2. Find their closest common parent component—a component above them all in the hierarchy.
  3. Decide where the state should live:
    1. Often, you can put the state directly into their common parent.
    2. You can also put the state into some component above their common parent.
    3. If you can't find a component where it makes sense to own the state, create a new component solely for holding the state and add it somewhere in the hierarchy above the common parent component.

In the previous step, you found two pieces of state in this application: the search input text, and the value of the checkbox. In this example, they always appear together, so it makes sense to put them into the same place.

Now let's run through our strategy for them:

  1. Identify components that use state:
    • product_table needs to filter the product list based on that state (search text and checkbox value).
    • search_bar needs to display that state (search text and checkbox value).
  2. Find their common parent: The first parent component both components share is filterable_product_table.
  3. Decide where the state lives: We'll keep the filter text and checked state values in filterable_product_table.

So the state values will live in filterable_product_table.

Add state to the component with the use_state() Hook. Hooks are special functions that let you "hook into" React. Add two state variables at the top of filterable_product_table and specify their initial state:

@component
def filterable_product_table(products):
    filter_text, set_filter_text = use_state("")
    in_stock_only, set_in_stock_only = use_state(False)

Then, pass filter_text and in_stock_only to product_table and search_bar as props:

html.div(
    search_bar(filter_text=filter_text, in_stock_only=in_stock_only),
    product_table(
        products=products, filter_text=filter_text, in_stock_only=in_stock_only
    ),
)

You can start seeing how your application will behave. Edit the filter_text initial value from use_state('') to use_state('fruit') in the sandbox code below. You'll see both the search input text and the table update:

Notice that editing the form doesn't work yet.

In the code above, product_table and search_bar read the filter_text and in_stock_only props to render the table, the input, and the checkbox. For example, here is how search_bar populates the input value:

@component

        html.input(

                "type": "text",

However, you haven't added any code to respond to the user actions like typing yet. This will be your final step.

docs.title: Step 5: Add inverse data flow
docs.text:
Currently your app renders correctly with props and state flowing down the hierarchy. But to change the state according to user input, you will need to support data flowing the other way: the form components deep in the hierarchy need to update the state in filterable_product_table.

React makes this data flow explicit, but it requires a little more typing than two-way data binding. If you try to type or check the box in the example above, you'll see that React ignores your input. This is intentional. By writing html.input({"value": filter_text}), you've set the value attribute of the html.input to always be equal to the filter_text state passed in from filterable_product_table. Since filter_text state is never set, the input never changes.

You want to make it so whenever the user changes the form inputs, the state updates to reflect those changes. The state is owned by filterable_product_table, so only it can call set_filter_text and set_in_stock_only. To let search_bar update the filterable_product_table's state, you need to pass these functions down to search_bar:

@component
def filterable_product_table(products):
    filter_text, set_filter_text = hooks.use_state("")
    in_stock_only, set_in_stock_only = hooks.use_state(False)

    return html.div(
        search_bar(
            filter_text=filter_text,
            in_stock_only=in_stock_only,
            set_filter_text=set_filter_text,
            set_in_stock_only=set_in_stock_only,
        )
    )

Inside the search_bar, you will add the onChange event handlers and set the parent state from them:

html.input(
    {
        "type": "text",
        "value": filter_text,
        "placeholder": "Search...",
        "onChange": lambda event: set_filter_text(event["target"]["value"]),
    }
)

Now the application fully works!

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You will build a small tic-tac-toe game. This tutorial assumes no prior ReactPy knowledge, and the techniques it covers — components, props, state, and lifting state up — are the ones you will use in every app you write.

Note

This tutorial is for people who prefer to learn by doing. If you would rather meet each concept one at a time, start with Your First Component instead.

The tutorial is divided into four sections:

  • Setup for the tutorial gives you a starting point.
  • The basics teaches you the fundamentals: components, props, and state.
  • Completing the game teaches you the most common techniques.
  • Adding time travel shows why immutability matters.

docs.title: What are you building?
docs.text:
You will build an interactive tic-tac-toe game. Here is the finished result:

app.pystyles.css Run 
from reactpy import component, html, use_state


@component
def square(value, on_click):
    return html.button(
        {"className": "square", "onClick": on_click},
        value,
    )


@component
def board(x_is_next, squares, on_play):
    def handle_click(i):
        def inner(event):
            """
            Due to a quirk of Python, if your event handler needs args other than
            `event`, you will need to create a wrapper function as seen above.
            Ref: https://pylint.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user_guide/messages/warning/cell-var-from-loop.html
            """
            if calculate_winner(squares) or squares[i]:
                return

            next_squares = squares.copy()
            next_squares[i] = "X" if x_is_next else "O"
            on_play(next_squares)

        return inner

    winner = calculate_winner(squares)
    status = (
        f"Winner: {winner}" if winner else "Next player: " + ("X" if x_is_next else "O")
    )

    return html.fragment(
        html.div({"className": "status"}, status),
        html.div(
            {"className": "board-row"},
            square(squares[0], handle_click(0)),
            square(squares[1], handle_click(1)),
            square(squares[2], handle_click(2)),
        ),
        html.div(
            {"className": "board-row"},
            square(squares[3], handle_click(3)),
            square(squares[4], handle_click(4)),
            square(squares[5], handle_click(5)),
        ),
        html.div(
            {"className": "board-row"},
            square(squares[6], handle_click(6)),
            square(squares[7], handle_click(7)),
            square(squares[8], handle_click(8)),
        ),
    )


@component
def game():
    history, set_history = use_state([[None] * 9])
    current_move, set_current_move = use_state(0)
    x_is_next = current_move % 2 == 0
    current_squares = history[current_move]

    def handle_play(next_squares):
        next_history = history[: current_move + 1]
        next_history.append(next_squares)
        set_history(next_history)
        set_current_move(len(next_history) - 1)

    def jump_to(next_move):
        return lambda _event: set_current_move(next_move)

    moves = []
    for move, _squares in enumerate(history):
        description = f"Go to move #{move}" if move > 0 else "Go to game start"

        moves.append(
            html.li(
                {"key": move},
                html.button({"onClick": jump_to(move)}, description),
            )
        )

    return html.div(
        {"className": "game"},
        html.div(
            {"className": "game-board"},
            board(x_is_next, current_squares, handle_play),
        ),
        html.div({"className": "game-info"}, html.ol(moves)),
    )


def calculate_winner(squares):
    lines = [
        [0, 1, 2],
        [3, 4, 5],
        [6, 7, 8],
        [0, 3, 6],
        [1, 4, 7],
        [2, 5, 8],
        [0, 4, 8],
        [2, 4, 6],
    ]
    for line in lines:
        a, b, c = line
        if not squares:
            continue
        if squares[a] and squares[a] == squares[b] and squares[a] == squares[c]:
            return squares[a]

    return None

* {
    box-sizing: border-box;
}

docs.title: The basics: components, props, and state
Inspecting the starter code
docs.text:
The example defines a component. In ReactPy, a component is a function that returns what part of the interface should look like. Read it line by line:

@component
def square():
    return html.button({"className": "square"}, "X")

The first two lines are boilerplate: @component turns the function below it into a component, and html gives you a function for every HTML tag.

The def square(): line defines a function called square. Unlike React, ReactPy component names are snake_case and lowercase — there is no capital-letter rule, because ReactPy tells a component from an HTML tag by whether you call it, not by how it is spelled.

The return line gives back a button. html.button(...) is a call to a function, not an element literal: children come after the attribute dictionary as positional arguments, so "X" is the text inside the button. {"className": "square"} is that attribute dictionary, and className is the DOM attribute name — attribute keys are forwarded to the browser verbatim, so they keep React's camelCase spelling.

docs.title: Building the board
docs.text:
The board needs nine squares, not one. Copying the button twice is tempting:

@component
def square():
    return html.button({"className": "square"}, "X"), html.button({"className": "square"}, "X")

That does not fail the way React's "adjacent JSX elements" error does. The comma builds a two-item tuple; ReactPy does not know you meant two children, coerces it with str(), and the page shows the VDOM dictionaries as literal text:

({'children': ['X'], 'attributes': {'className': 'square'}, 'tagName': 'button'}, ...)

Verified through Layout.render(): the model's only child is that string. If the page ever shows you a Python repr, a missing call or a stray comma is the usual cause. A component returns exactly one thing. To return several children, wrap them in a fragment with html.fragment(...), which groups children without adding an element of its own:

@component
def square():
    return html.fragment(
        html.button({"className": "square"}, "X"),
        html.button({"className": "square"}, "X"),
    )

Now copy-paste your way to nine squares and... they come out in a single line, not a grid. Group them into rows with divs carrying the className the stylesheet already defines, and number the squares so you can tell them apart:

docs.title: Passing data through props
docs.text:
Nine hardcoded buttons means nine places to change when a square's content becomes dynamic. Instead, extract a square component and give it the value to display — a prop:

@component
def square(value):
    return html.button({"className": "square"}, value)

There is no JSX, so props are simply Python parameters. Call the component and pass the argument:

square("A")

Update board to call square nine times, passing a different letter each time so you can see the values arrive:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component

Notice how board and square are both called the same way, with no ceremony, while html.div and html.button are calls into the html object. Components are just functions you wrote; tags are functions ReactPy provides.

Props are read-only. square cannot assign to value to change what its parent passed, and ReactPy has no mechanism to help it try. Data flows down; to change it, the component that owns it must change it.

docs.title: Making an interactive component
docs.text:
Now make a square fill itself when clicked. Add a handler inside square and register it under onClick:

@component
def square():
    def handle_click(event):
        print("clicked!")

    return html.button({"className": "square", "onClick": handle_click})

A handler is any callable, and ReactPy calls it with exactly one argument — the event payload. Name it event, even if you ignore it.

Unlike React, there is no browser console to open: ReactPy components run on the server, so print lands in the terminal running your app, next to the URL. Click a square several times and you will see the line repeat there.

Pitfall

The key must be camelCase onClick. The React-looking on_click is accepted and shipped to the browser like any other on* key — and then nothing listens for it, because no browser event is named on_click. Verified: the server-side model holds a registered on_click handler while clicking the button leaves the component's state at 0. The button renders, looks normal, and never fires, with no error and no log line anywhere. If a control does nothing, check the spelling of the key first. See Responding to Events.

Next, make the square remember that it was clicked. ReactPy gives components memory with the use_state hook, which returns the current value and the function that changes it:

app.pystyles.css Run 
# None is what an unfilled square holds; ReactPy renders None as nothing.
EMPTY_SQUARE: str | None = None


@component
def square():
    value, set_value = use_state(EMPTY_SQUARE)

    def handle_click(event):
        set_value("X")

    return html.button({"className": "square", "onClick": handle_click}, value)


@component
def board():
    return html.fragment(
        html.div(
            {"className": "board-row"},
            square(),
            square(),
            square(),
        ),
        html.div(
            {"className": "board-row"},
            square(),
            square(),
            square(),
        ),
        html.div(
            {"className": "board-row"},
            square(),
            square(),
            square(),
        ),
    )

value, set_value = use_state(EMPTY_SQUARE) unpacks a pair: the state you read and the setter you call. Its argument is the starting value, used only on the component's first render. Calling set_value asks ReactPy to render the component again, and that render sees the new value.

The value is None, meaning "empty", and ReactPy renders None as nothing, so a fresh board is blank. It lives in a module-level constant annotated str | None, which is what lets a type checker accept both None and "X" in that square — without it, the type is inferred from None alone and assigning a mark is flagged. See Use State.

Note that ReactPy renders True and False as the words True and False, so None is the only value that disappears — React's habit of writing cond && <X/> has no working Python equivalent. See Conditional Rendering.

Click each square and watch them fill independently. Nine square() calls contain nine separate use_state calls, and each one keeps its own value.

That is a defect, not a feature. Each square's value lives inside that square, so no other part of the program can see the whole board — which means nothing can answer "has someone won?". The next section fixes this by moving the state to where the whole board is visible.

docs.title: Completing the game
docs.text: Right now the game has a serious limitation: nobody can win.

docs.title: Lifting state up
docs.text:
To detect a winner you need the whole board in one place. The fix is to move the state out of square and into board, which already renders all nine squares — a move called lifting state up.

board owns a list of nine values and passes each one down:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def square(value, on_click):
    return html.button({"className": "square", "onClick": on_click}, value)


@component
def board():
    initial_board: list[str | None] = [None] * 9
    squares, set_squares = use_state(initial_board)

    def handle_click(i):
        def inner(event):
            if squares[i]:
                return
            next_squares = squares.copy()
            next_squares[i] = "X"
            set_squares(next_squares)

        return inner

    return html.fragment(
        html.div(
            {"className": "board-row"},
            square(squares[0], handle_click(0)),
            square(squares[1], handle_click(1)),
            square(squares[2], handle_click(2)),
        ),
        html.div(
            {"className": "board-row"},
            square(squares[3], handle_click(3)),
            square(squares[4], handle_click(4)),
            square(squares[5], handle_click(5)),
        ),
        html.div(
            {"className": "board-row"},
            square(squares[6], handle_click(6)),
            square(squares[7], handle_click(7)),
            square(squares[8], handle_click(8)),
        ),
    )

* {
    box-sizing: border-box;
}

    font-family: sans-serif;
    margin: 20px;
    padding: 0;

.square {
    background: #fff;
    border: 1px solid #999;
    float: left;
    font-size: 24px;
    font-weight: bold;
    line-height: 34px;
    height: 34px;
    margin-right: -1px;
    margin-top: -1px;
    padding: 0;
    text-align: center;
    width: 34px;
}

    clear: both;
    content: "";
    display: table;
}

    margin-bottom: 10px;
}

    flex-direction: row;
}

    margin-left: 20px;
}

# TODO

square is now stateless: it takes value to display and on_click to call, and remembers nothing. That is the shape of most components you will write — they take data in and report events out, and the state lives above them.

Note the spelling distinction, because both forms are correct in different places. on_click above is a Python parameter — a prop name you invented, so it is snake_case like every other identifier you define. onClick is the attribute dictionary key the browser needs, so it keeps its camelCase spelling. Naming a prop onClick or writing the attribute key on_click are both mistakes, in opposite directions.

Two details are worth pausing on.

First, the handler needs to know which square was clicked, but ReactPy hands a handler exactly one argument: the event. The usual answer is a factory, as handle_click(i) does here — it returns the handler that closes over i. You will also see this written as a lambda:

html.button({"onClick": lambda event: handle_click(i)}, squares[i])

That works when written out per square. It has a sharp edge inside a loop, which Picking a key demonstrates.

Second, board renders three rows by hand, so square(...) appears nine times with nine different indices. A loop is shorter, and once you write one you will need keys — see Rendering Lists.

docs.title: Why immutability is important
docs.text:
Look closely at what the handler does before it calls the setter:

next_squares = squares.copy()
next_squares[i] = "X"
set_squares(next_squares)

It copies the list, changes the copy, and hands the copy to the setter. There are two ways to change data: mutate it in place, or replace it with a modified copy. The obvious Python code takes the first route, and it fails in a way that is hard to diagnose:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def board():
    initial_board: list[str | None] = [None] * 9
    squares, set_squares = use_state(initial_board)

    def handle_click(i):
        # Mutating in place and handing back the same object: ReactPy compares
        # the new value with the old one, sees the same object, and schedules no
        # render at all. The button looks fine and never responds.
        def inner(event):
            squares[i] = "X"
            set_squares(squares)

        return inner

    return html.fragment(
        html.div(
            {"className": "board-row"},
            square(squares[0], handle_click(0)),
            square(squares[1], handle_click(1)),
            square(squares[2], handle_click(2)),
        ),
        html.div(
            {"className": "board-row"},
            square(squares[3], handle_click(3)),
            square(squares[4], handle_click(4)),
            square(squares[5], handle_click(5)),

# TODO

Click a square. Nothing happens — no error, no log line, no warning. The handler runs; the board just never changes.

Verified against this example: after three clicks on that square, the board is still nine empty cells. The cause is that set_squares(squares) passes back the very same object that is already in state. ReactPy compares the new value against the current one, finds them equal, and skips the render — an optimisation that turns an in-place mutation into a silent no-op.

Pitfall

Mutate-then-set-the-same-object is the most common ReactPy bug and the quietest one. squares[i] = "X" followed by set_squares(squares) schedules no render at all. Neither does mutating without calling the setter. Always build a new list — squares.copy(), a list comprehension, or slicing — and pass that. See Updating Arrays in State.

Immutability earns its keep twice here. It is what makes the board update at all, and it is what lets the last section keep every past move around: because old lists are never modified, they stay valid and can be re-displayed later.

Deep Dive

React's version of this section argues that immutability lets React skip re-rendering parts of the tree that did not change. That argument does not apply to ReactPy: there is no memo and no render bailout, so a child component's body re-runs whenever its parent renders, even with identical props. Immutable data is still required — for the reason above, and so equality checks mean what you expect — but do not expect it to save you renders. See You Might Not Need an Effect.

docs.title: Declaring a winner
docs.text:
Add a helper that checks the eight winning lines. It knows nothing about ReactPy, so read it as plain Python:

def calculate_winner(squares):
    lines = [
        [0, 1, 2],
        [3, 4, 5],
        [6, 7, 8],
        [0, 3, 6],
        [1, 4, 7],
        [2, 5, 8],
        [0, 4, 8],
        [2, 4, 6],
    ]
    for a, b, c in lines:
        if squares[a] and squares[a] == squares[b] and squares[a] == squares[c]:
            return squares[a]
    return None

It returns "X", "O", or None. Where you put it in the file does not matter; keeping it at the bottom means you do not scroll past it every time.

Call it in two places — to stop play after a win, and to write the status line:

docs.title: Adding time travel
docs.text:
Because every move produced a new list instead of modifying the old one, the previous boards still exist. All that is left is to keep them.

The history is a list of boards, one per move:

[
    # before the first move
    [None] * 9,
    # after the first move
    [None, None, None, None, "X", None, None, None, None],
    # after the second move
    [None, None, None, None, "X", None, None, None, "O"],
]

docs.title: Lifting state up, again
docs.text:
Add a game component above board to hold that history. It will also decide which move you are looking at, so board must stop owning state and start receiving what to draw.

Start by having game render board inside the layout the stylesheet expects, and keep the history and the current move as its own state. board keeps its own handle_click, but now reports the finished move upward through an on_play prop instead of storing it:

@component
def game():
    history, set_history = use_state([[None] * 9])

    def handle_play(next_squares):
        set_history([*history, next_squares])

    current_move = len(history) - 1
    x_is_next = current_move % 2 == 0
    current_squares = history[current_move]

    return html.div(
        {"className": "game"},
        html.div(
            {"className": "game-board"},
            board(x_is_next, current_squares, handle_play),
        ),
        html.div({"className": "game-info"}, html.ol()),
    )

x_is_next and current_squares are not state. They are computed from history during the render, which is why they cannot drift out of sync with it.

docs.title: Showing the past moves
docs.text:
You have a list of moves in state; render it as a list of buttons. Where React reaches for map, Python reaches for a comprehension or a loop:

moves = []
for move in range(len(history)):
    description = f"Go to move #{move}" if move > 0 else "Go to game start"
    moves.append(html.li(html.button({"onClick": jump_to(move)}, description)))

Then render html.ol(moves) inside the game-info div. Add a current_move state variable and an empty jump_to(move) that does nothing yet, so the list has somewhere to go:

Pitfall

With REACTPY_DEBUG on, the server logs Key not specified for child in list ... for every row. ReactPy is telling you the same thing React does: a list you will re-render needs a key on each item. It is a warning, not an error, so a list can ship without one — and misbehave later in ways that are hard to trace back. The fix is Picking a key.

A related trap: pass a list, not a generator. html.ol(html.li(...) for ... in ...) skips the key check entirely, with the warning Did not verify key-path integrity of children in generator ... - pass a sequence, and an iterator stored in state is worse still — it is single-use, so the first render shows the rows and every later render shows nothing.

docs.title: Picking a key
docs.text:
When you re-render a list, ReactPy has to work out which item is which. It cannot read your intent, so you tell it: give each item a key.

html.li({"key": move}, html.button({"onClick": jump_to(move)}, description))

key is a reserved name, and it is spelled two different ways depending on what you are creating — mixing them up is a hard error:

You are creating Spell it Passing it the other way raises an element inside the attribute dict: html.li({"key": move}, ...) TypeError: Vdom.__call__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'key' a component as a keyword: row(item, key=item["id"]) silently meaningless, since the dict is the attribute dict

A key identifies an item across renders. Change a component's key and ReactPy destroys it and builds a fresh one, discarding its state — which is a useful trick on its own, and the subject of Preserving and Resetting State. Keys need only be unique among siblings, not globally.

For the move list, the move's index is a legitimate key: moves are never reordered, inserted in the middle, or deleted, so index and identity agree. That is the exception. When items can be added or removed, the array index stops identifying anything, and state quietly lands on the wrong row — use a real identifier instead. See Rendering Lists.

docs.title: Implementing time travel
docs.text:
jump_to(move) only has to say which move you are looking at:

def jump_to(move):
    def inner(event):
        set_current_move(move)

    return inner

And the values derived during render must follow current_move rather than the end of the list:

x_is_next = current_move % 2 == 0
current_squares = history[current_move]

Playing a move now has one more rule. If you jump back and play from there, the moves after that point are no longer the future — they are discarded:

def handle_play(next_squares):
    next_history = history[: current_move + 1]
    next_history.append(next_squares)
    set_history(next_history)
    set_current_move(len(next_history) - 1)

The slice history[: current_move + 1] keeps everything up to and including the move you jumped back to, dropping the rest, and set_current_move puts you at the new end.

def square(value, on_click):

def board(x_is_next, squares, on_play):
    def handle_click(i):
        def inner(event):
            """
            Due to a quirk of Python, if your event handler needs args other than
            `event`, you will need to create a wrapper function as seen above.
            Ref: https://pylint.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user_guide/messages/warning/cell-var-from-loop.html
            """
            if calculate_winner(squares) or squares[i]:
                return

            next_squares = squares.copy()
            next_squares[i] = "X" if x_is_next else "O"
            on_play(next_squares)

        return inner

    winner = calculate_winner(squares)
    status = (
        f"Winner: {winner}" if winner else "Next player: " + ("X" if x_is_next else "O")
    )

    return html.fragment(
        html.div({"className": "status"}, status),
        html.div(
            {"className": "board-row"},
            square(squares[0], handle_click(0)),
            square(squares[1], handle_click(1)),
            square(squares[2], handle_click(2)),

            square(squares[3], handle_click(3)),
            square(squares[4], handle_click(4)),
            square(squares[5], handle_click(5)),
        ),
        html.div(
            {"className": "board-row"},
            square(squares[6], handle_click(6)),
            square(squares[7], handle_click(7)),
            square(squares[8], handle_click(8)),
        ),
    )


@component
def game():
    history, set_history = use_state([[None] * 9])
    current_move, set_current_move = use_state(0)
    x_is_next = current_move % 2 == 0
    current_squares = history[current_move]

    def handle_play(next_squares):
        next_history = history[: current_move + 1]
        next_history.append(next_squares)
        set_history(next_history)
        set_current_move(len(next_history) - 1)

    def jump_to(next_move):
        return lambda _event: set_current_move(next_move)

    moves = []
    for move, _squares in enumerate(history):
        description = f"Go to move #{move}" if move > 0 else "Go to game start"

        moves.append(
            html.li(
                {"key": move},
                html.button({"onClick": jump_to(move)}, description),
            )
        )

    return html.div(
        {"className": "game"},
        html.div(
            {"className": "game-board"},
            board(x_is_next, current_squares, handle_play),
        ),
        html.div({"className": "game-info"}, html.ol(moves)),
    )


def calculate_winner(squares):
    lines = [
        [0, 1, 2],
        [3, 4, 5],
        [6, 7, 8],
        [0, 3, 6],
        [1, 4, 7],
        [2, 5, 8],
        [0, 4, 8],
        [2, 4, 6],
    ]
    for line in lines:
        a, b, c = line
        if not squares:
            continue
        if squares[a] and squares[a] == squares[b] and squares[a] == squares[c]:
            return squares[a]

    return None

Pitfall

Do not store one board and a separate list of moves that points into it. The history must own the boards, and the boards must never change once stored. If you find yourself reaching for deepcopy here, that is a sign something is still being mutated — with the code above, the boards are never modified after they are created, so a plain slice is enough.

docs.title: Final cleanup
docs.text:
The finished game holds its state in three places, each as low as it can be while still seeing what it needs:

  • game owns history and current_move, because it renders both the board and the move list.
  • board owns nothing. It receives x_is_next, squares, and on_play.
  • square owns nothing. It receives value and on_click.

That is the pattern this tutorial was built around. State belongs to the component that needs it and to every component above it — no lower, because then a sibling cannot see it, and no higher, because then unrelated renders redo the work. When two components need the same data, lift it to their nearest common ancestor.

docs.title: Wrapping up
docs.text:
• A component is a @component function returning one thing; several children go inside html.fragment(...) or a list.
  • Props are ordinary Python parameters, and they are read-only.
  • use_state gives a component memory; calling the setter re-renders it.
  • Handlers take exactly one argument, the event. Extra context is bound on the Python side, usually with a factory function.
  • Never mutate a list you have put in state — copy it, or the setter silently does nothing.
  • Derive what you can during render instead of storing it: winner, x_is_next, current_squares.
  • Lift state to the lowest component that can see everything that needs it.
  • Give list items a key — in the attribute dict for elements, as a keyword for components.
  • Time travel is free once your data is immutable, and impossible when it is not.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Lists are mutable in Python, but you should treat them as immutable when you store them in state. Just like with objects, when you want to update a list stored in state, you need to create a new one (or make a copy of an existing one), and then set state to use the new list.

You will learn

  • How to add, remove, or change items in a list in ReactPy state
  • How to update an object inside of a list
  • Why a mutating update is dropped without any error

docs.title: Updating lists without mutation
docs.text:
In JavaScript you copy arrays with the spread syntax, and mutating methods like push() and pop() are easy to reach for by mistake. Python's equivalent methods — append(), extend(), insert(), remove(), pop(), sort(), reverse() — are in-place and return None, so the mistake looks different and fails harder:

def handle_add(event):
    items.append({"id": next_id, "text": text})   # mutates, returns None
    set_items(items)                              # same object -> ignored

Nothing happens. ReactPy compares the new value against the old one with == (core/hooks.py, strictly_equal), sees nothing changed, and schedules no render. There is no error, no warning, and nothing in the browser console. Verified directly: mutating then setting the same list produces no render at all. Nor does setting a new list that happens to compare equal — which is why set_rows([*rows, 4]) works while mutating rows and passing it back does not.

So whenever you want to update a list, pass a new list to the setter. Python gives you two tools for that:

Instead of (mutates) Use (new list) items.append(x) [*items, x] items.remove(x) [i for i in items if i is not x] items[i] = x [*items[:i], x, *items[i + 1:]] items.pop(i) [*items[:i], *items[i + 1:]] items.insert(i, x) [*items[:i], x, *items[i:]] items.reverse() list(reversed(items)) items.sort(key=f) sorted(items, key=f)

Never store an iterator in state

This one has no JavaScript analogue and will bite you. Python's filter() and map() return lazy, single-use iterators, not lists:

set_items(filter(lambda i: i["id"] != id_to_delete, items))   # 🚩

That renders correctly once, which is exactly what makes it so hard to diagnose. The iterator is consumed while ReactPy walks the children, so the next render of that same state sees an exhausted iterator and displays nothing. Verified: a list of three items filtered to "a,c" on the first render, then an unrelated state change rendered an empty line.

Always build a list — a comprehension is clearest, list(filter(...)) if you must:

set_items([i for i in items if i["id"] != id_to_delete])   # correct

docs.title: Adding to a list
docs.text:
The common case is adding an item. The handler creates a new list ending with the new item:

app.py Run 
@component
def todo_list():
    items, set_items = use_state([{"id": 0, "text": "Walk the dog"}])
    text, set_text = use_state("")

    def handle_add(event):
        event.preventDefault()
        if not text:
            return
        # A new list; `items.append(...)` would be silently ignored.
        next_id = max((item["id"] for item in items), default=-1) + 1
        set_items([*items, {"id": next_id, "text": text}])
        set_text("")

    return html.div(
        html.form(
            {"onSubmit": handle_add},
            html.input(
                {
                    "value": text,
                    "placeholder": "To do...",
                    "onChange": lambda event: set_text(event["target"]["value"]),
                }
            ),
            html.button({"type": "submit"}, "Add"),
        ),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": item["id"]}, item["text"]) for item in items]),
    )

# TODO

Type a task and submit; it appends while the existing ones stay put. Note that the new id is computed from the existing items rather than from a module-level counter. A global counter is shared by every visitor to the server, so two users would collide on the same key — derive ids from the state you already have, or use uuid4().

docs.title: Removing from a list
docs.text:
The most common removal is filtering out one item:

app.py Run 
@component
def todo_list():
    items, set_items = use_state(
        [
            {"id": 0, "text": "Walk the dog"},
            {"id": 1, "text": "Brush the cat"},
            {"id": 2, "text": "Teach the fish to juggle"},
        ]
    )

    def handle_delete(id_to_keep):
        def handler(event):
            # filter() gives a new list; items.remove(...) would mutate it.
            set_items([item for item in items if item["id"] != id_to_keep])

        return handler

    return html.ul(
        [
            html.li(
                {"key": item["id"]},
                item["text"],
                html.button({"onClick": handle_delete(item["id"])}, "Delete"),
            )
            for item in items
        ]
    )

# TODO

[item for item in items if item["id"] != id_to_keep] produces a brand-new list containing everything except the deleted item, and the original is left alone.

docs.title: Transforming every item
docs.text:
To apply a change to every item, build a new list by transforming each element:

app.py Run 
@component
def todo_list():
    items, set_items = use_state(
        [
            {"id": 0, "text": "Walk the dog"},
            {"id": 1, "text": "Brush the cat"},
        ]
    )

    def handle_click(event):
        # map() becomes a comprehension; the old items stay untouched.
        set_items([{"id": item["id"], "text": item["text"] + "!"} for item in items])

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": handle_click}, "Add !"),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": item["id"]}, item["text"]) for item in items]),
    )

# TODO

Each item becomes a new dict, because mutating item["text"] in place would leave the previous state pointing at the same mutated object.

Comprehensions do not modify the original

React's docs point out that filter() doesn't touch the original array, and a Python comprehension has the same property — it reads the old list and returns a fresh one. The catch, stated above, is that the built-in filter() does not return a list at all.

docs.title: Replacing an item
docs.text:
Unlike most languages, Python has no setAt(i, x) method, and the obvious items[i] = x mutates. Build the list from slices instead:

app.py Run 
@component
def todo_list():
    items, set_items = use_state(
        [
            {"id": 0, "text": "Walk the dog"},
            {"id": 1, "text": "Brush the cat"},
        ]
    )
    text, set_text = use_state("")

    def handle_replace(event):
        event.preventDefault()
        if not text:
            return
        # Replace one item by building a whole new list. Mutating
        # items[0]["text"] would be invisible to ReactPy.
        set_items([{"id": 0, "text": text}, *items[1:]])
        set_text("")

    return html.div(
        html.form(
            {"onSubmit": handle_replace},
            html.input(
                {
                    "value": text,
                    "placeholder": "Replace the first item",
                    "onChange": lambda event: set_text(event["target"]["value"]),
                }
            ),
            html.button({"type": "submit"}, "Replace"),
        ),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": item["id"]}, item["text"]) for item in items]),
    )

# TODO

[{"id": 0, "text": text}, *items[1:]] replaces the first item and copies the rest. For an arbitrary index, [*items[:i], new_item, *items[i + 1:]] is the general form.

docs.title: Inserting into a list
docs.text:
To insert an item somewhere other than the end, slice around the insertion point:

app.py Run 
@component
def todo_list():
    items, set_items = use_state(
        [
            {"id": 0, "text": "Walk the dog"},
            {"id": 1, "text": "Brush the cat"},
        ]
    )
    text, set_text = use_state("")

    def handle_insert(event):
        event.preventDefault()
        if not text:
            return
        # Slicing builds the new list; list.insert() would mutate in place.
        set_items([*items[:1], {"id": 3, "text": text}, *items[1:]])
        set_text("")

    return html.div(
        html.form(
            {"onSubmit": handle_insert},
            html.input(
                {
                    "value": text,
                    "placeholder": "Insert at index 1",
                    "onChange": lambda event: set_text(event["target"]["value"]),
                }
            ),
            html.button({"type": "submit"}, "Insert"),
        ),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": item["id"]}, item["text"]) for item in items]),
    )

# TODO

[*items[:1], new_item, *items[1:]] puts the new item at index 1. This is how React's "insert into an array" example translates; list.insert() mutates and is unusable here.

docs.title: Making other changes to a list
docs.text:
The rule is uniform: copy first, then operate on the copy, or use a function that already returns a new list.

app.py Run 
@component
def todo_list():
    items, set_items = use_state(
        [
            {"id": 0, "text": "Walk the dog"},
            {"id": 1, "text": "Brush the cat"},
            {"id": 2, "text": "Feed the fish"},
        ]
    )
    log, set_log = use_state([])

    def record(label, next_items):
        set_items(next_items)
        set_log([*log, f"{label}: {', '.join(i['text'] for i in next_items)}"])

    return html.div(
        html.div(
            html.button(
                {"onClick": lambda event: record("reversed", list(reversed(items)))},
                "Reverse",
            ),
            html.button(
                {
                    "onClick": lambda event: record(
                        "sorted", sorted(items, key=lambda i: i["text"])
                    )
                },
                "Sort",
            ),
            html.button(
                {"onClick": lambda event: record("filtered", items[:2])},
                "Keep first two",
            ),
        ),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": item["id"]}, item["text"]) for item in items]),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": i}, line) for i, line in enumerate(log)]),
    )

# TODO

reversed() returns an iterator, so wrap it in list(...); sorted() already returns a new list; items[:2] is a slice, which is already a new list.

list.sort() and list.reverse() return None

These two are the most expensive traps because the failure is invisible. items.sort() sorts in place and returns None, so set_items(items.sort()) stores None in state. Use sorted(items) and list(reversed(items)).

docs.title: Updating objects inside lists
docs.text:
The examples above replaced whole dicts, which is the safe default. When an item is a dict whose fields you want to change one at a time, you need two copies: a new list, and a new dict for the item that changed.

app.py Run 
@component
def form():
    artworks, set_artworks = use_state(initial_artworks())

    def handle_toggle(id_to_toggle):
        def handler(event):
            # Copy the LIST, and copy the one dict inside it that changed.
            # A shallow copy would leave the dict shared with the old state.
            set_artworks(
                [
                    {**artwork, "seen": not artwork["seen"]}
                    if artwork["id"] == id_to_toggle
                    else artwork
                    for artwork in artworks
                ]
            )

        return handler

    return html.ul(
        [
            html.li(
                {"key": artwork["id"]},
                html.label(
                    html.input(
                        {
                            "type": "checkbox",
                            "checked": artwork["seen"],
                            "onChange": handle_toggle(artwork["id"]),
                        }
                    ),
                    f"{artwork['title']} - {artwork['artist']}",
                ),
            )
            for artwork in artworks
        ]
    )

# TODO

Tick one checkbox and only that artwork's "seen" flips — verified, the pair goes from [False, False] to [True, False]. The comprehension copies every item, and only the targeted one is rebuilt with the changed field.

A shallow copy of the list is not enough

It is tempting to write:

next_items = list(artworks)          # new list...
next_items[0]["seen"] = True         # ...but the SAME dicts inside
set_items(next_items)

That is a new list containing the same dict objects. Two problems follow. The assignment mutates a dict the previous state still references, so the change is invisible to ReactPy's comparison. And anything else holding that dict — another component seeded from the same fixture, a cached render — sees it flip too.

Copying is shallow at every level in Python; there is no deep copy on assignment or unpacking. Build the changed dict explicitly, as the example does. See Updating a nested object for the object-side version of this.

Keep identity stable for unchanged items

Notice the else artwork branch: unchanged items are passed through as the same objects, not rebuilt. That is both cheaper and useful — if you rebuild everything on each keystroke, nothing can be recognised as unchanged later.

docs.title: Writing concise update logic
docs.text:
React's docs finish this page with Immer, which lets you write draft.push(...) behind a proxy. ReactPy has no Immer and no equivalent. There is no proxy layer to record your mutations, and no use_immer to import.

What you have instead is what this page already used:

  • List unpacking and comprehensions — [*items, x], [f(i) for i in items], [*items[:i], x, *items[i:]]. Verbose but explicit, and it fails loudly rather than silently.
  • copy.deepcopy — for a structure too nested to copy by hand.
  • use_reducer — moves the update logic out of the component, which is where the verbosity actually starts to hurt. See Extracting State Logic into a Reducer.

A homegrown Immer is worth avoiding specifically because it would paper over the failure mode this page is about: mutations are more dangerous here than in the browser, because ReactPy decides whether to render by comparing the old and new values on the server — so a mutation that hands back the same object, or an equal one, is dropped without a trace.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Treat lists in state as read-only: never call append(), sort(), insert(), remove(), and friends on them.
  • Build a new list with [*items, x] or a comprehension, and pass that to the setter.
  • Mutating and passing the same list back is silently dropped — no render, no error.
  • Never store filter()/map() results in state; they are single-use iterators and the second render will be empty.
  • To change an object inside a list, copy the list and copy the changed dict.
  • There is no Immer in ReactPy; use comprehensions, deepcopy, or use_reducer.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
State can hold any kind of value, including dicts and lists. But you shouldn't change objects that you hold in ReactPy state directly. Instead, when you want to update an object, you need to create a new one (or make a copy of an existing one), and then set the state to use that copy.

You will learn

  • How to correctly update an object in ReactPy state
  • How to update a nested object without mutating it
  • What immutability is, and how not to break it
  • Why a mutating update can be dropped without any error

docs.title: What's a mutation?
docs.text:
To mutate something means to change it after it was created.

Objects and lists in Python are mutable: you can change their contents in place. The mutating operations are usually visible in the code you write — obj["key"] = value, list.append(x), list.pop(), del list[i], d.update(other) — but there are more hiding behind method names that don't announce themselves (list.sort(), list.extend(), list.reverse(), dict.setdefault()).

In ReactPy, treat state as read-only. Every time your code renders, you work with the state that already exists, and you want to cause changes over time based on user input. Leaving all mutation to the setter keeps your code easy to understand. This applies to state in general, not just object state.

Mutating state doesn't just risk a bug — it can silently do nothing

In React, mutating state is a "may render stale UI" hazard. In ReactPy it is sharper, because the setter compares the new value against the old one before scheduling anything — and that comparison accepts equality, not just identity (core/hooks.py, strictly_equal). Anything that compares equal, including a brand-new object, schedules no render.

Measured behaviour, each case dispatched through reactpy.core.layout.Layout:

What the handler does Result Mutates a list in place, then set_x(same_list) no render at all Mutates in place, calls no setter no render set_x([*old, item]) — a new object renders

The failure is completely silent: no error, no warning, nothing in the browser console. Your handler ran, ReactPy agreed that nothing changed, and the UI never updates. This is why the read-only rule is not a style preference here.

docs.title: Treat state as read-only
docs.text:
Consider a form that lets the user change their profile. This handler reaches into the state object and assigns a field directly:

def handle_first_name(event):
    person["firstName"] = event["target"]["value"]   # 🚩 Mutate!
    set_person(person)                                # same object -> ignored

person is the very object ReactPy already holds, so the assignment changes it in place and then hands the same object back. ReactPy compares it against what it already has, finds nothing changed, and skips the render — the field appears frozen while your dict quietly holds the new value.

The fix is to always create a new object for the next state:

def handle_first_name(event):
    set_person({**person, "firstName": event["target"]["value"]})

That is the pattern for every state update in ReactPy: build a new value, pass it to the setter.

A pointer-tracking dot shows the same rule with no form in sight. The handler builds a brand-new position dict on every move:

app.py Run 
@component
def moving_dot():
    position, set_position = use_state({"x": 0, "y": 0})

    def handle_move(event):
        # Replace the whole object: ReactPy never merges a partial update.
        set_position({"x": event["clientX"], "y": event["clientY"]})

    return html.div(
        {
            "onPointerMove": handle_move,
            "style": {
                "position": "relative",
                "width": "100%",
                "height": "180px",
                "background": "#f0f0f0",
            },
        },
        html.div(
            {
                "style": {
                    "position": "absolute",
                    "background": "black",
                    "borderRadius": "50%",
                    "width": "20px",
                    "height": "20px",
                    "left": "-10px",
                    "top": "-10px",
                    "transform": f"translate({position['x']}px, {position['y']}px)",
                }
            }
        ),
    )

# TODO

The "onPointerMove" handler is on the grey container, and the dot is positioned from the coordinates it receives. Move the pointer anywhere inside the box and the dot follows. event["clientX"] and event["clientY"] are part of what the client sends for pointer events — verified against a real browser, which reported clientX/clientY matching the synthesized pointer position — so React's pointer and drag demos port across unchanged.

There is no automatic merge

set_x(...) replaces the state. It does not merge a partial object into what was there. Verified: setting {"a": 9} over {"a": 1, "b": 2} leaves {'a': 9} — "b" is simply gone.

If you have read React tutorials, you may remember setState merging objects. That was the class API. React's own useState replaces, and so does ReactPy (core/hooks.py, _CurrentState.dispatch assigns self.value = new). Any ReactJS text saying "React merges the object into your current state" is describing an API that no longer applies — port those examples with an explicit {**old, ...}.

Local mutation is fine

Mutating a value you just created inside the current render is safe, because nothing else has ever seen it. The same applies to the rows = [] plus rows.append(...) loop you will write constantly when building children:

@component
def list_of_parts(parts):
    # Built during this render, never handed out before.
    sorted_parts = sorted(parts, key=lambda p: p["importance"])
    return html.ul(
        [html.li({"key": p["id"]}, p["title"]) for p in sorted_parts]
    )

What must not be mutated is state ReactPy gave you, and props you received. See Local mutation: Your component's little secret for the rendering-side version of this rule.

docs.title: Copying objects with the spread syntax
docs.text:
To update an object, create a new one from the old one so you can change any of its properties. Python has no ... spread operator, but {**obj, "key": value} is the same operation on dicts, and [*items, x] is its twin for lists.

Here the form keeps the other fields intact while replacing one:

app.py Run 
@component
def form():
    person, set_person = use_state(
        {
            "firstName": "Jane",
            "lastName": "Jacobs",
            "email": "jane@example.com",
        }
    )

    def handle_first_name(event):
        # Copy everything, then override just this one field.
        set_person({**person, "firstName": event["target"]["value"]})

    def handle_last_name(event):
        set_person({**person, "lastName": event["target"]["value"]})

    def handle_email(event):
        set_person({**person, "email": event["target"]["value"]})

    return html.div(
        html.input({"value": person["firstName"], "onChange": handle_first_name}),
        html.input({"value": person["lastName"], "onChange": handle_last_name}),
        html.input({"value": person["email"], "onChange": handle_email}),
        html.hr(),
        html.h1(f"Hello, {person['firstName']} {person['lastName']}!"),
        html.a({"href": f"mailto:{person['email']}"}, person["email"]),
    )

# TODO

Type in any field and watch the heading update. Each handler spreads the current person into a fresh dict and overrides exactly one key.

An unpacked dict is a shallow copy

{**person} copies the top level only. Any nested dict or list inside it is still shared with the previous state — see Updating a nested object.

The destructuring equivalents

Where React's docs reach for const { a, ...rest } = obj, Python reads with indexing and writes with unpacking. For the "everything but one key" shape, the direct translation is a comprehension:

rest = {k: v for k, v in obj.items() if k != "drop"}

docs.title: Using a single event handler for multiple fields
docs.text:
Repeating a near-identical handler per field gets tedious. One handler can take the field name:

app.py Run 
@component
def form():
    person, set_person = use_state(
        {"firstName": "Jane", "lastName": "Jacobs", "email": "jane@example.com"}
    )

    # One handler for every field. ReactPy always calls a handler with the
    # event as its single positional argument, so the field name is bound by
    # the lambdas below rather than delivered by the client.
    def handle_change(field, event):
        set_person({**person, field: event["target"]["value"]})

    return html.div(
        html.input(
            {
                "value": person["firstName"],
                "onChange": lambda event: handle_change("firstName", event),
            }
        ),
        html.input(
            {
                "value": person["lastName"],
                "onChange": lambda event: handle_change("lastName", event),
            }
        ),
        html.input(
            {
                "value": person["email"],
                "onChange": lambda event: handle_change("email", event),
            }
        ),
        html.hr(),
        html.h1(f"Hello, {person['firstName']} {person['lastName']}!"),
    )

# TODO

Note how the field name is supplied by the lambda. ReactPy invokes every event handler with the event as its single positional argument — verified, a handler declaring two required parameters fails with TypeError: ... missing 1 required positional argument: 'event'. There is no e.target.name to read either, because the client does not send DOM attributes; any extra context has to be bound on the Python side.

Reach for use_reducer when handlers multiply

Several handlers that all edit one object is a sign the update logic wants its own home. See Extracting State Logic into a Reducer.

docs.title: Updating a nested object
docs.text:
State often contains nested objects. To update a deeply nested value, copy the object all the way up from where the change happens.

app.py Run 
@component
def form():
    person, set_person = use_state(
        {
            "firstName": "Jane",
            "lastName": "Jacobs",
            "email": "jane@example.com",
            "shippingAddress": {
                "street": "123 Maple Street",
                "city": "Pretendville",
            },
        }
    )

    def handle_city(event):
        address = {**person["shippingAddress"], "city": event["target"]["value"]}
        set_person({**person, "shippingAddress": address})

    return html.div(
        html.label(
            "City: ",
            html.input(
                {
                    "value": person["shippingAddress"]["city"],
                    "onChange": handle_city,
                }
            ),
        ),
        html.h1(person["firstName"]),
        html.p(person["shippingAddress"]["street"]),
        html.p(person["shippingAddress"]["city"]),
    )

# TODO

Two copies are required:

  1. Copy person["shippingAddress"] with the new "city".
  2. Copy person, replacing "shippingAddress" with that new dict.

Writing person["shippingAddress"]["city"] = ... would mutate the nested dict in place. Because that nested dict is the same object the previous state still refers to, the change is invisible to ReactPy's comparison and the update is dropped.

Objects are not really nested

Python makes this point sharper than JavaScript does. Given:

person = {"name": "Jane", "theme": {"background": "white"}}
copy = {**person}

copy["theme"] and person["theme"] are the same dict. Python never deep-copies on assignment or on unpacking — copying is shallow for dicts, lists, and everything else. To get a genuinely independent copy you either copy each level explicitly, as the example does, or use copy.deepcopy:

import copy

set_people(copy.deepcopy(people))

deepcopy is the blunt instrument: correct, but slower, and it copies everything reachable, including objects you did not mean to duplicate. Prefer explicit copies for the paths you actually change, and keep state to plain dicts, lists, and primitives so deepcopy remains a safe fallback.

Shallow sharing is also why two components seeded from the same module-level fixture end up aliasing each other's data — see Updating Arrays in State for the list version of that bug.

docs.title: Writing concise update logic
docs.text:
React's docs reach for Immer here, which records your mutations through a proxy and turns them into copies. ReactPy has no Immer and no equivalent. There is no proxy layer, so nothing could observe your mutations, and there is no use_immer to import.

What you have instead:

  • Dict and list unpacking — {**obj, "k": v}, [*items, x]. This covers the overwhelming majority of updates and is what every example above uses.
  • copy.deepcopy — for the rare shape too deep to copy by hand.
  • use_reducer — does not shorten updates, but moves them out of the component so their verbosity costs you less. See Extracting State Logic into a Reducer.

Resist building your own Immer. A proxy that logs mutations would have to run on the server, after a websocket round trip, which is not the problem Immer solves in the browser. If update logic feels genuinely painful, that usually means the state shape is wrong — see Choosing the State Structure.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• Treat everything ReactPy hands you as state or props as read-only: never assign into it, never call a mutating method on it.
  • Build a new object with {**old, ...} and pass that to the setter.
  • Mutating in place and passing the same object back is silently dropped — ReactPy compares the new value with the old and schedules no render when they are equal. Nothing in the browser will tell you.
  • Copying is shallow at every level; copy all the way up from the field that changed, or use copy.deepcopy.
  • Mutating a value you created during this render is fine.
  • There is no Immer in ReactPy; use dict and list unpacking, or restructure the state.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A ReactPy element is a dict, and Python lets you assign into it. That is the whole topic of this page: what is safe to change, what is merely pointless, and what quietly corrupts the model that the server is holding on behalf of every connected browser. The rule that decides all of it is that a model is owned by exactly one render — before it, yours to shape; after it, ReactPy's.

You will learn

  • Why mutation before a render is fine and after it is not
  • Which parts of a built element are copies and which are shared
  • The module-level element that leaks one user's change into everyone's page
  • Safe shapes: build fresh, deepcopy, and transform at build time

docs.title: The rule: a model belongs to its render
docs.text:
ReactPy serializes your element to JSON and sends it. Once that has happened, the dictionary is no longer purely yours — the layout keeps live references to the same objects so it can patch a subtree later (core/layout.py, Layout._create_layout_update reuses model.current rather than rebuilding it).

Split your code on that line:

  • Before the element is returned — mutate freely. Building a model incrementally out of helper functions is normal Python and nothing is watching.
  • After it has been returned from a render — treat it as frozen. Changes now affect a model the client has already received, and the server has no idea they happened.

Nothing in ReactPy enforces this. There is no freeze, no copy-on-render, no warning. That is why the failure modes below are worth memorizing.

docs.title: What is safe before the render
docs.text:
VdomDict is a light dict subclass, and it is strict about its top-level keys — exactly tagName, children, attributes, eventHandlers, inlineJavaScript, importSource:

d = html.div({"id": "pre"}, "x")

d["tagName"] = "section"       # fine
d["attributes"]["id"] = "a"    # fine — but only because "attributes" exists
d["children"].append("tail")   # fine
d["key"] = 1                   # KeyError: 'Invalid key: key'
d["ref"] = object()            # KeyError: 'Invalid key: ref'

Note the first line passes an attributes dict. html.div("x") omits the attributes key entirely when there are none — verified, it returns {'children': ['x'], 'tagName': 'div'} — so d["attributes"]["id"] = "a" on such an element raises KeyError: 'attributes' before any guard is reached. Use d.setdefault("attributes", {})["id"] = "a" when the element may not have had one.

The guard only covers the six top-level names. d["attributes"]["anything"] is unvalidated, and so is every nested value — the validation happens at serialization, and only in debug mode.

Keys and refs are not top-level keys

The React shapes {"key": ...} and {"ref": ...} raise, because a VdomDict has no such slot. A key goes inside attributes for an element (html.li({"key": 1}, ...)) or is passed as a keyword to a component (Item(x, key=1)). A ref does not exist at all — see Manipulating the DOM with Refs.

docs.title: Shallow copy, deep sharing
docs.text:
The constructors copy the top level, so the containers you passed in are not aliased into the element — but the copy is shallow, and nested values still point at your objects:

app.py Run 
# The tag constructors copy the top level, so the element's own attributes and
# children containers are separate objects from the ones you passed in.
style = {"color": "red"}
attributes = {"id": "card", "style": style}
children = ["hello"]

element = html.div(attributes, *children)

print(element["attributes"] is attributes)  # False -- a copy
print(element["children"] is children)  # False -- a fresh list

# But the copy is shallow: nested values are still the objects you handed over.
print(element["attributes"].get("style") is style)  # True

style["color"] = "blue"
print(element["attributes"].get("style"))  # {'color': 'blue'} -- changed after the fact

# TODO

The same applies to child elements: pass a model you built earlier and the parent stores that object, not a copy. Mutating the child later changes the parent. This is convenient for builders that assemble a tree in stages, and dangerous for anything that outlives the render — which is the subject of the next section.

docs.title: Mutating after the render
docs.text: There are two ways this goes wrong, and they look nothing alike.

docs.title: Case 1: the mutation is never sent
docs.text:
Change a rendered element and ask for no re-render, and the browser never learns. This is the same class of bug as mutating state in place, and it shares the cause: ReactPy decides what to send from state changes, not from the shape of your dictionaries.

There is no error, no log line, and no console message. The element in the browser keeps its old text and you keep staring at the assignment that "obviously" should have worked.

A mutation you make while handling an event is invisible until something else renders

This is the version that costs an afternoon. In a real browser, against the shared-element example below: click mutate and the page does not change; click bump, which changes unrelated state, and the mutation appears — as if it had been waiting. Because the re-render walks the model again, it re-reads the dictionary you edited and ships the change with the next patch. A user's action becomes visible on the next action, which is a bug that looks like a timing problem and is not one.

docs.title: Case 2: the mutation escapes to other users
docs.text:
The more damaging case, and the one unique to a server-side framework.

A model built at module level is one object shared by every connection to the server. Each connection gets its own Layout and its own hook state, but they all render the same dictionary. One visitor's handler mutates the object that everyone else's next render reads:

app.py Run 
# Built once, at module scope. Every visitor's Layout renders this same dict.
STATUS = html.p({"id": "status"}, "idle")


@component
def panel():
    n, set_n = use_state(0)

    def mark_dirty(event):
        # Mutates the shared element and asks for no render: nothing changes
        # on screen, and the server's model now disagrees with every client.
        STATUS["children"] = [f"mutated by visitor {n}"]

    def bump(event):
        # The next render of ANY state in this component re-sends STATUS --
        # including the mutation, whoever made it.
        set_n(n + 1)

    return html.div(
        html.h1({"id": "counter"}, f"n={n}"),
        html.button({"id": "dirty", "onClick": mark_dirty}, "mutate"),
        html.button({"id": "bump", "onClick": bump}, "bump"),
        STATUS,
    )

# TODO

Verified in a real browser with two separate tabs and two separate websockets against one server: tab A clicks mutate, then bump; tab B, which never clicked anything, then clicks bump and sees mutated by visitor 0 in its own page. Neither user can make it go away, because the mutated module-level dict is now the source of truth for every future render.

Module-level elements are shared across all connections

This has no browser-side analogue — in React, module scope is per-tab. Here module scope is per-process, and the process is shared. The rule follows directly: build elements inside the component. A function that returns html.p(...) costs one dictionary construction and removes the whole class of bug:

app.py Run 
# A function that builds a fresh element on every call: the safe shape.
def status_banner(text, tone):
    return html.p(
        {"id": "status", "className": f"status-{tone}"},
        text,
    )


@component
def panel():
    n, set_n = use_state(0)
    tone = "ok" if n == 0 else "warn"

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"n={n}"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_n(n + 1)}, "bump"),
        status_banner(f"{n} items", tone),  # a new dict every render
    )

# TODO

Module-level constants are still fine when they are genuinely inert — a style dict, a list of option labels, an html.head() passed once to ReactPy(html_head=...) — because nothing writes to them. The bug needs a write. If nothing in your program assigns into it, module scope is safe.

docs.title: The two mutation habits that also defeat state
docs.text:
These belong to Updating Objects in State and Updating Arrays in State, but they are VDOM mutation seen from the other side, so they are repeated here because the symptom — a control that stops responding with no error — is the one people hunt for longest.

use_state's setter compares the new value against the old with == (core/hooks.py, strictly_equal). So:

rows.append(x)
set_rows(rows)          # same object -> compares equal -> no render, no error

And the corollary that surprises people: a new object that merely compares equal is dropped too, so set_rows([*rows]) when rows is unchanged also renders nothing. Replace state with new, non-equal objects; never edit in place.

The same comparison is what makes use_memo fail to recompute after a mutate-then-set — the dependency compares equal to itself.

docs.title: Safe ways to shape a model
docs.text: Reach for these in order.

docs.title: Build it, do not edit it
docs.text:
The default. Compose with functions, keep elements as return values, and pass data in as arguments. Conditional structure is an expression, not a post-construction edit:

def row(item):
    return html.li(
        {"key": item["id"], "className": "row" if item["done"] else "row pending"},
        item["text"],
    )

docs.title: deepcopy for a genuine fork
docs.text:
When you must derive a variant from a model you do not own — typically something that came back from string_to_reactpy() or a cached template — copy it first:

from copy import deepcopy

TEMPLATE = html.div({"className": "card"}, html.p("placeholder"))


def card(body_text):
    model = deepcopy(TEMPLATE)
    model["children"][0]["children"] = [body_text]
    return model

deepcopy preserves the VdomDict class and its key guard, and leaves the original intact — verified. It is the right tool for a template you parse or build once at module level; it is not a licence to mutate a model that has already been rendered.

Deep-copying a model with handlers duplicates the handler objects

deepcopy succeeds on a model that has eventHandlers. It builds a new EventHandler but shares the wrapped function, so both copies still invoke the same Python code. That is fine for a fork you intend to render; it is not a way to hand two elements independent handlers — build those separately.

docs.title: Transform at parse time
docs.text: For HTML that arrives as a string, pass *transforms to string_to_reactpy() and edit nodes before anyone has a reference to them — see Convert Between VDOM and HTML.

docs.title: Turn the check on while developing
docs.text:
REACTPY_CHECK_VDOM_SPEC validates each rendered model against the JSON schema in core/vdom.py — but only catches structural damage (a child that is not a VDOM dict, a missing tagName), and it is off unless REACTPY_DEBUG is on:

from reactpy import config

config.REACTPY_DEBUG.current = True   # parents REACTPY_CHECK_VDOM_SPEC on

It will not catch a className you changed to the wrong string, or a text node you rewrote — those are valid VDOM. Treat it as a schema check, not a mutation detector.

docs.title: What you may still touch: the DOM, briefly
docs.text: Nothing here applies to the browser's DOM, which ReactPy does not share with you. The one sanctioned route is an inline-JavaScript handler, and the same discipline applies there — do not mutate nodes ReactPy owns, since the next patch against a node you removed breaks the diff. That is covered in Manipulating the DOM with Refs.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• A model is yours until it is returned from a render; after that the layout holds the same objects.
  • VdomDict guards its six top-level keys — key belongs inside attributes, and there is no ref.
  • Constructors copy the top level but share nested values, so a child element you built is the object the parent holds.
  • Mutating a rendered element sends nothing; the change surfaces on the next unrelated render, which makes it look like a timing bug.
  • A module-level element is shared by every connection, so one user's mutation appears in everyone's page. Build elements inside components.
  • Mutate-then-set-the-same-object is dropped by use_state's equality check, with no error.
  • Prefer building fresh; use deepcopy for a real fork; use parse-time transforms for parsed HTML.
