docs.title: You Might Not Need an Effect
Overview
docs.text:
Most Effects are unnecessary. If your logic only adjusts one thing based on another thing you already have, it belongs in the render — not in an Effect. This page walks through the common cases where an Effect looks right and isn't, with the render counts each one costs.

You will learn

  • How to recognize an Effect that is doing a render's job
  • What to write instead, case by case
  • Why ReactPy cannot use React's "set state during render" escape hatch
  • Which Effects genuinely are necessary

docs.title: How to remove unnecessary Effects
docs.text:
Work through each Effect in your code and ask: does this code need to run after a render, or could it run while rendering?

An Effect is genuinely necessary when the component must reach something outside ReactPy — subscribing to a queue, opening a socket, starting a task. Everything below is the opposite case: the "external system" is a value your component already has.

If you're not sure what Effects are for in the first place, start with Synchronizing with Effects.

docs.title: Updating state based on props or state
docs.text:
A component shows a name built from two fields. The tempting version stores the combination and keeps it in step with an Effect:

app.py Run 
@component
def form():
    first_name, set_first_name = use_state("Ada")
    last_name, set_last_name = use_state("Lovelace")
    # Wrong: this value is not state, it is a calculation of other state.
    full_name, set_full_name = use_state("")

    def effect():
        set_full_name(f"{first_name} {last_name}")

    use_effect(effect, dependencies=[first_name, last_name])

    return html.div(
        html.h1(full_name or "(nothing yet)"),
        html.input(
            {
                "value": first_name,
                "onChange": lambda event: set_first_name(event["target"]["value"]),
            }
        ),
        html.input(
            {
                "value": last_name,
                "onChange": lambda event: set_last_name(event["target"]["value"]),
            }
        ),
    )

# TODO

Remove the state variable and the Effect, and calculate it during render:

app.py Run 
@component
def form():
    first_name, set_first_name = use_state("Ada")
    last_name, set_last_name = use_state("Lovelace")
    # Right: calculated during rendering, so it is always in sync.
    full_name = f"{first_name} {last_name}"

    return html.div(
        html.h1(full_name),
        html.input(
            {
                "value": first_name,
                "onChange": lambda event: set_first_name(event["target"]["value"]),
            }
        ),
        html.input(
            {
                "value": last_name,
                "onChange": lambda event: set_last_name(event["target"]["value"]),
            }
        ),
    )

# TODO

The difference is measurable, and the first row of each is the part users actually see:

First paint Renders for two keystrokes Effect + stored state "(nothing yet)" 6 Derived during render "Ada Lovelace" 3

Verified in a Layout. The Effect version renders once with an empty name, sets state from the Effect, renders again — every keystroke costs two renders instead of one, and the very first paint is wrong. Nothing downstream can rescue that first frame, because it is a real render that a real client receives.

When something can be calculated from existing props or state, don't put it in state. Calculate it during render. Fewer state variables means less code, no way for two of them to drift apart, and half the renders. If this feels unfamiliar, Thinking in React covers what belongs in state.

How expensive is too expensive?

If you're not sure whether a calculation is costly enough to worry about, write it without caching first, then measure it: time the component body, or count how often it runs. In practice the work that is genuinely slow is usually obvious — parsing, sorting or filtering thousands of rows, regex over a large string, cryptographic hashes. String concatenation, len(), and a loop over a page's worth of items are not worth a cache, and a cache costs more than it saves when its dependency list is wrong.

docs.title: Caching expensive calculations
docs.text:
When a calculation genuinely is expensive, the answer is still not state plus an Effect — it is use_memo, which caches a value without adding a render:

app.py Run 
@component
def todo_list():
    filter_name, set_filter_name = use_state("all")
    new_todo, set_new_todo = use_state("")

    def visible_todos():
        # A real filter over a real dataset. It records every run so the
        # effect of use_memo is countable.
        filter_runs.append(filter_name)
        if filter_name == "all":
            return todos
        if filter_name == "active":
            return [todo for todo in todos if not todo["completed"]]
        return [todo for todo in todos if todo["completed"]]

    shown = use_memo(visible_todos)

    return html.div(
        html.p(f"{len(shown)} of {len(todos)} shown (filter: {filter_name})"),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": todo["id"]}, todo["text"]) for todo in shown]),
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": lambda event: set_filter_name(
                    {"all": "active", "active": "completed", "completed": "all"}[
                        filter_name
                    ]
                )
            },
            "Change filter",
        ),
        html.input(
            {
                "placeholder": "new todo",
                "value": new_todo,
                "onChange": lambda event: set_new_todo(event["target"]["value"]),
            }
        ),
    )

# TODO

The filter records each run so the result is countable. Verified: after two keystrokes the component has rendered three times and the filter has run once; pressing Change filter adds a render and a second run. The value is recomputed exactly when the inputs it reads change, and never on a render that didn't change them.

Two properties worth knowing, both verified:

  • use_memo infers its dependencies the same way use_effect does — from the names the function reads. Pass dependencies=[] to pin a value forever, or dependencies=None to recompute on every render. See Use Memo.
  • It caches the value, not the render. The component body still runs on every render; ReactPy has no component-level memo, so a child re-runs whenever its parent does. use_memo saves the computation, never the render — see Render and Commit.

Mutating a value in place and "setting" it back defeats use_memo too, for the same reason it defeats use_state: the new value compares equal to the old one. Build a new object instead (Updating Arrays in State).

docs.title: Resetting all state when a prop changes
docs.text:
A profile page holds a comment draft. When the user navigates to a different profile, the draft should not follow them:

app.py Run 
@component
def profile(user_id):
    # Any state declared here is thrown away whenever the key changes, along
    # with the state of every component below it. No Effect needed.
    comment, set_comment = use_state("")

    return html.div(
        html.h2(f"profile {user_id}"),
        html.textarea(
            {
                "value": comment,
                "placeholder": "leave a comment",
                "onChange": lambda event: set_comment(event["target"]["value"]),
            }
        ),
        html.p(f"draft: {comment or '(empty)'}"),
    )


@component
def profile_page():
    user_id, set_user_id = use_state("ada")

    return html.div(
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": lambda event: set_user_id(
                    "grace" if user_id == "ada" else "ada"
                )
            },
            "Next profile",
        ),
        # The key is what makes ReactPy treat this as a different profile.
        profile(user_id, key=user_id),
    )

# TODO

Verified: type a draft, press Next profile, and the draft is empty on the new profile — in a single extra render.

Passing key=user_id tells ReactPy that a different user_id means a different component instance. It tears down profile() and everything below it and builds them again, so all of their state starts fresh. One line, and it covers every piece of state in the whole subtree — no Effect, and no remembering to add one to each nested component.

The Effect version (set_comment("") in an Effect depending on user_id) is worse in three ways: the subtree renders once with the previous user's draft still in it, every nested component needs its own copy, and a piece of state added later silently fails to reset. See Preserving and Resetting State for the full mechanism.

key is spelled differently for elements and components

Here it is a keyword argument to the component call: profile(user_id, key=user_id). On an element it goes in the attribute dict instead: html.li({"key": 1}, ...). Put it in the wrong place and you get TypeError: Vdom.__call__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'key', or a literal key="..." attribute in the page.

docs.title: Adjusting some state when a prop changes
docs.text:
Sometimes you don't want to throw state away — just invalidate part of it when an input changes. A list keeps a selection, and a new items prop should clear it. React's advice is to call the setter during render, and that escape hatch does not work in ReactPy. Measured, the render-phase-setter version takes four renders and the client receives this sequence:

<root>                     items: [a,b,c]     selected: None
/children/0/children/1     items: [a,b,c]     selected: a
<root>                     items: [a,b,c,i4]  selected: a     <-- stale, and delivered
/children/0/children/1     items: [a,b,c,i4]  selected: None

React throws the discarded render away; ReactPy hands the model to the socket as soon as it exists, so the stale frame ships. Use a derived read instead. Store the value alongside what it belonged to, and let the read decide whether it is still valid:

app.py Run 
@component
def list_box(items):
    is_reverse, set_is_reverse = use_state(False)
    # One state value that remembers which list the choice belonged to. The
    # selection is *derived*: if the items changed, the old choice is not
    # valid for the new list, so it reads back as None. No Effect, no
    # intermediate render with a stale selection.
    chosen, set_chosen = use_state({"items": None, "value": None})
    selection = chosen["value"] if chosen["items"] == items else None

    shown = items[::-1] if is_reverse else items

    return html.div(
        html.p(f"items: {shown}  selected: {selection}"),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_is_reverse(not is_reverse)}, "Reverse"
        ),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_chosen({"items": items, "value": shown[0]})},
            "Select",
        ),
    )


@component
def app():
    items, set_items = use_state(["a", "b", "c"])

    return html.div(
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_items([*items, f"item {len(items) + 1}"])},
            "Add item",
        ),
        list_box(items),
    )

# TODO

Verified: Select costs one render and shows the selection; Add item costs one render and the selection is already gone in that same patch — three renders total, no stale frame.

The general shape is a guard on the read rather than a call to the setter:

is_valid = chosen["items"] == items
selection = chosen["value"] if is_valid else None

Do not set state from an Effect that depends on it

The reflexive alternative — an Effect calling set_selection(None) with dependencies=[items] — is not merely slow. When the value it sets is one it also reads, it is a loop, and ReactPy has no detector for one. Measured: an Effect that set a counter it depended on rendered 86 times before the probe gave up. If a component visibly spins, read what the Effect awaits, what it depends on, and what it sets.

docs.title: Sharing logic between event handlers
docs.text:
Two handlers should do the same thing on input. There is no reason for this to involve an Effect:

app.py Run 
@component
def shipping_form():
    shipping_city, set_shipping_city = use_state("")
    billing_city, set_billing_city = use_state("")

    def handle_shipping_change(event):
        city = event["target"]["value"]
        set_shipping_city(city)
        # Shared logic: just call the other setter. Handlers are ordinary
        # functions; there is nothing to schedule and nothing to re-sync.
        set_billing_city(city)

    return html.div(
        html.p(f"shipping: {shipping_city or '(empty)'}"),
        html.p(f"billing:  {billing_city or '(empty)'}"),
        html.input(
            {"value": shipping_city, "onChange": handle_shipping_change},
        ),
        html.input(
            {
                "value": billing_city,
                "onChange": lambda event: set_billing_city(event["target"]["value"]),
            }
        ),
    )

# TODO

Verified: type in the shipping field and the billing readout changes with it, in one render, because both setters were called from one handler.

Event handlers are ordinary functions. Call one from the other, extract the shared part into a plain function, or pass the other setter as a parameter. Whatever React's docs tell you here transfers unchanged, because none of it is rendering work.

docs.title: Sending a POST request
docs.text:
Submitting a form is an event, not a consequence of rendering. Do the work in the handler:

app.py Run 
@component
def signup():
    email, set_email = use_state("")
    status, set_status = use_state("idle")

    async def handle_submit(event):
        event.preventDefault()
        # Wrong: set a "pending" flag and let an Effect notice it. That costs
        # a state variable, a render, and a way to submit the same value twice.
        #     set_pending(True)
        #
        # Right: do the work from the handler. It runs once per submission.
        set_status("sending...")
        await send_email(email)
        set_status(f"sent to {email}")

    return html.div(
        html.p(status),
        html.form(
            {"onSubmit": handle_submit},
            html.input(
                {
                    "value": email,
                    "placeholder": "you@example.com",
                    "onChange": lambda event: set_email(event["target"]["value"]),
                }
            ),
            html.button({"type": "submit"}, "Sign up"),
        ),
    )

# TODO

Verified: fill the field, submit, and the transport recorded exactly one send — ['ada@example.com'].

The version to avoid is a flag plus an Effect: set_pending(True), and an Effect that watches pending. It costs a state variable, an extra render per submission, and — because Effects re-run on dependency changes and remounts — a way to send twice. event.preventDefault() stops the page navigating, and must appear literally in the handler's body, since ReactPy detects it by bytecode inspection (Creating VDOM Event Handlers).

docs.title: Notifying parent components about state changes
docs.text:
A child should tell its parent something happened. Pass a callback and call it from the child's event handler — this works exactly as it does in React:

app.py Run 
@component
def search_box(on_search):
    query, set_query = use_state("")

    def handle_submit(event):
        event.preventDefault()
        # Not an Effect: the search happens because the user submitted.
        on_search(query)

    return html.form(
        {"onSubmit": handle_submit},
        html.input(
            {
                "value": query,
                "placeholder": "search",
                "onChange": lambda event: set_query(event["target"]["value"]),
            }
        ),
        html.button({"type": "submit"}, "Search"),
    )


@component
def app():
    results, set_results = use_state("Type something and submit.")

    def handle_search(query):
        set_results(f"searching for {query!r}..." if query else "empty query")

    return html.div(html.p(results), search_box(handle_search))

# TODO

Verified: type ada, submit, and the parent's paragraph reads searching for 'ada'....

What you must not do is call the parent's function from an Effect that watches a value. Handlers run once per user action; Effects run once per dependency change, which includes renders the user never caused. There is also no use_imperative_handle for the reverse direction — pass data down as props and callbacks up as arguments (Sharing State Between Components).

docs.title: Chains of computations
docs.text:
When several values feed each other, keep the whole chain in render. Each intermediate is a local variable, not a state variable:

@component
def report(rows, currency):
    priced = [(*row, row[1] * RATES[currency]) for row in rows]
    total = sum(item[-1] for item in priced)
    heading = f"{currency.upper()}: {total:,.2f}"
    return html.div(html.h1(heading))

An Effect at any link in that chain means every upstream change costs an extra full render — and, as above, each of those renders is visible to the client. If one link is genuinely expensive, wrap that one in use_memo rather than putting the whole chain in state.

docs.title: Initializing the application
docs.text:
Code that should run once per process does not belong in a component at all — a component's Effect runs once per connection, and a server serves many connections:

# module level, or the ASGI app's startup: runs once
configure_logging()
POOL = create_pool()

Keep a dependencies=[] Effect for work that is genuinely per-connection, such as a subscription or a session-scoped task. Never guard a process-level side effect with my_component.started = True: the function object is module-scope, so the first visitor flips the flag for everyone (VDOM Mutations).

docs.title: Subscribing to an external store
docs.text:
Here is the case where the Effect is correct. The value does not live in ReactPy at all, so there is nothing to derive it from — ReactPy has to be told when it changes:

app.py Run 
@component
def clock_view():
    # The value is owned by `clock`, not by this component, so it cannot be
    # derived during render -- ReactPy has to be told when it changes.
    ticks, set_ticks = use_state(clock.get())

    def effect():
        # Subscribe, and hand back the unsubscribe. This is what an Effect
        # is for: the source of truth lives outside ReactPy.
        def on_change():
            set_ticks(clock.get())

        return clock.subscribe(on_change)

    use_effect(effect, dependencies=[])

    return html.div(html.h1(f"{ticks} ticks"))


@component
def app():
    watching, set_watching = use_state(True)

    return html.div(
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: clock.tick()}, "Tick"),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_watching(not watching)},
            "Stop watching" if watching else "Watch",
        ),
        *([] if not watching else [clock_view()]),
    )

# TODO

Verified: pressing Tick once shows 1 ticks; pressing Stop watching unmounts the view and leaves 0 listeners registered on the store.

Three things make this one legitimate where the others were not:

  1. The source of truth is outside ReactPy. Deriving would mean reading clock.get() during render, which has no way to know when to run again.
  2. The subscription needs a lifetime, and the clean-up is what returns the store to zero listeners.
  3. The state exists to trigger a render — that is its whole purpose.

This is also where use_async_effect earns its place, when the external system is an async stream rather than a callback. See Synchronizing with Effects for cancellation and the four-way dependency table.

docs.title: Fetching data, without the extra Effects
docs.text:
Fetching genuinely needs an Effect — the network is external. Everything you would otherwise stack on top of it does not. Store the response, and shape it in render:

app.py Run 
@component
def report_view(name):
    # Store the response *with the name it belongs to*, so a render for a new
    # report cannot display the old one's rows. The empty read is the
    # "loading" state -- derived, not a second state variable.
    loaded, set_loaded = use_state({"name": None, "data": {}})

    async def load():
        data = await catalog.fetch(name)
        set_loaded({"name": name, "data": data})

    use_async_effect(load, dependencies=[name])

    raw = loaded["data"] if loaded["name"] == name else {}

    if not raw:
        return html.p("loading...")

    # Right: the shape the page needs is computed here, from the data that
    # arrived. There is no second state variable to keep in step, so there is
    # nothing for an Effect to synchronise.
    rows = [{"label": key.title(), "value": value} for key, value in raw.items()]
    total = sum(row["value"] for row in rows)
    lines = [
        html.li({"key": row["label"]}, f"{row['label']}: {row['value']}")
        for row in rows
    ]

    return html.div(
        html.h2(f"{name}: {total} total"),
        html.ul(lines),
    )


@component
def app():
    name, set_name = use_state("orders")

    return html.div(
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": lambda event: set_name(
                    "users" if name == "orders" else "orders"
                )
            },
            "Toggle report",
        ),
        # No `key` here on purpose: the derived read in report_view is what
        # keeps the old report off the screen, so nothing has to be remounted.
        report_view(name),
    )

# TODO

Verified: the Effect stores the raw response; the labels, the per-row formatting, and the total are computed during render. One request per report name (['orders', 'users']), and no rows or total state variables that could fall out of step with the response.

The example carries one more lesson in its state shape. It stores the response together with the name that produced it and derives the read:

raw = loaded["data"] if loaded["name"] == name else {}

Storing the response alone looks fine and is wrong: switch from orders to users and the component re-renders immediately, before the new response arrives, so the client receives users: 55 total above the orders rows — 55 being orders' total. Measured, and the derived read above is what fixes it, without remounting the component.

The anti-pattern is a second Effect that watches the response and sets three more state variables from it. Each of those is a value you can calculate, and each adds a render in which the page is half-updated.

Because ReactPy already runs on the server, there is usually a better option than fetching in the child at all: fetch in a parent during render, or at startup, and pass the result down as a prop. Then the child has no Effect and no loading state, and the response is shared rather than re-requested. Keep the Effect for data that depends on something only the connection knows, like use_location.

docs.title: How to tell whether an Effect is necessary
docs.text:
The Effect... Verdict reads state or props and sets other state unnecessary — compute it during render caches a calculation unnecessary — use_memo resets state when a prop changes unnecessary — pass a key invalidates state when a prop changes unnecessary — derive the read from what it belonged to runs logic shared by two handlers unnecessary — call a function reacts to a user action unnecessary — put it in the event handler calls a parent's callback when a value changes unnecessary — call it from the handler subscribes to a queue, socket, or store necessary, with a clean-up starts async work that outlives the render necessary, with use_async_effect starts per-connection work on mount necessary, with dependencies=[]

If you cannot name what the Effect is synchronizing with, it is probably doing a render's job.

Two failure modes that cost hours

  • An Effect that sets state it depends on loops silently. ReactPy has no loop detector. Measured: 86 renders and counting before the probe stopped.
  • Hooks do not work inside an effect body. use_context, use_state, and friends all raise RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout? — effects run in their own task, with no hook on the stack. Read what you need during render and let the closure carry it in. The traceback appears only in the server log; the page just goes quiet.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
• An Effect runs after a render. If the work could happen during the render, it should.
  • Values calculated from props or state are not state. Compute them; do not store and re-sync them. Measured: the Effect version costs twice the renders and ships a wrong first frame.
  • use_memo caches expensive calculations without adding a render — but it caches values, not component renders.
  • Reset state with a key, not with an Effect.
  • ReactPy cannot use React's render-phase setter trick: the stale patch reaches the client. Derive the value instead.
  • Sharing logic between handlers, notifying a parent, and submitting a form are all handler work.
  • Subscriptions and async streams are the real use for Effects — with a clean-up, always.

docs.text:

  • Choosing the State Structure — avoid redundant state in the first place
  • Preserving and Resetting State — resetting with key
  • Use Memo and Use Callback
  • Separating Events from Effects — the remaining case where reading fresh state matters

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Components are one of the core concepts of ReactPy. They are the foundation upon which you build user interfaces (UI), which makes them the perfect place to start your ReactPy journey!

You will learn

  • What a component is
  • What role components play in a ReactPy application
  • How to write your first ReactPy component

docs.title: Components: UI building blocks
docs.text:
On the Web, HTML lets us create rich structured documents with its built-in set of tags like <h1> and <li>:

<article>
    <h1>My First Component</h1>
    <ol>
        <li>Components: UI Building Blocks</li>
        <li>Defining a Component</li>
        <li>Using a Component</li>
    </ol>
</article>

This markup represents this article <article>, its heading <h1>, and an (abbreviated) table of contents as an ordered list <ol>. Markup like this, combined with CSS for style, and Python for interactivity, lies behind every sidebar, avatar, modal, dropdown—every piece of UI you see on the Web.

ReactPy lets you combine your markup, CSS, and Python into custom "components", reusable UI elements for your app. The table of contents code you saw above could be turned into a table_of_contents() component you could render on every page. Under the hood, it still uses the same HTML tags like html.article, html.h1, etc.

Just like with HTML tags, you can compose, order and nest components to design whole pages. For example, the documentation page you're reading is made out of ReactPy components:

html.div(
    html.header(
        search_bar(),
        html.a({"href": "/docs"}, "Docs"),
    ),
    sidebar(),
    html.main(
        table_of_contents(),
        documentation_text(),
    ),
)

As your project grows, you will notice that many of your designs can be composed by reusing components you already wrote, speeding up your development. Our table of contents above could be added to any screen with table_of_contents()! You can even jumpstart your project with components shared by the community.

docs.title: Defining a component
docs.text:
Traditionally when creating web pages, web developers marked up their content and then added interaction by sprinkling on some JavaScript. This worked great when interaction was a nice-to-have on the web. Now it is expected for many sites and all apps. ReactPy puts interactivity first while still using the same technology: a ReactPy component is a Python function that you can sprinkle with markup. Here's what that looks like:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def profile():
    return html.img(
        {"src": "https://i.imgur.com/MK3eW3Am.jpg", "alt": "Katherine Johnson"}
    )

img {
    height: 200px;
}

# TODO

And here's how to build a component:

docs.title: Step 1: Import what you need
docs.text:
Every component needs the @component decorator and the html tag constructor:

from reactpy import component, html

Unlike ReactJS, there is no export statement. To use a component from another file you import it like any other Python object, which you will learn about in Importing and Exporting Components.

docs.title: Step 2: Define the function
docs.text:
With def profile(): you define a Python function with the name profile. The @component decorator turns that function into something ReactPy can render.

Pitfall

ReactPy components are ordinary Python functions, so follow Python's naming conventions and write them in snake_case.

The ReactJS rule that "component names must start with a capital letter" does not apply. ReactJS needs that rule to tell components apart from HTML tags in its markup syntax. ReactPy has no markup syntax: HTML tags are reached through html. and components are called directly, so the difference is already unambiguous.

docs.title: Step 3: Add markup
docs.text:
The component returns an html.img element with src and alt attributes. There is no JSX or PSX in ReactPy — a tag is a normal Python call whose first argument is a dictionary of attributes and whose remaining arguments are its children.

Return statements can be written all on one line when the element is short:

return html.h1("Amazing scientists")

For anything longer, wrap the element in parentheses rather than relying on a backslash continuation:

return html.img(
    {"src": "https://i.imgur.com/MK3eW3As.jpg", "alt": "Katherine Johnson"}
)

docs.title: Using a component
docs.text:
Now that you've defined your profile component, you can nest it inside other components. For example, you can define a gallery component that uses multiple profile components:

app.pystyles.css Run 
@component
def profile():
    return html.img(
        {"src": "https://i.imgur.com/MK3eW3As.jpg", "alt": "Katherine Johnson"}
    )


@component
def gallery():
    return html.section(
        html.h1("Amazing scientists"),
        profile(),
        profile(),
        profile(),
    )

img {
    margin: 0 10px 10px 0;
    height: 90px;
}

# TODO

docs.title: What the browser sees
docs.text:
Notice the difference in how the two kinds of calls are made:

  • html.section(...) and html.h1(...) are attributes on the html object, so ReactPy knows they are HTML tags.
  • profile() is a function you wrote and decorated with @component, so ReactPy knows it is a component.

And profile contains even more HTML: html.img. In the end, this is what the browser sees:

<section>
    <h1>Amazing scientists</h1>
    <img src="https://i.imgur.com/MK3eW3As.jpg" alt="Katherine Johnson" />
    <img src="https://i.imgur.com/MK3eW3As.jpg" alt="Katherine Johnson" />
    <img src="https://i.imgur.com/MK3eW3As.jpg" alt="Katherine Johnson" />
</section>

docs.title: Nesting and organizing components
docs.text:
Components are regular Python functions, so you can keep multiple components in the same file. This is convenient when components are relatively small or tightly related to each other. If this file gets crowded, you can always move profile to a separate file. You will learn how to do this shortly on the page about imports.

Because the profile components are rendered inside gallery—even several times!—we can say that gallery is a parent component, rendering each profile as a "child". This is part of the magic of ReactPy: you can define a component once, and then use it in as many places and as many times as you like.

Pitfall

Components can render other components, but you must never nest their definitions:

from reactpy import component, html


# Do not do this: a component defined inside another component.
@component
def gallery():
    @component
    def profile():
        return html.img({"src": "https://i.imgur.com/MK3eW3As.jpg"})

    return html.section(
        html.h1("Amazing scientists"),
        profile(),
        profile(),
        profile(),
    )

Instead, define every component at the top level of your module:

@component
def profile():
    return html.img(
        {"src": "https://i.imgur.com/MK3eW3As.jpg", "alt": "Katherine Johnson"}
    )


@component
def gallery():
    return html.section(
        html.h1("Amazing scientists"),
        profile(),
        profile(),
        profile(),
    )

Here is why. When ReactPy re-renders gallery, it matches each child against the child from the previous render by the identity of its function. A component defined inside another function is a brand new function object every time the parent runs, so ReactPy concludes the old child is gone: it unmounts the previous profile, throws away its state and Effects, and mounts a fresh one. Rendering still looks correct, which makes this bug easy to miss and hard to trace.

When a child component needs some data from a parent, pass it by props instead of nesting definitions.

Deep Dive

docs.title: Components all the way down
docs.text:
Your ReactPy application begins at a "root" component. This is the component you hand to an executor — for example the hello_world component passed to ReactPy in Creating a Standalone React App.

Most ReactPy apps use components all the way down. This means that you won't only use components for reusable pieces like buttons, but also for larger pieces like sidebars, lists, and ultimately, complete pages! Components are a handy way to organize UI code and markup, even if some of them are only used once.

Because your components run on the server, ReactPy can also render them into the initial HTML response instead of waiting for a browser to do the work. See Add React to an Existing Project to render components inside pages you already have.

Still, many websites only use ReactPy to add interactivity to existing HTML pages. They have many root components instead of a single one for the entire page. You can use as much—or as little—ReactPy as you need.

docs.title: Recap
docs.text:
You've just gotten your first taste of ReactPy! Let's recap some key points.

  • ReactPy lets you create components, reusable UI elements for your app.
  • In a ReactPy app, every piece of UI is a component.

  • ReactPy components are regular Python functions except:

    1. They are decorated with @component.
    2. They return elements built with html.

  • Attributes are a dict, children are the remaining arguments, and both are ordinary Python — which means for loops, if statements, and variables work exactly as you would expect.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: Check out Importing and Exporting Components to organize components across files, or jump straight to Passing Props to a Component to make yours configurable.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
mountReactPy is the browser-side entry point: one exported function, one websocket, no build step. Everything else in the browser is the server's business. 

import { mountReactPy } from "/reactpy/static/index.js";

mountReactPy({
  mountElement: document.getElementById("app"),
  pathPrefix: "/reactpy/",
  componentPath: "main.counter/",
});

The executors emit this call for you — see ReactPy and ReactPyMiddleware. You need to write it yourself only when you serve the document from your own route, or when the defaults do not fit.

docs.title: mountReactPy(options)
docs.text:
import { mountReactPy } from "{pathPrefix}static/index.js";

The bundle is served by ReactPy itself, under {pathPrefix}static/, alongside two chunks it imports by relative path. There is nothing to install and nothing to build: it is preact and the client, pre-bundled.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
A single object.

  • mountElement: The DOM node to render into. Not optional in effect — passing null, which is what getElementById returns for a missing id, dies with TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading '__k') before anything is logged.

  • pathPrefix: string. Must start and end with /. Concatenated verbatim with componentPath, so a missing slash on either side produces a URL that is wrong rather than invalid — which is worse, because nothing rejects it. A value with no leading slash ("reactpy/") or no pathPrefix at all may fail early with TypeError: Failed to construct 'URL': Invalid URL, but only when the page's host includes a port. See The URL is built by concatenation.

  • componentPath: string, optional. The dotted path of the root component, with a trailing slash: "main.counter/". ReactPyMiddleware requires it. ReactPy takes the opposite view and requires it be omitted — see The executors route differently.

  • reconnectInterval: number of ms. 750.

  • reconnectMaxInterval: number of ms. 60000.

  • reconnectMaxRetries: number. 150.

  • reconnectBackoffMultiplier: number. 1.25.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
Nothing.

There is no unmountReactPy

The bundle exports exactly one name. Verified by importing it and listing the keys: mountReactPy, nothing else. mountReactPy returns nothing and takes no callback, so you get no handle to keep and no supported way to stop a component.

Removing the mount element from the DOM does not stop it either. The subtree is detached, not unmounted: mountReactPy calls preact's render(...) into the node and never the matching unmount. Verified in a browser — after removing the node, a click dispatched into the detached subtree still reached the server and incremented its state, and the websocket stayed OPEN in both directions. The component keeps reconciling into an orphan nobody can see.

The only clean teardown is to navigate or reload. If you are building a single-page app that swaps components on the client, the closest available tool is onMessage's return value, which unsubscribes a handler — that stops the client applying updates, but leaves the socket and the server's layout alive.

Reconnect options reject zero, not just wrong types

The defaults are applied with JavaScript's ||, not ??, so any falsy value is replaced by the default. Passing reconnectMaxRetries: 0 to mean "do not retry" gets you the default 150 instead, and reconnectInterval: 0 gets you 750 ms.

To actually stop retrying, pass a negative reconnectMaxRetries. The retry test is retries >= maxRetries and negatives survive ||, so reconnectMaxRetries: -1 connects once and then gives up — measured at exactly one attempt, by running the client's own createReconnectingWebSocket against a stub socket.

The retry counter is also not what it appears to be. It counts consecutive failures, because a successful open resets it to zero along with the backoff interval. Measured against a stub that accepts each connection and closes it 2 ms later, reconnectMaxRetries: 2 with a 1 ms interval produced 342 attempts in 1.5 s: every reconnect succeeds, so the counter never reaches the limit. Only attempts that fail to open at all accumulate.

Which leads to the sharper edge: a handshake that is refused is never retried at all. If the socket never reaches OPEN, the close handler logs Failed to connect! and returns without scheduling anything. So ReactPyMiddleware answering 403 — a wrong componentPath, a wrong path_prefix — gives you one attempt, one line in the console, and a permanently empty element. Nothing recovers without a reload. Retries exist only for connections that opened and then dropped.

docs.title: What mountReactPy does
docs.text:
mountReactPy does five things (static/index.js):

  1. Picks the websocket scheme from the page: wss: under https:, otherwise ws:.
  2. Builds the URL as scheme // host + pathPrefix + componentPath, then appends path=window.location.pathname and, only if the page has a query string, qs=window.location.search.
  3. Sets jsModulesPath to origin + pathPrefix + "modules/", the base from which JavaScript modules named by an element's importSource are imported.
  4. Constructs the client, which wires up a reconnecting websocket.
  5. Renders the layout into mountElement.

Steps 2 and 3 are the only places the browser's own URL is read. Once the socket is open, the server's view of the URL is whatever those two parameters said — see Use Location.

docs.title: The URL is built by concatenation
docs.text:
Nothing inserts a slash for you, so both halves have to arrive correctly formed. The four ways to get it wrong, each verified from a page with the resulting socket URL (against ReactPyMiddleware on a host with a port):

pathPrefix componentPath Socket path Result "/reactpy/" "main.counter/" /reactpy/main.counter/ Connects. "/reactpy" "main.counter/" /reactpymain.counter/ 403, then Failed to connect! "/reactpy/" "main.counter" /reactpy/main.counter 403, then Failed to connect! "/reactpy/" omitted /reactpy/ 403, then Failed to connect!

ReactPyMiddleware matches the websocket path against ^{path_prefix}(?P<dotted_path>[a-zA-Z0-9_.]+)/$. Rows two through four fail that pattern, so they fall through to your own ASGI app, which answers 403.

Read the browser's own error line, not ReactPy's. The client emits a bare Failed to connect!; the URL that caused it is on the line above, in the browser's message, without the [ReactPy] prefix.

The || defaults and the URL constructor make this host-dependent

Two of these fail earlier than the table suggests, and only sometimes. new URL(...) throws TypeError: Failed to construct 'URL': Invalid URL for a missing or slashless pathPrefix — but only when the host carries a port, because ws://example.comreactpy/main.counter/ parses happily as host example.comreactpy. Verified with Node's URL, the same implementation Chrome uses:

Host pathPrefix Outcome 127.0.0.1:8842 "" TypeError: Invalid URL 127.0.0.1:8842 "reactpy/" TypeError: Invalid URL example.com "" Connects to host example.commain.counter example.com "reactpy/" Connects to host example.comreactpy

So the mistake that fails loudly in development fails silently in production, sending the socket to a hostname that does not exist. Check the host, not just the path.

docs.title: The executors route differently
docs.text:
The last table row is not a universal truth, and this is where the two executors part company. ReactPy — the standalone app — overrides the matcher:

def match_dispatch_path(self, scope):
    """Method override to remove `dotted_path` from the dispatcher URL."""
    return str(scope["path"]) == self.dispatcher_path

So the two want opposite things:

componentPath Unmatched dotted path ReactPyMiddleware required, with trailing slash Falls through to your app (with Starlette's websocket handler, a 403 handshake rejection) ReactPy must be omitted — the bare {pathPrefix} is the route socket error; the server logs NotImplementedError (see below)

Verified against both executors on the same build: the middleware accepts /reactpy/main.counter/ and refuses /reactpy/; the standalone app does exactly the reverse. A mount snippet copied from one executor to the other therefore produces a socket that never opens.

The standalone rejection does not read like a normal exception. executors/asgi/standalone.py, ReactPyApp.__call__ builds msg as a tuple of a %-format template and its arguments and raises NotImplementedError(msg) without ever formatting it, so the server logs it verbatim — the placeholders survive and the path is appended:

NotImplementedError: ("ReactPy app received unsupported request of type '%s' at path '%s'", 'websocket', '/reactpy//')

Do not search the log for ...type 'websocket'; search for unsupported request of type. The same tuple is written by _logger.warning immediately before the raise.

docs.title: The socket does not open immediately
docs.text:
Constructing the client does not connect. The websocket waits on a ready promise, and that promise is resolved by the first onMessage registration — nothing else in the codebase resolves it. The layout registers its handler from an effect, so the client connects only after that effect runs, which is why [ReactPy] Starting client... always precedes Connected! and never follows it.

Because onMessage is the sole resolver, a run where the layout's effect never fires produces a fourth console state: no Starting client..., no socket attempt, and no error. Treat that as "the bundle ran but the component never mounted" rather than a network problem — the other four messages below are all post-connect.

Two consequences of the gating:

  • Reconnection refreshes path and qs from the live page on every attempt, but never re-reads componentPath — that was baked into the URL at mount time.
  • Messages sent before the socket reports OPEN are buffered rather than dropped, and flushed on the next open. They survive a reconnect — but once retries are exhausted the buffer is never drained.

Note that path and qs are query parameters, not path segments. The full form is ws://127.0.0.1:8000/reactpy/main.counter/?path=%2F&qs=%3Ftab%3D1, and the server reads them with strict_parsing=True. When building a test client by hand, copy a real frame from the browser rather than assembling one from the tables on this page.

docs.title: The import map
docs.text:
For a server-rendered component, no import map is needed. The bundle imports its own two chunks by relative path and has preact inlined, so nothing it loads statically is a bare specifier. Verified: a page with no map at all mounted, connected, and the server never received a single request for preact.js.

The map becomes load-bearing only when the model contains importSource and the resolved module does not export its own bind. Rendering such an element goes through loadImportSource, which uses the module's bind when it is a function and only otherwise calls infer_bind_from_environment() — the function that runs await import("react") and await import("react-dom/client"). Those are dynamic imports, which are exactly what an import map resolves. If they succeed, real React renders the subtree; if they fail, the client falls back to its own preact bindings and says so:

ReactPy will render JavaScript components using internal bindings for 'react'.

Note the level and the prefix: that line is console.debug with no [ReactPy] prefix, so it is invisible in a console filtered to warnings, and it is not caught by filtering on [ReactPy].

The executors' bootstrap injects a map only if none is present — and the check is keyed on one specific id:

if (!document.querySelector("#reactpy-importmap")) { /* inject ReactPy's map */ }

The id is the trigger, not the content. Verified across three pages, all served through the same executor bootstrap:

Page ReactPy injects What you see No map Yes, as <script type="importmap" id="reactpy-importmap"> ReactPy did not detect a suitable JavaScript import map. Falling back to ReactPy's internal framework (Preact). Your own map, any other id Yes — a second map appears, alongside yours The same did not detect line, plus the browser's own An import map rule for specifier 'react' was removed, as it conflicted with an existing rule. Your own map with id="reactpy-importmap" No Nothing at all.

The two messages have different authors, which matters when you search a minified bundle. The did not detect line is written by the Python side of the bootstrap — executors/utils.py, server_side_component_html emits it inside the inline <script> it generates, so it is in the served HTML, not in the bundle. The internal bindings for 'react' line comes from the client — infer_bind_from_environment in bind.tsx, reached from loadImportSource in vdom.tsx. Both are unprefixed console.debug, so neither shows up under a [ReactPy] filter.

To control resolution yourself, use that exact id. Two maps is worse than untidy: the browser keeps the first rule it sees for a specifier and discards the later one, so with two maps the winner is decided by document order — which is why the warning above names a rule being removed.

The map ReactPy writes maps all four React specifiers onto its own preact files under {pathPrefix}static/. Save the page and the app under those exact names — the dotted path in componentPath is a Python module path, and main.counter only resolves when this file is called main.py:

page.htmlmain.py Run 
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>Counter</title>
    <script type="importmap" id="reactpy-importmap">
      {
        "imports": {
          "react": "/reactpy/static/preact.js",
          "react-dom": "/reactpy/static/preact-dom.js",
          "react-dom/client": "/reactpy/static/preact-dom.js",
          "react/jsx-runtime": "/reactpy/static/preact-jsx-runtime.js"
        }
      }
    </script>
  </head>
  <body>
    <div id="app"></div>
    <script type="module" crossorigin="anonymous">
      import { mountReactPy } from "/reactpy/static/index.js";

      mountReactPy({
        mountElement: document.getElementById("app"),
        pathPrefix: "/reactpy/",
        componentPath: "main.counter/",
      });
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

from pathlib import Path

from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.responses import FileResponse
from starlette.routing import Route

from reactpy import component, html, use_state
from reactpy.executors.asgi import ReactPyMiddleware


@component
def counter():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    def increment(_event):
        set_count(count + 1)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"count is {count}"),
        html.button({"onClick": increment}, "Add"),
    )


async def home(request):
    return FileResponse(Path(__file__).parent / "page.html")


my_app = ReactPyMiddleware(
    Starlette(routes=[Route("/", home)]),
    root_components=["main.counter"],
)

# TODO

Serve it with uvicorn main:my_app. Verified in a browser: the counter rendered and logged [ReactPy] Connected!, and no request for preact.js reached the server — confirming the client never consulted the map.

docs.title: The client object
docs.text:
mountReactPy builds on two classes from the @reactpy/client source package. Neither is reachable from a page — the shipped bundle exports mountReactPy and nothing else — but you meet them reading the bundle, and they are what a custom binding's sendMessage and onMessage come from.

BaseReactPyClient is the transport-independent half:

Member Purpose onMessage(type, handler) Register a handler for a message type. Returns an unsubscribe function. handleIncoming(message) Dispatch to the handlers for message.type. ready Promise, resolved by the first onMessage call. Gates the connection.

Messages with no type, or with one nobody registered for, are logged and dropped — the connection is never closed over a bad message:

Received message without type {…}
Received message without handler {…}

ReactPyClient adds the websocket, plus sendMessage(message) and loadModule(name). They are not peers. sendMessage is handed to a JavaScript binding as its way to talk back; loadModule is called for the binding, by ReactPy, to pull in a web module named by an importSource whose sourceType is "NAME" — it resolves against jsModulesPath, which is what the server's web modules directory is mounted under.

docs.title: The console
docs.text:
Every message ReactPy writes is prefixed [ReactPy], so filtering the console by that string shows the whole story of a mount. The set is finite:

Message Meaning Starting client... The layout registered its handler; a connection attempt is about to start. Connected! The handshake completed. Resets the retry counter and the backoff interval. Failed to connect! The socket closed without ever having opened. Usually a routing miss — see The URL is built by concatenation. Disconnected! The socket closed after at least one successful open. Reconnecting in 0.7500 seconds... A retry is scheduled. The number is the current backoff interval. Connection max retries exhausted! Giving up. The page needs a reload; nothing recovers after this. did not detect a suitable JavaScript import map... <script type="importmap" id="reactpy-importmap"> was absent. Informational — see The import map.

Failed to connect! and Disconnected! are distinguished by whether the socket ever opened, which makes them useful as a diagnosis: the first means the server never routed the request, the second means it did and then the link dropped. Both are logged at console.info level, so a console set to warnings-only shows nothing at all — check the level before concluding the client is silent.

docs.title: A hand-written mount
docs.text:
Nothing is required beyond an element and the call. Both files below were run to produce the [ReactPy] Connected! and the incremented counter quoted on this page.

main.py Run 
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.responses import HTMLResponse
from starlette.routing import Route

from reactpy import component, html, use_state
from reactpy.executors.asgi import ReactPyMiddleware

PATH_PREFIX = "/reactpy/"


@component
def counter():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    def increment(_event):
        set_count(count + 1)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"count is {count}"),
        html.button({"onClick": increment}, "Add"),
    )


async def home(request):
    # pathPrefix and the bundle's URL both have to agree with the server's,
    # so both are interpolated from one value rather than typed twice.
    return HTMLResponse(
        f"""<!doctype html>
        <html>
          <body>
            <div id="app"></div>
            <script type="module" crossorigin="anonymous">
              import {{ mountReactPy }} from "{PATH_PREFIX}static/index.js";

              mountReactPy({{
                mountElement: document.getElementById("app"),
                pathPrefix: "{PATH_PREFIX}",
                componentPath: "main.counter/",
              }});
            </script>
          </body>
        </html>"""
    )


my_app = ReactPyMiddleware(
    Starlette(routes=[Route("/", home)]),
    root_components=["main.counter"],
)

# TODO

The component is registered with root_components, and the componentPath in the page — "main.counter/" — is that dotted path with a slash appended.

The 404 in the console is usually not yours

A page like this logs one Failed to load resource: 404 on every load. It is /favicon.ico, which no browser should be told about by a component framework. Verified: it appears with everything else working. Ignore it; a second 404 naming a /reactpy/... path means the bundle could not be fetched, which does mean the mount will not happen.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text: Symptom Cause TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading '__k') mountElement is None. The id does not exist, or the script ran before the element was parsed. TypeError: Failed to construct 'URL': Invalid URL pathPrefix missing, or missing a leading or trailing slash. No request is ever made. mountReactPy() throws Cannot read properties of undefined No options object at all. Failed to connect!, nothing rendered The socket URL did not match the server's route. Read the URL in the browser's own error line. [ReactPy] Connected!, empty element, nothing in the browser console The component path is unknown to the server. The failure is server-side: RuntimeError: Attempting to use an unregistered root component <path>. Check the server log, not the browser. Renders once, never updates Handlers are not firing — usually a snake_case event name such as on_click. See Responding to Events. Component vanishes when you remove it from the DOM, socket still open Expected. There is no unmount that closes the socket. Two import maps in the document, React warnings about a removed rule Your map does not use id="reactpy-importmap".
