docs.text:
• Protocol Structure — what travels over the socket this function opens.
  • ReactPy and ReactPyMiddleware — the executors that generate this call.
  • Jinja — emitting mounts from templates, including {% pyscript_component %} for running Python in the page.
  • Use Location — reading back the path and qs the client sends.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Every element a ReactPy component renders is a plain dict with a fixed set of keys, and the attributes you pass to a tag end up on the DOM node nearly untouched. This page is the reference for what you may put in there — and for the handful of places ReactPy behaves differently from React. 

{
    "tagName": "div",
    "children": [...],
    "attributes": {...},
    "eventHandlers": {...},
    "inlineJavaScript": {...},
    "importSource": {...},
}

Only "tagName" is required. You almost never write this by hand — reactpy.html builds it for you — but everything below is what a tag call can carry.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
An attribute is any key/value pair in the first argument to a tag:

html.input({"type": "search", "placeholder": "Filter", "autoFocus": True})

ReactPy forwards the name and the value to the browser verbatim. There is no translation layer, which is the main difference from React, where JSX rewrites props before they reach the DOM.

The value must be JSON-serializable, because the model is sent to the browser as JSON. Nothing stops you from putting something else in there: with debug mode off, the value is accepted at the tag call and only fails when the layout tries to send the model, deep inside the connection:

TypeError: Type is not JSON serializable: object

Run with REACTPY_DEBUG=1 and the same mistake fails at the tag call, where you can see which element caused it:

TypeError: Object of type object is not JSON serializable

Write the name the browser expects

Attribute names are not validated against any allow-list. If the browser understands an attribute, ReactPy delivers it — including data-*, aria-*, and attributes ReactPy has never heard of:

html.div({"aria-live": "polite", "data-row-id": 7, "spellcheck": False})

docs.title: class and className
docs.text:
Both work, and both produce class="..." in the DOM:

html.div({"class": "one two"}, "...")
html.div({"className": "one two"}, "...")

There is no JSX in Python, so nothing forces you toward className. Pick one and stay consistent — class reads better beside the HTML it mirrors, className is familiar to anyone arriving from React.

docs.title: for and htmlFor
docs.text: Both work on <label>, and both produce for="...". Prefer for; htmlFor exists only for readers who expect it.

docs.title: style
docs.text:
Pass a dict. Keys may be camelCase or kebab-case — both are accepted, and both reach the browser in a form it understands:

html.div(
    {
        "style": {
            "backgroundColor": "rgb(255, 0, 0)",  # camelCase
            "font-size": "20px",  # kebab-case
        }
    }
)

Always write the unit as part of the string

Do not rely on a bare number being given a unit. React appends px to numeric style values; ReactPy's executors do not agree with each other on this. Measured in Chrome, the same component rendered through each executor:

style value ReactPy / ReactPyMiddleware ReactPyCsr {"fontSize": "30px"} font-size: 30px font-size: 30px {"font-size": "30px"} font-size: 30px font-size: 30px {"fontSize": 30} font-size: 30px nothing at all {"fontSize": "30"} nothing nothing {"zIndex": 5} z-index: 5 z-index: 5 {"opacity": 0.5} opacity: 0.5 opacity: 0.5

A number that needs a unit is dropped in silence — no warning, no log line, and the layout model shows the value untouched, so it is nowhere to be found by reading the server side. Unitless properties like z-index and opacity are the exception: a number is already a valid value there.

The portable rule: put units in the string, everywhere.

{"style": {"font-size": 20}}  # works by accident in some executors
{"style": {"font-size": "20px"}}  # works everywhere

docs.title: All together
docs.text:
A table of rows is where most of these rules meet at once — key in attributes, data-* and aria-* passed straight through, and units inside style strings:

app.py Run 
ROWS = [
    {"id": 1, "name": "Dana", "role": "admin", "active": True},
    {"id": 2, "name": "Sam", "role": "viewer", "active": False},
]


@component
def row(person):
    # `key` lives in attributes, `data-*` and `aria-*` are forwarded verbatim,
    # and `class` works exactly like `className`. Style values carry their own
    # units, because a bare number is not portable across executors.
    return html.tr(
        {
            "key": person["id"],
            "class": "is-active" if person["active"] else "is-inactive",
            "data-role": person["role"],
            "aria-label": f"{person['name']}, {person['role']}",
            "style": {"opacity": "1" if person["active"] else "0.55"},
        },
        html.td(person["name"]),
        html.td(person["role"]),
        html.td(
            {"style": {"text-align": "right", "font-variant-numeric": "tabular-nums"}},
            "yes" if person["active"] else "no",
        ),
    )


@component
def people_table():
    return html.table(
        None,
        html.thead(
            html.tr(
                None,
                html.th("Name"),
                html.th("Role"),
                html.th({"scope": "col"}, "Active"),
            )
        ),
        # A list of children: every row needs a key or state will follow the
        # row's position rather than the person.
        html.tbody(None, [row(person) for person in ROWS]),
    )

# TODO

Rendering this through Layout gives rows whose attributes are exactly what was written:

{
    "tagName": "tr",
    "attributes": {
        "key": 1,
        "class": "is-active",
        "data-role": "admin",
        "aria-label": "Dana, admin",
        "style": {"opacity": "1"},
    },
    "children": [...],
}

Nothing was renamed, and nothing was dropped. In the DOM the row arrives as:

<tr data-role="admin" aria-label="Dana, admin" class="is-active" style="opacity: 1;">

The one attribute that does not reach the DOM is key itself: ReactPy and ReactPyMiddleware consume it for reconciliation and never set it on the element. ReactPyCsr does leak it, so a key="1" attribute shows up in the page — harmless, but do not rely on the attribute being absent or present. Every other name you write arrives as written.

docs.title: Booleans and numbers
docs.text:
Values are serialized as JSON and coerced by the browser:

You write The browser receives {"hidden": True} hidden="" — present, therefore true {"hidden": False} no attribute at all {"readonly": True} readonly="true" {"data-x": "1"} data-x="1", readable as element.dataset.x {"tabindex": 2} tabindex="2"

React's attribute quirks do not carry over. There is no htmlFor requirement, no auto-px, and no special-casing of value versus defaultValue — what you write is what arrives.

docs.title: dangerouslySetInnerHTML
docs.text:
Injects a raw HTML string, exactly as in React:

html.div({"dangerouslySetInnerHTML": {"__html": "<b>bold</b>"}})

The key is the plain string "dangerouslySetInnerHTML" — not a class to import — and its only field is "__html".

This is the XSS hole

ReactPy does nothing to sanitize the string. Never put user input in it.

A dangerouslySetInnerHTML attribute also suppresses children. Nothing enforces the combination — no error, no warning, at the tag call or at render time — so the children you passed are simply never displayed. Verified in the browser: for html.div({"dangerouslySetInnerHTML": {"__html": "<b>RAW</b>"}}, "CHILDTEXT") the server sends both the attribute and "children": ["CHILDTEXT"], and the rendered element contains only <b>RAW</b>. Pass the children or the raw HTML, never both, because the silent one is your children.

docs.title: Children
docs.text:
Children are the arguments that follow the attribute dict. ReactPy accepts a wide range of types and normalizes each one:

Child Becomes str a text node, verbatim int / float its str(), so 7 renders as "7" None dropped — renders nothing True / False the literal text True / False list / tuple flattened into the children another dict an element a @component instance that component's rendered output

Nested lists are flattened, so [items, "more"] is the same as one flat list.

Only None renders nothing

False renders the word False. React-style short-circuits therefore misfire:

html.div(None, items or False)  # renders the word "False" when items is empty
html.div(None, banner if is_visible else None)  # renders nothing

Replace every x and <element> habit with a conditional expression ending in else None.

docs.title: Void elements
docs.text:
html.br, html.img, html.input, html.hr, html.meta and the rest of the void-element set reject children:

html.br("oops")

TypeError: 'br' nodes cannot have children.

Nothing special is needed for self-closing tags — a tag with no children is simply:

html.img({"src": "/logo.png", "alt": "Logo"})

docs.title: Fragments
docs.text:
html.fragment groups children without adding an element to the DOM. It renders as an element with an empty tagName, which the client renders as its children:

html.fragment(
    html.h1("Title"),
    html.p("Body"),
)

A fragment accepts key and nothing else:

html.fragment({"id": "x"}, html.p("..."))

TypeError: Fragments cannot have attributes besides 'key'

html(...) — calling html directly — is the same fragment constructor.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
ReactPy matches children between renders to decide what to update versus what to rebuild. It reads the key out of attributes["key"]:

html.ul(
    None,
    [html.li({"key": person["id"]}, person["name"]) for person in people],
)

key is an attribute, not a sibling of tagName

React treats key as a top-level prop. ReactPy reads it from attributes, so this has no effect — the key is silently ignored:

{"tagName": "li", "key": "row-1", "children": ["..."]}

Write {"tagName": "li", "attributes": {"key": "row-1"}, "children": ["..."]}, or simply html.li({"key": "row-1"}, "..."). Passing key= to VdomDict directly raises ValueError: Invalid keys: {'key'}.

Without a key, a child's position in the list becomes its key. That is why reordering a list makes state stick to the wrong row: nothing moved as far as ReactPy is concerned. Keys must be unique among siblings.

When debug mode is on, ReactPy warns for each unkeyed child that came out of a list:

UserWarning: Key not specified for child in list {'children': ..., 'tagName': 'li'}

Run your app with REACTPY_DEBUG=1 to see them — see Rendering Lists for the same warning in context. The check only fires for children inside a list; the direct children of a tag are never warned about, and a generator cannot be inspected at all:

UserWarning: Did not verify key-path integrity of children in generator <generator object ...> - pass a sequence (i.e. list of finite length) in order to verify

Pass a list — a comprehension is usually the smallest change.

docs.title: Event handlers
docs.text:
Any callable under any attribute name becomes an event handler:

async def save(event):
    await store.save(event["target"]["value"])


html.button({"onClick": save}, "Save")

The name is forwarded as the DOM event to listen for, so the names that work are the DOM event names in camelCase — onClick, onInput, onKeyDown. The handler receives one argument: the event data as a JSON-serializable dict, wrapped in reactpy.types.Event so nested keys are also readable as attributes. There is no "data" key to unwrap — the browser sends a list of arguments, and ReactPy hands you its single element. Make the handler async when the work is slow, because a plain def handler runs to completion inside the server's event loop: core/events.py, to_event_handler_function wraps a non-coroutine in an async def wrapper that simply calls it, so nothing is handed to a thread. A slow or blocking handler stalls every connection in the process, not just the one that clicked. See Responding to Events.

A handler wrapped in EventHandler receives the raw list

A plain callable is called with the browser's argument list unpacked, so def f(event) gets the event dict. An EventHandler does the opposite: it is called with the list itself, so def f(data) must index into it. The difference stays invisible until a handler is converted, and then event["target"] becomes TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not str:

from reactpy.core.events import EventHandler

def save(event):      # plain callable: receives the event dict
    store.save(event["target"]["value"])


def save_all(data):   # EventHandler: receives the list of arguments
    store.save(data[0]["target"]["value"])


html.button({"onClick": save}, "Save")
html.button({"onClick": EventHandler(save_all, prevent_default=True)}, "Save")

docs.title: ReactPy's own options
docs.text:
Four behaviours run in the browser before the event is sent to the server. Configure them by wrapping the function, not by an attribute:

from reactpy.core.events import EventHandler

html.form(
    {"onSubmit": EventHandler(submit, prevent_default=True)},
    html.button({"type": "submit"}, "Submit"),
)
Parameter Value Effect prevent_default bool calls preventDefault() in the browser before sending stop_propagation bool calls stopPropagation() in the browser before sending debounce int ms rate-limits value updates on user-input elements throttle int ms rate-limits outgoing events

A non-negative integer is required for debounce and throttle; anything else is ignored with a browser-console warning rather than an error:

Ignoring invalid debounce value "fast" on event handler "onInput": expected a non-negative integer.

A dict is not an event handler

The React-style {"function": ..., "preventDefault": True} shape does not work here. A dict is not callable, so ReactPy treats it as an ordinary attribute and no listener is ever registered. With debug mode on you get an immediate error instead of silence:

TypeError: Object of type function is not JSON serializable

# wrong: no listener is attached
html.button({"onClick": {"function": save, "preventDefault": True}}, "...")

# right
html.button({"onClick": EventHandler(save, prevent_default=True)}, "...")

docs.title: Inline JavaScript
docs.text:
A str under an event handler attribute is treated as JavaScript to run in the page instead of being sent to Python:

html.button({"onClick": "console.log(event)"}, "Log the event")

ReactPy records it under the element's inlineJavaScript rather than eventHandlers:

{
    "tagName": "button",
    "children": ["Log the event"],
    "inlineJavaScript": {"onClick": "console.log(event)"},
}

The string is eval'd in the page; if it evaluates to a function, that function is called with the event.

Trusted strings only

This runs with your application's privileges. Never build the string from user input — use a Python handler and pass data through state.

<script> elements reject handlers

html.script raises ValueError: 'script' elements do not support event handlers. It also infers a key from its content or src, so the same script is not re-run on every render.

docs.title: importSource
docs.text:
importSource marks an element as coming from a JavaScript module rather than a built-in tag. ReactPy's web module support produces it for you; you rarely set it by hand. Its keys are source, fallback, sourceType and unmountBeforeUpdate, and sourceType must be "URL" or "NAME":

JsonSchemaValueException: data.children[0].importSource.sourceType must be one of ['URL', 'NAME']

docs.title: Invalid dictionaries
docs.text:
ReactPy validates the six key names as it builds an element:

from reactpy.types import VdomDict

VdomDict(tagName="div", bogus=1)

ValueError: Invalid keys: {'bogus'}.

element = VdomDict(tagName="div")
element["bogus"] = 1

KeyError: 'Invalid key: bogus'

A dict used as a child with no "tagName" does not raise on the server. The layout catches it, logs the traceback, and sends an element whose error field carries the message — which the client prints in the page, in a <pre> that replaces the component, not in the console:

html.div(None, {"children": ["x"]})

ValueError: Expected a VDOM element dict, not {'children': ['x']}

That text exists only under REACTPY_DEBUG=1. Verified in a browser with a bad child between two headings: with debug on, the page read above / ValueError: Expected a VDOM element dict… / below; with debug off the bad component simply vanished — above / below, no <pre>, and nothing at all in the console. The server log has the traceback either way. So when an element renders as nothing, check the server log first and re-run with REACTPY_DEBUG=1 before trusting the page. See Protocol Structure.

docs.title: VdomDict keys
docs.text:
Key Type Notes tagName str required; "" means a fragment children list any accepted child type, flattened attributes dict[str, Any] must be JSON-serializable eventHandlers dict[str, EventHandler] written for you from callables inlineJavaScript dict[str, str] written for you from str handlers importSource dict written for you by web modules

Any other key raises, as shown above. VdomDict is a dict subclass, so you can read and update it with normal dict access — but not add a seventh key.

docs.title: Attribute names worth knowing
docs.text: Attribute Value class / className str of space-separated class names for / htmlFor str, the id of the labelled control style dict of CSS property to value; include units in strings dangerouslySetInnerHTML {"__html": str} key str or int, unique among siblings anything else forwarded to the browser verbatim

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Usage — the tag API itself: naming rules, custom tags, SVG
  • Responding to Events — the event dict, async handlers
  • Rendering Lists — keys and why rows keep the wrong state
  • Use Ref — ReactPy's Ref, which is never attached to an element

docs.title: Components and Hooks must be pure
Overview
docs.text:
A component is a formula: given the same arguments, it must return the same VDOM, and it must change nothing outside itself. This page states that contract precisely — for components and for hooks — and names the places ReactPy expects side effects instead.

The short version:

  • A component may read its arguments, call hooks, and return VDOM. It must not mutate anything that existed before it was called, and its output must not depend on anything it did not receive.
  • A hook follows the same rule, plus one of its own: it must be called in the same order on every render — see Rules of Hooks.

This is not a style preference. ReactPy calls your component at times and frequencies you do not control, and rendering is where the shared-state bug below lives — because in ReactPy components run on a server, inside one long-lived Python process.

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
A component body is allowed to:

Do Example Read its own arguments html.p(title) Call hooks count, set_count = use_state(0) Compute from those values html.p(f"{count} item(s)") Define functions it hands to the client {"onClick": save} Call other components html.div(None, Row(item))

A component body is not allowed to:

Don't Why it fails Assign to a module-level or global variable Shared by every connection in the process; see The server makes this worse Mutate an object it received as an argument The caller still holds it, so the change is visible outside the render Mutate a value read from use_state The comparison that decides whether to re-render can drop an in-place mutation silently Read the clock, random, or the environment Same inputs, different output — the formula is broken Do I/O: open, requests, a database, print Runs on every render, at a frequency you do not control Start a task, thread, or timer Leaks one per render

The two halves of the rule are independent. random.choice mutates nothing and is still impure of output; writing a module-level dict is an outside effect whether or not it changes what you return.

The pair below is the difference, side by side. Both render identically on the first pass. The first one counts renders in a module-level variable, so the number it prints is a property of the process, not of the component — press the button twice in two browser tabs and the two pages disagree about what "the same render" produced:

impure.pypure.py Run 
# Module-level state is shared by every connection and survives across renders,
# so `total` is not part of the component's inputs at all. Two browsers, or two
# renders of the same component, see the same counter.
total = 0


@component
def impure_counter():
    global total
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    # Render mutates module state: an outside effect, and a value that changes
    # what the next render returns even though nothing the component received
    # changed. Nothing warns about this -- the symptom is a number that does not
    # match the button presses.
    total += 1

    return html.div(
        html.h1(count),
        html.p(f"renders (module-wide): {total}"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_count(count + 1)}, "Add 1"),
    )

@component
def counter():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    # Nothing outside this component is touched. `count` comes from use_state,
    # which ReactPy keeps per component instance -- so two connections to this
    # same component each have their own number, and re-running the render
    # changes nothing but the value returned.
    return html.div(
        html.h1(count),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_count(count + 1)}, "Add 1"),
    )

# TODO

docs.title: The server makes this worse
docs.text:
In a browser, module-level state belongs to one user. In ReactPy it belongs to every connection your process serves, for the whole life of the process. Rendering into a shared container is therefore not a code smell but a data leak — and it produces no error.

Three separate layouts, three separate visitors, one module-level dict:

SESSION = {}


@component
def account(name):
    SESSION.setdefault("cart", [])
    SESSION["cart"].append(f"{name}-item")
    return html.div(f"{name}: cart has {len(SESSION['cart'])} item(s)")

Measured output from three independent layouts:

visitor A: cart has 1 item(s): ['A-item']
visitor B: cart has 2 item(s): ['A-item', 'B-item']
visitor C: cart has 3 item(s): ['A-item', 'B-item', 'C-item']

Nothing crashes, each page looks plausible, and every visitor after the first sees other people's data. The same failure appears with total += 1 at module scope, a module-level cache, or a mutable default argument on a component.

Per-user state belongs in use_state or use_reducer, which ReactPy keeps per component instance. State genuinely shared across connections belongs in an explicit store you pass in — through context or an argument — never in a bare module global that rendering reaches for.

docs.title: Where side effects belong
docs.text:
Need Put it in React to a click, keystroke, submit An event handler (Responding to Events) Run once on mount, or when values change use_effect (Use Effect) Await something outside the render use_async_effect (Use Async Effect) Read a request's headers or URL use_connection, use_scope, use_location Build a value for the render, only when inputs change use_memo (Use Memo) Log for debugging use_debug_value, or a logging logger outside the render Load data at process start Executor startup (ReactPy)

An event handler is the default answer. It is defined inside the component but runs later, in response to something the user did, so it may do anything a pure function may not.

use_effect is the escape hatch, not the habit

Effects run after the render, which makes them correct for touching the outside world and awkward for expressing logic. Most of the data you would reach for an effect for can be computed during the render instead. If you find yourself writing an effect to derive a value, stop and compute it in the body.

docs.title: Hooks must be pure too
docs.text:
A hook body is a function your component calls during its render, so it inherits every rule above, plus these:

  • No global, no module mutation. Same leak, harder to see because the hook is shared by several components.
  • No time, no randomness. use_memo(lambda: random.random(), []) fixes each instance to whatever the first render produced. Pass the value in as an argument instead.
  • No I/O. A custom hook that queries a database runs that query on every render of every component that uses it.
  • No conditional hook calls, and no hooks in loops. That is the Rules of Hooks, and it is the one a reviewer can catch by reading.

A custom hook that needs the outside world should take the data as an argument, or expose an event handler that does the work when called.

docs.title: What ReactPy cannot do with purity
docs.text:
React skips re-rendering a component whose props are unchanged — safe because pure functions are safe to cache. ReactPy has no such bailout: a child component re-runs whenever its parent renders, no matter how pure it is.

There is use_memo for values and use_callback for function identity, which reduce the work a render does, but neither stops the render. So purity here buys correctness, testability, and safety under restart — not performance. Do not add memoization on the theory that ReactPy will skip the render; it will not.

Why the rule is enforced by review, not by tests

ReactPy cannot detect impurity — reading a global is a legal Python statement. The rule is about where the language lets you put things, which is why it belongs in code review.

docs.title: Testing purity
docs.text:
A pure component is an ordinary function, so test it as one — no browser:

import asyncio

from reactpy.core.layout import Layout


def render_model(component):
    async def go():
        async with Layout(component) as layout:
            return (await layout.render())["model"]

    return asyncio.run(go())


def test_same_arguments_same_output():
    assert render_model(Greeting("a")) == render_model(Greeting("a"))

Run each layout in its own event loop and build a fresh component instance per call. If a component renders differently the second time, or one layout's render changes another's output, it is impure and the test says so — which is exactly what happens for a component that counts its own renders.

docs.title: Symptoms
docs.text: You see Likely cause Two users see each other's data Module-level state written during render A counter is higher than the number of clicks The component rendered more often than you assumed, and it counts renders Numbers change on reload with no user action Clock or random during render A list mutation does nothing State mutated in place; see Updating Arrays in State One component's render changes another's output A shared object reached through a global, a default argument, or a class attribute

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ReactPyJinja adds three tags to a Jinja2 environment so an existing Python web app can mount ReactPy components inside templates it already owns — one tag for server-rendered components, two for components that run in the browser via PyScript. 

{% component "my_app.pages.counter" %}

Install the extra the extension needs:

pip install "reactpy[asgi,jinja]"

It lives at reactpy.templatetags.ReactPyJinja. Despite the templatetags name it is not a Django app — it is a jinja2-simple-tags StandaloneTag, so it works with any Jinja2 environment.

docs.title: Registering the extension
docs.text:
Two equivalent forms:

from jinja2 import Environment, FileSystemLoader

from reactpy.templatetags import ReactPyJinja

# at construction
env = Environment(loader=FileSystemLoader("templates"), extensions=[ReactPyJinja])

# or afterwards
env = Environment(loader=FileSystemLoader("templates"))
env.add_extension(ReactPyJinja)

Both register all three tags at once; there is no way to register one alone, and no configuration to pass. Registering ReactPyJinja(...) as an instance and calling .register() does not work — that object has no register method.

Register before a template is compiled

Tags are resolved when a template is parsed. If the environment has already compiled a template that uses them, you get jinja2.exceptions.TemplateSyntaxError: Encountered unknown tag 'component'. Frameworks that cache templates at startup make this a startup-time error, which is easy to attribute to something else.

docs.title: {% component "dotted.path" %}
docs.text:
Emits the markup that mounts a server-side component: an empty mount element, an import-map fallback, and a module script that calls mountReactPy.

{% component "my_app.pages.counter" %}
{% component "my_app.pages.badge", class="badge" %}
  • The dotted path (required): the import path of the root component function — the same string you give ReactPyMiddleware's root_components. It is embedded verbatim into the emitted JavaScript; ReactPy imports it on the server when the browser asks to connect.
  • class (optional): a CSS class for the generated mount element, producing <div id="..." class="badge"></div>.

safe_output is set on the tag, so Jinja does not escape the returned HTML even under autoescape=True.

Arguments are parsed as Python expressions

The tag uses Jinja's argument parser, so keyword arguments must follow a comma — {% component "m.f" class="x" %} fails at template-compile time with TemplateSyntaxError: expected token ',', got 'class'. Write {% component "m.f", class="x" %}.

The path may be a quoted string (as above) or a Jinja expression that resolves to one; in the latter case it is read from the template context, so an unquoted my_app.pages.counter requires my_app to be a context variable.

docs.title: Errors this tag raises
docs.text:
Mistake Error Omitting the path TypeError: component() missing 1 required positional argument: 'dotted_path' Passing a second positional TypeError: component() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given Any other keyword ValueError: Unexpected keyword arguments: id, style A typo in the tag name TemplateSyntaxError: Encountered unknown tag 'bogus_tag'.

A wrong dotted path is not one of them. Nothing checks that the module or attribute exists: the tag happily emits markup pointing at a path that will never connect, and the only symptom is a permanently empty element plus a failed request in the browser console. Verify the path against what you passed to root_components.

docs.title: {% pyscript_setup %}
docs.text:
Emits the PyScript bootstrap — stylesheet, module script, and the config that installs ReactPy into the browser.

<head>
    {% pyscript_setup %}
</head>
  • extra_py (optional, positional, repeatable): extra Python packages for the PyScript runtime — {% pyscript_setup "numpy", "rich" %}. They are appended to the package list alongside ReactPy's own wheel.
  • extra_js (optional, keyword): a JSON object mapping module URLs to names, e.g. extra_js='{"./my.js": "mylib"}'. It is merged into the config's js_modules.main. A plain string that is not valid JSON raises json.decoder.JSONDecodeError.
  • config (optional, keyword): a JSON object (or JSON string) merged over the generated config, letting you set anything PyScript accepts.

Put this tag in the document head, once. A page with several pyscript_component tags needs one bootstrap, not one per component.

Packages install in the browser

Anything in extra_py must be installable under Pyodide — pure Python, or a wheel built for it. A package with C extensions that installs cleanly on the server will fail in the browser, and the failure appears only in the browser console.

docs.title: {% pyscript_component "path/to/file.py" %}
docs.text:
Emits a <div> plus a <script type='py'> that runs the named file's component in the browser.

{% pyscript_component "components/counter.py" initial="Loading..." %}
  • File paths (required, positional, repeatable): paths to Python files, resolved relative to the process's current working directory at template-render time. Several files may be passed; they are concatenated into one script.
  • initial (optional): markup rendered inside the mount element while PyScript boots.
  • root (optional): the name of the root component function, default "root".

Because the files are read and inlined, the browser never fetches them and your app serves no route for them.

The file's source ships to the client

Nearly the whole file is embedded in the HTML: executors/pyscript/utils.py, minify_python deletes # comments and inner docstrings before inlining, but the code and every string literal survive. One docstring does escape the filter — the module docstring, because the regex that removes docstrings needs a newline before the opening quotes and that docstring sits at the very start of the file (measured: a module docstring reached the page, a function docstring and both comment styles did not). Treat all of it as published, including any secret read into a string at render time. This is unrelated to debug mode: turning reactpy.config.REACTPY_DEBUG off hides nothing here.

Mistake Error File does not exist (wrong cwd or path) FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'components/missing.py' No root function in the file ValueError: Could not find the root component function 'root' in your PyScript file(s).

Both are raised at render time, so they surface as a 500 on the page — not as a broken widget.

Prefer ReactPyCsr unless you are embedding

For a page built from scratch, ReactPyCsr is an ASGI app with its own URL and handles the setup tag for you. These two tags exist for putting a component inside a template you do not control. See ReactPyCsr.

docs.title: A server-rendered component in an existing page
A client-side component
docs.text:
Setup in the head, the component where it belongs:

home.htmlcounter.py Run 
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>Counter</title>
    {% pyscript_setup %}
  </head>
  <body>
    {% pyscript_component "components/counter.py" initial="Loading..." %}
  </body>
</html>

@component
def root():
    # `root` is the name the tag looks for by default; pass root="other" to
    # point it somewhere else. This file is inlined into the page at render
    # time and runs in the browser, so treat all of it as public.
    count, set_count = use_state(0)
    return html.div(
        html.h1(count),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_count(count + 1)}, "Add 1"),
    )

# TODO

There is no websocket, so use_connection, use_scope, and use_location have no connection to read and raise — see Use Connection.

docs.title: Which one to use
docs.text: {% component %} {% pyscript_setup %} + {% pyscript_component %} Component runs Server Browser Needs a websocket Yes No Component source visible to users No Yes First paint Server HTML, then it connects initial until PyScript boots Can read the request Yes (use_connection, use_scope, use_location) No Needs a route on your app Yes No Packages must be Pyodide-compatible No Yes

  • ReactPyMiddleware — the middleware that serves server-rendered components, and the markup this tag generates

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This section is the detailed reference for ReactPy. For an introduction, start with the Learn section.

The reference is split into functional subsections:

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
Call these at the top level of a component. ReactPy provides twelve:

  • use_state — declare a state variable.
  • use_effect — run a synchronous side effect.
  • use_async_effect — run an async def effect, or one that keeps running across renders.
  • use_reducer — hold state behind a reducer.
  • use_context — read a value provided higher in the tree.
  • use_ref — hold a mutable box that survives renders.
  • use_memo — cache a computed value.
  • use_callback — cache a function.
  • use_debug_value — attach a debug label to a component.
  • use_connection — inspect the current websocket connection.
  • use_scope — read the ASGI connection scope.
  • use_location — read the browser's current URL.

There is no use_id, use_transition, use_deferred_value, use_layout_effect, use_insertion_effect, use_imperative_handle, or use_sync_external_store. Texts ported from React that rely on them have no ReactPy equivalent.

docs.title: HTML
docs.text:
How to describe markup. ReactPy has no JSX; you call functions.

  • Common Props — attributes shared by every tag.
  • Usage — the html.* functions and the shape of a VDOM dictionary.

docs.title: Executors
docs.text:
The ASGI applications that serve your components:

  • ReactPy — standalone single-page app; components render on the server.
  • ReactPyMiddleware — add ReactPy routes to an ASGI app you already have.
  • ReactPyCsr — run component code in the browser via PyScript.

docs.title: Template integration
docs.text: • Jinja — render components from Jinja templates.

docs.title: Rules of React
docs.text:
Idioms for expressing React patterns so they stay understandable and correct:

  • Components and Hooks must be pure
  • React calls Components and Hooks
  • Rules of Hooks

docs.title: Internals
docs.text:
• Protocol Structure — the messages exchanged between server and client.
  • Client API — the browser-side entry point.

docs.title: Where React differs
docs.text: ReactPy models React's function-component API, but it is not React. Effects infer their dependencies instead of requiring an array, state updates are replaced rather than merged, an update that mutates in place is dropped without any error, and several React hooks do not exist at all. Each page calls out the differences that matter to it, so when porting code or prose from a React tutorial, read the ReactPy page rather than assume parity.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ReactPy renders on the server and paints in the browser. A single websocket carries two message types: the server sends "layout-update" patches, the client sends "layout-event" interactions. 

server --{"type": "layout-update", "path": ..., "model": ...}-->  client
server <--{"type": "layout-event", "target": ..., "data": [...]}--  client

docs.title: The connection
docs.text:
Every mounted component opens exactly one websocket. The client builds it from the pathPrefix and componentPath it was handed at mount time (static/index.js, mountReactPy):

ws://<host><pathPrefix><componentPath>?path=<page path>&qs=<page query string>

With the default REACTPY_PATH_PREFIX of "/reactpy/" and a component registered as "main.counter/", mounting on /page?tab=1 opens:

ws://127.0.0.1:8000/reactpy/main.counter/?path=%2Fpage&qs=%3Ftab%3D1

Two things about that URL are load-bearing:

  • The trailing slash after the dotted path is required. The server matches the websocket path against

    ^{path_prefix}(?P<dotted_path>[a-zA-Z0-9_.]+)/$

    which ends in /$. Without the slash the route never matches, the request falls through to your own ASGI app, and the handshake is refused. Verified from a page: ws://…/reactpy/main.counter/?path=/ opens, ws://…/reactpy/main.counter?path=/ fails with Unexpected response code, and the console logs [ReactPy] Failed to connect!.

  • path and qs are how the component learns its URL. ReactPy runs on the server, where the browser's location does not exist. The client copies window.location.pathname into path and window.location.search into qs; the server parses them back out (executors/asgi/middleware.py, _location_from_websocket_query_string) into the Location that use_location() returns. They are percent-encoded and carried in the websocket's own query string, so a server that normalises the handshake URL cannot silently rewrite them.

Reconnection does not re-read the mount

When the socket drops, the client waits and reconnects. Each attempt refreshes path and qs from the current page, but it never re-reads componentPath or the connect options — those were captured when the element mounted. A client-side navigation that changes which component belongs on the page needs a fresh mount, not a reconnect.

The client retries with exponential backoff: REACTPY_RECONNECT_INTERVAL (750 ms) times REACTPY_RECONNECT_BACKOFF_MULTIPLIER (1.25) per attempt, capped at REACTPY_RECONNECT_MAX_INTERVAL (60 s), for REACTPY_RECONNECT_MAX_RETRIES (150) tries. Those are arguments to mountReactPy(...); see ReactPyMiddleware for the bootstrap that emits them.

docs.title: The server-to-client message
docs.text:
One message type goes down the wire. Its keys are fixed (reactpy.types.LayoutUpdateMessage):

Key Value Meaning "type" "layout-update" Always this literal. "path" str A JSON Pointer into the client's copy of the model. "" means replace everything. "model" dict The value to place at that pointer.

The model is JSON, not a VdomDict. Six key names are legal (core/vdom.py, VDOM_JSON_SCHEMA), and only tagName is required:

Key Value Notes "tagName" str The DOM tag, or "" for a wrapper element. "children" list Nested models or plain strings. "attributes" dict Sent to the client as written, and written to the DOM essentially verbatim. Two ReactPy-specific exceptions: key is read for reconciliation and consumed, never becoming an attribute, and _reactpy_ack_seq is deleted by the client before render. "eventHandlers" dict Handler name to target spec, described below. "inlineJavaScript" dict Handler name to JavaScript source string. "importSource" dict Marks an element as coming from a JavaScript module.

Any other key name is rejected while the element is being built:

ValueError: Invalid keys: {'bogus'}.

Here is a real mount message for a counter, captured off the wire:

{
  "type": "layout-update",
  "path": "",
  "model": {
    "tagName": "",
    "children": [
      {
        "tagName": "",
        "children": [
          {
            "tagName": "",
            "children": [
              {
                "tagName": "div",
                "children": [
                  {"tagName": "h1", "children": ["count is 0"]},
                  {
                    "tagName": "button",
                    "eventHandlers": {
                      "onClick": {
                        "target": "/0/0/0/1:onClick",
                        "preventDefault": false,
                        "stopPropagation": false
                      }
                    },
                    "children": ["Add"]
                  }
                ]
              }
            ]
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: Wrapper elements
docs.text:
Read from the top, that model is three elements with "tagName": "" before the div appears. ReactPy needs somewhere to put a component's output that is not itself a DOM node, and it does not reuse your tag for the purpose.

Do not depend on how many there are. The count is an implementation detail that shifts with structure: the same component produced one wrapper rendered bare through Layout, and three behind the ASGI executor's context provider. Never index the tree by position, and never assume the root has a tag name. The client renders a wrapper as a fragment, so it costs you nothing on screen.

docs.title: Patches, not re-renders
docs.text:
The server does not resend the tree. When only an inner component's state changes, it sends the subtree rooted where that component renders:

{
  "type": "layout-update",
  "path": "/children/0/children/0",
  "model": {
    "tagName": "",
    "children": [
      {
        "tagName": "div",
        "children": [
          {"tagName": "h1", "children": ["count is 1"]},
          {
            "tagName": "button",
            "eventHandlers": {
              "onClick": {
                "target": "/0/0/0/1:onClick",
                "preventDefault": false,
                "stopPropagation": false
              }
            },
            "children": ["Add"]
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

That is the whole reply to a click: one-third the depth of the mount, and the only text that changed is inside it. The pointer indexes the model, and path: "" replaces the root — which is what a state change in the topmost component produces.

A patch replaces rather than merges, so whatever subtree it carries is complete: keys you would expect to be sticky, eventHandlers among them, are resent inside it. Nothing is deleted by a patch; a smaller subtree simply arrives with fewer children.

docs.title: Errors arrive as a model
docs.text:
A component that raises during render does not kill the socket. The layout sends an element whose tagName is empty and whose error is the message, which the client prints in a <pre> in place of the component:

{
  "type": "layout-update",
  "path": "",
  "model": {
    "tagName": "",
    "error": "ValueError: Expected a VDOM element dict, not {'noTag': True}"
  }
}

The schema ties the two together: when error is present, tagName must be empty. Without REACTPY_DEBUG=1 the same element carries "error": "" — an empty string, which the client renders as nothing, so the component silently disappears instead of showing a blank box.

docs.title: The client-to-server message
docs.text:
One message type goes up (reactpy.types.LayoutEventMessage):

Key Value Meaning "type" "layout-event" Always this literal. "target" str The handler's target, copied from the model. "data" list The arguments for the handler. Usually one event dict. "seq" int Optional. A client-assigned counter, per element.

A real click on the button above:

{
  "type": "layout-event",
  "target": "/0/0/0/1:onClick",
  "data": [{"type": "click", "target": {"tagName": "BUTTON"}}],
  "seq": 1
}

docs.title: How data is built
docs.text:
The browser serializes the DOM event by walking it: enumerable properties, plus value, checked, files, type and name read off the element even though they are accessors, plus dataset, plus every named control of a form on submit. Functions, DOM nodes, and anything else unserializable are skipped; a cycle or an object nested too deep is cut rather than raising.

That is why the handler receives a dict and not a live event, and why it cannot call into the page. It also means the contents depend on what the walk happened to reach: an <input> arrives as the whole element, hundreds of fields of which you read one. Index data positionally rather than counting on a specific key surviving.

docs.title: Unpacking, and why the two handler forms differ
docs.text:
Layout._process_event_queue turns data into arguments and calls the handler — but not the same way for both kinds of handler (core/events.py, to_event_handler_function):

function(*data)   # a plain callable: the list is unpacked
function(data)    # an EventHandler: the list itself

So def f(event) receives the event dict when passed directly, while def f(data) must index into the list once wrapped in EventHandler. Converting a working handler just to add prevent_default breaks it in a way the traceback does not explain. Common Props shows both shapes side by side.

docs.title: The target string
docs.text:
"/0/0/0/1:onClick" is two parts joined by a colon:

  • Before the colon, the element's position: child index, then child index, walking down from the root. It indexes the same tree the patch path does, so the two line up.
  • After the colon, the attribute name the handler was declared under. It is whatever key you used, which is why {"onMyThing": f} produces a target ending in :onMyThing.

Treat the whole thing as an opaque handle. It is generated per render and is not meant to be constructed by hand; two structurally identical elements get distinct targets because their index paths differ.

Events for unmounted elements are dropped, not queued

If the server has no handler for a target — because the element was removed since the client last rendered, or the target was mistyped — the event is discarded with an informational log and the socket stays open:

Ignored event - handler '/99/99:nope' does not exist or its component unmounted

ReactPy retries the lookup three times at 10 ms intervals first, to cover a handler that is briefly absent mid-render. That window is a race guard, not a queue: nothing is replayed later. A click that happens while the socket is down is held in a client-side send buffer and flushed if the connection reopens — but once REACTPY_RECONNECT_MAX_RETRIES is exhausted the client stops trying, and everything buffered stays unsent.

docs.title: seq and typed input
docs.text:
Typing needs a protocol answer that a plain request/response does not give. Each keystroke sends an event carrying a counter the client incremented for that element. The server records the highest number seen per target, and on the next render of an <input>, <select>, or <textarea> stamps the largest one into the element's attributes under _reactpy_ack_seq:

{
  "type": "layout-update",
  "path": "/children/0/children/0",
  "model": {
    "tagName": "",
    "children": [
      {
        "tagName": "input",
        "attributes": {"value": "hello world", "_reactpy_ack_seq": 1},
        "eventHandlers": {
          "onInput": {
            "target": "/0/0/0:onInput",
            "preventDefault": false,
            "stopPropagation": false
          }
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}

The client compares that number against its own counter to decide whether the server has caught up with the latest keystrokes. If the server is still behind, the client keeps what the user typed instead of overwriting the box with a stale value. Without it, a slow handler erases text mid-word — the classic complaint about server-rendered inputs.

The value lives in a dedicated attribute rather than among your own so it cannot collide with, or leak into, a real DOM attribute. It is added only to those three tags, and only once at least one event has arrived for the element.

Debounce and throttle do travel on the wire

They change when events leave the browser, not what is in them — but the layout still has to tell the client about them. core/layout.py, _serialize_event_handler copies both into the handler's model entry whenever they are not None, and vdom.tsx reads them back off that entry. @event(handler, debounce=250, throttle=500) arrives as:

{
  "onClick": {
    "target": "/0:onClick",
    "preventDefault": false,
    "stopPropagation": false,
    "debounce": 250,
    "throttle": 500
  }
}

Both are omitted entirely when None, which is what keeps the common case minimal. On arrival the client validates each with isValidDebounce — finite, non-negative integer — and an invalid one is dropped with a console.warn naming the handler rather than an error, leaving the handler live but un-debounced. Build a non-Python client from this page and you must carry these two fields; skipping them silently loses the throttling. See Common Props.

docs.title: Watching it yourself
docs.text:
The protocol is plain JSON text frames, so an ordinary websocket client is a sufficient observer. Start this app:

main.py Run 
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.responses import HTMLResponse
from starlette.routing import Route

from reactpy import component, html, use_state
from reactpy.executors.asgi import ReactPyMiddleware
from reactpy.executors.utils import server_side_component_html


@component
def counter():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    def increment(_event):
        set_count(count + 1)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"count is {count}"),
        html.button({"onClick": increment}, "Add"),
    )


async def home(request):
    return HTMLResponse(
        "<!doctype html>"
        "<html><body>"
        + server_side_component_html("root", "", "main.counter/")
        + "</body></html>"
    )


my_app = ReactPyMiddleware(
    Starlette(routes=[Route("/", home)]),
    root_components=["main.counter"],
)

# TODO

Then read the mount message, send a click, and read the patch:

client.py Run 
import asyncio
import json

import websockets


async def main():
    url = "ws://127.0.0.1:8000/reactpy/main.counter/?path=%2F"

    async with websockets.connect(url) as socket:
        mount = json.loads(await socket.recv())
        print("1. the mount update:", mount["path"] or "(root)")
        print(json.dumps(mount["model"], indent=2))

        target = find_handler_target(mount["model"])
        print("\n2. sending a click to", target)
        await socket.send(
            json.dumps(
                {
                    "type": "layout-event",
                    "target": target,
                    "data": [{"type": "click", "target": {"tagName": "BUTTON"}}],
                    "seq": 1,
                }
            )
        )

        patch = json.loads(await socket.recv())
        print("\n3. the reply is a patch at path:", repr(patch["path"]))
        print(json.dumps(patch["model"], indent=2))


def find_handler_target(model):
    """Return the target of the first event handler found in a model."""
    if isinstance(model, dict):
        for spec in (model.get("eventHandlers") or {}).values():
            return spec["target"]
        for child in model.get("children", []):
            found = find_handler_target(child)
            if found:
                return found
    return None


asyncio.run(main())

# TODO

Both were run against each other to produce every JSON block on this page. Nothing about the protocol is private to ReactPy's client — given a mount element and a correct target, you can drive a server-rendered component from any language.

The server trusts the client completely

Nothing checks that target names a real handler, that data describes a real event, or that the sender is the page that mounted the component. Whatever your handler reads out of data, it read because the browser asserted it. Treat it as user input: event["target"]["value"] is a string an attacker chose, at any length. The one thing the client cannot forge is the ASGI scope, which is server-side — see Use Connection.

docs.title: Failure modes
docs.text: Symptom Cause Handshake refused, [ReactPy] Failed to connect! Missing trailing slash in componentPath, or a path_prefix that differs between the bootstrap and the server. Socket opens then closes; server logs RuntimeError: Attempting to use an unregistered root component <path>. The dotted path is not in root_components. The socket is accepted before the component is resolved, so the failure is visible only in the server log. Server log: Unknown message type: <type> Anything other than "layout-event". The server accepts that one type and drops the rest, leaving the connection open. Server log: Ignored event - handler ... does not exist or its component unmounted Stale or wrong target. Console: Received message without type or Received message without handler A frame the client has no handler for. Ignored; the connection stays up. A <pre> with an exception message appears in the page The component raised. See Errors arrive as a model. Component renders once and never updates The handler never fires — usually a snake_case event name such as on_click, so no event is ever sent. [ReactPy] Disconnected! then Reconnecting in … The socket dropped and backoff is in effect. If Connection max retries exhausted! follows, the page needs a reload.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You do not call a component or a hook — ReactPy does. Understanding who calls what explains why components must be pure, why hook order matters, and why calling a component yourself almost never does what you meant. 

@component
def counter():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)  # ReactPy runs this, not you
    return html.h1(count)

Writing counter() does not run the function. And use_state does not work from anywhere you like — it works only while ReactPy is in the middle of rendering the component that called it.

docs.title: ReactPy calls components
docs.text:
@component turns a function into a constructor. Calling it returns a Component object — a description of "render this function with these arguments", to be rendered later, by the layout:

>>> type(counter())
<class 'reactpy.types.Component'>

Component is defined in reactpy/types.py; core/component.py only imports it to build these objects, so reactpy.core.component.Component is an alias, not the class's own module.

The layout is what invokes your function body, at times it decides:

ReactPy calls your component When On mount The first time it appears in the tree On state change A use_state or use_reducer in that component is updated On parent render Whenever the component that renders it re-renders On an event Indirectly — your handler runs, and any state it sets schedules a render

Two consequences follow immediately.

You do not control how often it runs. A parent re-render re-renders its children, and ReactPy has no memo bailout for components. Code that counts, logs, or accumulates in a component body accumulates faster than the number of user actions. Measured: one press of a parent's button produced exactly one render of the parent and one of an unrelated child — but nothing guarantees those counts match your mental model once several state updates are in play.

Calling it yourself does not render it. Two mistakes, both silent:

html.div(None, my_component)  # passing the function, not calling it
html.div(None, my_component())  # correct: an instance to be rendered

The first is accepted, and the function's repr becomes a text child — the page shows something like <function my_component at 0x7f0d1b2c4e00>. There is no error, because a callable that is not a known child type is stringified like a number would be. If your page ever displays a hex address, this is why.

Calling .render() on an instance does not work either:

await my_component().render()

RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout?

Rendering needs a life cycle hook, which only a layout provides. To see what a component produces, put it in one:

import asyncio

from reactpy.core.layout import Layout


def render_model(component):
    async def go():
        async with Layout(component) as layout:
            return (await layout.render())["model"]

    return asyncio.run(go())

docs.title: Components are values
docs.text:
An instance is an ordinary Python object, so you can build one in a loop or pass it as an argument — the way ReactPy expects you to compose:

html.ul(None, [row(item) for item in items])

Each call creates a fresh instance, and each gets its own state. Reusing one instance in two positions in the tree is the thing to avoid: build a new one per position, and key them when they come from a loop.

docs.title: key is a reserved parameter
docs.text:
A component constructor accepts an optional key keyword, which the layout uses for reconciliation:

[row(item, key=item["id"]) for item in items]

Because of that, key is reserved as a component parameter name, and a component that declares one is rejected at import time — before anything renders:

@component
def row(key):  # do not do this
    return html.li(key)

TypeError: Component render function <function row at 0x...> uses reserved parameter 'key'

Name the argument something else — row_key, label, item_id — and pass the reconciliation key as key= at the call site.

Note this differs from plain elements, where the key lives inside the attributes dict. See Common Props.

docs.title: Hooks are called by ReactPy, during a render
docs.text:
A hook is a plain function that reads the current life cycle hook off a task-local stack. That is why it raises outside a render — and in several places that look like renders:

You call a hook from Result A component body Works — the intended place A custom hook called from a component body Works, and is how you build one Module level, directly RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout? await component().render() The same RuntimeError An event handler The same RuntimeError, logged on the server as Failed to execute event handler ... An use_effect callback body The same RuntimeError, logged on the server as Error in effect — a different log line, from a different place

The last two are the trap, and they look alike from the browser and nothing like each other in the log. Calling use_state from inside an event handler does not crash the app; it kills that handler, and the traceback goes to the server log:

Failed to execute event handler EventHandler(...)
...
RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout?

That line comes only from core/layout.py, _process_event_queue — delivered browser events. An effect body is a task, not a delivered event, so it fails through core/_life_cycle_hook.py, affect_component_will_unmount, and you see Error in effect instead. Search the log for both strings, not one.

Nothing changes in the browser, so the symptom is "the button does nothing". Move the hook call to the component body and close over the value instead.

docs.title: The mental model
docs.text:
You ReactPy Define what to render Decide when to render Return VDOM from a component Call the component Declare state with a hook Store it, per component instance Write an event handler Run it, when the event arrives Declare dependencies Compare them, and decide whether to re-run an effect

Everything in the Rules of React follows from the left column being yours and the right column being ReactPy's. You cannot ask ReactPy to render less often, so you write components that are safe to render often.

docs.title: A custom hook is a component's helper, not a standalone function
docs.text:
Because a hook is called during a render, a custom hook is only usable from a render:

def use_cart():
    items, set_items = use_state([])  # fine: runs during the caller's render
    return items, add_item

Calling use_cart() from an event handler, a utility function, or a background task raises the same RuntimeError. If logic must be callable from there, write it as a normal function that takes what it needs as arguments.

docs.title: A hex address appeared on the page
docs.text: You passed a component instead of calling it: html.div(None, my_component). Add the parentheses.

docs.title: RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout?
docs.text: A hook ran with no render in progress. Usual causes: called from an event handler, from an effect body, from a helper that a handler calls, or by awaiting .render() yourself. Read the server log for the traceback — the browser will not show it.

docs.title: TypeError: ... uses reserved parameter 'key'
docs.text: A component parameter is named key. Rename it, and pass the reconciliation key as key= at the call site.

docs.title: A button does nothing, and the browser shows no error
docs.text: The handler raised on the server. Handlers that call hooks fail this way. Check the server log.
