docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ReactPyCsr serves a page that runs your component code in the browser via PyScript. There is no websocket: the component renders entirely client-side. 

from reactpy.executors.asgi import ReactPyCsr

my_app = ReactPyCsr("root.py", initial="Loading...")

docs.title: ReactPyCsr(*file_paths, **settings)
docs.text: from reactpy.executors.asgi import ReactPyCsr

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• *file_paths: One or more paths to Python files containing components. Their source is inlined into the served HTML. Accepts str or pathlib.Path.

    Read once, then cached for the life of the process: executors/pyscript/utils.py, fetch_cached_python_file is decorated with functools.cache, keyed on the path. Editing the file does not change the page on reload — restart the server. The same call minifies the source before inlining — # comments and inner docstrings are stripped, the module docstring is not — so what reaches the browser is not quite what you wrote (see Jinja).

  • root_name (optional): The name of the root component inside your Python file. Defaults to "root". The file may define any number of components; this one is mounted.

    ReactPyCsr("components.py", root_name="my_app")

    The name must match exactly, and the object must be a component.

  • initial (optional): Content shown while PyScript boots. A string or a VdomDict. Defaults to "".

  • extra_py (optional): Additional Python packages to install into the PyScript runtime, as version specifier strings.

  • extra_js (optional): Additional JavaScript modules, as a dict[str, str] where each key is the URL of the JavaScript file and the value is the name to export it as — {"/static/foo.js": "foo"}. The name is how the module is reached from the component, via pyscript.js_modules.foo. Same direction as the js_modules.main block PyScript itself consumes.

  • pyscript_config (optional): Raw PyScript configuration dictionary.

  • http_headers, html_head, prepend_body, html_lang: Same meaning as in ReactPy.

  • **settings: Any key from ReactPyConfig.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: An ASGI application.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Two files: the ASGI app, and the root component.

main.pyroot.py Run 
my_app = ReactPyCsr(
    Path(__file__).parent / "root.py",
    initial="Loading...",
    root_name="root",
)

from reactpy import component, html, use_state


@component
def root():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)
    return html.div(
        html.h1(count),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_count(count + 1)}, "Add 1"),
    )

# TODO

Serve with uvicorn main:my_app. The served page carries the Loading... placeholder, the PyScript bootstrap, and your component source.

Your component source is public

ReactPyCsr embeds the text of every file you pass into the HTML response, so the browser can execute it. Verified: requesting the index route returned the full body of the component file, including components that are not mounted.

Treat these files as client-side code. Do not read secrets, query a database, or call privileged APIs from a CSR component — anything reachable from that file is reachable by anyone who loads the page. CSR is for genuinely client-side work: offline apps, demos, UI that needs no server authority. For anything that touches data you do not publish, use ReactPy or ReactPyMiddleware, which keep your Python on the server.

docs.title: How it loads
docs.text:
The page ReactPy generates does three things:

  1. Links PyScript's CSS and module script from {path_prefix}static/.
  2. Declares what PyScript should fetch: a packages list for Python — ReactPy's own wheel from {path_prefix}static/wheels/ and jsonpointer==3.* — and a separate js_modules entry for morphdom, served from {path_prefix}static/morphdom/morphdom-esm.js. They are different lists with different installers; morphdom is not a packages entry.
  3. Inlines your Python, then runs it under PyScript.

Verified against a running server: the initial response carries the PyScript core.js, "packages": ["/reactpy/static/wheels/reactpy-2.0.0b13-py3-none-any.whl", "jsonpointer==3.*"], "js_modules": {"main": {"/reactpy/static/morphdom/morphdom-esm.js": "morphdom"}}, and the initial placeholder inside a <div class="pyscript">. pyscript_config lets you replace either list.

The first load is slow

The browser downloads and installs a CPython runtime plus your packages before anything renders. That is what initial is for. pyscript_config and extra_py let you pin packages, and packages_cache controls re-download, but the cold start is inherent to running Python in the browser.

docs.title: Choosing CSR over the other executors
docs.text:
Where your Python runs Needs a websocket Source visible to the client ReactPy server yes no ReactPyMiddleware server yes no ReactPyCsr browser no yes

Pick CSR when the client must work without a server connection. Pick one of the others whenever the component touches anything you would not publish.

PyScript without CSR

ReactPy accepts pyscript_setup=True to load PyScript alongside server-rendered components, for mixed setups. ReactPyCsr is the fully client-side case.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Creating a Standalone React App
  • Adding ReactPy to an Existing Project — the Jinja template tags include a CSR variant.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ReactPyMiddleware adds ReactPy routes to an ASGI application you already have. Requests ReactPy does not recognise fall through to your app. 

from reactpy.executors.asgi import ReactPyMiddleware

my_app = ReactPyMiddleware(existing_asgi_app, root_components=["main.component"])

docs.title: ReactPyMiddleware(app, root_components, **settings)
docs.text: from reactpy.executors.asgi import ReactPyMiddleware

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• app: The ASGI application to serve when a request does not match a ReactPy route. Any ASGI app works — Starlette, FastAPI, or hand-written.

  • root_components: A list, set, or tuple of dotted paths to root components, e.g. ["main.counter"]. The path must be importable by Python's import system: module path, dot, attribute name. Resolution is module.rsplit(".", 1) followed by getattr, so it must name a module that is importable from the server's working directory.

  • **settings: Any key from ReactPyConfig. See Configuration. path_prefix is validated at construction and raises ValueError if malformed.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: An ASGI application.

docs.title: Wrapping an existing app
docs.text:
main.py Run 
my_app = ReactPyMiddleware(starlette_app, root_components=["main.counter"])

# TODO

The wrapped app is untouched. Verified with Starlette: a plain /healthz route still returned its text response through the middleware.

docs.title: What the middleware actually claims
docs.text:
ReactPyMiddleware.__call__ handles exactly three kinds of request and forwards everything else:

Path Handled by websocket matching {path_prefix}{dotted_path}/ ReactPy render stream {path_prefix}static/... ReactPy client bundle {path_prefix}modules/... built web modules anything else your app

There is no fourth row. ReactPyMiddleware.match_extra_paths is a hook that returns None — its own comment says custom routes are "unused by default to encourage users to handle routing within your ASGI framework of choice". The @my_app.route(...) registry people expect belongs to the standalone ReactPy executor, which overrides that method to match extra_http_routes / extra_ws_routes. Under the middleware, every route is your app's.

The middleware never serves your HTML

This is the part that surprises people. Registering a dotted path does not create a page. Requesting "/" falls through to your app, and there is no {path_prefix}{dotted_path}/ HTTP route either — that pattern is matched only when the ASGI scope type is "websocket". Verified: requesting /reactpy/main.counter/ over HTTP returns 404, while the websocket on the same path streams the model.

You produce the document yourself, by emitting an empty mount element and the client bootstrap that points at one registered component.

docs.title: Serving a component from your own route
docs.text:
main.py Run 
async def home(request):
    # The mount point plus the client bootstrap, for one registered component.
    mount = server_side_component_html(
        element_id="app",
        class_="",
        # Trailing slash required: the websocket route matches `<prefix><dotted_path>/`.
        component_path="main.counter/",
    )
    return HTMLResponse(f'<html><body><div id="wrapper">{mount}</div></body></html>')


starlette_app = Starlette(routes=[Route("/", home)])

my_app = ReactPyMiddleware(starlette_app, root_components=["main.counter"])

# TODO

server_side_component_html emits the <div id="app">, the import map fallback, and the mountReactPy(...) call. Verified in a real browser: the counter rendered into <div id="app"> with [ReactPy] Connected! in the console.

The trailing slash in component_path is required

Pass "main.counter/", not "main.counter". The client opens ws://host/reactpy/<component_path>?path=/, and the server matches the websocket path against

^{path_prefix}(?P<dotted_path>[a-zA-Z0-9_.]+)/$

which requires the trailing slash. Verified both ways: without it the handshake fails with Unexpected response code and the console logs [ReactPy] Failed to connect!, leaving an empty div; with it, the component renders.

docs.title: Multiple components
docs.text:
Register several and choose per page. Each page mounts exactly one:

my_app = ReactPyMiddleware(
    starlette_app,
    root_components=["main.counter", "main.settings", "main.profile"],
)

Then emit a different component_path from each of your routes.

Unregistered paths are rejected

"Attempting to use an unregistered root component <path>." is raised when a websocket asks for a dotted path you never listed. Register every component you intend to mount.

docs.title: Import errors
docs.text:
A dotted path that cannot be imported fails at construction, with a message naming the part that failed:

ImportError: ReactPy failed to import "main"
AttributeError: ReactPy failed to import "counter" from "main"

The first means the module was not found; the second means the module loaded but has no such attribute. ValueError is raised earlier still if the path has no dot at all.

docs.title: Choosing an executor
docs.text:
Goal Use Whole app is ReactPy, no existing server code ReactPy Add components to an existing ASGI app ReactPyMiddleware Run component code in the browser via PyScript ReactPyCsr

ReactPy is itself a subclass of ReactPyMiddleware that registers a single root and serves its own index document, which is why the standalone executor can do the HTML the middleware leaves to you.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Adding ReactPy to an Existing Project
  • ReactPy — the standalone executor.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ReactPy is ReactPy's standalone ASGI application. It serves the HTML document, the client bundle, and the websocket through which components render. 

from reactpy.executors.asgi import ReactPy

my_app = ReactPy(root_component)

docs.title: ReactPy(root_component, **settings)
docs.text:
Instantiate ReactPy once, at module level, and hand the instance to any ASGI server:

uvicorn main:my_app

ReactPy serves the page at every route that is not claimed by its own static or websocket paths.

from reactpy.executors.asgi import ReactPy

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• root_component: The component to mount. A component constructor — the @component function itself, not a call to it. This app is a single-page application: there is exactly one root.

  • html_head (optional): Extra content for the document's <head>.

    Must be built with html.head

    Pass html.head(...) — not a bare html.title(...) or a html.div(...). Anything else raises at request time:

    ValueError: Head element must be constructed with `html.head`.

    Verified: this surfaces as a 500 on the index route, not at import time, so a typo here only shows up once the server is running.

  • prepend_body (optional): Content rendered at the start of the <body>, before the mount point. Accepts a VdomDict built with html.*, or None to omit. Defaults to html.noscript("Enable JavaScript to view this site.").

    This is the one part of the tree that is genuinely server-rendered. See what ReactPy does and does not render.

  • html_lang (optional): Value for the document's lang attribute. Defaults to "en".

  • http_headers (optional): Extra response headers for the index document — a plain dict[str, str]. Use it for CSP, X-Frame-Options, caching, and similar.

  • pyscript_setup (optional): Load PyScript into the document head, for running component code in the browser. Defaults to False. ReactPyCsr sets this for you.

  • pyscript_options (optional): A PyScriptOptions configuring that behaviour.

  • **settings: Any key from ReactPyConfig. Despite appearances these are not scoped to this app instance — each one is written to the matching global in reactpy.config, so the last executor constructed wins process-wide. See Configuration.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: An ASGI application.

docs.title: A standalone app
docs.text:
app.py Run 
my_app = ReactPy(counter)

# TODO

Serve it with uvicorn main:my_app. The name you assign matters, because it is what uvicorn module:name refers to.

docs.title: Page metadata and headers
docs.text:
app.py Run 
my_app = ReactPy(
    page,
    # Must be built with html.head(); any other tag raises ValueError.
    html_head=html.head(
        html.title("My ReactPy App"),
        html.meta({"name": "description", "content": "A ReactPy app"}),
    ),
    html_lang="fr",
    http_headers={"X-Frame-Options": "DENY"},
    # Rendered into the <body> before the mount point, on the server.
    prepend_body=html.header({"id": "nav"}, "Server-rendered navigation"),
)

# TODO

Verified against a running server: lang="fr", the custom <title>, the custom response header, and the prepend_body markup all appear in the initial HTML.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Settings are ordinary keyword arguments, and they reach the browser-side client:

app.py Run 
my_app = ReactPy(
    page,
    path_prefix="/apps/reactpy/",
    reconnect_interval=500,
    reconnect_max_interval=30000,
    reconnect_max_retries=50,
    async_rendering=True,
    debug=False,
)

# TODO
Setting Default Meaning path_prefix /reactpy/ Base path ReactPy serves its own static assets and websocket from. web_modules_dir temp dir Where built web modules are cached. reconnect_interval 750 Milliseconds before the first reconnect attempt. reconnect_max_interval 60000 Ceiling on the reconnect backoff. reconnect_max_retries 150 Attempts before giving up. reconnect_backoff_multiplier 1.25 Growth factor between attempts. async_rendering True Allow renders to overlap. debug False Server-side checks and richer error text — see the note below. max_queue_size 1000 Bound on the pending event queue per connection. tests_default_timeout 15.0 Default timeout for reactpy.testing. Not settable this way — see the note below.

Verified: setting path_prefix="/apps/reactpy/" moves asset serving to that prefix, and the reconnect values appear in the generated mount call.

These keywords are process-wide, not per-app

executors/utils.py, process_settings walks the keywords and calls set_current() on the matching reactpy.config Option object. Those objects are module-level globals, so the last constructor to run wins for the whole process — including for any app built before it. Verified: two ReactPy instances created with reconnect_interval=111 and reconnect_interval=999 leave REACTPY_RECONNECT_INTERVAL.current at 999 for both. There is no per-app configuration layer; do not host two apps that need different values.

tests_default_timeout is worse than ineffective. Its Option is declared mutable=False in reactpy/config.py, and _option.py, set_current raises TypeError on an immutable option — so passing it raises Option(REACTPY_TESTS_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT=15.0) cannot be modified after initial load out of the constructor. Set it via the REACTPY_TESTS_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT environment variable before import, or not at all.

debug is not a client switch. REACTPY_DEBUG turns on server-side VDOM and JSON-attribute validation, populates the model's error text (without it, a failed component ships "error": "" and renders as nothing), and changes a few asset URLs to their ?dev forms. See Common Props.

Each setting also has an environment-variable twin in reactpy.config — REACTPY_PATH_PREFIX, REACTPY_RECONNECT_INTERVAL, and so on. Since the keyword already writes to that same global option, the two differ only in timing: the environment variable is read when the module is first imported, the keyword whenever an executor is constructed.

docs.title: What ReactPy does and does not render
docs.text:
This is the distinction that trips people up, because the executor has historically been described as "SSR".

The initial HTML document contains an empty mount point:

<body>
  <noscript>Enable JavaScript to view this site.</noscript>
  <div id="app" class=""></div>
  <script type="module" crossorigin="anonymous">
    import { mountReactPy } from "/reactpy/static/index.js";
    mountReactPy({ mountElement: document.getElementById("app"), ... });
  </script>
</body>

Verified by fetching the index route: your root component's markup is not in the response. The browser connects over the websocket and ReactPy renders and streams from there.

What is server-rendered into the first response:

  • prepend_body, converted with reactpy_to_string.
  • html_head.
  • The document shell: lang, static asset paths, the mount script.

Practical consequences:

  • Search engines and curl see an empty app. For content that must exist without JavaScript, render it yourself — reactpy_to_string turns a component into an HTML string, which you can place in prepend_body or emit from your own route. It renders the component's first render directly, without a layout, so the component cannot use any hook: use_state, use_ref, use_effect, use_location and the rest all raise RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout?. Pass plain html.* elements, or a component that calls none of them.
  • There is no first-paint flash to optimise away, because there is no first paint to replace.
  • A component that fails on the server fails after the page loads, leaving a blank <div id="app">. When the page loads but shows nothing, check the server log before the browser console.

Not the same as ReactPyCsr

ReactPyCsr is the one that runs component code in the browser via PyScript. ReactPy runs components on the server and sends VDOM over a websocket. Both need a server; they differ in where your Python executes. See ReactPyMiddleware for mounting into an existing ASGI app.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Call hooks at the top level of a component, in the same order, on every render. No loops, no conditions, no early returns, no nesting inside a function that runs later. ReactPy will not always tell you when you break this rule — in one case it corrupts state in silence. 

@component
def form():
    name, set_name = use_state("")  # top level, every render, same order
    email, set_email = use_state("")
    return html.form(name, email)

ReactPy identifies a hook's state by where it was called, not by what it is called into. The nth use_state in a component body gets the nth stored slot. Change which hooks run, and you change which slot each one reads.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
• Only call hooks from a component body or another hook — never from an event handler, an effect body, a plain function, or module level. See React calls Components and Hooks.
  • Call them at the top level — not inside if, for, try, a while, a comprehension, or a nested function that runs later.
  • Always call the same hooks in the same order — which hooks run may not depend on props, state, or anything else that can change between renders.
  • No early return before a hook — an early exit skips the hooks after it.

The one exception is use_context: it takes no slot at all (core/hooks.py reads the provider off the current hook and never touches the state list), so calling it conditionally shifts nothing — verified, a component whose use_context call runs on only some renders keeps _state at the same length throughout. It is still a hook and still needs an active render to call.

docs.title: Why: hooks are slots, not names
docs.text:
ReactPy keeps a component's hook values in a plain list and hands out the next entry on each call — a running index, not a name. From reactpy/core/_life_cycle_hook.py, LifeCycleHook.use_state:

if not self._rendered_atleast_once:
    # since we're not initialized yet we're just appending state
    result = function()
    self._state.append(result)
else:
    # once finalized we iterate over each succesively used piece of state
    result = self._state[self._current_state_index]
self._current_state_index += 1

The first render appends one entry per hook call, in order. Every later render reads back by position. Nothing records the variable name, the hook's type, or what it stores — so position is identity.

That is why the rules are phrased as "same order". The component cannot tell ReactPy which value is which; only the sequence of calls says so.

docs.title: What breaking the rules actually does
docs.text: This is where ReactPy and React part ways, and why the rules must be enforced by review rather than trusted to a loud failure.

docs.title: More hooks than the first render: a crash
docs.text:
A component that mounts with one hook and later calls two tries to read a slot that was never appended:

@component
def grow():
    n, set_n = use_state(0)
    if n >= 1:  # a second hook appears only after the first click
        extra, set_extra = use_state("EXTRA")
        return html.div(f"n={n} extra={extra}")
    return html.div(f"n={n}", html.button({"onClick": lambda e: set_n(n + 1)}, "bump"))

With debug mode on, the component is replaced by an error node and the server logs the cause:

IndexError: list index out of range

With debug mode off, the error field is an empty string, so the region simply renders as nothing. This case fails loudly enough to find.

docs.title: Fewer hooks than the first render: silent state corruption
docs.text:
This is the dangerous one. A hook call that disappears from above another one shifts every later index by one — and the shift is invisible:

@component
def shifting():
    show, set_show = use_state(True)  # slot 0
    if show:
        hidden, set_hidden = use_state("HIDDEN")  # slot 1, only while show
    n, set_n = use_state("N")  # slot 1 while show, slot 2 once it is off
    return html.div(f"show={show} n={n}")

Measured, flipping show from True to False once (through its setter — this snippet has no button; the runnable broken_toggle below wires the same shape to a real Toggle button):

mount:          show=True  n=N
after toggle:   show=False  n=HIDDEN     <-- `n` is now reading `hidden`'s slot

No error, no warning, no traceback. n starts showing another hook's value and keeps doing so until the branches line up again. React, by contrast, throws Rendered fewer hooks than expected. A ported component can therefore be wrong in ReactPy where it was a crash in React.

The corruption usually surfaces later, somewhere that looks unrelated. With a counter that should hold an int, the shifted read hands a string to arithmetic, and the next click dies in the handler:

TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

That traceback names the event handler, not the hook — so the hunt starts in the wrong file. The button stops working, and the error is on the server log only.

app.py Run 
@component
def broken_toggle():
    """Do not copy this: a hook behind a condition that can change.

    `hidden` occupies slot 1 only while `show` is true. Clicking Toggle makes
    that call disappear, so every hook after it shifts up one slot and starts
    reading somebody else's value -- `count` begins showing the string that
    belongs to `hidden`. No error is raised, on the server or in the browser.
    """
    show, set_show = use_state(True)  # slot 0

    if show:
        hidden, set_hidden = use_state("NOT-A-NUMBER")  # slot 1, conditionally

    count, set_count = use_state(0)  # slot 1 when `show` is False

    return html.div(
        html.h1(count),
        html.p(f"show={show}"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_show(not show)}, "Toggle"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_count(count + 1)}, "Add 1"),
    )


@component
def fixed_toggle():
    """The same component with the hook order held constant.

    Every hook runs on every render, so the slots stay aligned with the
    variables they belong to. Branching happens in the *return value*, which is
    what rendering is for.
    """
    show, set_show = use_state(True)
    hidden, set_hidden = use_state("NOT-A-NUMBER")
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(count),
        html.p(f"show={show} hidden={hidden}"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_show(not show)}, "Toggle"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_count(count + 1)}, "Add 1"),
    )

# TODO

In broken_toggle, Add 1 works, then Toggle makes the heading read NOT-A-NUMBER, and the next Add 1 does nothing at all — the handler raised TypeError on the server. fixed_toggle is the same component with the hooks moved out of the condition: both of its buttons keep working through every toggle.

docs.title: A hook in a loop: frozen values, then a crash
docs.text:
@component
def rows(n):
    out = []
    for i in range(n):
        value, set_value = use_state(f"v{i}")
        out.append(value)
    return html.div(out)

Measured with n going 3 → 2 → 1 → 0:

vals=['v0', 'v1', 'v2']
vals=['v0', 'v1']
vals=['v0']
vals=[]

It looks correct. It is not: use_state(f"v{i}") applies its initial value only on the first render, so the i in it is decoration, and the list's length is driven by an argument while its contents come from frozen slots. Growing n past its first-render value raises the IndexError from the first case. A loop of hooks is wrong either way — build one component per item, which gives each its own state legitimately:

html.div(None, [row(item, key=item["id"]) for item in items])

docs.title: An early return before a hook
docs.text:
@component
def loading():
    n, set_n = use_state(0)
    if n == 2:
        return html.div("early")  # skips the hook below
    label, set_label = use_state("LABEL")
    return html.div(f"{n} {label}")

ReactPy does not crash, and label survives while the branch is away. But this is the same slot-shifting hazard as above, arriving whenever the condition flips. Put the early return after every hook, or move the conditional content into a child component:

@component
def loading():
    n, set_n = use_state(0)
    label, set_label = use_state("LABEL")  # all hooks first
    if n == 2:
        return html.div("early")
    return html.div(f"{n} {label}")

Tolerance is not safety

ReactPy lets several of these through; React does not. The case above corrupts state without a word, and the same code raises the moment it is ported, tested against React semantics, or read by someone who assumes React's guarantees. Treat the rules as absolute.

docs.title: Custom hooks follow the same rules
docs.text:
A custom hook is only a function, so nothing checks it:

def use_auth(token):
    if not token:
        return None, None  # hooks skipped on some calls
    user, set_user = use_state(None)
    return user, set_user

Call it with a falsy token and the caller silently loses a slot — measured, the happy path consumes one hook slot and the falsy path consumes none. Return early only after every hook has run, or split into two hooks and choose between them at the call site, where the choice is visible in the component body:

@component
def page(token):
    return authed(token) if token else anonymous()

Because a hook's name is all a reviewer has, name custom hooks use_* and call them only from component bodies or other hooks.

docs.title: Catching violations
docs.text:
There is a linter: reactpy-flake8, the plugin this repository pins (reactpy-flake8 >=0.7 in pyproject.toml, select = ["RPY"]). Its RulesOfHooksVisitor is the working equivalent of eslint-plugin-react-hooks for the call-site rule, and it reports:

Code Catches REACTPY100 a hook defined as a closure inside another function REACTPY101 a hook used outside any component or hook REACTPY102 a hook used inside an if / if expression / try / match / for / while REACTPY103 a hook used after an early return

Run it as part of flake8 (the repo config selects only its RPY codes), or drive it directly:

import ast
from reactpy_flake8.run import run_checks

for line, col, msg in run_checks(ast.parse(source), exhaustive_hook_deps=False):
    print(line, col, msg)

Verified against a component with a hook after an early return and a hook inside an if: it reports exactly REACTPY103 hook 'use_state' used after an early return on line 7 and REACTPY102 hook 'use_state' used inside if statement. Pass exhaustive_hook_deps=True to add the dependency-shape checks (REACTPY200–REACTPY202), which cover far less than people expect — see Lifecycle of Reactive Effects.

What the linter cannot do is check the order rule, because order is a runtime property. There is still no runtime check, so the two habits remain:

  • Run with REACTPY_DEBUG=1 during development, so a hook-count increase becomes a visible error instead of an empty region.
  • Treat any use_ call that appears below the first non-hook statement of a component body, or inside an if / for / try / nested def, as a review defect — and wire reactpy-flake8 into CI so you are not the only one who spots it.

The linter also matches on names: it flags anything whose name fits ^_*use_\w+ and treats a function as a component only if decorated with something matching ^(component|[\w.]+\.component)$. Rename the decorator or the hook and the checks silently stop applying; the patterns are configurable via --component-decorator-pattern and --hook-function-pattern.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Two rules make ReactPy predictable: components and hooks must be pure, and ReactPy must be the one that calls them. They look like style advice. They are load-bearing — and in ReactPy, one of them is not enforced by anything except you.

Rule In one line Read Purity A component or hook returns the same output for the same inputs, and changes nothing outside itself. Components and Hooks must be pure Who calls what You write components and hooks; ReactPy calls them — always from the top level of a component, in the same order. React calls Components and Hooks, Rules of Hooks

The two are one idea seen from either side. ReactPy is free to call your component whenever it likes, as often as it likes, because purity makes that safe. In return, your component gets to assume nothing about when it ran — which is why state lives in hooks rather than in variables.

docs.title: Why the rules exist
docs.text:
ReactPy renders on a server, inside one Python process that serves many connections, and re-renders a component whenever its state changes or its parent renders. Both facts are what the rules protect against.

  • Impure rendering leaks between users. A module-level dict written during a render is shared by every connection in the process. Three visitors, one cart. No error, and each page looks fine. Measured in Components and Hooks must be pure.
  • Render frequency is not yours to predict. Code that counts, accumulates, or logs in a component body runs more often than the user acts. A child re-renders every time its parent does — ReactPy has no memo bailout for components.
  • Hook state is positional. ReactPy hands out hook values from a list by index, so changing which hooks run changes which value each hook reads. The usual outcome is not an error but a component quietly reading its neighbour's state. See Rules of Hooks.

The last point is the one that surprises people coming from React. React's hook dispatcher validates call order and throws; ReactPy's does not. Several violations are tolerated silently, and one of them corrupts state with nothing logged anywhere. The rules are still exactly React's — the safety net underneath them is not.

docs.title: The rules, as a checklist
docs.text:
For a component body:

  • reads only its arguments, and values from its own hooks
  • assigns no global or module-level name
  • mutates no object it did not create during this render
  • reads no clock, random, environment, or I/O
  • starts no task, thread, or timer
  • may freely define event handlers — they run later, and may do all of the above

For a hook call site:

  • called from a component body or another hook — never an event handler, effect body, or plain function
  • at the top level of that body: not under if, for, try, and not inside a nested def that runs outside the render (an event handler, an effect callback). A nested def whose name starts with use_ and which the body calls during the render is a custom hook, and calling hooks in it is the point.
  • the same hooks, in the same order, on every render
  • no early return before a hook

use_context is the one hook that takes no slot, so it alone may be called on only some renders without shifting the others. See Rules of Hooks.

For a custom hook (use_*): everything above, plus it must not skip its own hooks on some calls.

docs.title: What ReactPy cannot check for you
docs.text:
reactpy-flake8 covers the call-site rule at build time (see Rules of Hooks), but there is no runtime assertion for hook order, and that is the one that bites silently. Two settings get you most of the way:

  • REACTPY_DEBUG=1 turns a render failure into a visible error in the model instead of a blank region, and enables the VDOM checks described in Common Props.
  • Tests are cheap precisely because of the rules: a pure component is an ordinary function — call it inside reactpy.core.layout.Layout, render it twice, assert the models are equal. No browser involved.

Everything else is review. The greppable version: any use_ call that appears below the first non-hook statement of a component body, or inside a conditional, loop, or nested function, is a defect until proven otherwise.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: You might be tempted to Instead Cache a computation in a module-level dict use_memo Keep a per-user counter in a global use_state or use_reducer Fetch data in the component body An event handler, or use_async_effect Fetch request headers with os.environ use_scope / use_location Call a hook from an event handler Call it in the body and close over the value Skip a hook when a prop is falsy Return early only after all hooks, or split into two components Loop over use_state One component per item, keyed Reach for use_effect to derive a value Compute it in the body

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
reactpy.html is how you write markup in ReactPy. It is an object whose attributes are tag constructors: html.div(...) builds a <div>, and there is no template language, no JSX, and no parser involved. 

from reactpy import html

html.div({"class": "card"}, html.h2("Title"), html.p("Body"))

That call produces a plain dict:

{
    "children": [
        {"children": ["Title"], "tagName": "h2"},
        {"children": ["Body"], "tagName": "p"},
    ],
    "attributes": {"class": "card"},
    "tagName": "div",
}

reactpy.h is the same object under a shorter name — h is html is True — so use whichever reads better in a given file. Importing both and mixing them in one module buys nothing.

docs.title: html.<tag_name>(attributes, *children)
docs.text:
Every attribute of html is a tag constructor. The common tags are declared for autocomplete, but any name works — see Any name is a tag.

  • First argument: the attributes — but only when it is a plain dict. A VdomDict, or any dict subclass, is treated as a child instead. This single rule is the most common source of confusion, and it is worth internalizing:

    html.div({"class": "card"}, html.p("Body"))  # dict -> attributes
html.div(html.p("Body"))  # no dict -> no attributes
html.div(None, html.p("Body"))  # None -> an explicit "no attributes"

    Leading None is the conventional way to say "no attributes" and keep the arguments in a predictable shape. It renders nothing.

    A VdomDict as the first argument is a child

    VdomDict is a dict subclass, and the check is for the exact plain dict type. So a VdomDict is never mistaken for attributes — even when you meant it that way:

    from reactpy.types import VdomDict

html.div(VdomDict(tagName="span"))  # -> a <span> *child* of the div

  • Remaining arguments: children, of any type Common Props accepts — strings, numbers, None, lists, dicts, components. Lists are flattened.

  • Returns: a VdomDict. Tag constructors are cached, so html.div is html.div — the same object every time. Nothing is rendered until a component returns it.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• A plain dict that is meant as an element can be read as attributes. html.div({"children": ["x"]}) produces a div with an attribute literally named children, not a child — because the first argument was a plain dict. When in doubt, pass the element as the second argument after None.
  • Void tags reject children. html.br("x") raises TypeError: 'br' nodes cannot have children. See Common Props.
  • Tags do not validate their own attributes. html.img({"scr": "typo.png"}) is accepted and renders an image with no source. There is no prop-type check; a misspelled attribute name is a silent no-op.

docs.title: html(*children) — fragments
docs.text: Calling html itself is the fragment constructor: children with no wrapper element. See Common Props — a fragment accepts key and nothing else.

docs.title: Any name is a tag
docs.text:
ReactPy does not keep a list of valid HTML tags. It converts the attribute name and sends it as the tag name, so you can reach tags the module has never declared:

You write You get html.div <div> html.data_table <data-table> html.my_widget <my-widget> html.del_ <del> html.class_ <class>

Two transformations: a trailing underscore is stripped (so you can name tags that are Python keywords, like del and class), and remaining underscores become dashes (so you can name custom elements and hyphenated tags that are not valid Python identifiers).

That makes custom elements first-class — no registration step, no wrapper component:

app.py Run 
# Any name is a tag: underscores become dashes, so this is <user-badge>.
user_badge = html.user_badge


@component
def profile(name, role):
    return html.section(
        {"class": "profile", "data-role": role},
        html.h2(name),
        # A plain string is a text child; an attribute dict is always first.
        html.p({"class": "muted"}, "Signed in as ", html.strong(name)),
        user_badge({"role": role, "label": role.title()}),
        html.footer(
            html.small(
                {"style": {"font-size": "12px", "color": "#666"}},
                "Last seen today",
            )
        ),
    )


@component
def app():
    return html.main(
        None,
        html.h1("Accounts"),
        profile("Ada", "admin"),
        profile("Linus", "viewer"),
    )

# TODO

The <user-badge> element reaches the browser as written. Whether it does anything is up to whatever defines it — a web component, an external script, or nothing at all. A tag the browser does not know renders as an unknown element: its children show up, its attributes are set, and it is laid out inline by default.

Prefer a component over a mystery tag

A custom tag is only worth it when something on the client implements it. For grouping your own markup, write a @component — it takes part in rendering, can hold state, and is checkable by a type checker.

docs.title: Tags versus components
docs.text:
Both are called the same way and both produce VDOM, and the difference is what happens next:

html.div(...) my_component(...) Returns A VdomDict, immediately A Component, rendered later by the layout Owns state No Yes — hooks belong to it Re-rendered Only when its parent returns a new value When its state changes or its parent re-renders it Defined with Provided by html @component over a function

The practical rule: a tag is for HTML elements, a component is for anything with behaviour. A <div> that has to remember something is not a div any more — it is a component that returns a div. See Your First Component.

docs.title: Nested and adjacent tags
docs.text:
Tags nest by call nesting, and read left-to-right, innermost first:

html.p(html.em("emphasized"), " and ", html.strong("bold"))

Because Python evaluates arguments eagerly, the inner call completes before the outer one runs. There is no indentation-scope or closing-tag syntax to get wrong, and no unbalanced-tag error — the structure either parses or it does not.

The one habit to build is the leading None. Without it, a first child that is a plain dict is consumed as attributes:

html.div({"tagName": "span"})  # attributes named "tagName" — not a child
html.div(None, {"tagName": "span"})  # a <span> child

A complete page reads like the HTML it produces:

app.py Run 
@component
def article_card():
    # Children are positional. The first argument is attributes only if it is a
    # plain dict, which is why a leading `None` is needed when there are no
    # attributes but the first child could look like one.
    return html.article(
        {"class": "card"},
        html.h2("Naming rules"),
        html.p(
            html.em("html.del_"),
            " is ",
            html.code("<del>"),
            ", ",
            html.code("html.data_table"),
            " is ",
            html.code("<data-table>"),
            ".",
        ),
        html.ul(
            None,
            [html.li({"key": word}, word) for word in ("class", "style", "key")],
        ),
        html.hr(),
        html.p({"class": "muted"}, "Void tags take no children."),
    )


@component
def app():
    return html.main(None, article_card(), html.br(), html.p("End of page."))

# TODO

docs.title: Lists of tags
docs.text:
A list comprehension produces children directly; give each one a key:

html.ul(None, [html.li({"key": word}, word) for word in words])

See Rendering Lists for why the key matters, and Common Props for where it lives in the dictionary.

docs.title: Classes and inline styles
docs.text:
class and className both work, and style takes a dict. Include units inside the strings — a bare number is applied by some executors and silently dropped by others:

html.p({"class": "muted"}, "...")
html.p({"style": {"font-size": "12px", "color": "#666"}}, "...")

Details, including the executor difference, are in Common Props.

docs.title: SVG
docs.text:
SVG elements live under html.svg, because their tag names collide with HTML ones (<title>, <a>, <style>):

html.svg(
    {"viewBox": "0 0 24 24", "width": "24"},
    html.svg.circle({"cx": "12", "cy": "12", "r": "10"}),
)

html.svg is itself a tag constructor, and nested names follow the same rules — trailing underscore stripped, underscores to dashes. Camel-cased SVG names are used as written, so html.svg.clipPath produces <clipPath>.

Names are not case-normalized

viewBox works because the name is forwarded exactly. Write SVG attribute names the way the spec spells them, capitals included.

docs.title: Raw HTML
docs.text:
Two different jobs get confused here. To put a raw HTML string into the page as-is, without ReactPy parsing it, use dangerouslySetInnerHTML:

html.div({"dangerouslySetInnerHTML": {"__html": "<b>bold</b>"}})

To hand ReactPy a block of HTML and have it parsed into VDOM — real elements you can then inspect and transform — use string_to_reactpy() instead, which is exported at the top of the package:

from reactpy import string_to_reactpy

string_to_reactpy("<b>bold</b>")
# {'children': ['bold'], 'tagName': 'b'}

See Convert Between VDOM and HTML for the parse direction in full, including the *transforms argument.

Never pass untrusted input to either one: dangerouslySetInnerHTML is inserted without sanitizing, and string_to_reactpy() parses whatever you give it. Note also that a dangerouslySetInnerHTML attribute suppresses children rather than raising — nothing checks the combination, the raw HTML simply wins and the children are dropped. See Common Props.

docs.title: Inspecting what a tag produced
docs.text:
A tag call is a plain dict, so print it:

>>> from reactpy import html
>>> html.li({"key": "a"}, "Item")
{'children': ['Item'], 'attributes': {'key': 'a'}, 'tagName': 'li'}

Key order can differ, and empty keys are omitted — a tag with no attributes has no "attributes" entry at all. To see what a component renders, drive it through reactpy.core.layout.Layout rather than printing the component instance, which shows only its arguments.

docs.title: Script tags
docs.text:
html.script is special-cased. It rejects event handlers:

html.script({"onLoad": handler})

ValueError: 'script' elements do not support event handlers

and it infers its own key from its content, falling back to src, so the script is not re-run on every render:

>>> html.script({"src": "/analytics.js"})
{'tagName': 'script', 'attributes': {'src': '/analytics.js', 'key': '/analytics.js'}}

Because the key drives re-execution, giving a script an explicit key is how you make it run again on purpose. As with dangerouslySetInnerHTML, keep untrusted data out of the body of a script.

docs.title: The first argument became an attribute
docs.text: If your element has an attribute named children or tagName and renders nothing, a plain dict child was read as the attributes dict. Pass None first.

docs.title: TypeError: '<tag>' nodes cannot have children.
docs.text: You passed content to a void tag. Remove the children.

docs.title: TypeError: Fragments cannot have attributes besides 'key'
docs.text: Give the fragment a real element, or move the attributes onto a child.

docs.title: An attribute has no effect
docs.text: The name is forwarded verbatim and never validated, so a typo is invisible. Print the dict and compare the key against what the browser expects. Only class/className and for/htmlFor have aliases; nothing else does.

docs.title: A numeric style does nothing
docs.text: Add the unit to the string. See Common Props.

docs.title: Tag names
docs.text: You write You get Rule html.div <div> as-is html.data_table <data-table> _ → - html.del_ <del> trailing _ stripped html.class_ <class> trailing _ stripped html.svg.clipPath <clipPath> as-is, under svg

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: Position Type Meaning first plain dict attributes, or pass None for none first (otherwise) any accepted child a child rest any accepted child children, flattened

docs.title: Accepted children
docs.text: Child Renders as str text, verbatim int / float str(value) None nothing True / False the words True / False list / tuple flattened children dict an element (needs "tagName") @component instance that component's output

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
use_async_effect is a ReactPy hook that lets you run an async def effect, and keep it running across renders. 

use_async_effect(effect)
use_async_effect(effect, dependencies=[value])

docs.title: use_async_effect(effect, dependencies=..., shield=False)
docs.text:
Call use_async_effect at the top level of your component to run an asynchronous effect. ReactPy wraps the coroutine in an asyncio.Task, so it runs on the connection's event loop rather than blocking the render.

from reactpy import use_async_effect

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• effect: An async def function taking no arguments. To run work in the background and stop it later, loop and handle cancellation — see running a long-lived effect.

  • dependencies (optional): Same four-way meaning as in use_effect, and the default is again not React's:

    Value Behaviour (verified) omitted (...) Inferred from the free variables of your closure. dependencies=[] Starts once, on mount. dependencies=[a, b] Restarts when a or b changes. dependencies=None Restarts after every render.

    Comparison is strictly_equal (core/hooks.py), not is — see Use Effect for the rule.

  • shield (optional): When True, an in-flight effect is not cancelled when the component unmounts or the effect is superseded. Default False.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: None when given the effect, or a decorator when called without one.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The effect must take zero arguments. ReactPy calls asyncio.create_task(func()) (core/hooks.py). The 1.x signature async def effect(stop): is therefore broken — and it fails silently. Verified: the component renders normally, the model carries no error, the browser shows nothing wrong; the only trace is Error in effect / TypeError: ... missing 1 required positional argument: 'stop' in the server log. If your async effect "does nothing", check the server log first.
  • There is no stop event to wait on. Cancellation is ordinary asyncio.CancelledError; a long-running effect should loop and break out of it.
  • Cancelling is one of two clean-up paths: when dependencies change, the running task is cancelled before the new one starts. The other is the function your coroutine returns — see Cleanup.
  • The default dependency behaviour is inference, not "every render". See use_effect for the full table.
  • Effects run on the server. document and window do not exist.
  • An exception raised inside the coroutine is logged on the server only — no error reaches the model or the browser.
  • The new effect cancels and awaits the previous task before starting its own (core/hooks.py), but that hand-off is best-effort: the bookkeeping that locates the previous task can miss it, so two effect coroutines can be alive at once. Measured over five runs each, with three dependency changes per run: changes spaced 0.3 s apart produced zero overlaps, anything faster produced two. Do not write an effect that assumes it is the only one running; make teardown idempotent.

docs.title: Importing use_async_effect
docs.text: from reactpy import use_async_effect

docs.title: Running a one-shot async effect
docs.text:
For a single await — a request, a slow lookup — write the coroutine straight:

@component
def stats(repo):
    data, set_data = use_state(None)

    async def effect():
        result = await fetch_stats(repo)
        set_data(result)

    use_async_effect(effect, dependencies=[repo])

    return html.p(data if data is not None else "loading...")

Setting state from the effect schedules the re-render; nothing else is needed.

docs.title: Running a long-lived effect
docs.text:
To keep work running across renders, loop and honour cancellation. This is what ReactPy's version of React's setInterval example looks like:

app.py Run 
import asyncio
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from reactpy import component, html, use_async_effect, use_state


@component
def clock():
    now, set_now = use_state(datetime.now(timezone.utc))

    async def effect():
        # Zero arguments. A long-running effect loops and honours cancellation.
        while True:
            set_now(datetime.now(timezone.utc))
            try:
                await asyncio.sleep(1)
            except asyncio.CancelledError:
                break

    use_async_effect(effect)

    return html.h1(now.strftime("%H:%M:%S"))

# TODO

The clock advances on its own — verified, one update per second. When dependencies change or the component unmounts, ReactPy cancels the task and the loop exits through CancelledError.

Do not wait for a stop event

ReactPy 1.x passed a stop event into async effects. That parameter no longer exists, and passing it is not reported anywhere the user can see. Write this:

async def effect():
    while True:
        do_work()
        try:
            await asyncio.sleep(1)
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            break

Not this:

async def effect(stop):  # 🚩 silent failure
    while not stop.is_set():
        ...

docs.title: Shielding an effect from cancellation
docs.text:
shield=True lets an in-flight effect run to completion even as the component unmounts — useful for finishing a request whose result must not be discarded:

use_async_effect(effect, dependencies=[], shield=True)

Verified: with shield=True a sleeping effect reached its completion line after the layout exited; with the default it was cancelled at that same moment. Leave this off unless you specifically want work to outlive the component, since it also means the effect keeps holding references and consuming the loop.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
Async effects have two clean-up paths, and which one applies depends on whether your coroutine finishes.

A coroutine that completes may return a clean-up function. ReactPy stores the coroutine's result (core/hooks.py, cleanup_func.current = task.result()) and runs it when the effect is next stopped — before a replacement effect starts, and again on unmount. Verified across three dependency changes and an unmount: every (start, n) was followed by its own (cleanup, n).

async def effect():
    handle = await open_connection()
    return handle.close  # runs at the next dependency change, and on unmount

A coroutine that never completes — the while True: loop — never returns, so its return value cannot be the clean-up. Cancellation is:

async def effect():
    handle = await open_connection()
    try:
        while True:
            await handle.poll()
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        handle.close()
        raise

Re-raising matters: swallowing CancelledError leaves the task in a state asyncio did not expect.

docs.title: Choosing between use_effect and use_async_effect
docs.text:
Need Use A synchronous side effect use_effect Anything await-based use_async_effect A repeating timer, polling, a subscription stream use_async_effect with a loop Work that must block the render neither — do it during render, or raise

Passing an async def to use_effect fails loudly, which is the one mismatch ReactPy does report: TypeError: use_effect does not support async functions. Use use_async_effect instead.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
use_callback is a ReactPy hook that caches a function, replacing it only when one of its listed dependencies changes. 

cached_handler = use_callback(handler, dependencies=[dep_1, dep_2])

It is the function-shaped counterpart of use_memo: same rules, same dependency behaviour, but the thing you cache is a callable rather than a value.

You probably do not need it

In React, useCallback earns its place by keeping a child from re-rendering behind memo and by keeping effect dependencies from thrashing. Neither reason applies to ReactPy. There is no render bailout and no memo, and a function you define in the component body already counts as an unchanged dependency, because ReactPy compares local functions by their code rather than by identity. So the effect-churn problem useCallback exists to solve does not occur here.

What it does give you is a genuinely stable function object, which matters only when the function leaves ReactPy and something else keys on its identity — a subscription registry, an event bus, a cached table. If none of that describes your code, write a plain def and skip this page.

docs.title: use_callback(function, dependencies)
docs.text:
Call use_callback at the top level of your component to cache an event handler or other callback.

from reactpy import use_callback

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• function: The function you want to keep. It must be pure in the sense that matters here: same closure, same behaviour.

  • dependencies: The values the function reads. ReactPy replaces the cached function when any of them changes. Three shapes, identical to use_memo:

    You pass Meaning dependencies=[a, b] Replace the function when a or b changes. omitted (the default) Infer the dependencies from the function's closure. dependencies=None Return a new function on every render — no caching at all.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: The cached function — either the one from a previous render, or, if a dependency changed, the one you just passed in.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The function you pass is not discarded, it is stored. ReactPy does not call it; it keeps the object. That is why caching a function that closes over state can hand you an old closure — see A cached handler sees stale values.
  • dependencies=[] pins the function forever. The same object comes back on every render, including the one holding the values it closed over on the first render. This is the single most common use_callback bug, and ReactPy will not warn you.
  • Listing a dependency you read is not optional. Forgetting one produces a handler that quietly acts on outdated values. Nothing checks this for you.
  • Stable identity does not mean stable behaviour. A function can be the same object across renders and still be wrong, because identity was the point and the closure went stale. Cache identity when something external needs identity; do not use it as a performance gesture.
  • Comparison follows strictly_equal, not identity — see the equivalent caveat in use_memo: same type first, code comparison for local functions, == otherwise.
  • The decorated name is the function, not a wrapper. @use_callback(dependencies=[x]) receives your function and returns a function, so the name still calls fine — unlike use_memo, where the name becomes the value.
  • Like every hook, call it only at the top level — never in a loop, a conditional, or after an early return.

docs.title: When a stable identity matters
docs.text:
Here is the case use_callback is actually for. The component subscribes to a bus that lives outside ReactPy. That bus stores handlers in a list and skips duplicates by identity — so a new function object on each render registers another handler, and every handler receives each message.

Press Re-render three times. handlers registered stays at 1, because the handler really is the same object each time. Press Publish and it is delivered once. Replace the use_callback line with a plain def and the same interaction registers four handlers.

app.pydata.py Run 
@component
def listener():
    renders, set_renders = use_state(0)
    heard, set_heard = use_state(0)

    # The registry lives outside ReactPy, so nothing deduplicates it for you.
    # A plain `def` here would be a brand new function object on every render,
    # and the registry would therefore collect another handler each time --
    # all of which receive every message. Pinning the identity keeps exactly
    # one handler, however often this component renders.
    handler = use_callback(
        lambda message: set_heard(lambda previous: previous + 1), dependencies=[]
    )

    def subscribe():
        bus.subscribe(handler)

    use_effect(subscribe, dependencies=None)

    return html.div(
        html.p(f"renders: {renders}"),
        html.p(f"handlers registered: {len(bus.handlers)}"),
        html.p(f"this component heard: {heard}"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_renders(renders + 1)}, "Re-render"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: bus.publish("ping")}, "Publish"),
    )

"""A stand-in for any registry that lives outside ReactPy.

This is the shape of code where a callback's identity actually matters: the
registry is ordinary Python, so nothing deduplicates it for you -- it stores
handlers by identity, and a *new* function object on each render means a new
entry each render.
"""


class Bus:
    def __init__(self):
        self.handlers = []
        self.handled = []

    def subscribe(self, handler):
        # `in` on a list of plain functions compares by identity, which is
        # exactly what a new `def` per render changes.
        if handler not in self.handlers:
            self.handlers.append(handler)

    def publish(self, message):
        for handler in list(self.handlers):
            handler(message)


bus = Bus()

# TODO

Note the heard updater: set_heard(lambda previous: previous + 1). It reads no state, which is what lets this handler keep an empty dependency list honestly — an updater function gets the current value at the moment the setter runs, so the handler does not need to close over anything.

docs.title: A cached handler sees stale values
docs.text:
The notes app below caches a handler with dependencies=[] while the handler reads draft. ReactPy keeps the first function, which closed over an empty draft, so every click adds a blank note no matter what you type.

app.py Run 
@component
def notes():
    notes_list, set_notes_list = use_state([])
    draft, set_draft = use_state("")

    # `draft` is read here, but `dependencies=[]` promises the function never
    # changes -- so ReactPy keeps handing back the *first* function, which
    # closed over an empty `draft`. Each click adds a blank note no matter what
    # you typed. Listing what the handler reads is what fixes it.
    add_note = use_callback(
        lambda event=None: set_notes_list([*notes_list, draft]),
        dependencies=[],
    )

    return html.div(
        html.h1("Notes"),
        html.ul(
            [
                html.li({"key": str(i)}, note or "(blank)")
                for i, note in enumerate(notes_list)
            ]
        ),
        html.input(
            {
                "value": draft,
                "onChange": lambda event: set_draft(event["target"]["value"]),
            }
        ),
        html.button({"onClick": add_note}, "Add note"),
    )

# TODO

Type something and press Add note: the list gains (blank). The handler is working perfectly — on the render it was created on.

docs.title: Listing what the handler reads
docs.text:
The fix is to name the values the function reads. Now the cached function is replaced whenever notes_list or draft changes, so a click always sees what is currently in the box — while the identity still stays put between changes.

app.py Run 
@component
def notes():
    notes_list, set_notes_list = use_state([])
    draft, set_draft = use_state("")

    # List what the handler reads and the cached function is replaced exactly
    # when those values change: the click always sees the current draft, while
    # the identity still stays put between changes.
    add_note = use_callback(
        lambda event=None: set_notes_list([*notes_list, draft]),
        dependencies=[notes_list, draft],
    )

    return html.div(
        html.h1("Notes"),
        html.ul(
            [
                html.li({"key": str(i)}, note or "(blank)")
                for i, note in enumerate(notes_list)
            ]
        ),
        html.input(
            {
                "value": draft,
                "onChange": lambda event: set_draft(event["target"]["value"]),
            }
        ),
        html.button({"onClick": add_note}, "Add note"),
    )

# TODO

Type something and press Add note: the text lands. These two files differ by one line; the behaviour difference is the whole point.

docs.title: Omitting the dependency list
docs.text: Leave out dependencies and ReactPy infers them from the function's closure, exactly as it does for use_memo and use_effect. For a handler that reads component state this is usually what you want, and it removes the "forgot a dependency" class of bug. Omitting is not the same as dependencies=[] — the inferred list is built from what the function actually reads, which is rarely empty.

docs.title: My handler acts on old values
docs.text: You cached it with an empty or incomplete dependency list. The function is the same object, and so is everything it closed over. Either list the values it reads, or stop the value from being read at all by using an updater — set_items(lambda previous: [*previous, new]) instead of set_items([*items, new]).

docs.title: My handler never fires
docs.text: Check the attribute name. {"on_click": handler} renders without complaint, lands in eventHandlers, and is never called — the client registers a DOM listener for the key with on stripped, so the underscore spelling subscribes to an event named _click that no browser ever fires. The key must be the DOM event name in camelCase ("onClick"), and the value must be your function, not a call to it. A wrong name is invisible: the only difference is that nothing happens.

docs.title: I still get a new function every render
docs.text:
• You passed dependencies=None, which means exactly that.
  • A dependency is rebuilt each render and does not compare equal — a plain class instance without __eq__, for instance.
  • The function is defined outside the component and you expect it to be cached; use_callback caches what you hand it, per component instance.

docs.title: Do I need this to stop a child re-rendering?
docs.text: No — that mechanism does not exist in ReactPy. See the note at the top of the page: children re-render whenever their parent does, regardless of prop or handler identity.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
use_connection is a ReactPy hook that returns the Connection object describing the websocket your component is rendering into. 

connection = use_connection()

Each connected browser tab has its own. The object carries three things: the ASGI scope of the websocket, the location the browser reports, and the server's object mediating the connection.

docs.title: use_connection()
docs.text:
Call it at the top level of a component. It takes no arguments.

from reactpy import use_connection

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
A reactpy.types.Connection dataclass with three fields:

  • scope: The ASGI scope of the websocket — the same dict use_scope returns.
  • location: A Location describing the page the browser is on — the same object use_location() returns.
  • carrier: The object mediating the connection. What it is depends on the executor; under the ASGI executors it is a ReactPyWebsocket. Capture type(connection.carrier).__name__ rather than assuming.

Import the type with from reactpy.types import Connection; it is not exported from the reactpy namespace.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• This is a read-only view. Connection has no deliver, no send, no close, no id — verified against the class. You cannot push a message to this client from here; communicate through state, effects, and event handlers. The carrier object under the ASGI executors is an internal ReactPyWebsocket, not a supported API to call into.
  • scope and location are live, mutable objects, not copies. Writing into connection.scope changes what every other read sees. Treat both as read-only.
  • There is one per connection, not per render. Each connected tab gets its own — verified: two concurrent clients saw distinct scopes and distinct locations — but within one tab the same object comes back on every render.

  • It needs a live connection. Two distinct failures:

    • Called outside any component render → RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout?
    • Called inside a plain Layout render with no provider → RuntimeError: No backend established a connection.

    Both messages are verbatim. In practice the second is the one you meet in tests; see injecting a connection in tests. - It does not exist under client-side rendering. ReactPyCsr runs components without a Connection at all, so the hook raises there even though Python is in the browser. Verified in Chrome. - Like every hook, call it only at the top level.

docs.title: Who is connected
docs.text:
Each field answers a different question, and mixing them up is the usual source of confusion.

app.py Run 
@component
def connection_report():
    connection = use_connection()

    # Three things, three sources: `scope` is what the ASGI server received,
    # `location` is the URL the browser reported, `carrier` is the object
    # mediating the connection (a websocket for the ASGI executors).
    return html.div(
        html.h1("Who is connected"),
        html.p(f"peer: {connection.scope['client']}"),
        html.p(f"page: {connection.location.path}"),
        html.p(f"protocol: {connection.scope['type']}"),
        html.p(f"carrier: {type(connection.carrier).__name__}"),
    )

# TODO

scope['client'] is what the server saw when the websocket opened. location.path is what the browser reported. They are independent sources, which is why the page path is not in the scope — see use_location for why that matters.

docs.title: Injecting a connection in tests
docs.text:
Components that use any of the connection hooks fail in a bare Layout render. For a unit test, build the Connection yourself and wrap the component in the provider — ConnectionContext is meant to be set by the backend at the root of an app, and a test is a backend.

import asyncio

from reactpy.core.hooks import ConnectionContext
from reactpy.core.layout import Layout
from reactpy.types import Connection, Location

from .app import page  # the component under test

connection = Connection(
    scope={"type": "websocket", "client": ("127.0.0.1", 5000)},
    location=Location(path="/reports", query_string="?tab=2"),
    carrier=None,
)


def test_page():
    async def render():
        async with Layout(ConnectionContext(page(), value=connection)) as layout:
            update = await layout.render()
        return str(update["model"])

    rendered = asyncio.run(render())
    assert "/reports" in rendered  # came from the injected Location

carrier can be anything — None is fine, since nothing in a unit test dispatches over it. Note that ConnectionContext lives in reactpy.core.hooks rather than the public reactpy namespace: it is deliberately the backend's knob, and in a test your code is the backend.

The hooks consume no hook slot

All three connection hooks ultimately call use_context, which reads the provider without reserving a hook slot. Unlike use_state or use_effect, they are safe to call conditionally or on only some renders; they will not shift other hooks' state. Verified: a component calling use_connection() only on even renders re-rendered cleanly across five renders.

docs.title: RuntimeError: No backend established a connection.
docs.text:
No ConnectionContext was set. Under ReactPy or ReactPyMiddleware it is set for you once the websocket opens, so in production this means the component rendered somewhere the executor does not cover — most commonly a plain Layout render, a reactpy_to_string call, or a ReactPyCsr page. Either inject one as above, or make the component tolerate its absence:

try:
    connection = use_connection()
except RuntimeError:
    return html.p("(not connected yet)")

docs.title: RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout?
docs.text: You called the hook outside a render — at module level, in a plain function the component calls before rendering, or directly in your test body. Hooks only work while a component is rendering inside a Layout.

docs.title: connection.carrier is None in my test
docs.text: Correct — you passed None, and nothing reads it. Only the executor's own plumbing touches the carrier.

docs.title: I need to send something to this specific client
docs.text: There is no supported way to reach a single connection from a component. State changes re-render that client's own components; anything beyond that is outside the scope of these hooks.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
use_context is a ReactPy hook that reads a value provided by a component higher in the tree, without every component in between having to pass it along. 

value = use_context(SomeContext)

Context is for values a whole subtree needs and the middle of the tree does not: a theme, the current user, the active locale, a store. If a component would only forward a prop to its children, context removes both the prop and the component's reason to exist.

docs.title: use_context(context)
docs.text:
Call it at the top level of a component, passing the context object you created with create_context.

from reactpy import use_context

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: • context: The object returned by create_context. It is matched by identity, so the same object must be used on both the provider and the reader — import it from one place.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: The value of the nearest context provider above the component. With no provider anywhere above, it returns the default given to create_context.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Reading context is not a subscription that spares renders. When a provider re-renders with a new value, its children re-render — which they would have anyway, since ReactPy re-renders children unconditionally. Context hands you the new value; it does not narrow the work. See What context does not do.
  • It returns the default, not None, when nothing provides it. create_context("light") yields "light" to an unprovided reader, so a component renders on its own without a wrapper. Pick a default that makes sense standalone, or None plus an explicit fallback branch.
  • Call it during the render, not from an effect body. An effect runs later, in its own task, where no hook is active; calling use_context there raises RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout? Read it in the component and let the closure carry the value in — see Reading context inside an effect.
  • The context object must be hashable and must be the same object. Passing something else raises: TypeError: <x> is not a Context for a class or string, TypeError: unhashable type: 'dict' if you hand it a dict or list. Two create_context calls over the same default are two unrelated contexts.
  • A None default narrows the type. create_context(None) infers a value type of None, so a type checker rejects value=[...]. Annotate the name to widen it: Cart: Context[list[str] | None] = create_context(None).
  • Like every hook, call it only at the top level. Unusually, context is safe to call conditionally — it reserves no hook slot, so unlike use_state it cannot shift other hooks' state.

docs.title: Creating and providing a context
docs.text:
A context is created once, at module level, with create_context:

from reactpy import create_context

Theme = create_context("light")

What comes back is an ordinary function, and calling it is the provider: pass the children positionally and the value as a keyword.

Theme(child_a, child_b, value="dark")

There is no Theme.Provider — calling the context is the only form. The provider renders a nameless fragment around its children, so it adds nothing to the output.

The value= keyword is optional; omit it and the default from create_context is used. A key= keyword is also accepted, with the same meaning as on any other element.

docs.title: Passing data deeply
docs.text:
swatch needs the theme. toolbar does not — it renders swatch and never mentions it. Without context, toolbar would take a theme argument purely to forward it, and every component added in between would inherit that obligation.

Press Switch to dark: the provider gets a new value, and the component far below reads it.

app.py Run 
# One context per concept, created once at module level. The argument is the
# value descendants get when nothing provides one -- a sensible default means
# a component can render before any provider exists.
Theme = create_context("light")


@component
def swatch():
    # Reads whatever the nearest provider above it supplied. It takes no props:
    # the value arrives without anything in between having to pass it along.
    theme = use_context(Theme)
    return html.div(
        html.p(f"theme: {theme}"),
        html.div({"style": {"background": theme, "height": "2rem"}}, ""),
    )


@component
def toolbar():
    # A component in the middle. It neither receives nor cares about `theme`;
    # it only has to render its children for them to reach the provider above.
    return html.div(html.h2("Toolbar"), swatch())


@component
def app():
    theme, set_theme = use_state("light")
    return html.div(
        Theme(toolbar(), value=theme),
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": lambda event: set_theme(
                    "dark" if theme == "light" else "light"
                )
            },
            f"Switch to {'dark' if theme == 'light' else 'light'}",
        ),
    )
