docs.title: Choosing a default
docs.text:
The default is what a component sees when no provider is above it, which is exactly the situation in a unit test or a standalone render. Make it something the component can handle.

cart_badge below copes with either — rendered bare it says the cart is unavailable, wrapped in the provider it counts the items.

app.py Run 
from reactpy import component, create_context, html, use_context
from reactpy.types import Context

# The annotation is what lets the value be a list *or* the None default. Without
# it, create_context(None) fixes the value type to None and a type checker then
# rejects `value=[...]`.
Cart: Context[list[str] | None] = create_context(None)


@component
def cart_badge():
    # With no provider above, use_context returns the default given to
    # create_context. Choosing that default well is what lets a component
    # render -- or be tested -- on its own, with no provider wrapper.
    items = use_context(Cart)
    if items is None:
        return html.p("cart: not available")
    return html.p(f"cart: {len(items)} item(s)")


@component
def shop():
    return html.div(cart_badge())


@component
def shop_with_cart():
    return Cart(shop(), value=["widget", "gadget", "gizmo"])

# TODO

Note the type annotation on Cart. Because the default is None, without the annotation a type checker infers the value type as None and rejects Cart(shop(), value=["widget", ...]).

docs.title: Nesting providers
docs.text:
The provider nearest above the reader wins, and sibling subtrees are independent. "Above" means in the tree that renders it, so the reader has to live inside a child component — reading in the enclosing body runs before the provider is rendered:

Theme = create_context("light")


@component
def swatch():
    # A child component: it renders after the provider above it has registered.
    return html.p(use_context(Theme))


@component
def page():
    return Theme(
        swatch(),                                     # "outer"
        Theme(swatch(), value="inner"),               # "inner"
        value="outer",
    )

Verified: the first reads "outer", the second "inner"; two sibling providers with different values each see their own.

Do not read the context in the same body that renders the provider

@component
def page():
    return Theme(
        html.p(use_context(Theme)),   # "light", not "outer"
        value="outer",
    )

Arguments are evaluated while page() runs, and the provider registers its value only when the layout later renders it. Both reads here return the create_context("light") default. Move the read into a child component. The same rule explains why reading inside an effect fails (below).

Removing a provider returns its descendants to the default. What actually produces that is the remount: a provider is a component node in the tree, so dropping it moves its children to a different position and ReactPy rebuilds them — verified, a counter below a removed provider went back to 0 along with its value. Do not lean on that. core/_life_cycle_hook.py, set_current only ever merges the parent's providers into a hook (_context_providers.update(...)) and nothing prunes the dict, so a component that survives a render keeps whatever it inherited. If you need a guaranteed reset, change the child's "key".

docs.title: Reading context inside an effect
docs.text:
Effects run in their own task, outside any component render, so no hook is active there and use_context will not work. Read it in the component and use the local:

app.py Run 
Config = create_context({"endpoint": "https://api.example"})


@component
def status():
    # Read the context HERE, during the render. An effect body runs later, in
    # its own task, where no hook is active -- calling use_context there fails
    # with `RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active.` Capture the value in a
    # local and let the closure carry it into the effect.
    config = use_context(Config)

    def on_mount():
        print(f"polling {config['endpoint']}")

    use_effect(on_mount, dependencies=[config])
    return html.p(f"endpoint: {config['endpoint']}")

# TODO

Putting use_context(Config) inside on_mount instead raises RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout? — and since an effect error is logged only on the server, it is easy to miss.

docs.title: What context does not do
docs.text:
Context solves plumbing: it moves a value past components that do not care about it. It is not a performance feature.

  • It does not stop children from re-rendering. ReactPy has no render bailout, so when the provider re-renders, everything below it re-renders too. A component reading a context whose value did not change still re-renders — verified: toggling a theme re-ran the bodies of both a context reader and an unrelated sibling.
  • It does not make a value reactive by itself. The value changes because the component that renders the provider re-rendered with a new one. If nothing re-renders the provider, readers keep seeing the old value.
  • It does not replace state. Context carries values down. To let a component change a shared value, put the state in a common ancestor and pass the setter down alongside it — or move to a reducer, see use_reducer.

For a value that only one component's subtree uses, a prop is simpler and easier to trace. Reach for context when the value genuinely crosses several levels that have no use for it.

docs.title: Readers always get the default
docs.text:
Usually one of:

  • The provider is not above the reader in the tree. Theme(child, value=...) must be an ancestor — calling it and discarding the result provides nothing.
  • The provider and the reader hold different context objects. Two create_context calls are different contexts even with the same default, so create it once and import it.
  • The provider's value= never changes, so readers keep seeing the value from the render that set it.

docs.title: RuntimeError: No life cycle hook is active. Are you rendering in a layout?
docs.text: You called use_context outside a render — from an effect body, from a plain function called before the component runs, or directly in a test. Move the call into the component body.

docs.title: TypeError: ... is not a Context
docs.text: You passed something other than the result of create_context — often the provider instead of the context (use_context(Theme(child, value="x"))), or the class of a value rather than a context.

docs.title: My type checker rejects the provider's value
docs.text: The default narrowed the type. Annotate the module-level name with Context[<your type> | None], as in the default-value example above.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
use_debug_value is a ReactPy hook that writes a message to the server log whenever it changes, for the component that calls it. 

use_debug_value(message, dependencies)

ReactPy components run on the server, so there is no DevTools panel to label. This is the equivalent: a value that shows up in your server's log output, tagged with the component that produced it, printed only when it differs from the last thing printed.

It needs debug mode, and logs go to the server

Nothing happens unless REACTPY_DEBUG is on. Set it before importing ReactPy — REACTPY_DEBUG=1 python app.py, or os.environ["REACTPY_DEBUG"] = "1" at the top of your entry point. Output goes through the standard logging module under the reactpy.core.hooks logger, so it lands wherever your logging configuration sends it, not in the browser console. A reader who expects DevTools will conclude the hook is broken; it is not.

docs.title: use_debug_value(message, dependencies)
docs.text:
Call it at the top level of a component, or at the top level of one of your own hooks.

from reactpy import use_debug_value

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• message: The value to log, or a function of no arguments that produces it. Pass a function when building the message costs something — ReactPy memoizes it, so it re-runs only when its dependencies change.

  • dependencies: Only meaningful with a function message. Same three shapes as every other hook that takes them:

    You pass Meaning dependencies=[a, b] Rebuild the message when a or b changes. omitted (the default) Infer them from the function's closure. dependencies=None Rebuild the message on every render.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Silent without debug mode. With REACTPY_DEBUG off, the hook logs nothing. Whether it still builds the message is decided by the dependency comparison, not by debug mode: the message is produced through use_memo, so a builder whose dependencies never change runs once and its result is discarded on every later render. A builder that closes over changing state runs every render, debug or no debug. If the build is expensive, control it with the dependency argument — do not assume the hook skipped it, and do not assume it ran.
  • "Changed" means !=, not identity. Unlike every other hook, which compares dependencies with strictly_equal, this one compares the new message against the previous one with plain !=. So a freshly constructed {"kind": "rows"} logs once and then stays quiet, because it compares equal to what was logged last time. Verified.
  • The comparison runs on every render, on the value you supply. For a large or slow-to-compare object that is a real cost, paid whether or not anything gets logged. This is the one hook where the docstring's performance note is worth taking literally.
  • An uncomparable message breaks the component. If message != previous raises, the exception is not caught: it surfaces as a render error in the model. A class with a __eq__ that raises will fail the component, so keep messages to plain data — strings, numbers, dicts, lists.
  • The value is memoized like any other hook value. With a stable message, the builder function runs once; with a message that changes each render, it runs each render. Measured across four renders: stable → 1 call, changing → 4 calls.
  • Like every hook, call it only at the top level — never in a loop, a conditional, or after an early return.

docs.title: Labelling a custom hook
docs.text:
The useful case. When a component calls three of your own hooks, a log line that says only shop(...) tells you nothing; a message naming what the hook holds tells you which hook is behaving oddly, and when.

Run this with debug on and press Add item. Each add logs one line through the reactpy.core.hooks logger, prefixed with the component and its id:

shop(7f7ef6f0d540) 0 item(s): -
shop(7f7ef6f0d540) 1 item(s): item 1
shop(7f7ef6f0d540) 2 item(s): item 1, item 2
shop(7f7ef6f0d540) 3 item(s): item 1, item 2, item 3

Pressing a button that leaves the cart alone logs nothing, because the message did not change.

app.py Run 
def use_cart():
    """A custom hook: it holds the cart and reports what it holds."""
    items, set_items = use_state([])

    # Logged to the server as `use_cart's component(...) <message>` whenever the
    # message differs from the last one logged. A plain string here would be
    # built on every render; reading state makes it change only when it should.
    use_debug_value(f"{len(items)} item(s): {', '.join(items) or '-'}")

    def add(event=None):
        set_items([*items, f"item {len(items) + 1}"])

    return items, add


@component
def shop():
    items, add = use_cart()
    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"Cart ({len(items)})"),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": i}, item) for i, item in enumerate(items)]),
        html.button({"onClick": add}, "Add item"),
    )

# TODO

docs.title: Passing a function as the message
docs.text:
If producing the message is more than string formatting, pass a function and let ReactPy memoize it. The report below finds the highest score to build its label; that walk happens once per distinct rows, not once per render.

Run it with debug on and press Add row:

report(7f7ef6f0da80) 1 rows, best=ada:91
report(7f7ef6f0da80) 2 rows, best=ada:91
report(7f7ef6f0da80) 3 rows, best=ada:91
app.py Run 
@component
def report():
    rows, set_rows = use_state([{"name": "ada", "score": 91}])

    # Pass a function when turning the message into text is not free. ReactPy
    # memoizes it like any other hook, so it re-runs only when what it reads
    # changes -- and not at all on renders that would not have logged anything.
    def describe():
        best = max(rows, key=lambda row: row["score"])
        return f"{len(rows)} rows, best={best['name']}:{best['score']}"

    use_debug_value(describe)

    def add_row(event=None):
        set_rows([*rows, {"name": f"row {len(rows)}", "score": len(rows) * 7}])

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"{len(rows)} rows"),
        html.button({"onClick": add_row}, "Add row"),
    )

# TODO

Keep the message honest about what it reads. A function that reads no state is computed once and then logs nothing ever again, which usually reads as "the hook stopped working" rather than as correct memoization.

docs.title: Nothing is logged
docs.text:
Almost always debug mode. The REACTPY_DEBUG environment variable is read when reactpy.config is first imported, so setting os.environ after ReactPy is already imported has no effect — start the process with REACTPY_DEBUG=1, or set the variable before importing anything from reactpy.

The option object can also be flipped at any point, which is the version that works from inside a test or a REPL:

from reactpy.config import REACTPY_DEBUG

REACTPY_DEBUG.current = True

If debug is on and you still see nothing, the logger is being filtered. ReactPy logs at DEBUG level under reactpy.core.hooks; a configuration that shows only warnings will hide these lines.

docs.title: It logs on every render
docs.text: Your message changes every render. A timestamp, id(self), a freshly built object compared by identity, or a counter you increment during rendering all do this. Make the message describe state rather than the render.

docs.title: It stopped logging
docs.text: The message has not changed since the last line, which is the hook working as designed. If you expected a change, either the value genuinely did not change or your function is memoized on dependencies that never move — pass dependencies=None briefly to confirm which.

docs.title: My component fails to render after adding it
docs.text: You passed something whose != raises. The comparison is not guarded, so the exception becomes a render error. Pass plain data instead, and format it lazily in a function if it is large.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
use_effect is a ReactPy hook that lets you synchronize a component with an external system. 

use_effect(effect)
use_effect(effect, dependencies=[value])

docs.title: use_effect(effect, dependencies=...)
docs.text:
Call use_effect at the top level of your component to run an effect after rendering.

from reactpy import use_effect

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• effect: A function taking no arguments. ReactPy calls it after the component renders. It may return a clean-up function (also taking no arguments), which ReactPy runs before the next time this effect runs and again when the component unmounts.

    The effect must be pure, and it must not be declared async def — ReactPy raises for that; use use_async_effect instead.

  • dependencies (optional): Controls when the effect re-runs. Unlike React, this argument has four distinct settings, and the default is not React's:

    Value Behaviour (verified) omitted (...) Inferred. ReactPy reads the free variables of your closure (core/hooks.py, _try_to_infer_closure_values) and re-runs when any of them changes. A closure that reads nothing runs once. dependencies=[] Runs once, after mount. dependencies=[a, b] Runs when a or b changes. dependencies=None Runs after every render.

    "Changes" means strictly_equal (core/hooks.py), not is: the two values must share a type, two locally-defined functions or lambdas are compared by bytecode, and everything else falls through to == with is as the last resort. A rebuilt list or dict with equal contents does not re-run the effect. Use Memo documents the same function in full.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: None when given the effect, or a decorator when called without one.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The default is inference, not "every render". In React, omitting the dependency array means the effect runs after every render. In ReactPy it means "re-run when the variables my closure reads change". Code ported from React will therefore behave differently — pass dependencies=None if you really want every-render behaviour, though usually you want to be explicit instead.
  • Inference is structural, not declared, and it does not compare by id. A closure that happens to read an extra local variable gains an extra dependency, and the comparison is strictly_equal — type, then bytecode for local functions, then == — so a rebuilt-but-equal container counts as unchanged. If the effect runs more or less often than you expect, look at which names it actually reads, and then at how those values compare.
  • Effects run on the server, after rendering, not in the browser. There is no DOM to touch: document and window do not exist here. There is no document or window to reach for, and no ReactPy equivalent of attaching a listener to a node — see Responding to Events for the supported way to react to the browser.
  • Children's effects run before their parent's, and siblings run in reverse order. Verified output: ['child effect b', 'child effect a', 'parent effect']. Two effects in one component run in declaration order. Do not rely on React's parent-first or source-order guarantees.
  • Passing async def to use_effect fails loudly: TypeError: use_effect does not support async functions. Use use_async_effect instead. The error lands in the model's error field and the component stops rendering.
  • An exception raised inside an effect body is logged on the server only; the model carries no error and the UI looks unchanged. Check the server log.
  • Effects are not a substitute for computing values. Derive them during render or with use_memo.
  • There is no use_layout_effect, use_insertion_effect, or use_imperative_handle. Nothing runs synchronously during the render phase.

docs.title: Importing use_effect
docs.text: from reactpy import use_effect

docs.title: Describing an effect
docs.text:
Pass the setup function directly:

app.pydata.py Run 
@component
def live_feed():
    latest, set_latest = use_state("waiting for a message...")

    def effect():
        # Runs once on mount; the returned function runs on unmount.
        unsubscribe = ticker.subscribe("news", set_latest)
        return unsubscribe

    use_effect(effect, dependencies=[])

    return html.div(
        html.h1(latest),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: ticker.publish("news", "Hello!")},
            "Publish",
        ),
    )

"""A stand-in for any external system with subscribe/unsubscribe semantics."""


class Ticker:
    def __init__(self):
        self.topics = {}

    def subscribe(self, topic, callback):
        self.topics.setdefault(topic, []).append(callback)

        def unsubscribe():
            self.topics[topic].remove(callback)

        return unsubscribe

    def publish(self, topic, message):
        for callback in list(self.topics.get(topic, [])):
            callback(message)

    def count(self):
        return sum(len(v) for v in self.topics.values())


ticker = Ticker()

# TODO

Or use it as a decorator, which is equivalent:

@use_effect
def effect():
    print("mounted")

docs.title: Telling ReactPy when to re-run the effect
docs.text:
Pass a dependency list to re-run only when something relevant changes:

app.pydata.py Run 
@component
def live_feed():
    topic, set_topic = use_state("news")
    latest, set_latest = use_state("")

    def effect():
        # Re-runs whenever `topic` changes; the returned clean-up unsubscribes
        # the previous topic first, so you never keep two subscriptions.
        unsubscribe = ticker.subscribe(topic, set_latest)
        return unsubscribe

    use_effect(effect, dependencies=[topic])

    return html.div(
        html.p(f"Subscribed to: {topic}"),
        html.p(latest or "(nothing yet)"),
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": lambda event: set_topic(
                    "sports" if topic == "news" else "news"
                )
            },
            "Switch topic",
        ),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: ticker.publish(topic, "ping")}, "Publish"
        ),
    )

"""A stand-in for any external system with subscribe/unsubscribe semantics."""


class Ticker:
    def __init__(self):
        self.topics = {}

    def subscribe(self, topic, callback):
        self.topics.setdefault(topic, []).append(callback)

        def unsubscribe():
            self.topics[topic].remove(callback)

        return unsubscribe

    def publish(self, topic, message):
        for callback in list(self.topics.get(topic, [])):
            callback(message)

    def count(self):
        return sum(len(v) for v in self.topics.values())


ticker = Ticker()

# TODO

Switching topic tears down the old subscription before creating the new one — verified, the subscriber count stays at 1 across switches and drops to 0 on unmount.

docs.title: Omitting the dependencies argument
docs.text:
use_effect(effect)               # inferred from what the closure reads

The example below makes inference visible. The effect reads count but not label, so renaming re-renders the component without re-running the effect:

app.py Run 
@component
def logger():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)
    label, set_label = use_state("counter")
    runs, set_runs = use_state([])

    def effect():
        # No `dependencies` argument, so ReactPy infers them from the names
        # this closure reads. Only `count` is a real dependency here -- the
        # setter is stable, and `label` is not read at all. So pressing
        # Rename re-renders the component but does NOT re-run this effect.
        set_runs(lambda previous: [*previous, f"effect ran with count={count}"])

    use_effect(effect)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(count),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_count(count + 1)}, "Add 1"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_label(label + "!")}, "Rename"),
        html.p(f"Label: {label}"),
        html.ul([html.li({"key": i}, line) for i, line in enumerate(runs)]),
    )

# TODO

Pressing Rename twice adds no new log line — verified. Be aware this works because of which names the closure reads; it is implicit, so many teams prefer to spell the list out.

docs.title: Passing an empty dependency array
docs.text:
use_effect(effect, dependencies=[])   # once, after mount

For mount-only work — subscribing, starting a timer, reading a config — say so explicitly.

docs.title: Passing None
docs.text:
use_effect(effect, dependencies=None)  # after every render

This is the closest ReactPy gets to React's "no array" behaviour. It re-runs the effect after every render, verified. Reach for it rarely: it usually means the effect is doing work that belongs in render or in use_memo.

docs.title: Adding clean-up
docs.text:
Return a function from the effect. ReactPy calls it before the next run of that effect and when the component unmounts:

app.py Run 
@component
def app():
    connected, set_connected = use_state(False)

    return html.div(
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_connected(not connected)},
            "Connect" if not connected else "Disconnect",
        ),
        *([] if not connected else [connection()]),
    )

# TODO

Connecting and disconnecting runs the pair in order — verified: connected, disconnected, connected across connect / disconnect / reconnect.

Clean-up is the difference between a leak and a working app

Because ReactPy components live in long-lived server processes, a forgotten subscription is not a brief flash of stale data — it is a permanent leak that outlives every browser tab that opened it. Every subscribe, every timer, every held connection needs a clean-up function.

docs.title: Effects and the request lifecycle
docs.text:
An effect runs in the connection's own task, after the render that scheduled it. It can call setters, and those schedule further renders. Two consequences:

  • An effect that awaits gives the event loop control. Long awaits belong in use_async_effect, which is built for it.
  • Setting state from an effect that depends on that same state loops forever. If an effect seems to spin, read what it sets and what it depends on.

docs.title: Reading the latest state inside an effect
docs.text:
An effect closes over the render that created it. If it then runs for a long time — an interval callback, a subscription handler — it can act on values that are no longer current. Two ways to handle it:

  • Put the value in the dependency list, so a change tears the effect down and starts a new one with fresh values.
  • Keep the value in a use_ref box and read ref.current when you need it. The box persists across renders, so readers see the newest value — as long as the write happens somewhere legal. Do not assign ref.current from the component body: a render-phase write is exactly the impurity Use Ref warns about, and ReactPy has no Strict Mode to catch it. Assign it where the value is already produced — the event handler that changed it — or in its own effect, which runs after the render.

If an effect reads state it does not declare, that is usually a sign the effect should be re-created when that state changes — reach for the dependency list first.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
use_location is a ReactPy hook that returns the URL the browser is currently showing. 

location = use_location()

Your components run on the server and know nothing about the browser unless you ask. use_location is how you ask: it reports the page the visitor is looking at, so navigation, breadcrumbs, and query-driven views can be built from it.

docs.title: use_location()
docs.text:
Call it at the top level of a component. It takes no arguments.

from reactpy import use_location

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
A reactpy.types.Location — a plain dataclass with two fields, both required:

  • path: The URL path, mirroring window.location.pathname. For example "/reports/2024/q1".
  • query_string: The query string, mirroring window.location.search — including the leading "?". For example "?tab=2&user=ada", or "" when there is no query.

It is mutable and compares by value. Import the type with from reactpy.types import Location; it is not exported from the reactpy namespace.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The "?" is part of the value. parse_qs(location.query_string) mis-parses the first parameter, producing a key "?tab" instead of "tab". Strip it: parse_qs(location.query_string.lstrip("?")). See the example below.
  • It is not the ASGI scope's path. use_scope()["path"] is the ReactPy websocket endpoint — "/reactpy/" — for every component on every page. use_location().path is the page the visitor is on. Verified in Chrome: visiting /some/deep/page?tab=2&user=ada gives Location(path='/some/deep/page', query_string='?tab=2&user=ada') while the scope still says "/reactpy/".
  • The browser reports it, so it is untrusted. The value arrives as parameters on the websocket URL and ReactPy does not validate it against your routes. Treat it as input: match it, never interpolate it into a "href" or a filesystem path without checking.
  • It needs a live connection. Called in a test's plain Layout render, it raises RuntimeError: No backend established a connection.. See working without a connection.
  • It does not exist under client-side rendering. With ReactPyCsr, Python runs in the browser but no ReactPy connection object is established, so the hook raises the same RuntimeError. Verified in Chrome against a CSR app. Read window.location through JavaScript there instead.
  • Like every hook, call it only at the top level — never in a loop, a conditional, or after an early return.

docs.title: Reading query parameters
docs.text:
query_string arrives exactly as the browser shows it, which means the leading "?" is attached to the first parameter's name. That is the one detail that trips people up.

app.py Run 
@component
def product_page():
    location = use_location()

    # `query_string` mirrors `window.location.search`, so it *keeps* the
    # leading "?". Strip it first or the first parameter gets a mangled name:
    # parse_qs("?tab=2&sort=price") yields the key "?tab", not "tab".
    params = parse_qs(location.query_string.lstrip("?"))
    tab = params.get("tab", ["overview"])[0]
    sort = params.get("sort", ["name"])[0]

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"Products — {tab}"),
        html.p(f"sorted by: {sort}"),
        html.p(f"raw query string: {location.query_string!r}"),
        html.p(f"path: {location.path}"),
    )
