With ?tab=sales&sort=price this renders "Products — sales", sorted by price. With no query string at all it falls back to the defaults.

docs.title: Building navigation from the current path
docs.text:
Splitting the path gives you the trail from the site root to wherever the visitor is.

app.py Run 
@component
def breadcrumb():
    location = use_location()

    # `path` mirrors `window.location.pathname`, so a component rendered on the
    # ReactPy server can describe the page the browser is actually on -- useful
    # for navigation that needs to know where it is.
    parts = [part for part in location.path.split("/") if part]

    return html.nav(
        html.a({"href": "/"}, "home"),
        *[
            html.span(" / ", html.a({"href": "/" + "/".join(parts[: i + 1])}, part))
            for i, part in enumerate(parts)
        ],
    )

# TODO

On /reports/2024/q1 this produces links to /reports, /reports/2024, and /reports/2024/q1. Build the URLs yourself rather than pasting path segments in raw if they can contain anything you did not choose.

docs.title: Working without a connection
docs.text:
A component that reads the location should say what it shows when there is none — a unit test, a reactpy_to_string call, or a CSR page all take this path.

@component
def page_title():
    try:
        location = use_location()
    except RuntimeError:
        return html.h1("(no browser yet)")
    return html.h1(f"at {location.path}")

Verified both ways through Layout: with no provider it renders the fallback; with one it renders the path.

docs.title: My query parameters never match
docs.text: The leading "?". parse_qs("?tab=2") gives {"?tab": ["2"]}. Strip it before parsing.

docs.title: It says /reactpy/
docs.text: You are reading use_scope()["path"], which is the websocket endpoint. Use use_location().path for the page.

docs.title: It raises in my tests
docs.text: Expected: a bare Layout render has no connection. Either wrap the call as shown above, or inject one — see use_connection.

docs.title: It raises inside a ReactPyCsr app
docs.text: Client-side rendering establishes no connection, so there is nothing to report. Read the URL from JavaScript instead, or move that component server-side.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
use_memo is a ReactPy hook that caches the result of a calculation, recomputing it only when one of its listed dependencies changes. 

cached_value = use_memo(calculate_value, dependencies=[dep_1, dep_2])

Use it when a calculation is genuinely expensive and the inputs it depends on change less often than the component renders. It caches a value; it does not stop anything from rendering.

What use_memo does not do in ReactPy

It does not prevent a child component from re-rendering. ReactPy has no render bailout and no memo: a child's body runs whenever its parent re-renders, even with identical props, and even if you cache the child element itself with use_memo. Texts ported from React that use useMemo to "skip re-rendering of components" describe a mechanism that is not here. use_memo saves the computation, nothing else.

docs.title: use_memo(function, dependencies)
docs.text:
Call use_memo at the top level of your component to cache a calculation.

from reactpy import use_memo

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• function: A function taking no arguments that returns the value you want. ReactPy calls it only when it must. It must be pure: same inputs, same output, no side effects.

  • dependencies: The values the calculation reads. ReactPy recomputes when any of them changes. It accepts three shapes:

    You pass Meaning dependencies=[a, b] Recompute when a or b changes. omitted (the default) ReactPy reads the function's closure and infers the free variables. dependencies=None Recompute on every render.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: The current value — either freshly computed, or the one cached from the last render in which a dependency changed.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The decorated name holds the value, not a function. The decorator form is the call form under another name, and the call form returns the value -- so after decorating, my_value is the cached result, and calling it raises TypeError: 'int' object is not callable. To keep the name callable, give the inner function its own name and pass it to use_memo.
  • Caching lasts for the lifetime of the component. A cached value survives as long as the component stays mounted; there is no way to invalidate it from inside. Mounting the component under a new "key" throws it away, because that unmounts and remounts the component and every hook starts over.
  • You must list every value the function reads. ReactPy does not check, and does not warn. A missing dependency produces a silently stale value, not an error. See I removed a dependency and nothing complained.
  • Comparison is not plain identity. Dependencies go through reactpy.core.hooks.strictly_equal, which requires the two values to be the same type first, compares two locally-defined functions or lambdas by their code objects (so a fresh, structurally identical lambda counts as unchanged), and otherwise compares with ==, falling back to is only if that raises. Two practical consequences: a freshly built list or dict with equal contents does not force a recompute, and a value that changes type between renders — 1 then 1.0, or 0 then False — always counts as changed.
  • Mutating a dependency in place defeats the cache. Change an object and pass the same object back, and it compares equal to itself, so the cached value is kept. Build a new object instead — see Updating Objects in State.
  • A ref never invalidates a memo. Writing to some_ref.current does not change how the ref compares, so listing a use_ref box in dependencies accomplishes nothing.
  • Like every hook, call it only at the top level — never in a loop, a conditional, or after an early return. ReactPy does not check; a hook that runs on some renders but not others produces a scrambled component and a cryptic IndexError.

docs.title: Skipping an expensive calculation
docs.text:
Give use_memo the function that does the work, and list what it reads. The leaderboard sorts seven rows here, which is nothing — but it is the same shape you would use for a sort over ten thousand, and the counter on screen shows exactly how often the sort runs.

Press Change highlight: the component re-renders, the sort does not run, and sorted 1 time(s) stays put. Press Everyone scores +1: players changes, so the sort runs again.

app.py Run 
ROSTER = [
    ("ada", 91),
    ("grace", 120),
    ("alan", 77),
    ("edsger", 64),
    ("katherine", 143),
    ("dorothy", 88),
    ("margaret", 155),
]

sorts = []  # demo-only: lets you *see* how often `rank` actually runs


@component
def leaderboard():
    players, set_players = use_state(
        [{"name": name, "score": score} for name, score in ROSTER]
    )
    highlight, set_highlight = use_state("ada")

    def rank():
        # The work you want to skip: sorting the whole table. Listing
        # `dependencies=[players]` runs this only when the roster changes, so
        # changing the highlight leaves the sorted list alone.
        sorts.append(1)
        return sorted(players, key=lambda player: -player["score"])

    ranked = use_memo(rank, dependencies=[players])

    return html.div(
        html.h1("Leaderboard"),
        html.ol([html.li(f"{player['name']}: {player['score']}") for player in ranked]),
        html.p(f"sorted {len(sorts)} time(s)"),
        html.p(f"highlighted: {highlight}"),
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": lambda event: set_highlight(
                    "grace" if highlight == "ada" else "ada"
                )
            },
            "Change highlight",
        ),
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": lambda event: set_players(
                    [{**player, "score": player["score"] + 1} for player in players]
                )
            },
            "Everyone scores +1",
        ),
    )

# TODO

The counter (sorts) and both buttons exist only to make the caching observable. In real code you would keep the use_memo call and drop the rest.

docs.title: How expensive is "expensive"?
docs.text:
Enough to measure. Sorting a small list, building a dict from a handful of items, or formatting a string is not worth it — the hook has a cost of its own, and a dependency list you must keep correct is a cost too.

Reach for it when you recognize one of these:

  • A sort, filter, or search over a large collection.
  • Parsing: JSON, CSV, a template, a source file.
  • Building a structure that then gets walked repeatedly.
  • Anything you have already timed and found annoying.

If you have not measured it, prefer the plain calculation. Adding use_memo later is a one-line change precisely because the calculation is already in its own function.

docs.title: Should you add use_memo everywhere?
docs.text: No. Each one is a dependency list you now have to maintain correctly, and a wrong list is a silent bug rather than a loud one. Memoize where you have measured, not everywhere.

docs.title: Omitting the dependency list
docs.text:
Leave out dependencies and ReactPy infers them from the free variables in the function's closure. This is a ReactPy feature with no React equivalent, and it removes the most common class of mistake, because a value the function reads is by definition a free variable.

The word count below reads text but not upper, so toggling the case re-renders the component without re-running the count. Watch counted 1 time(s).

app.py Run 
counts = []  # demo-only: lets you *see* how often `count` actually runs


@component
def word_count():
    text, set_text = use_state("reactpy is a python ui library")
    upper, set_upper = use_state(False)

    # No `dependencies` argument at all. ReactPy inspects the function's
    # closure and infers the free variables it reads -- here that is `text`,
    # but not `upper`, so toggling the case does not redo the count.
    def count():
        counts.append(1)
        return len(text.split())

    total = use_memo(count)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"{total} words"),
        html.p(text.upper() if upper else text),
        html.p(f"counted {len(counts)} time(s)"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_upper(not upper)}, "Toggle case"),
        html.input(
            {
                "value": text,
                "onChange": lambda event: set_text(event["target"]["value"]),
            }
        ),
    )

# TODO

Two catches. Inference only sees closure variables, so a module-level name, or anything reached through an object, is invisible to it. And inference is a convenience for a function defined inside the component — pass the list explicitly when the function comes from elsewhere.

docs.title: Recomputing on every render
docs.text:
dependencies=None opts out of caching entirely: the function runs on every render. That is what you want when the calculation reads something no dependency list can express, such as a module-level mutable.

The label below reads config, which lives at module scope. Inference only sees closure variables, so it would pick up count and suffix and miss config entirely — the label would keep a stale prefix whenever config changed. dependencies=None sidesteps the question: label() runs each render.

app.py Run 
# Module-level, so it is *not* a closure variable and ReactPy cannot infer it
# as a dependency.
config = {"prefix": "count"}

calls = []  # demo-only


@component
def counter():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)
    suffix, set_suffix = use_state("")

    def label():
        # Reads `config`, which ReactPy cannot see as a dependency. With
        # inferred (i.e. empty) dependencies this would be computed once and
        # then never notice an edited `config`. `dependencies=None` says: this
        # depends on the render itself, so recompute every time.
        calls.append(1)
        return f"{config['prefix']}: {count}{suffix}"

    return html.div(
        html.h1(use_memo(label, dependencies=None)),
        html.p(f"label() ran {len(calls)} time(s)"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_count(count + 1)}, "Count +1"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_suffix("!")}, "Set suffix"),
    )

# TODO

docs.title: My memo value never updates
docs.text:
In order of likelihood:

  • You mutated a dependency instead of replacing it. Same object in, equal to itself, cached value kept. Build a new object.
  • You listed a ref as a dependency. Mutating some_ref.current never invalidates anything. Use state, or list the value itself.
  • The dependency compares equal to its replacement. Two [1, 2, 3] lists are equal, so rebuilding one each render changes nothing.
  • You left the value out of the list. See the next item.

docs.title: I removed a dependency and nothing complained
docs.text:
Because nothing checks. The example below omits tax_rate from the list, and it seems to work: press Add 10% tax twice and the rate climbs while the total stays frozen at whatever a 0% rate produced. Then press Add an item — a real dependency — and the total jumps to 12.00, silently incorporating both tax increases you could see never happened.

app.py Run 
@component
def totals():
    items, set_items = use_state([1, 2, 3])
    tax_rate, set_tax_rate = use_state(0.0)

    # `tax_rate` is read here but deliberately left out of `dependencies`.
    # ReactPy does not complain. The cached total just keeps the rate from the
    # render that last computed it, so "Add 10% tax" appears to do nothing --
    # until something that *is* a dependency changes, and the stale number
    # jumps to the right one all at once.
    def grand_total():
        return sum(items) * (1 + tax_rate)

    total = use_memo(grand_total, dependencies=[items])

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"total: {total:.2f}"),
        html.p(f"tax rate: {tax_rate:.0%}"),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_tax_rate(tax_rate + 0.1)}, "Add 10% tax"
        ),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_items([*items, len(items) + 1])},
            "Add an item",
        ),
    )

# TODO

This is the failure mode to watch for: a stale value that eventually arrives, so it reads as lag rather than as a bug. List everything the function reads, or omit dependencies and let ReactPy infer them.

docs.title: My calculation runs on every render anyway
docs.text:
• You passed dependencies=None.
  • A dependency really is new each render — commonly an object constructed in the component body above the use_memo call.
  • A dependency is an object whose == is identity-based and which you rebuild each time.

docs.title: I wanted to stop a child from re-rendering
docs.text: use_memo cannot do this in ReactPy, and caching the child element does not help either — a cached element is still re-rendered. ReactPy re-renders children unconditionally. If a child is genuinely expensive, the levers are to make its own calculations cheap (memoize inside it) or to avoid rendering it at all behind a conditional.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
use_reducer is a ReactPy hook that holds state behind a function: you send an action, and a reducer turns the current state plus that action into the next state. 

state, dispatch = use_reducer(reducer, initial_value)

Reach for it when a component's updates are more than "set this to that" — several fields that change together, transitions that depend on what is already there, or update logic you want out of the component so it can be tested as a plain function.

docs.title: use_reducer(reducer, initial_value)
docs.text:
Call use_reducer at the top level of your component.

from reactpy import use_reducer

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
• reducer: (state, action) -> new_state. A pure function: given the same two arguments it returns the same result, and it does not touch anything outside them. It must return a new object rather than modifying state — see the reducer must not mutate.
  • initial_value: The state to start with. Pass a function taking no arguments to build it lazily; ReactPy calls it on the first render only. See avoiding recreating the initial state.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
A two-item tuple, normally unpacked:

  • state: The current state, as of the start of this render.
  • dispatch: A function that takes an action and schedules the update. The same object on every render — verified, one dispatcher across four renders — so it is safe to pass into a child or a dependency list.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Define the reducer at module level. ReactPy builds the dispatcher once, on the first render, and the dispatcher closes over the reducer you passed then. A reducer defined inside the component is a new function object each render and ReactPy keeps using the first one, so any value it closes over is frozen at its first-render value. Measured: four renders, four distinct reducer objects passed in, and the state kept reporting seen_n=0. This differs from React, which re-reads the reducer every render. Anything the reducer needs must arrive in state or action. See The reducer never changes.
  • use_reducer is use_state underneath. The dispatcher calls the state setter with lambda last_state: reducer(last_state, action), so every rule from use_state applies here — replaced, never merged; equal values schedule no render; mutations vanish silently. See The reducer must not mutate.
  • The reducer runs eagerly, inside dispatch — not later during the render. Verified by ordering statements around the call. A reducer that raises is swallowed the same way any event-handler error is: logged on the server as Failed to execute event handler, with nothing in the browser console.
  • Actions are yours; ReactPy never inspects them. A dict with a "type" key is convention, not a requirement — you can dispatch a string, a number, or a tuple.
  • Like every hook, call it only at the top level — never in a loop, a conditional, or after an early return. ReactPy does not check; a hook that runs on some renders but not others produces a scrambled component and a cryptic IndexError.

docs.title: Managing complex state with a reducer
docs.text:
One reducer holds the whole shape, and each behaviour is a branch chosen by the action. Because it is an ordinary function of two arguments, you can test it without rendering anything.

Press Add task twice, task 1, then Clear done, and watch the reducer's branches run:

app.py Run 
def todos_reducer(state, action):
    """One function per behaviour, chosen by the action's type.

    Defined at module level on purpose: ReactPy builds the dispatcher once, on
    the first render, and keeps that reducer -- a reducer defined inside the
    component would keep its first-render closure forever.

    Every branch returns a NEW dict. Returning the mutated `state` would be
    dropped without a word.
    """
    if action["type"] == "add":
        return {
            **state,
            "items": [*state["items"], {"text": action["text"], "done": False}],
        }
    if action["type"] == "toggle":
        items = [
            {**item, "done": not item["done"]} if i == action["index"] else item
            for i, item in enumerate(state["items"])
        ]
        return {**state, "items": items}
    if action["type"] == "clear_done":
        return {**state, "items": [i for i in state["items"] if not i["done"]]}
    return state


@component
def todo_list():
    state, dispatch = use_reducer(todos_reducer, {"items": []})

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"To-do ({sum(1 for i in state['items'] if not i['done'])} left)"),
        html.ul(
            [
                html.li(
                    {"key": i},
                    html.button(
                        {
                            "onClick": lambda event, i=i: dispatch(
                                {"type": "toggle", "index": i}
                            )
                        },
                        state["items"][i]["text"],
                    ),
                )
                for i in range(len(state["items"]))
            ]
        ),
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": lambda event: dispatch(
                    {"type": "add", "text": f"task {len(state['items']) + 1}"}
                )
            },
            "Add task",
        ),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: dispatch({"type": "clear_done"})}, "Clear done"
        ),
    )

# TODO

Three things to notice in todos_reducer. It is at module level, so the closure trap above never arises. Every branch builds a new dict with {**state, ...} — none of them mutate. And the fallback return state makes an unhandled action a deliberate no-op rather than a crash.

docs.title: The reducer must not mutate
docs.text:
This is the failure mode most likely to cost you an afternoon, and it is silent. A reducer that modifies state and returns it hands back the very object ReactPy already holds; the comparison finds them equal and schedules nothing. No error, no warning, nothing in the console — the button just stops working while your data quietly changes underneath.

app.py Run 
def counter_reducer(state, action):
    # Always return a NEW object. `use_reducer` is built on `use_state`, which
    # compares what you return against what it already holds and schedules no
    # render when the two are equal. Mutating `state` here and returning it
    # would update the data, schedule nothing, and fail with no error and
    # nothing in the browser console.
    return {**state, "count": state["count"] + 1}


@component
def counter():
    state, dispatch = use_reducer(counter_reducer, {"count": 0})
    return html.div(
        html.h1(state["count"]),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: dispatch({"type": "inc"})}, "Add 1"),
    )

# TODO

Return {**state, "count": state["count"] + 1}, not state["count"] += 1; return state. The same applies one level down: {**state, "items": state["items"] + [new]}, never state["items"].append(new). See Updating Objects in State and Updating Arrays in State.

docs.title: The reducer never changes
docs.text:
Because the first reducer is the only one that ever runs, a reducer that closes over component state reads a value frozen at the first render — permanently, with no warning.

Run this, press Add step twice, then Bump step, then Add step again:

app.py Run 
@component
def stepper():
    step, set_step = use_state(1)

    def reducer(state, action):
        # BUG: this reducer closes over `step`, but ReactPy builds the
        # dispatcher once, on the first render, and keeps that reducer
        # forever. Bump `step` to 3 and this keeps adding 1.
        return {**state, "total": state["total"] + step}

    state, dispatch = use_reducer(reducer, {"total": 0})

    return html.div(
        html.p(f"total: {state['total']}"),
        html.p(f"step: {step}"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: dispatch({"type": "add"})}, "Add step"),
        html.button({"onClick": lambda event: set_step(step + 1)}, "Bump step"),
    )

# TODO

step goes to 2 on screen, but the total keeps rising by 1. The reducer still holds the step from the render that created it. Two ways out: keep the reducer at module level and put step in the state, or send it in the action — dispatch({"type": "add", "amount": step}).

docs.title: Avoiding recreating the initial state
docs.text:
Pass a function and ReactPy calls it once; pass a call and it runs on every render, with every result but the first discarded. Measured across four renders: 1 call versus 4. The counter on screen reports the total, and it stays at 1 no matter what you press.

app.py Run 
loads = []  # demo-only: shows how often the initializer actually runs


def load_config():
    """Stand-in for anything slow: reading a file, querying a database."""
    loads.append(1)
    return {"rows": [{"name": n} for n in ("alpha", "beta", "gamma")], "selected": None}


def reducer(state, action):
    if action["type"] == "select":
        return {**state, "selected": action["name"]}
    return state


@component
def report():
    # Pass a function as the initial state and ReactPy calls it once, on the
    # first render. Passing `load_config()` instead would call it on every
    # render and throw every result but the first away.
    state, dispatch = use_reducer(reducer, load_config)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"{len(state['rows'])} rows"),
        html.p(f"selected: {state['selected'] or '-'}"),
        html.p(f"initializer ran {len(loads)} time(s)"),
        html.button(
            {
                "onClick": lambda event: dispatch(
                    {"type": "select", "name": state["rows"][0]["name"]}
                )
            },
            "Select first",
        ),
    )

# TODO

docs.title: use_reducer or use_state?
docs.text:
Prefer use_state. It is shorter and there is no reducer-closure rule to remember. Switch when one of these is true:

  • Several pieces of state always change together, and updating them through separate setters lets the component render in between with an inconsistent mix.
  • The next state depends on the current one in a way you keep writing wrong.
  • The update logic has grown branches you want to name, or unit-test as a plain function.
  • Different parts of a tree need to trigger the same transitions — passing dispatch around is tidier than passing several setters.

docs.title: My dispatch does nothing
docs.text: Check the reducer's return value first — this is almost always a mutation. return state after modifying state schedules nothing. Also check for a branch that returns the state unchanged: an action whose "type" no branch matches falls through to your return state, which is correctly a no-op.

docs.title: My reducer sees an old value of some state
docs.text: You defined it inside the component, so ReactPy is running the first-render version with the first-render closure. Move it to module level and pass the value through state or the action.

docs.title: The initial value seems to be rebuilt every render
docs.text: You passed build_initial_state() instead of build_initial_state. ReactPy needs the function itself to know it may skip the work.

docs.title: My reducer raised and nothing said so
docs.text: Expected. Reducer errors land in the server log as Failed to execute event handler and are otherwise swallowed; the state is left unassigned. Look at the server output, not the browser console.

docs.title: I want an updater function instead of an action
docs.text: That is what use_state gives you: set_value(lambda previous: ...). If that is all you need, use_reducer is ceremony you do not owe yourself.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
use_ref is a ReactPy hook that gives you a mutable box which survives re-renders. Writing to it never causes a render. 

value_box = use_ref(initial_value)

A ref is for values your component uses but never renders. It is a plain Python object holding one field, so reading and writing it is just attribute access — no setter, no scheduling, no re-render.

There is no DOM ref in ReactPy

React's useRef is often used to grab a DOM node — inputRef.current.focus(), videoRef.current.play(), myDiv.current.scrollIntoView(). That use does not exist in ReactPy. Your components run on the server, where there is no DOM, and ReactPy has no mechanism for handing a browser node to Python. There is no ref_current attribute, no callback ref, nothing to attach a node to. Anything you write as a "ref_..." attribute is an unknown attribute the client silently ignores.

Express browser behavior through state and ordinary attributes instead: {"autoFocus": True}, {"value": text}, {"disabled": not ready}. If you need genuinely imperative browser code, that belongs in a client-side app, where your Python runs in the browser.

docs.title: use_ref(initial_value)
docs.text:
Call use_ref at the top level of your component to declare a value box.

from reactpy import use_ref

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: • initial_value: The value the box starts with. It can be any Python value, including a mutable one.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
A reactpy.utils.Ref object — the same object on every render of that component. It has two members:

  • current: The value. Read and write it directly: value_box.current = new_value. Reading it does not schedule a render.
  • set_current(new_value): Assigns current and returns the value it replaced. Because it is a call rather than an assignment, it fits where a statement cannot go — inside a lambda, for example.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• initial_value is evaluated on every render. use_ref(build_something_expensive()) calls build_something_expensive() each time the component renders, then throws all but the first result away. Verified: four renders, four calls. To build something once, start empty and fill it in:

    index = use_ref(None)
if index.current is None:
    index.current = build_something_expensive()

  • Writing to a ref never triggers a render. That is the point, and also the trap: if the value is something the screen shows, it will not update. See Ref versus state.

  • Mutating a ref does not invalidate anything. Dependency comparison treats the box as unchanged no matter what you write into it, because it compares equal to itself. Listing a ref in a dependencies list is therefore useless — the effect or memo will never re-run because of it. Verified: an effect with dependencies=[box] ran once while its box.current was written to three times.
  • A ref is unhashable. hash(use_ref(0)) raises TypeError, so it cannot be a dict key or a set member. Its == compares contents: two separate Ref(0) boxes are equal.
  • Render value_box.current, not the box. html.p(my_ref) does not raise; it renders the repr, so the reader sees Ref(0) on the page. Passing a ref as an attribute value fails at serialization instead.
  • Like every hook, call it only at the top level — never in a loop, a conditional, or after an early return. ReactPy does not check: shuffling which hooks run between renders yields a scrambled component and a cryptic IndexError, not a helpful message.
  • ReactPy has no Strict Mode, so nothing runs your component twice to catch impure code. A ref written to during rendering is exactly as unsafe here as in React, and nothing will warn you. See Keeping Components Pure.

docs.title: Ref versus state
docs.text:
The question is not "which is cheaper" but who needs to know. If changing the value must update the screen, it is state. If only the code needs it, it is a ref.

The two counters below start together and then drift apart, because only one of them causes a render. The ref counter's new value sits in the box unseen until something else renders the component.

app.py Run 
@component
def counter():
    # Two buttons, one counter each. Only the state one causes a render, so the
    # numbers only come back into sync on a render triggered by something else.
    state_count, set_state_count = use_state(0)
    ref_count = use_ref(0)

    def bump_state(event=None):
        set_state_count(state_count + 1)

    def bump_ref(event=None):
        ref_count.current += 1  # writes in place: no render is scheduled

    return html.div(
        html.p(f"state: {state_count}"),
        html.p(f"ref: {ref_count.current}"),
        html.button({"onClick": bump_state}, "Increment state"),
        html.button({"onClick": bump_ref}, "Increment ref"),
    )

# TODO

The usual split:

You need... Use A value the UI renders use_state A value only handlers or effects read use_ref A value that drives the UI and is written by a long-lived loop Both: state for the UI, ref for the loop Something built once, then read-only use_ref, with the guard A mutable value the UI renders use_state — replace the object instead of mutating it; see Updating Objects in State

docs.title: Remembering a value built once
docs.text:
Because the box is the same object across renders, it is the natural place for something expensive to construct and cheap to read: a parsed file, an index, a client object. Start it empty so the expensive call is not repeated on every render.

app.py Run 
def build_word_index():
    """Stand-in for something slow: reading a file, opening a connection, etc."""
    return {word: len(word) for word in "react py is a python ui library".split()}


@component
def word_counter():
    # Built once, on the first render, and then reused for the life of the
    # component -- no `dependencies`, no invalidation, nothing to keep in sync.
    index: Ref[dict[str, int] | None] = use_ref(None)
    if index.current is None:
        index.current = build_word_index()

    return html.div(
        html.h1("Word lengths"),
        html.ul(
            [
                html.li(f"{word}: {length}")
                for word, length in sorted(index.current.items())
            ]
        ),
    )

# TODO

If the value should be rebuilt when some input changes, a ref is the wrong tool — that is what a dependencies list is for. See use_memo.

docs.title: Sharing a value with a long-lived effect
docs.text:
An use_async_effect loop keeps running across renders, so it closes over the state values from the render that started it. A ref sidesteps this: it is the same object every render, so the loop reads whatever the handlers wrote after it started.

The stopwatch below keeps the start timestamp in a ref. The ticking effect reads it and the buttons write it, none of which needs a render of its own. The value the screen shows, elapsed, is state.

app.py Run 
@component
def stopwatch():
    # What the UI renders lives in state. What only the handlers and the
    # ticking effect read -- and which must never trigger a render of its own
    # -- lives in a ref.
    elapsed, set_elapsed = use_state(0.0)
    running, set_running = use_state(False)
    started_at: Ref[float | None] = use_ref(None)

    async def tick():
        # The ref is the same object on every render, so this long-lived loop
        # always sees whatever the button handlers wrote into it.
        while started_at.current is not None:
            await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
            set_elapsed(time.monotonic() - started_at.current)

    use_async_effect(tick, dependencies=[running])

    def start(event=None):
        started_at.current = time.monotonic()
        set_running(True)

    def stop(event=None):
        if started_at.current is not None:
            # Write the exact final value; the ticking effect only samples
            # every 0.1s, so relying on it alone would leave the display
            # slightly behind.
            set_elapsed(time.monotonic() - started_at.current)
            started_at.current = None
        set_running(False)

    def reset(event=None):
        started_at.current = None
        set_running(False)
        set_elapsed(0.0)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"{elapsed:.1f}s"),
        html.button(
            {"onClick": stop if running else start},
            "Stop" if running else "Start",
        ),
        html.button({"onClick": reset}, "Reset"),
    )

# TODO

docs.title: Writing from inside a lambda
docs.text:
box.current = value is an assignment, which is a statement, so it cannot be the body of a lambda. set_current exists for that case, and hands back what you replaced.

app.py Run 
@component
def theme_picker():
    # `ref.current = value` is a statement, so it cannot appear inside the
    # `lambda` a one-line handler needs. `set_current` is the expression-shaped
    # version of the same write, and it hands back the value you replaced --
    # which is exactly what you need to remember the previous choice.
    previous = use_ref("light")
    theme, set_theme = use_state("light")

    def pick(name):
        return lambda event=None: (previous.set_current(theme), set_theme(name))

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"{theme} theme"),
        html.p(f"you were just using: {previous.current}"),
        html.button({"onClick": pick("light")}, "Light"),
        html.button({"onClick": pick("dark")}, "Dark"),
    )

# TODO

pick returns a lambda precisely so each button gets its own handler, and previous.set_current(theme) is what makes the one-line body possible.

docs.title: My ref value is stale
docs.text:
Check which of these you did:

  • You rendered the box, not its contents. html.p(my_ref) prints Ref(...). Use my_ref.current.
  • You expected the write to re-render. A ref never schedules a render. If the screen must change, that value is state.
  • You listed the ref as a dependency. Mutating current does not invalidate effects or memos — the box always compares equal to itself. Put the value in the dependency list, or use state.
  • You read a ref through an old closure. Inside a long-lived effect, re-read box.current on each pass instead of binding it to a local once.

docs.title: My expensive setup runs on every render
docs.text:
You passed it as the argument: use_ref(build()) calls build() every render. Move it behind a guard:

box = use_ref(None)
if box.current is None:
    box.current = build()

docs.title: I need to focus an input, or scroll to an element
docs.text: There is no way to do this from a ReactPy server component, and no "ref_current" attribute will add one. Use the declarative attributes the browser already understands — "autoFocus", "checked", "value", "disabled" — and reach for a client-side app if you truly need imperative browser access.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
use_scope is a ReactPy hook that returns the ASGI connection scope behind the current websocket. 

scope = use_scope()

Use it for what the server knows about the connection: who the peer is, which headers arrived, which server accepted the request. For the page the visitor is looking at, use use_location instead.

docs.title: use_scope()
docs.text:
Call it at the top level of a component. It takes no arguments.

from reactpy import use_scope

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
The dict at use_connection().scope — the raw ASGI scope, with the same shape as any other ASGI app's scope. It is a live dictionary: nothing copies it for you.

Read ASGI: Websockets for the specification; the keys below are what uvicorn's websocket implementation actually delivered, captured from a live Chrome session against ReactPy:

Key What it holds "type" "websocket" for these connections. "path" The ReactPy websocket endpoint, e.g. "/reactpy/". Not the page. "headers" A list of (bytes, bytes) pairs, lower-cased by the server. "client" (ip, port) of the peer, or None if unknown. "server" (host, port) that accepted the connection. "scheme" "ws" or "wss". "query_string" The websocket URL's query string, as bytes — this carries ReactPy's own path/qs parameters. "raw_path" The request path, as bytes, un-decoded. "root_path" The ASGI root path, normally "". "http_version" e.g. "1.1". "asgi" {"version": ..., "spec_version": ...}. "subprotocols" Requested websocket subprotocols, usually []. "state" A dict shared across the connection's tasks; empty unless something put values in it. "extensions" Server-specific extras, e.g. {"websocket.http.response": {}} under uvicorn.

Which extras appear depends on the server: "state" and that "extensions" entry are uvicorn/websockets additions. Read them defensively, with scope.get(...).

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• "path" is not the page. For every component in the app it is the websocket endpoint — "/reactpy/" under the default path_prefix. Verified: on the page /some/deep/page?tab=2&user=ada, the scope still says "/reactpy/". Use use_location().path for the page.
  • Headers are bytes. Both halves of each pair are bytes and lower-cased, so compare against b"user-agent" and .decode() the value before using it. There is no dict of headers; see the example.
  • "query_string" is the websocket's, not the page's. It contains ReactPy's own path= and qs= parameters. Parse the page's query with use_location().
  • None is possible. "client" can be absent or None behind a proxy or in-process transport. scope["client"][0] will raise on None; check first.
  • It needs a live connection. In a plain Layout render it raises RuntimeError: No backend established a connection.
  • It does not exist under client-side rendering. With ReactPyCsr there is no connection object, so the hook raises the same RuntimeError.
  • Like every hook, call it only at the top level.

docs.title: Reading the peer and a header
docs.text:
app.py Run 
def header(scope, name):
    """Read one request header out of an ASGI scope.

    Headers arrive as a list of ``(bytes, bytes)`` pairs, lower-cased by the
    server, so both halves need decoding before you can compare them.
    """
    wanted = name.lower().encode()
    for key, value in scope.get("headers", []):
        if key == wanted:
            return value.decode()
    return None


@component
def visitor():
    scope = use_scope()
    # Note this is the *websocket* scope. Its "path" is the ReactPy websocket
    # path, not the page the visitor is on -- use use_location() for that.
    # `client` is legitimately absent or None behind some proxies, so read it
    # through a local and check it rather than subscripting the scope directly.
    client = scope.get("client")
    peer = client[0] if client else "unknown"
    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"Hello, {peer}"),
        html.p(f"browser: {header(scope, 'user-agent') or 'unknown'}"),
        html.p(f"connection type: {scope['type']}"),
    )

# TODO

header() exists because the ASGI scope hands you raw bytes: it lower-cases the name, matches on bytes, and decodes the value. The component reads scope["client"] defensively because a proxy can leave it unset.

docs.title: What belongs here and what does not
docs.text: You want Use The visitor's IP address use_scope()["client"] A request header use_scope()["headers"] The page the visitor is on use_location The query string use_location The object mediating the connection use_connection

docs.title: My header lookups always return None
docs.text: You compared against a str. The keys are bytes and lower-cased: (b"user-agent", b"Mozilla/5.0 ...").

docs.title: It raises in my tests
docs.text: A bare Layout render establishes no connection. Wrap the call in try/except RuntimeError, or inject a connection — see use_connection.

docs.title: Every page shows /reactpy/
docs.text: That is the scope's "path": the websocket endpoint, identical for all components. Use use_location().path.

docs.title: I need the request path before the websocket opens
docs.text: use_scope only exists inside a component, which means inside an established websocket. For pre-connection decisions, handle it in ASGI middleware in front of the ReactPy app — see ReactPyMiddleware.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
use_state is a ReactPy hook that lets you add a state variable to your component. 

value, set_value = use_state(initial_value)

docs.title: use_state(initial_value)
docs.text:
Call use_state at the top level of your component to declare a state variable.

from reactpy import use_state

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: • initial_value: The value you want the state to start with. It can be any Python value. Alternatively, pass a function taking no arguments and returning the initial value; ReactPy calls it on the first render only, which avoids rebuilding an expensive value on every render. See avoiding recreating the initial state.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text:
use_state returns a reactpy.types.State — a named tuple of two items, which is normally unpacked:

  • value: The current state, as of the start of this render.
  • set_value: A function that updates the state and schedules a re-render. See set_value.

Because State is a named tuple you can also reach the halves explicitly (state.value, state.set_value), but unpacking is the convention.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• use_state is a hook, so call it only at the top level of your component or of your own hooks — never in a loop, a conditional, or after an early return. ReactPy does not check for this: changing which hooks run between renders produces a scrambled component and a cryptic IndexError: list index out of range rather than a helpful message. If you need conditional state, extract a component.
  • initial_value is used only on the first render. Later changes to the expression are ignored — see resetting state with a key.
  • Do not pass a function you intend to store. A callable initial_value is treated as an initializer and called. use_state(lambda value: value * 2) does not store the lambda; ReactPy calls it with no arguments and the component fails. To keep a function in state, wrap it (use_state(lambda: my_function)) or store it in a use_ref.
  • Unlike React, ReactPy has no Strict Mode, so your initializer is called exactly once — verified: one call across four renders. Nothing will run it twice to expose impurity for you, so test purity yourself if it matters.

docs.title: set_value(next_value)
docs.text: The set_value function returned by use_state updates the state and schedules a re-render.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: • next_value: The value you want the state to become. Any Python value, or a function taking one argument and returning the next state. That function receives the current value, runs eagerly inside the setter, and must be pure. See updating state based on the previous state.

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: None.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Setting state does not change the variable you already have in this render — it schedules a new one. See State as a Snapshot.
  • Setting state to a value equal to the current one does not re-render. The comparison is core/hooks.py, strictly_equal — and it is not an identity check: the two values must share a type, two locally-defined functions or lambdas are compared by their code, and everything else is compared with ==, falling back to identity only if that raises. So a brand-new object is dropped too whenever it merely compares equal: setting [1, 2, 3] while the state is an equal list renders nothing, and the same goes for any class whose __eq__ matches. Only values with identity-based __eq__ — plain class instances, say — re-render when you replace them.
  • set_value replaces the state; it never merges a partial object into it. Verified: setting {"a": 9} over {"a": 1, "b": 2} yields {"a": 9}. Update objects with set_value({**value, "k": v}) — see Updating Objects in State.
  • Mutating the current value and passing it back does nothing. The comparison finds the value equal to itself, so no render is scheduled — and there is no error, no warning, and nothing in the console. set_value(items.append(x)) also stores None, because most mutating list methods return None.
  • If the updater function raises, the error is logged on the server as Failed to execute event handler and swallowed; the state is left unassigned and the UI simply stops updating. Check the server log, not the browser console.
  • set_value is a stable object: the same callable is returned on every render of that component. Verified across four renders. That makes it safe to put in a dependency list or pass to a child without causing extra renders.

docs.title: Adding state to a component
docs.text:
Call use_state at the top level of your component, and use the returned value while rendering:

app.py Run 
@component
def counter():
    step, set_step = use_state(1)

    def handle_add(event):
        set_step(step + 1)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(step),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_add}, "Add 1"),
    )

# TODO

Each state variable gets its own setter, so prefer several narrow variables over one crowded object:

first_name, set_first_name = use_state("Ada")
last_name, set_last_name = use_state("Lovelace")
age, set_age = use_state(42)

docs.title: Counter (number)
docs.text:
To update a number based on its current value, use a function:

def handle_add(event):
    set_step(lambda step: step + 1)

Or read the value from this render directly when you don't need the latest: set_step(step + 1).

docs.title: Text field (string)
docs.text:
A controlled input reads its "value" from state and writes back through "onChange":

app.py Run 
@component
def text_field():
    first_name, set_first_name = use_state("Ada")

    return html.div(
        html.input(
            {
                "value": first_name,
                "onChange": lambda event: set_first_name(event["target"]["value"]),
            }
        ),
        html.h1(f"Hello, {first_name}!"),
    )

# TODO

Type into the field and the heading follows. Note the key names: "value" and "onChange" are DOM attribute names inside the attributes dictionary, while the Python names around them are snake_case.

There is no e.target.name, because the client does not send DOM attributes — bind extra context with a lambda instead. See Responding to Events.

docs.title: Checkbox (boolean)
docs.text:
event["target"]["checked"] tells you whether the box is ticked:

app.py Run 
@component
def checkbox():
    enabled, set_enabled = use_state(False)

    def handle_change(event):
        # `checked` is delivered by the client for checkbox inputs.
        set_enabled(event["target"]["checked"])

    return html.div(
        html.label(
            html.input(
                {"type": "checkbox", "checked": enabled, "onChange": handle_change}
            ),
            "Enabled",
        ),
        html.p(f"Status: {'on' if enabled else 'off'}"),
    )

# TODO

Tick the box and the status line flips. The client deliberately re-reads value, checked, files, type, and name from the element, which is why they arrive even though most element properties are stripped to keep payloads small.

docs.title: Form (two variables)
docs.text:
Two inputs, two state variables, no interference between them:

app.py Run 
@component
def form():
    first_name, set_first_name = use_state("Ada")
    last_name, set_last_name = use_state("Lovelace")

    return html.div(
        html.label(
            "First name: ",
            html.input(
                {
                    "value": first_name,
                    "onChange": lambda event: set_first_name(event["target"]["value"]),
                }
            ),
        ),
        html.label(
            "Last name: ",
            html.input(
                {
                    "value": last_name,
                    "onChange": lambda event: set_last_name(event["target"]["value"]),
                }
            ),
        ),
        html.h1(f"Hello, {first_name} {last_name}!"),
    )

# TODO

docs.title: Updating state based on the previous state
docs.text:
A common case is updating state based on the value that came before. Pass a function instead of a value:

set_count(lambda count: count + 1)

ReactPy calls your function with the current state and assigns the result.

app.py Run 
@component
def counter():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)

    def handle_add_three(event):
        # Updaters receive the current value, so all three increments land.
        set_count(lambda previous: previous + 1)
        set_count(lambda previous: previous + 1)
        set_count(lambda previous: previous + 1)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(count),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_add_three}, "+3"),
    )

# TODO

Click "+3" and the counter reaches 3, because each updater sees what the previous one produced — verified. Had these been set_count(count + 1) instead, all three would compute from the same render-time count and the result would be 1. See Queueing a Series of State Updates.

docs.title: Is using an updater always preferred?
docs.text: No. If you are setting state to a value that does not depend on previous state, pass the value. Updaters are for when the next value is derived from the last, or when several updates to the same variable must compose within one handler.

docs.title: Passing the updater function
docs.text:
The function must be pure — it should only compute and return the next value. Do not send requests, mutate the argument, or set other state inside it.

# Correct: pure, returns the next value
set_count(lambda count: count + 1)

# Wrong: mutates, and returns None
set_items(lambda items: items.append("new"))

docs.title: Passing the next state directly
docs.text:
When the value comes from outside, pass it plainly:

set_first_name("Ada")

docs.title: Updating objects and arrays in state
docs.text:
Pass a new object; there is no merge. For dicts use unpacking, for lists use a comprehension or slicing:

set_person({**person, "firstName": event["target"]["value"]})
set_items([*items, {"id": next_id, "text": text}])

Full treatment, including nested updates and the silent-drop failure mode, is on Updating Objects in State and Updating Arrays in State.

docs.title: Avoiding recreating the initial state
docs.text:
ReactPy ignores initial_value after the first render, but the expression still runs on every render. If building it is expensive, pass a function:

app.py Run 
@component
def list_page():
    state, set_state = use_state(create_expensive_state)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(f"{len(state['items'])} items"),
        html.p(state["items"][0]),
    )

# TODO

create_expensive_state is called once, on mount — verified (one call across four renders).

docs.title: Passing the initializer function
docs.text: state, set_state = use_state(create_expensive_state)   # called once

docs.title: Passing the initial state directly
docs.text:
state, set_state = use_state(create_expensive_state())  # built every render

Correct, but wasteful. Note again that a bare function is interpreted as an initializer, which is why the second form calls it explicitly.

docs.title: Resetting state with a key
docs.text:
ReactPy normally preserves state between re-renders, matching children by position and key. To force a component to start fresh, give its call site a different key:

app.py Run 
@component
def inbox():
    email, set_email = use_state("ada@example.com")

    return html.div(
        html.button(
            {"onClick": lambda event: set_email("grace@example.com")},
            "Switch account",
        ),
        counter(email, key=email),
    )

# TODO

Switching accounts resets the counter to zero, because a changed key means a different component as far as ReactPy is concerned. Verified: a keyed child bumped to 2 came back at 0 after its key changed, while the identical child rendered without a key kept its count.

docs.title: Storing information from previous renders
docs.text:
To keep a history, read the previous list through an updater so it composes correctly, and capture this render's value:

app.py Run 
@component
def counter():
    count, set_count = use_state(0)
    history, set_history = use_state([])

    def handle_add(event):
        # Read history through an updater: `history` in this closure is the
        # value from the render that created the handler, not the latest.
        set_history(lambda previous: [*previous, count])
        set_count(count + 1)

    return html.div(
        html.h1(count),
        html.button({"onClick": handle_add}, "Add 1"),
        html.p("Previous values: " + (", ".join(map(str, history)) or "-")),
    )

# TODO

Clicking twice records Previous values: 0, 1 — verified. The history name in the closure would still be the render-time value, which is exactly why the updater form matters here. For genuinely mutable, non-rendering values, use use_ref instead.
